pub_title: Profiling people with Parkinson's disease at risk of cognitive decline: Insights from PPMI and ICICLE‐PD data
dataset_context_from_paper: Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) data were used, accessed on November 15, 2022. PPMI is an international, observational, cohort study with almost 50 sites across 13 countries. Eligibility was contingent on a diagnosis of PD no longer than 2 years prior to enrolment and drug naïve status. Participants with young-onset PD (age < 50) and dementia were excluded. Data were available annually from baseline up to year 7. Participants with two or more data points were included, resulting in N= 770 baseline participants. Latent class mixed models were created to identify subgroups with similar longitudinal cognitive trajectories using total MoCA score as the outcome variable.
dataset_keywords: Parkinson's disease, cognitive decline, longitudinal cohort

pub_title: Profiling people with Parkinson's disease at risk of cognitive decline: Insights from PPMI and ICICLE‐PD data
dataset_context_from_paper: Incidence of Cognitive Impairment in Cohorts with Longitudinal Evaluation-Parkinson's Disease (ICICLE-PD) data were used, accessed on October 10, 2022. ICICLE-PD was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and GCP guidelines. Ethical approval was provided by the Newcastle and North Tyneside Research Ethics Committee. Recruitment took place from the community in Cambridgeshire and Newcastle upon Tyne/Gateshead, United Kingdom. All participants were recently diagnosed people with PD meeting Queen's Square Brain Bank Criteria, with working knowledge of English and no significant baseline cognitive impairment. Data were available every 18-months from baseline to year 4.5. Participants with two or more data points were included, resulting in N= 212 baseline participants. Latent class mixed models were applied to identify cognitive subtypes based on rate of decline in MoCA scores.
dataset_keywords: Parkinson's disease, cognitive impairment, community-based cohort

dataset_keywords: Parkinson's disease, whole blood RNA sequencing, early-stage idiopathic PD

pub_title: Evaluation of amyloid change as a surrogate for cognitive decline: demonstration in individual‐level data from the A4 study of solanezumab
dataset_context_from_paper: The A4 study was a Phase 3 randomized-controlled clinical trial of solanezumab, an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody, for the reduction of cognitive decline in individuals with elevated amyloid assessed via amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) but no clinical symptoms. Individual-level data from the A4 study were used to evaluate amyloid change as a surrogate for cognitive decline using causal mediation analysis and instrumental-variable analysis. The study included 812 participants with complete before/after amyloid-PET measures and cognitive assessments. Participants underwent amyloid-PET imaging at baseline and final study visits, with standardized uptake value ratios converted to Centiloids. Cognitive outcomes measured included Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB), Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST), Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study-Activities of Daily Living (ADCS-ADL), and Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite (PACC).

Participants were selected by age-stratified random sampling from publicly available voter registration lists over two time periods: 2006–2008 and 2016–2019. At initial recruitment, n=2,036 and n=708 participants provided written informed consent in the first and second recruitment phases respectively. The study investigates the epidemiology of MCI, with n=1,982 and n=703 participants completing full assessment in the original and second recruitment cohorts respectively. Plasma samples were available from 920 participants, with 847 participants included in final analyses after quality control. Blood samples were collected during annual assessments in 2014 or later for the initial cohort and 2016 or later for the new cohort.

Participants were recruited from memory clinics in Stockholm Sweden, Toulouse France, Frankfurt Germany, and Kuopio Finland during September 2017-May 2019. pub_title: Constipation in a Large Online Cohort of Persons with Parkinson's Disease
dataset_context_from_paper: Using the Fox Insight database, we compared baseline characteristics, risk of progressive motor symptoms, and incidence of NMS between PD patients with versus without constipation. Of 20,352 participants, 16,611 (82%) reported infrequent bowel movements and/or excessive straining, 15,594 (77%) had incomplete evacuation, and 14,165 (70%) reported both symptoms. Patients with constipation were generally older, white, women, had PD>5 years, and had higher NMS and comorbidity scores. At a mean median follow-up of 2.8 years, constipation was associated with an increased risk of incident gastrointestinal, autonomic, neuropsychiatric, sleep-related, sensory NMS.

pub_title: Neuropsychiatric symptom subtypes and dementia‐associated neuropathologic change

pub_title: Cohort Profile Update: The Harmonised Cognitive Assessment Protocol sub-study of the Northern Ireland Cohort for the Longitudinal Study of Ageing (NICOLA-HCAP)

pub_title: Investigating Syndemic Effects of Air Pollution and Physical Inactivity on Cognitive Decline in Older Adults
dataset_context_from_paper: The Northern Ireland Cohort for the Longitudinal Study of Ageing (NICOLA) is a longitudinal prospective cohort of over 8000 community-dwelling adults aged 50 years or older in Northern Ireland. pub_title: Investigating the prevalence of cognitive impairment and dementia in the Northern Ireland Cohort for the Longitudinal Study of Ageing (NICOLA): the Harmonised Cognitive Assessment Protocol (HCAP) cross-sectional substudy
dataset_context_from_paper: The Northern Ireland Cohort for the Longitudinal Study of Ageing (NICOLA) is the largest public health cohort study of ageing in Northern Ireland. pub_title: Investigating the prevalence of cognitive impairment and dementia in the Northern Ireland Cohort for the Longitudinal Study of Ageing (NICOLA): the Harmonised Cognitive Assessment Protocol (HCAP) cross-sectional substudy

pub_title: Global trends in COVID-19 Alzheimer's related research: a bibliometric analysis

pub_title: Preclinical Alzheimer's and vascular biomarkers alter brain aging in cognitively normal adults: a MRI-based study

Following EPAD procedures and completion of a data access request through the ADDI Workbench, researchers gained access to the EPAD LCS Version.IMI (V.IMI) dataset, which comprises final longitudinal data with cognitive, clinical, biomarker, and neuroimaging and lifestyle risk factor datasets from over 2,000 participants. For this cross-sectional study, baseline data was utilized. The dataset included 1,380 cognitively unimpaired participants (50+ years) stratified into five groups based on cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers (Aβ42, t-tau, p-tau) and vascular pathology (Fazekas scale, microbleeds). Structural MRI volumes of cortical and subcortical regions were analyzed using Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression.
dataset_keywords: Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, structural MRI, cerebrospinal fluid

pub_title: Polygenic pathways shape white matter vulnerability to Alzheimer’s disease-related pathophysiological changes
dataset_context_from_paper: Data were drawn from the latest data release from the European Prevention of Alzheimer's Dementia (EPAD) multicenter study. EPAD general inclusion criteria were age above 50 years and no diagnosis of dementia (clinical dementia rating [CDR] score < 1). The study selected 803 participants who had CSF Aβ1−42 and p-Tau181 measurements available, full genotyping, as well as structural and diffusion MRI. MRI acquisition details and diffusion weighted images (DWI) were processed using QSIPrep 0.19.0. CSF biomarkers were quantified using a harmonized pre-analytical protocol with the fully automatised Roche cobas Elecsys System at the Clinical Neurochemistry Laboratory, Mölndal, Sweden.
dataset_keywords: Alzheimer's disease, cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, neuroimaging, genetic data

pub_title: Blood pressure and Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers in cognitively unimpaired adults: a multicenter study
dataset_context_from_paper: ALFA+ study is a unicentric, longitudinal observational study designed to explore AD early pathophysiological changes among cognitively unimpaired adults with increased genetic risk factors. Participants underwent baseline visits between 2016 and 2020, and follow-up visits between 2019 and 2023. The study included 405 participants with CSF biomarkers (CSF Aβ42, Aβ40, p-tau181, t-tau) and/or Aβ PET data. Blood pressure measurements and clinical variables including diabetes, antihypertensive medication use, and waist-to-hip ratio were available.
dataset_keywords: Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, cerebrospinal fluid, amyloid PET

pub_title: Blood pressure and Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers in cognitively unimpaired adults: a multicenter study
dataset_context_from_paper: European Prevention of Alzheimer's Dementia Longitudinal Cohort Study (EPAD-LCS) is a multicentric European study with over 2000 participants aiming to understand early stages of AD and prevent dementia before symptom onset. Data used were from EPAD-LCS dataset V.IMI comprising 2096 EPAD participants enrolled from 2016 to 2020, with last follow-up data acquired during 2020. The study included 1104 participants with CSF biomarkers (CSF Aβ42, p-tau181, t-tau) and available blood pressure measurements and clinical variables.
dataset_keywords: Alzheimer's disease, cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, European cohort

pub_title: Blood pressure and Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers in cognitively unimpaired adults: a multicenter study
dataset_context_from_paper: EPAD-LCS dataset V.IMI comprising 2096 EPAD participants enrolled from 2016 to 2020. CSF sampling followed a harmonized preclinical protocol with analyses performed with the fully automated Roche Elecsys System in a single laboratory at University of Gothenburg. CSF Aβ42 positivity was defined as CSF Aβ42<1000 pg/ml using previously validated cutoffs.

pub_title: Early detection of Alzheimer’s disease using small RNAs. Results from the EPAD cohort
dataset_context_from_paper: The European Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease (EPAD) clinical trial platform is a prospective, multi-center study designed to investigate biomarkers for preclinical and prodromal AD. The EPAD dataset contains more than 2096 individuals with each subject having made between 1 to 5 visits. Of these, 1934 individuals had available blood samples which were used in this study. Participants were recruited from 31 sites in 10 countries throughout Europe. During each visit, subjects performed cognitive tasks and some underwent MRI, CSF sampling, or blood donation. Ultra-deep small RNA sequencing was performed on whole blood samples using PAXgene tubes from 1913 participants, 50 years or older and free of dementia diagnosis at enrollment, stratified by cerebrospinal fluid amyloid levels. The study analyzed small RNAs as novel biomarkers for detecting early cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease.
dataset_keywords: Alzheimer's disease, small RNA biomarkers, cognitive impairment, blood-based biomarkers

pub_title: Brain MRI signatures across sex and CSF Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers
dataset_context_from_paper: Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database used as one of three independent validation datasets. MRI and CSF Alzheimer's disease biomarkers data were analyzed in participants. The study validated core analyses across ADNI totaling participants, and performed meta-analyses to obtain more robust estimates of brain volume associations with amyloid and tau biomarkers.

pub_title: Brain MRI signatures across sex and CSF Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers
dataset_context_from_paper: National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) database used as one of three independent validation datasets. pub_title: Brain MRI signatures across sex and CSF Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers
dataset_context_from_paper: European Prevention of Alzheimer's Dementia (EPAD) Consortium database used as one of three independent validation datasets. pub_title: Brain MRI signatures across sex and CSF Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers
dataset_context_from_paper: MGB dataset comprised 306 patients aged 50 years or older selected from the Mass General Brigham healthcare system. All image data were pre-existing clinical images from the MGB patient database within 1 year of lumbar puncture. Brain segmentation and volume calculation were performed via the SynthSeg+ pipeline. CSF levels of Aβ40, Aβ42 and p-Tau181 were measured at the MIND Biomarker Core using Euroimmun immunoassays.
dataset_keywords: clinical MRI, CSF biomarkers, Alzheimer's disease

pub_title: Deep normative modelling reveals insights into early-stage Alzheimer's disease using multi-modal neuroimaging data
dataset_context_from_paper: 12,844 healthy subjects from the UK Biobank were used to pre-train the deep normative model. The cohort was selected to have no neurological, psychiatric disorders or head trauma according to available ICD9 and ICD10 codes. Pre-processed FreeSurfer grey-matter volumes for 66 cortical (Desikan-Killiany atlas) and 16 subcortical brain regions, and Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and Mean Diffusivity (MD) measurements for 32 white matter tracts (John Hopkins University atlas) were used as input features to the normative model.
dataset_keywords: healthy brain MRI, structural neuroimaging, normative model training

pub_title: Deep normative modelling reveals insights into early-stage Alzheimer's disease using multi-modal neuroimaging data
dataset_context_from_paper: 929 subjects from the EPAD dataset were used for model analysis and validation. The dataset comprises healthy individuals recruited as a 'probability spectrum' population, covering the entire range of anticipated probabilities for Alzheimer's dementia development. The cohort was split into a 'super healthy' cohort (337 individuals) for fine-tuning and healthy holdout controls, and an 'at-risk' cohort (592 individuals) for analysis purposes. Multi-modal MRI data (T1 and diffusion MRI features) and AD CSF biomarkers (phosphorated tau, total tau, amyloid-beta 42, and p-tau/abeta42 ratio) were extracted. Cognitive assessments included Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE).
dataset_keywords: Alzheimer's disease risk, cognitive decline, CSF biomarkers, multi-modal MRI

pub_title: Accrual of Alzheimer's disease pathology as a function of proximity to parental dementia onset

The EPAD LCS is a prospective, multicenter study registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT02804789. Participants were recruited from parent cohorts throughout Europe as well as clinical settings. CSF samples were analyzed using the Roche cobas Elecsys System, yielding concentrations of Aβ1-42, p-tau181, and t-tau. pub_title: Association of Vascular Risk Factors and Cerebrovascular Pathology With Alzheimer Disease Pathologic Changes in Individuals Without Dementia
dataset_context_from_paper: The European Prevention of Alzheimer's Dementia (EPAD) cohort is a multicenter longitudinal study of nondemented participants (Clinical Dementia Rating < 1) from which data were drawn for this study. Participants underwent CSF and MRI acquisitions, with a subset having longitudinal MRI and cognitive evaluation data available. The study included 1,592 participants (mean age 65.5 ± 7.4 years; 56.16% female) evaluated for associations between vascular risk factors, cerebral small vessel disease features, and Alzheimer disease biomarkers including CSF amyloid-β (Aβ1-42) and phosphorylated tau (P-tau181), gray matter volume, and cognitive performance.
dataset_keywords: Alzheimer's disease, neuroimaging, cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, cognitive assessment

pub_title: Validation of the brain health index in the European Prevention of Alzheimer's Dementia cohort
dataset_context_from_paper: The European Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease Longitudinal Cohort Study (EPAD LCS) is a longitudinal, multi-centre, pan-European cohort study that recruited participants predominantly from various parent cohorts to create a cohort covering the full range of anticipated likelihood of Alzheimer's disease development. The current study used the EPAD-LCS-v.IMI dataset released in October 2020 and accessed via the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative (ADDI) workbench portal. The dataset includes T1, T2, T2*, and T2 FLAIR MRI sequences, cognitive test scores (MMSE, 4MT, RBANS), demographic information (age, gender), lifestyle data (physical activity, smoking status, alcohol consumption), genetic data (APOE status), and medical history information. Data from 1496 participants (50-88 years old, 43.32% male, predominantly Caucasian) were used for cross-sectional analysis, and 197 participants were included in longitudinal analysis with follow-up at 12 and 24 months.
dataset_keywords: Alzheimer's disease, neuroimaging, cognitive assessment, longitudinal cohort

pub_title: Modifiable dementia risk factors and AT(N) biomarkers: findings from the EPAD cohort
dataset_context_from_paper: Participants were drawn from the European Prevention of Alzheimer's Dementia (EPAD) Longitudinal Cohort Study (LCS), a prospective, multicenter, pan-European longitudinal cohort study. Participants were recruited across 21 different European sites and were eligible if they were at least 50 years of age, had completed at least 5 years of formal education, and did not have a dementia diagnosis at baseline. Participants underwent clinical and neurological assessments including a mini-mental state examination (MMSE), brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and comprehensive neuropsychological assessment. For this study, baseline data (V1) from 1,474 participants were included. All EPAD data are available via the NTKApp on the AD Workbench, designed by ADDI.
dataset_keywords: Alzheimer's disease, biomarkers, cognitive assessment, neuroimaging

pub_title: Models and methods: a perspective of the impact of six IMI translational data-centric initiatives for Alzheimer’s disease and other neuropsychiatric disorders
dataset_context_from_paper: EMIF built a common Information Framework (EMIF-Platform) to link up and facilitate access to diverse medical and research data sources. By integrating data from various sources such as electronic health records, biobanks, and clinical trials, EMIF enabled researchers to access a wealth of diverse and large-scale data sets. In its 5 years, EMIF successfully leveraged data from more than 62 million EU adults and children through federal databases and cohorts from 7 different countries. EMIF included two therapeutic areas: AD (EMIF-AD, with a focus on pre-dementia AD) and metabolic complications of obesity (EMIF-Metabolic).
dataset_keywords: patient-level data, electronic health records, biobanks, clinical trials

pub_title: Models and methods: a perspective of the impact of six IMI translational data-centric initiatives for Alzheimer’s disease and other neuropsychiatric disorders
dataset_context_from_paper: EPAD pooled existing national and regional registers of individuals at risk of developing AD to create a single, pan-European register of around 24,000 people. Of these, the 6,000 deemed to be at greatest risk of AD were placed into a specialized, at-risk subject cohort that underwent standardized tests and follow-up. Finally, 1,500 of these subjects participated in early stage 'adaptive' clinical trials of therapeutics intended to prevent the progression of AD. The compiling and streamlining of these disparate datasets led to the identification of four distinct subgroups based on cognitive function.
dataset_keywords: Alzheimer's disease, pre-symptomatic patients, cognitive function

pub_title: Models and methods: a perspective of the impact of six IMI translational data-centric initiatives for Alzheimer’s disease and other neuropsychiatric disorders
dataset_context_from_paper: The PRISM project carried out a range of tests on patients with neuropsychiatric disorders to determine which biological parameters can be matched with specific clinical symptoms like social dysfunction. They identified quantitative biological parameters that allowed the grouping of patients into clusters based on symptoms and underlying causes. PRISM found that social dysfunction is transdiagnostically associated with default mode network disconnectivity in schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. They also developed new behavioral readouts using passive remote smartphone monitoring with the aim of identifying novel digital biomarkers.

pub_title: Models and methods: a perspective of the impact of six IMI translational data-centric initiatives for Alzheimer’s disease and other neuropsychiatric disorders
dataset_context_from_paper: The Aetionomy project innovated classification approaches for neurodegenerative diseases by applying computational tools to molecular and biological data based on Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). Aetionomy used a broad range of datasets, ranging from molecular to symptom data, and organized, structured, integrated them to dissect the underlying mechanistic causes. The consortium successfully demonstrated that their prototype taxonomy could be used to identify patient subgroups in Parkinson's disease (PD). These efforts resulted in an open-access knowledge base with inventories of mechanistic hypotheses that form the basis for the prototype taxonomies.
dataset_keywords: Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, disease taxonomy

pub_title: Models and methods: a perspective of the impact of six IMI translational data-centric initiatives for Alzheimer’s disease and other neuropsychiatric disorders
dataset_context_from_paper: The eTRIKS collaboration with ELIXIR-Luxemburg Node is an IMI data repository that centralizes ongoing and past IMI project level metadata for translational research scientists who require information about study projects. eTRIKS places an emphasis on the findability of research study descriptions with the aim of linking global data in a way that can be optimally leveraged to improve biomedical research, creating value for public and private organizations and driving research collaboration towards precision medicine.
dataset_keywords: IMI project metadata, translational research, study descriptions

One of the main outcomes of the project was a novel quality management system as well as a range of other open-access tools and learning materials. EQIPD sought to provide various stakeholders groups with resources that would facilitate collaboration and ensure generation of robust and reliable data.

pub_title: Amyloid PET predicts atrophy in older adults without dementia: Results from the AMYPAD Prognostic & Natural History study
dataset_context_from_paper: Data for this study were drawn from the AMYPAD PNHS v202306 (N=1585). The AMYPAD PNHS is a multi-center cohort of non-demented participants to determine the value of amyloid PET in clinical and research settings. The study included 1329 participants (56% female) with an age of 68.2 ± 8.78 years who underwent [18F]Flutemetamol or [18F]Florbetaben Aβ-PET and T1-weighted MRI, with longitudinal data for 684 participants (median follow-up = 3.4 years). Participants were non-demented (CDR < 1), age above 50 years, and able to undergo amyloid-PET and MRI scans. The study examined the effect of baseline cortical amyloid-beta burden on regional brain atrophy in older adults without dementia.
dataset_keywords: amyloid PET, brain MRI, preclinical Alzheimer's disease, longitudinal neuroimaging

pub_title: Quantification Supports Amyloid PET Visual Assessment of Challenging Cases: Results from the AMYPAD Diagnostic and Patient Management Study
dataset_context_from_paper: The AMYPAD diagnostic and patient management study (DPMS) is a randomized controlled trial that recruited patients across the disease continuum, including subjective cognitive decline–plus (SCD+), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), or dementia from 8 memory clinics across Europe. All participants with an available baseline amyloid PET scan that passed quality control for quantification were included (n=741). The study assessed agreement between visual reads performed at each imaging site by local readers and quantification performed centrally using the PET-only AmyPype pipeline, providing global Centiloid and regional z-scores. The trial was registered with EudraCT (2017-002527-21).
dataset_keywords: amyloid PET imaging, Centiloid quantification, Alzheimer's disease biomarkers

pub_title: Association Between Years of Education and Amyloid Burden in Patients With Subjective Cognitive Decline, MCI, and Alzheimer Disease
dataset_context_from_paper: Amyloid-PET information ([18F]Flutemetamol or [18F]Florbetaben) of individuals with SCD+, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD were retrieved from the AMYPAD-DPMS cohort, a multicenter randomized controlled study. The cohort included 212 individuals with SCD+ (M(Age) = 69.17 years, F 42.45%), 258 individuals with MCI (M(Age) = 72.93, F 43.80%), and 195 individuals with dementia (M(Age) = 74.07, F 48.72%). Amyloid PET images were acquired within 8 months after initial screening and processed with AMYPYPE. Amyloid load was based on global Centiloid (CL) values. Educational level was indexed by formal schooling and subsequent higher education in years. The study examined the relationship between education and amyloid plaques using PET imaging in individuals with SCD+, MCI, and dementia across 8 European memory clinics.
dataset_keywords: amyloid PET imaging, Alzheimer disease, cognitive decline

pub_title: Clinical Effect of Early vs Late Amyloid Positron Emission Tomography in Memory Clinic Patients
dataset_context_from_paper: The AMYPAD-DPMS is a prospective, multicenter, randomized clinical trial conducted across 8 European memory clinics. Participants were allocated to 3 study groups based on timing of amyloid PET: arm 1 (early, within 1 month), arm 2 (late, after 8 months), or arm 3 (free-choice). A total of 840 participants were enrolled with baseline and 3-month follow-up data available for 532 participants (272 in arm 1, 260 in arm 2). Participants had subjective cognitive decline plus (SCD+), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), or dementia. The study assessed clinical effects of amyloid PET imaging using [18F]flutemetamol or [18F]florbetaben tracers on diagnostic confidence, etiological diagnosis, and treatment planning in memory clinic patients.
dataset_keywords: amyloid PET imaging, memory clinic, cognitive decline, Alzheimer disease biomarkers

pub_title: Unraveling the molecular mechanisms in severe Alzheimer’s disease based on transcriptomic data using next generation knowledge discovery methods
dataset_context_from_paper: RNA sequencing data from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) of individuals with severe Alzheimer's disease and healthy controls. The dataset was originally deposited by Scheckel et al. (2016) and derived from frozen brain tissues classified based on the Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) criteria. The original study included eight control subjects and nine patients with advanced or severe AD (CDR 4-5), matched for age and sex with brief postmortem intervals. The authors filtered and selected four controls and six advanced AD samples for downstream analysis using next-generation knowledge discovery methods. RNA was extracted using the TRIzol method and sequenced using an Illumina HiSeq 2500. The dataset was analyzed using GEO2R to identify 24,207 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) at P ≤0.05, further filtered to 3,103 genes using a fold change cut-off of ±1.5. WebGestalt and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis were used to identify dysregulated pathways including retrograde endocannabinoid signaling, motor proteins, oxidative phosphorylation, ribosome biogenesis, immune system activation, antigen processing and presentation, and cytokine signaling in severe AD.
dataset_keywords: RNA sequencing, Alzheimer's disease, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, gene expression, neuroinflammation

Gene expression was assessed via RNA-seq. Genome-wide genotypes were assessed using the Illumina Global Diversity Array (~1.8 million variants) and imputed using 1000 Genomes phase 3v5 reference data. The cohort was used to test association between significant variants with all expressed genes within 200 kb using regression models with covariates for RNA integrity number, age at death, sex, batch and estimated cell proportions.

pub_title: Multi-ancestry genome-wide meta-analysis of 56,241 individuals identifies known and novel cross-population and ancestry-specific associations as novel risk loci for Alzheimer’s disease
dataset_context_from_paper: The ADGC assembled the largest multi-ancestry collection of AD samples to date, containing 24,388 participants with AD and 31,853 cognitively unimpaired individuals passing quality control from 41 NHW, 12 AFA, eight HIS, and five EAS datasets. All samples utilized in these analyses were directly genotyped and either clinically assessed or pathologically evaluated and did not include proxy case/control definitions. AD cases were defined by either pathological confirmation of the presence of AD pathology or clinical diagnosis using NIA-AA Working Group criteria, while cognitively normal elders (CNEs) were determined to have intact cognition via cognitive examinations (including mini-mental status exam (MMSE) or modified MMSE (3MS) score ≥ 26) among living CNEs and absence of AD pathology among deceased CNEs.

Samples were expected to cluster with 1000 Genomes European populations for NHW samples and between European and African populations for admixed subjects.

LRRC4C and KIAA0825 were differentially expressed between autopsy-confirmed AD brains and brains of cognitively intact decedents with P < 0.05. pub_title: Linking spatial omics to patient phenotypes at the population scale by BSNMani: Bayesian scalar-on-network regression with manifold learning
dataset_context_from_paper: Spatial transcriptomics data generated by multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) from the SEA-AD project applied to the middle temporal gyrus (MTG) of 27 SEA-AD donors, resulting in 69 total brain sections. All spatial transcriptomics data and donor-level metadata are publicly available through the Allen Brain Map portal and the ABC Atlas platform. BSNMani framework achieved an accuracy of 0.74 for Alzheimer's disease (AD) prediction and revealed four distinct gene–gene co-expression subnetworks with clear biological relevance, such as glutamatergic synapses and neurogenesis.

Over a mean follow-up of 10.6 years, 346 participants (8.7%) developed dementia. pub_title: Midlife short sleep with and without obesity, and the risk of future dementia: a prospective cohort study
dataset_context_from_paper: The Whitehall II study is an ongoing prospective cohort study of British civil servants, aged 35–55 years, at study entry in 1985–1988. A total of 10,308 participants, including 6,895 men and 3,413 women, were asked to complete a series of self-administered questionnaires and attended a baseline screening examination. The present analysis uses data from phases 5 (1997–1999), 7 (2002–2004), 9 (2007–2009), 11 (2012–2013), and 12 (2015–2016), as well as linked electronic health records for the diagnosis of dementia until 2023. Phase 2 applied this framework to 29 large-scale genome-wide studies published since 2015, tiering 163 unique loci. Phase 1 yielded 17 high-confidence loci (12 linked to specific genes), and Phase 2 identified 111 high-confidence loci/genes with replicated associations across ancestries and convergent single-variant/variant-set evidence. Prioritized loci highlight APP processing, microglial immunity, and lipid metabolism pathways, including genes not captured by existing resources like Agora or Open Targets. Summarized results can be viewed at https://topgenes.niagads.org/.

Data organization began with the extraction of participant data from the NACC UDS, consolidating cognitive, neuropathological, and psychiatric evaluation data into a structured format for analysis. The NACC database is funded by the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and National Institutes of Health Grant U24 AG072122.

Data availability for NACC can be requested by qualified investigators. The dataset includes information relevant to Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, dementia with Lewy bodies, Lewy body disease, and Parkinson's disease research, with assessments including CERAD scores for β-amyloid neuritic plaques.

The datasets analyzed during the current study are publicly available from the Michael J. Fox PPMI database. Data used in the preparation of this article were obtained on April 22, 2026 from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database. PPMI is a public-private partnership funded by the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research. The study used PPMI data to develop disease-duration-specific subtyping algorithms for Parkinson's disease, with analysis of selective dropout from PPMI by baseline data-driven subtype.

An interactive web calculator that implements the disease-duration-specific subtyping algorithm described in this manuscript, with the full per-year reference statistics for all six subtyping scales, is freely accessible at https://negidamd.github.io/data-driven-pd-subtype-calculator/ (source code at https://github.com/negidamd/data-driven-pd-subtype-calculator).

CSF DDC measurements are available in the PPMI database (project 274). All samples from the PPMI cohort were run on the same day on four plates with four quality control samples (CSF pools) on each plate. The newly developed SMC assay was used to quantify DDC levels in cerebrospinal fluid samples from drug-naïve Parkinson's disease patients and controls, achieving an AUC of 0.89 in ROC analysis for discriminating dopaminergic drug-naïve PD patients from controls.

The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarker data used in this study were obtained from the Accelerating Medicines Partnership-Parkinson's disease (AMP-PD) consortium under approved data access agreements. AMP-PD cohort with PD, control, and SWEDD participants and six CSF biomarkers (Aβ42, α-syn, t-tau, p-tau181, hemoglobin). Preprocessing included missing-value imputation, standardization, and outlier screening. Five machine-learning models were trained with stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Data balancing used the SMOTE-Tomek method with performance evaluation based on AUC, PR-AUC, and Brier score.

MIMIC-III, an EHR dataset focusing on intensive care settings, used to assess the effectiveness of the proposed VTDNet framework. The study leveraged real-world electronic health record (EHR) data to estimate individualized treatment effects (ITE) in longitudinal observational settings. VTDNet achieved lower root mean squared error, mean absolute error, and influence function precision in the estimation of heterogeneous effects compared to existing state-of-the-art methods on this real-world EHR dataset.

NACC, emphasizing neurodegenerative disease, collected using a standardized protocol from participants enrolled in Alzheimer's Disease Research Center (ADRC) clinical cores. Used as a real-world dataset to assess the effectiveness of the proposed VTDNet framework for estimating individualized treatment effects in longitudinal settings. VTDNet achieves lower root mean squared error, mean absolute error, and influence function precision in the estimation of heterogeneous effects compared to existing state-of-the-art methods on this real-world EHR dataset.

A synthetic dataset was created and used to assess the effectiveness of the proposed VTDNet framework. Experimental results on the synthetic dataset demonstrate superior accuracy under varying levels of confounding, validating the framework's ability to handle hidden confounding in controlled conditions.

This study is a secondary analysis of de-identified data obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). ADNI data are available from the LONI Image and Data Archive subject to the ADNI Data Use Agreement. The dataset was used to develop and validate predictive models for cognitive decline, specifically examining the relationship between domain-specific cognitive measures and CDR-SB (Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes) scores. Participants were eligible with ≥3 item-level visits. The analysis demonstrated R² values of 0.497 for the inferred mask and 0.674 for total score in predicting CDR-SB.

NACC UDS3 data were obtained through the NACC data request process. This study is a secondary analysis of de-identified data from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC). The dataset was used alongside ADNI for validation of predictive models for cognitive decline. In NACC, the 19-item saturated vector substantially exceeded the total score (R² 0.707 vs 0.593) in predicting CDR-SB, showing that item-level detail carries clinically relevant information. Participants were eligible with ≥3 item-level visits.

Participants were 272 older adults diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and 1,344 cognitively healthy controls recruited from the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. Participants in each study were administered the FCI-SF, which evaluates coin/currency calculation, financial conceptual knowledge, use of a checkbook/register, and use of a bank statement.

Participants were 272 older adults diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and 1,344 cognitively healthy controls recruited from the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota and also from the Cognitive Observations in Seniors study at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. Participants in each study were administered the FCI-SF, which evaluates coin/currency calculation, financial conceptual knowledge, use of a checkbook/register, and use of a bank statement.

Retrospective examination of data from the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging cohort. Participants (n = 202, mean age of 78 years, 38% female) with diagnoses of cognitive unimpairment (n = 109), mild cognitive impairment (n = 71), and dementia (n = 22) were included. p-Tau217 was determined using the ALZpath Simoa p-tau217 immunoassay and an immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry assay. Amyloid positivity was defined by amyloid-PET with a centiloid of ≥25. The study investigated the relationship of plasma p-tau217 concentrations versus estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in individuals with CKD with and without amyloid pathology.

Retrospective examination of data from the Alzheimer's Disease Research Center cohort. Participants (n = 202, mean age of 78 years, 38% female) with diagnoses of cognitive unimpairment (n = 109), mild cognitive impairment (n = 71), and dementia (n = 22) were included. In all, 114 (56%) of all participants were amyloid-PET positive (A+) and 86 (43%) were classified as having CKD (stages 3–4). p-Tau217 concentrations were measured and analyzed in relation to eGFR and amyloid status.

The A4 (Anti-Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease) study is a longitudinal clinical trial investigating biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease progression. The study evaluates multiple biomarker modalities including brain imaging (18-F-Florbetapir PET), cognitive assessments (PACC, MMSE, logical memory), and retinal amyloid imaging. The research examines how combinations of biomarker tests can enhance diagnostic accuracy and specificity for Alzheimer's disease, testing additional diagnostic assays across different modalities to provide insights into AD progression.

The LEARN (Longitudinal Evaluation of Amyloid Risk and Neurodegeneration) study is a companion longitudinal study that evaluates amyloid risk and neurodegeneration markers in asymptomatic individuals. The study collects biomarker data including apolipoprotein E (APOE) genotyping and other neurodegeneration assessments to track disease progression and risk factors.

Summary statistics from the GWAS in this study are available at GWAS Catalog (GCST90727422). The GWAS identified four genome-wide significant loci associated with ADAD risk, with sentinel variants on chromosomes 14 (rs141931440 near RHOJ gene, p<0.0001, OR 5.96), 1 (rs74546314 in CNIH4, p<0.0001, OR 11.99), 5 (rs537168961 near CCNG1 gene, p<0.0001, OR 9.56), and 2 (rs78120946 in ALK gene, p<0.0001, OR 7.21). Analysis included common and low-frequency variants (MAF≥0.005) using logistic Firth regression adjusted for sex, cohort, and principal components.

dataset_context_from_paper: Meta-analysis of the discovery and ADSP R5 replication datasets was performed. The similarity between allele frequencies observed in the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) database and those in control groups offers supportive evidence for the reliability and validity of the GWAS findings.

Whole genome sequencing data were classified into genotype status groups based on availability of genomic data: those with both WGS and SNP data (G2), those with SNP data only (G1), and those with no genotype data (G0). The use of genotype status groups allowed evaluation of, and eventual adjustment for, genotyping accuracy/error.

The dataset was used to analyze associations of AXIN1 polymorphisms (rs13337493 and rs9921222) with clinical manifestations and biomarkers in white populations with Parkinson's disease, including DATSCAN imaging, motor function assessments (H&Y stage, UPDRS), nonmotor function measures (MoCA, RBD, ESS, olfactory disorders, depression), and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers (α-Synuclein, dopamine metabolites, tau, and amyloid-beta).

This study included participants with normal cognition (CN) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. Cognitive IIV was computed as the within-person standard deviation of five domain-specific neuropsychological test z-scores. Four neuroimaging biomarker IIV metrics were similarly derived using regional amyloid-β (n = 1,021), tau (n = 719), cortical thickness (n = 2,148), and combined amyloid-tau-neurodegeneration (ATN, n = 258). Associations between cognitive IIV and each biomarker IIV were evaluated using linear regression models, adjusted for relevant covariates.

Whole-genome-sequencing (WGS) was carried out for 244 AJ participants. Of them 221 were sequenced as previously described. Sequencing was done with DNBSEQ technology at the BGI facility, China, with an average 30X-depth-coverage. Paired-end reads (each of 100 bp length) were aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38 build) using the BWA tool, and Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK4) was used for variant calling. An additional 23 PD patients were whole-genome-sequenced at 30X-depth-coverage on Illumina NovaSeq6000 platform (PCR-free libraries), with paired-end reads (150 bp length each) and secondary analysis was done using Illumina DRAGEN software with human reference genome GRCh38 build.

Primary cohort used for training set thresholds in plasma-based staging model for Alzheimer's disease biomarkers. The dataset includes cross-sectional and longitudinal measurements of AD biomarkers. Thresholds derived from BioFINDER-2 training set were applied to validation cohort (Knight ADRC), achieving high concordance with PET (C index, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.87-0.94) and clinical categorization (C index, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.82-0.89). SHAP values were calculated to investigate each biomarker's contribution to the final model.

Validation cohort used for external replication of plasma-based staging model. Thresholds derived from BioFINDER-2 training set were applied to Knight ADRC validation cohort under similar analytical conditions, demonstrating out-of-sample performance with high concordance between plasma-based staging and PET (C index, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.87-0.94) and clinical categorization (C index, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.82-0.89).

Mass spectrometry quantified post-translational modifications (PTMs) in prefrontal cortex tissue from Alzheimer's disease patients. Data used in this study are available from ADNI. The study compared thalamic nuclei volumes derived from HIPS-THOMAS across groups of cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients. Analyses included: (1) comparison of thalamic nuclei volumes across groups; (2) examination of relationship between amyloid PET load and thalamic nuclei volume; (3) assessment of diagnostic value of thalamic nuclei in Random Forest classification of CN (amyloid-negative and amyloid-positive), amyloid-positive MCI, and amyloid-positive AD groups; (4) construction of UMAP model integrating thalamic nuclei volumes, CSF biomarkers (p-tau181/Aβ42 ratio), cognitive scores (RAVLT delayed recall, TMT-B, BNT, clock drawing, phonemic and category fluencies, MMSE, ANART errors), everyday function (CDR Sum of Boxes), and demographics. Study populations included amyloid-negative CN (n=180), amyloid-positive MCI (n=171), amyloid-positive AD (n=92), amyloid-positive CN (n=74), amyloid-negative MCI (n=133), and amyloid-negative dementia (n=14).

The study integrates multimodal imaging and biomarkers to construct a comprehensive predictive framework that incorporates multiple memory dimensions for early identification and precise intervention in Alzheimer's Disease (AD).

PD GENEration is an international, observational, clinical research study that offers genetic testing and counseling to people living with Parkinson's disease (PwP) at no cost, sponsored by the Parkinson's Foundation in partnership with Aligning Science Across Parkinson's (ASAP) through the Global Parkinson's Genetics Program (GP2). Since its launch in 2019, the study has expanded to enroll over 32,000 PwP (as of March 31, 2026), from 10 countries across North, Central, and South America, the Caribbean, and Israel. Participants undergo whole genome sequencing with variants curated for a primary panel of seven PD-associated genes. A central pillar of the study design has been the open sharing of genomic data to advance discovery in PD research in partnership with ASAP and GP2.

dataset_context_from_paper: Multicenter, prospectively enrolled cohort of 87 older adults with focal epilepsy (age=66.10 [SD=6.86]), including early-onset (<55 years at seizure onset) and late-onset (≥55 years at seizure onset) epilepsy. Participants underwent neuroimaging to derive AD signatures from regional cortical thickness and hippocampal volume. Associations between the AD signature, epilepsy characteristics, plasma biomarkers (β-amyloid 42/40, phosphorylated tau [pTau217, pTau181], neurofilament light chain [NfL]), and cognition were evaluated. AD signature correlated with NfL (β= −0.30, p adj =0.050), memory performance (β= 0.30, p adj =0.006), and predicted greater odds of cognitive impairment specifically among those with early-onset epilepsy.

362 participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), including cognitively unimpaired (CU) healthy controls and individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or AD dementia. Used as comparison group to examine AD-related neuroimaging signatures. Participants with epilepsy demonstrated more AD-like signatures compared to ADNI CU controls (β= −0.43, p adj <0.001), reflecting reduced thickness/volume in AD-vulnerable regions.

T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging scans from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative were analyzed using a region-wise radiomics framework across 10 anatomically defined brain regions. Radiomic features were extracted following automated segmentation, bias field correction, and intensity normalization. Age-associated radiomic patterns were first identified in cognitively normal subjects using Spearman correlation analysis. Features demonstrating significant age sensitivity were subsequently compared between cognitively normal and Alzheimer's disease cohorts across age bins using Welch's two-sample t-tests with permutation-based significance estimation and false discovery rate correction.

Participants include CU individuals, those with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and patients with AD type dementia, diagnosed using standardized clinical and neuropsychological criteria such as the NINCDS-ADRDA guidelines and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores. Raw imaging and clinical data were obtained from the ADNI dataset under data-sharing agreements. Data are publicly available upon registration and agreement to the data use terms. MCSA data are available to qualified investigators by request through MCSA website. Serial amyloid-PET scans using 11(C-PiB) were conducted with a median interval of 2.5 years (IQR 2.25 – 3.7). Each scan included four 5-minute dynamic frames acquired 40 to 60 minutes post-injection. Data were processed at each time point using a validated, fully automated in-house pipeline. Regional uptake values were extracted from bilateral Aβ-vulnerable regions of interest (ROIs), including the orbitofrontal, prefrontal, anterior cingulate (anterior and mid cingulate), posterior cingulate/precuneus, parietal, and temporal regions. Standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) were calculated by normalizing median uptake in each region to that of the cerebellar crus gray matter. Global PiB SUVRs were computed as a weighted average across these regions and converted to centiloid units (CL) for comparability with other studies.

This study is a secondary data analysis of a publicly available dataset of the A4-LEARN trial. The A4 and LEARN study received ethics approval by Institutional Review Boards at each of the 67 trial sites in Australia, Canada, Japan, and the USA. The present study analyzed de-identified data including tau-PET SUVR values in composite MTL, temporal, and neocortical regions, and cognitive scores for CDR-SB (Clinical Dementia Rating Scale-Sum of Boxes) to examine longitudinal trajectories of clinico-biological staging across groups using linear mixed-effects models.

100 non-demented PD patients underwent assessment using BDI and SPECT with 123I-FP-CIT imaging. Severity of depression had an inverse correlation with DaT binding in the right caudate (r = −0.27, p = 0.007). UPDRS-III score was significantly associated with DaT binding ratio in the right putamen (β = −0.26, p = 0.03) but not in the right caudate (β = −0.09, p = 0.38). Study suggests depressed PD may be associated with DA deficit in the caudate nucleus, whilst motor symptoms accrue in part from putaminal dopaminergic deficit.

109 newly diagnosed drug-naïve PD patients underwent 2-4 year follow-up for RLS assessment. DaT scan at baseline was used to assess DaT availability. Increase in DaT availability in caudate and putamen was found to be more likely associated with baseline RLS (n = 5, OR = 75.7, p = 0.077) and RLS follow-up (n = 16, OR = 12.0, P = 0.059). Study suggests PD patients with RLS have comparatively preserved dopaminergic pathways.

Large-scale imaging initiatives, such as the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (Mueller et al., 2005) which provide unrestricted access to image data (Butcher, 2007) are an important resource in this regard. While they are not currently associated with pathological features, there are increasing numbers of MCI patients who convert to Alzheimer's disease. The detection of MCI is another important potential application of classification-based methods.

The authors used support vector machines (SVMs) to separate mild to severe sporadic Alzheimer's disease from normal ageing using structural MRI. The first dataset comprised 20 Alzheimer's disease patients and 20 healthy controls matched for age and scanner. Neuropathological examination served as a gold standard against which classification accuracy was compared. Grey matter segments were extracted from T1-weighted brain scans and normalized into standard anatomical space, with each voxel reflecting the magnitude of local grey matter volume.

The second set comprised 18 pathologically proven sporadic Alzheimer's disease scans and 19 scans from patients with pathologically proven FTLD, matched for age, scanner and mini mental state examination (MMSE) score. The Alzheimer's disease patients all fulfilled NINCDS-ADRDA criteria for definite Alzheimer's disease in that the clinical diagnoses were confirmed histopathologically after cerebral biopsy or at autopsy according to CERAD and NIA-RIA criteria.

The third dataset comprised 14 Alzheimer's disease patients and 14 healthy controls, used for SVM-based classification to separate Alzheimer's disease from normal ageing using structural MRI with grey matter segmentation and normalization to standard anatomical space.

This study leverages the extraordinarily rich data resources of the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) dataset, representing a well-characterized and multicenter sample of people living with AD. The dataset is uniquely suited for this analysis due to its breadth, rigorous diagnostic procedures, standardized collection by trained clinicians, and its large representation of EOAD—a population often underrepresented in large-scale studies. Item parameters were applied to the longitudinal data set (e.g. all visits, not just the most recent visit) to obtain factor scores for the language domain. The study leveraged a uniquely robust sample of individuals with EOAD and LOAD from a large, multi-site cohort of incident and prevalent AD from NACC. The standardized data collection across Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers (ADRCs), conducted by highly trained clinicians and research personnel with deep expertise in dementia diagnosis and assessment, ensures the clinical rigor of EOAD and LOAD classification, and ascertainment of language performance in standardized fashion across all participant encounters. Classification resulted in a participant sample of 1,189 EOAD and 4,646 LOAD.

The data used in this study were obtained from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database (www.ppmi-info.org), which requires formal application and approval for access. The dataset was used for machine learning classification of three-class cognitive status in Parkinson's Disease patients. Authors applied cognitive battery assessments and domain-informed classification strategies to develop models for individualized cognitive profiling in PD, with the goal of facilitating earlier recognition of cognitive impairment. A limitation noted is that the PPMI cognitive battery lacks two tests per domain and an independent language domain, so the labeling is MDS-inspired rather than fully MDS Level II-conformant.

Data used in the preparation of this article were obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. The ADNI was launched in 2003 as a public-private partnership, led by Principal Investigator Michael W. Weiner, MD. The original goal of ADNI was to test whether serial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), other biological markers, and clinical and neuropsychological assessment can be combined to measure the progression of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and early Alzheimer's disease (AD). The analysis was limited to structural MRI data for validating the cognitiveTree automated pipeline for dementia classification, achieving high discrimination performance (AUC = 0.90) compared to radiologists (AUC = 0.71 and 0.62).

Data used in this study are available through standard application procedures on the BIOCARD website. The study analyzed biomarker data including amyloid-beta (Aβ), neurofilament light chain (NfL), phosphorylated tau at threonine 181 (p-tau181), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and other Alzheimer's disease-related biomarkers in the context of cognitive impairment and disease progression.

The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database includes longitudinal clinical, cognitive, imaging, genetic, autopsy, and biomarker data from more than 2400 participants. The resource comprises over 185,000 imaging datasets. More than 26,000 investigators across 169 countries have accessed ADNI's database, which has supported more than 405 million data downloads. Over 7000 publications have used ADNI data and/or samples. This review synthesizes 122 high-impact studies using ADNI data or biospecimens from 2023 to mid-2025 to clarify mechanisms of Alzheimer's disease progression. By integrating imaging, fluid biomarkers, genetics, and clinical measures, ADNI provides a comprehensive research dataset for unraveling mechanisms underlying AD progression.

The NACC database is funded by NIA/NIH Grant U24 AG072122. NACC data are contributed by the NIA-funded ADRCs including multiple Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers across the United States. The database includes cognitive assessment data including measures such as the Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) and Mini-Mental Status Examination (MMSE), as well as clinical and demographic information from patients with cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease.

Raw total and small RNA sequencing data for the PPMI Cohort used in this study. Analysis used RNA-Seq data and metadata from selected participants obtained from PPMI upon request and approval of the PPMI Data Access Committee. Raw total RNA sequencing data from the PDBP Cohort available at AMP-PD. All R scripts used for data analysis and visualization are publicly available in this GitHub repository. These scripts were used for processing RNA-Seq data, identifying and annotating circRNAs, and performing comparative analysis between PPMI and PDBP cohorts.

TaqMan assays (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, USA) for both rs429358 (ABI#C 3084793 20) and rs7412 (ABI#C 904973 10) were used for APOE genotyping. Allele calling was performed using the allelic discrimination analysis module of ABI Sequence Detection Software. The Imaging Core provided structural MRI data. Authors used this data for hippocampal subdivision delineation with assistance from John Paul Bonadonna.

Health variables (mild heart problems, hypertension, diabetes, brief head trauma) were coded for absence (0) or history (1). Depressive symptomatology was measured using the GDS. Depression information was not available for one AD and two cognitively normal participants. Their values were imputed with the mean score for their respective group. The Clinical Core of the Knight ADRC at Washington University performed participant assessments.

The study aimed to characterize biological heterogeneity in early-onset Alzheimer's disease using tau-PET biomarkers and clinical phenotypes including amnestic predominant cognitive impairment, non-amnestic predominant cognitive impairment, primary progressive aphasia, and posterior cortical atrophy. Tissue-specific enrichment used published findings that mapped organ-specific proteomes using human organ bulk RNA-seq data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression project (GTEx); a cognate gene encoding a plasma protein was considered enriched if it was expressed at least four times higher in a single organ (or groups of organs) compared to any other organ. For assessing expression across cell and tissue types, we used RNA sequencing data from the HPA and GTEx.

Cell-specific enrichment utilized published findings that mapped cell-specific proteomes using single-cell RNA sequencing data from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA); a cognate gene encoding a protein was considered enriched if it was expressed at least two standard deviations higher in a single cell type compared to its relative expression across all other cell types. Single cell and bulk RNA sequencing (normalized transcripts per million; nTPM) were obtained from the Human Protein Atlas.

Protein interaction networks were assessed using STRING (Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes/Proteins). Enrichment analyses used publicly available databases via STRING and Enrichr platforms.

Enrichment analyses also used publicly available databases via the Enrichr platform. Supplementary information on individual SNPs was obtained with the OpenTargets and GTEx platforms.

Exploratory biomarker analyses were conducted in smaller subsets. Data preprocessing pipelines incorporated internal imputation and scaling steps to prevent information leakage between training and validation phases.

Data used in the preparation of this article were obtained from the Department of Defense–Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (DoD-ADNI) database. The DoD-ADNI is a multi-site extension of ADNI designed to investigate the effects of TBI and PTSD on AD-related pathology in Vietnam-era Veterans. Participants underwent structured clinical interviews, neuropsychological assessment, MRI, and collection of genetic and biomarker data. The study included structural MRI markers such as white matter hyperintensities (WMHs), hippocampal volume, and cortical thickness to understand brain changes associated with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and early Alzheimer's disease (AD). Neuropsychological assessments included measures such as the Wechsler Memory Scale Revised Edition (WMS-R) and Mini-Mental Status Examination (MMSE).

The study analyzed longitudinal relationships between tooth loss and white matter integrity using neuroimaging markers, biomarkers including white blood cell counts, neutrophil counts, and albumin, as well as DTI (diffusion tensor imaging) data acquired on 2 KKI scanners and 1 NIA scanner with detailed acquisition protocols specified.

This study leverages data from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) dataset, one of the most comprehensive dementia datasets in the United States. NACC serves as a centralized data repository, aggregating longitudinal data from over 30 Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers (ADRCs) from across the country. Participants are recruited through clinician referrals, self-referrals, and active recruitment in community organizations. The primary outcome of our study was dementia status, defined using the NACC variable NACCETPR or its equivalent in earlier UDS versions. This clinician-assigned variable captures the presence of all-cause dementia, regardless of subtype, as recorded at baseline and at each follow-up visit. Data for this study were obtained from the NACC database, which is funded by NIA/NIH Grant U24 AG072122.
In 2005 NACC established the Uniform Data Set (UDS), a standardized, longitudinal protocol that facilitates harmonized clinical, cognitive, and diagnostic data across centers.

Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project participants free of clinical dementia or stroke (n=156, 72±6 years, 37% mild cognitive impairment, 33% female) completed fasting lumbar puncture, SCD assessment, and Wide Range Achievement Test-III Reading subtest to assess reading level at baseline. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers for AD (β-amyloid 42 (Aβ42), Aβ42/40 ratio, phosphorylated tau (p-tau), tau, and neurofilament light (NfL)) were analyzed in batch. Linear mixed effects models related SCD to CSF AD biomarkers and follow-up models assessed SCD x sex, SCD x reading level, and SCD x education interactions on AD biomarkers.

The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) data are publicly available and can be accessed upon request via the LONI Image and Data Archive (IDA LONI). Both ADNI and AIBL datasets were aligned to the GRCh37/hg19 reference genome for GWAS analysis.

The Australian Imaging, Biomarkers and Lifestyle (AIBL) study of aging is publicly available and can be accessed upon request through expression of interest to AIBL data access committee. Both datasets were aligned to the GRCh37/hg19 reference genome for GWAS analysis.

1000 Genomes European panel was used to account for linkage disequilibrium (LD) structure in GWAS summary statistics analysis. MAF annotations from the 1000 Genomes Phase 3 GRCh38 EUR panel were used for colocalisation analysis.

MetaBrain eQTLs from five brain regions (Cortex, Hippocampus, Basal nuclei, Spinal cord, and Cerebellum) were used for colocalisation analysis. The cis-eQTLs were obtained from https://metabrain.nl/cis-eqtls.html for the European cohort, processed per locus mapped to GRCh38. Colocalisation was performed using GWAS summary statistics from 384 individuals and MetaBrain eQTLs to identify shared causal variants.

Promoter and enhancer coordinates and chromatin interaction data for six brain cell types (microglia, oligodendrocytes, neurons, brain endothelial cells, mural cells, and astrocytes) were derived from a recent study of brain cell-type-specific chromatin architecture. These data were used in H-MAGMA analysis to map non-coding GWAS variants to their target genes through physical chromatin contacts.

Downloaded 'UPENN_CSF_Biomarkers_ROCHE_ELECSYS [ADNI1,GO, 2,3]' dataset from the LONI website. The study used ADNI data to conduct mediation analyses examining relationships between cardiovascular risk factors (FRS and CVR) and cognitive domains (Memory, Language, Executive Function) in Alzheimer's disease research. Analysis included MIMIC models, LME growth models, and LGCM parallel process mediation models with factor score extraction.

CNV-Finder utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory neural network trained on expert-annotated LRR and BAF signals to detect deletions and duplications within predefined genomic regions.

ADNI remains the most widely used benchmark, appearing in at least 18 out of 28 studies. It is typically used for baseline T1-weighted MRI for AD vs. CN and MCI-related tasks, and occasionally for external validation when paired with other cohorts. Almost all studies (90) used publicly available repositories of neuroimaging repositories, including ADNI, which facilitate partial reproducibility in terms of data access.

The second most common source is OASIS (and its derivatives, such as the Kaggle OASIS split), which is often used for multiclass dementia severity classification (for example, CDR 0, 0.5, 1). The table highlights the dominance of ADNI and OASIS, the variability in pre-processing protocols, and the limited use of harmonisation and cross-cohort testing.

Other datasets include MIRIAD (a longitudinal volumetric MRI dataset), AIBL (a frequently used dataset for external validation), and local clinical cohorts. Almost all studies (90) used publicly available repositories of neuroimaging repositories, including ADNI, OASIS, AIBL, and MIRIAD.

Other datasets include MIRIAD (a longitudinal volumetric MRI dataset), AIBL (a frequently used dataset for external validation), and local clinical cohorts. Almost all studies (90) used publicly available repositories of neuroimaging repositories, including ADNI, OASIS, AIBL, and MIRIAD.

Beyond these, UK Biobank (UKB)—a large general-population cohort with standardised brain MRI data (for example, T1, T2-FLAIR, diffusion and resting-state fMRI) is increasingly cited for pre-training, representation learning, and robustness analyses.

The Harvard Ageing Brain Study (HABS) provides longitudinal imaging of older-adults, including MRI and amyloid PET data from smaller, deeply phenotyped cohorts that support early-stage and trajectory modelling.

Several studies have conducted cross-cohort testing to evaluate generalisation, for example by training on ADNI and testing on independent clinical cohorts, or by training on a combination of ADNI, OASIS, and A4, and testing on an external hospital dataset.

This analysis used data from the PPMI database. Data were drawn from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center Uniform Data Set (NACC UDS). We included all participants who were age ≥65 at their most recent visit (N=34,154). Participants were classified according to reported parental history of dementia (neither parent, mother only, father only, both parents, and unknown). Multinomial regression was used to estimate the adjusted odds ratios for reported parental history of dementia. Dementia in at least one parent was reported by 40% of participants (n=13,596), 52% (n=17,881) reported that neither parent had dementia, and 8% (n=2,677) did not know. Participants reporting neither parent had dementia, or reported unknown history, were older, less educated, more likely to be minoritized, and were also most likely to be missing APOE genotype (28% and 37%, respectively) and to be diagnosed with cognitive impairment at baseline (62% and 75%, respectively).

The external dataset was obtained on 24 June 2024 from the PPMI database. The model was evaluated on this external PPMI dataset, which showed notably wider and lower ROC curves reflecting a drop in discriminative ability compared to internal datasets. The PPMI set demonstrated substantial reduction in precision and recall in external validation, consistent with lower prevalence and class imbalance. The PPMI calibration curve showed systematic overconfidence in the external cohort, with the model tending to overestimate risk.

The NACC UDS is a dataset of clinical variables collected from 2005 to 2021 from 42 past and present ADRCs funded by the National Institute of Aging. The UDS collects data on neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) in 5 places: Subject Health History (Form A5), NPIQ (Form B5), Geriatric Depression Scale (Form B6), Clinician Judgment of Symptoms (Form B9), and Clinician Diagnosis (Form D1). For depression, all five metrics were available. For anxiety, all sections except the GDS were available. For apathy, only Clinician-rated and NPIQ were available. The dataset includes longitudinally tracked participants from multiple centers with a unified set of clinical variables collected on every participant, though with significant heterogeneity in patient populations and clinical focus.

An international, longitudinal cohort launched in 2010 to accelerate biomarker discovery in Parkinson's disease. PPMI enrolls three broad cohorts across multiple international sites under a harmonized protocol: recently diagnosed, untreated PD; healthy controls; and prodromal/genetic-risk groups. Participants undergo standardized clinical motor assessments, imaging, and biospecimen collection, with dense visits in year 1 and semiannual to annual follow-up thereafter. The study emphasizes deep phenotyping and open data sharing through a centralized repository. Peripheral whole blood was collected at baseline and at planned follow-up visits following PPMI's longitudinal protocol. DNA methylation profiling is released as raw Illumina Infinium array .idat files in the PPMI Methylation Profiling dataset (Projects 120/140), predominantly HumanMethylationEPIC BeadChips. The authors utilized longitudinal phenotype and whole-blood DNA methylation data from the PPMI cohort to calculate seven epigenetic aging measures (Horvath v1, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge v1/v2, AltumAge, DunedinPACE) and assess motor function using the MDS-UPDRS.

Data used in the preparation of this article was obtained on 2024-06-20 from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database. The dataset comprised 100 PD and 100 CT (control) MRI volumes in T1-weighted format used to train a neural network for PD classification. Authors note that the dataset of 100 PD and 100 CT MRI volumes was limited and did not capture a complete profile of the heterogeneous PD-associated structural features available in T1w MRI, and the model would have benefitted from more MRI data from PPMI to further increase performance on the task of classifying early PD.

Statistical atlas parcellations were retrieved on 2025-06-17 from the Julich Brain Cytoarchitectonic Atlas v3.1 using the Siibra Python Package. A full list of atlas areas is available in Supplementary Data 1.

The Health and Retirement Study data are publicly available from the HRS website. The HRS relied on validated cognitive testing algorithms for identifying incident dementia cases. The HRS was approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Review Board (IRB). The three cohort studies employed distinct strategies for identifying incident dementia cases, with all utilizing all-cause dementia definitions rather than subtype-specific classifications due to methodological differences in ascertainment approaches.

Data from the Framingham Heart Study can be accessed by submitting a research proposal through the study group upon reasonable request. The FOS incorporated multidisciplinary expert adjudication for identifying incident dementia cases. The FOS was approved by the Boston University Medical Center IRB. The NICOLA-HCAP dataset was used for confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) with missing data handled using Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) to generate 10 imputed datasets before analysis. The study replicated an analytical approach in R, addressing missing data that may be informative (e.g., signalling cognitive decline) using MLR estimators and MICE to maintain categorical structure of indicators while minimising data loss.

Longitudinal AD-related cohort used to examine the association between age at biomarker-clock events and remaining time to clinical symptom onset. Authors analyzed five biomarkers in this cohort: (1) CSF Abeta42/Abeta40, (2) CSF p-tau181, (3) plasma p-tau181, (4) amyloid PET, and (5) plasma p-tau217. The standard analysis produced uniformly significant associations for ages at biomarker-clock events based on all five biomarkers (hazard ratios 1.94-3.34, all P < 0.01). Time-varying analysis showed that younger age at biomarker-clock events is associated with higher hazard for symptom onset on the age scale.
