The authors analyze brain morphometry and cognition in ADNI datasets using their proposed ProJIVE method for data integration. The analysis includes multiple measures: cortical thickness (CT), surface area (SA), cortical volume (CVol), and subcortical volume (SVol). The joint subject scores derived from this analysis were associated with ApoE4, diagnosis, and PET biomarkers. The largest joint variable loadings show patterns consistent with associations found in the literature between measures of cognition, brain morphometry, and Alzheimer's disease.

Retrospective longitudinal data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative was used to train supervised logistic regression models to estimate the probability of undergoing DBS during follow-up. Separate models were developed for bradykinesia/rigidity–predominant, tremor‐predominant phenotypes, and the total cohort. Analyses were restricted to visits within a clinically plausible DBS screening window (age <75 years, Hoehn & Yahr stage 2–3, MoCA ≥26). Across 1,227 patients, phenotype‐specific and combined models demonstrated moderate discrimination for eventual DBS implantation (AUC 0.80–0.82).

Publicly available transcriptomic and metadata from human brain samples were obtained from the Accelerating Medicines Partnership–Alzheimer's Disease (AMP-AD) Knowledge Portal. The AMP-AD consortium provides harmonized multi-omics datasets generated from post-mortem brain tissue of individuals with Alzheimer's disease and age-matched cognitively normal controls, including RNA sequencing data from multiple brain regions and independent cohorts. Data were accessed through the AMP-AD Knowledge Portal, which supports standardized processing pipelines, metadata annotation, and cross-cohort analyses. For this study, AMP-AD datasets were queried to assess the expression patterns of the DEGs identified. AMP-AD is a large-scale integrative resource that provides multi-omic data, including transcriptomic, proteomic, and genomic profiles from multiple brain regions of well-characterized human cohorts. AMP-AD datasets are derived from bulk RNA sequencing of post-mortem human brain tissue.

OASIS dataset used for neuroimaging analysis. The dataset contains MRI neuroimaging data and structured clinical data including numerical features (age, MMSE score, hippocampus volume) and categorical features (gender, education level, genetic markers such as APOE4). The framework processes these data modalities while preserving data privacy across multiple healthcare institutions.

ADNI sorted data used for federated learning analysis. The dataset includes MRI neuroimaging data and structured clinical data with numerical features (age, MMSE score, hippocampus volume) and categorical features (gender, education level, genetic markers including APOE4). Authors applied fuzzy inference and federated training to boost generalization across heterogeneous data sources while maintaining diagnostic accuracy and interpretability.

The Bio-Hermes plasma proteomic dataset and associated phenotypic data are available through the AD Workbench platform of the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative under a controlled-access Data Use Agreement. Plasma proteomic measurements were collected from individuals with known amyloid status using tandem mass spectrometry with a TMTpro18 pipeline. The dataset included 992 participants after quality control and normalisation, with 881 proteins initially available. After complete-case analysis excluding features with missing values, the final dataset comprised 988 samples and 295 proteins. Five proteins showed significant differential expression after FDR correction, and 31 proteins with amyloid-status group differences were selected for machine learning training.

Bio-Hermes Data Challenge data are publicly available through the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative platform via the AD Discovery Portal on AD Workbench. The dataset was provided by the Global Alzheimer's Platform Foundation and the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative, with plasma proteomic data generated by EMTherapro (Atlanta, GA, USA) as part of the Bio-Hermes controlled-access dataset and analysed as de-identified abundance measurements.

The NACC database is funded by NIA/NIH Grant U24 AG072122. Following initial training on the UK Biobank dataset, an adaptive transfer learning approach was employed to calibrate estimates to the clinical dataset from NACC. 80% of NACC healthy controls (NC train, N=1,624) were used to recalibrate model parameters, establishing a NACC-specific normative baseline. The remaining 20% of healthy controls (NC test, N=394), along with all patients diagnosed with Alzheimer's Disease (AD, N=618), MCI Stable (N=632), and MCI Progressive (N=299), formed the test set for evaluating deviations from the normative model (total test set N=1,943). All sites included in the test set were also represented in the adaptation dataset to ensure proper calibration of site-specific parameters.

This research has been conducted using the UK Biobank Resource under Application Number 20904. The UK Biobank dataset was used for initial training before employing an adaptive transfer learning approach to calibrate estimates to the clinical dataset from NACC.

Data presented in this manuscript are derived from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) dataset, available upon request from https://naccdata.org/. The dataset includes cognitive assessment variables: CDR-SB (CDRSUM), Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE; NACCMMSE), logical memory immediate recall (LMI; LOGIMEM), logical memory delayed recall (LMD; MEMUNITS), time elapsed since LMI (MEMTIME), digit span forward (DSF; DIGIF), digit span forward length (DSFL; DIGIFLEN), digit span backward (DSB; DIGIB), digit span backward length (DSBL; DIGIBLEN), Trail Making Test Part A (TMT-A; TRAILA), Trail Making Test Part B (TMT-B; TRAILB), Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale Digit Symbol Substitution Test (WAIS), animal fluency (ANIMALS), vegetable fluency (VEG), and Boston Naming Test 30 odd items (BNT; BOSTON). Data were downloaded with permission from NACC and sourced from 37 Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers (ADRCs) located across the United States. Standardized Uniform Data Set (UDS) version 3 variables, Neuropathology (NP) Data Set version 11 variables, and Genetic Data Set variables were used. Study analyzed trajectories of global cognitive assessments in subjects with various isolated neurodegenerative pathologies including Alzheimer's disease neuropathologic change, Lewy body dementia, and other pathologies.

This is a secondary analysis of data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). The ADNI was launched in 2003 as a public-private partnership, led by Principal Investigator Michael W. Weiner, MD. The original goal of ADNI was to test whether serial MRI, PET, other biological markers, and clinical and neuropsychological assessment can be combined to measure the progression of MCI and early AD. The current goals include validating biomarkers for clinical trials, improving the generalizability of ADNI data by increasing diversity in the participant cohort, and to provide data concerning the diagnosis and progression of AD to the scientific community. The authors used ADNI data to demonstrate subgroups that are 'resilient' against versus 'afflicted' by adipokines, inflammatory cytokines, Aβ PET, and neurodegeneration using a novel Line of Identity (LOI) algorithm.

The data underlying the findings of this study are not publicly available because they contain sensitive human participant information and are subject to ethical and legal restrictions on sharing. The data are available from the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project, collected by the Vanderbilt Memory and Alzheimer's Center, for researchers who meet criteria for access to confidential data. Requests for data access should be directed to the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project / Vanderbilt Memory and Alzheimer's Center at 3319 West End Avenue, 8th Floor, Nashville, TN 37203. The study analyzed diffusion metrics (FA and MD) from 948 imaging sessions using mixed-effects models to assess associations between aging and diffusion metrics, with gradient nonlinearity (GNL) correction applied to the imaging data.

Longitudinal Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) biomarker data used to develop and demonstrate interactive visualization tools. The web-based application enables users to explore longitudinal AD biomarker data, including plasma biomarker collection at baseline and follow-up timepoints. Dataset includes multiple biomarkers tracked over time to visualize non-linearity and heterogeneity of biomarker relationships in Alzheimer's disease progression.

This study uses anonymised human participant data accessed through the UK Brain Banks Network database. The human participant data were not collected directly by the authors, and all personal identifiers were removed prior to access. Access to the database was approved by the Brains for Dementia Research (BDR) Assessment Team. All data within the database are provided by individual brain banks in the UK Brain Banks Network, each of which holds its own research ethics approval process. All data supporting these analyses are available through the UK Brain Banks Network.

The Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer's Network (DIAN) dataset is referenced throughout the publication as the source of clinical and biomarker data. The dataset includes measurements of amyloid beta (Aβ), phosphorylated tau (pT), total tau (tTau), and neurofilament light chain (NfL) in cerebrospinal fluid, as well as PET imaging data using Pittsburgh compound B (PiB) and fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG). Clinical assessments include Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores. The study population includes asymptomatic mutation carriers (aMC), symptomatic mutation carriers (sMC), and mutation non-carriers (NC) with APOE genotyping.

The data that support the findings of this study are available on reasonable request from the corresponding author. The data are not publicly available due to privacy or ethical restrictions. The online UCSF MAC Resource Request Form can be used to submit your request. The dataset includes clinical and biomarker measurements from patients with behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), and primary psychiatric disorders (PPDs). Measurements include frontotemporal atrophy assessments, neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels, phosphorylated tau (p-tau217), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) biomarkers. Data were used to develop logistic regression models to distinguish between bvFTD-FTLD and PPDs using leave-one-out cross-validation.

Large-scale proteomics (6907 features) and metabolomics (1508 features) datasets generated from 3060 samples comprising 1655 control and 1362 Alzheimer's Disease (AD) samples. Two datasets: 2200 samples collected from 1995-1997 and 2007-2021; 860 samples collected from 1998-2006. Data collected via SomaScan platform from the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium (GNPC), an international effort consolidating proteomic data from over 40,000 samples across 23 international cohorts covering neurodegenerative conditions including AD, Parkinson's Disease, Frontotemporal Dementia, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Proteomics data were normalized using log10 transformation and batch effects removed using limma R package. Gene Ontology enrichment analysis was conducted to identify activated biological processes with p-value ≤ 0.05.

FDA approved drug and target information derived from DrugBank database. The 'Target Drug-UniProt Links' file of 'Approved' drugs was downloaded from the 'EXTERNAL LINKS' tab to identify FDA drugs and associated drug-target information. FDA approved drugs inhibiting selected genes were identified as drug candidates for potential perturbation of uncovered signaling networks.

Connectivity Map (CMAP) database accessed via clue.io API for drug repositioning analysis. Consistently up-regulated and down-regulated proteins were used as biomarkers for drug repositioning. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) algorithm was used to rank drugs that can potentially reverse abundance of these proteins, with top ranked drugs selected and analyzed.

Raw sequence and processed data of single-nucleus RNA-seq are available at Synapse. Access to the datasets is restricted and requires a Data Use Certificate (DUC) to be submitted to preserve anonymity of study participants. The snRNAseq library consisted of nuclei from eight individuals, with UMI counts aggregated from duplicate libraries. Pseudobulk UMI count matrices were generated for each cell type by extracting and aggregating counts per gene per individual, with low expression genes filtered using edgeR and normalized using TMM method.

Cell (sub)type annotation and cell (sub)type-level eQTL summary statistics are available at Synapse. Cell type-level eQTL of this study are also available from this dataset and accessible through an interactive Shiny application.

Variant Call Format (VCF) files of WGS are available at Synapse. WGS-based VCF file of 1,196 ROS/MAP individuals was used to extract SNPs in transcribed regions that passed GATK filter, with at least one of eight individuals having its alternate allele. These SNP genotype data were used with demuxlet software to assign nuclei back to their participant of origin.

The reference human genome GRCh37 that was used for WGS variant calling is available from EMBL-EBI. This reference genome was employed for aligning and calling variants in the whole genome sequencing data.

Custom code for preparing pseudobulk gene expression and mapping cis-eQTL can be found at Zenodo. This code implements the complete TWAS pipeline using FUSION tools for heritability estimation, expression weight computation with multiple modeling approaches (BLUP, Bayesian sparse linear mixed model, LASSO, Elastic Net), and cross-validation.

Pseudobulk RNA-seq data and genotypes from ROSMAP (424 brain subjects) were used to impute the cis genetic component of expression into multiple GWAS summary statistics. The study used snRNAseq libraries prepared from nuclei of eight individuals, with genotype data obtained from snRNAseq reads and WGS data from 1,196 ROS/MAP individuals.

Raw and processed datasets associated with this study are publicly available from the Gene Expression Omnibus at accession number GSE268609. The dataset contains single-cell transcriptomic data from human forebrain tissue. Cell types identified include astrocytes, neuroblasts, developmentally immature neurons, CA neurons, CA2–4 neurons, microglia, OPCs, mOLs, mGCs, endothelial cells and ependymal cells. Analysis used the top 5,000 most variable genes in the combined dataset with batch effect correction based on data source.

Reference data were obtained from a previous study which reported a human developmental forebrain dataset. This reference dataset was used in a transfer-learning approach based on scVI and scANVI, in which reference dataset annotations were transferred to annotate subpopulations in the query dataset. The latent representation was modelled using the top 5,000 most variable genes in the combined dataset.

Reference data were obtained from another study of the human hippocampus. This reference dataset was used in a transfer-learning approach based on scVI and scANVI to transfer the most likely label from the reference datasets to the unannotated cells in the query dataset.
Mouse reference genome assembly GRCm38.99 was used for data analysis. This reference genome was utilized as the basis for genomic data analysis in the study.

Cross-sectional analyses were performed using data from the Amyloid Biomarker Study data pooling initiative. Data from 49 research, population-based, and memory clinic studies were pooled and harmonized. The Amyloid Biomarker Study has been collecting data since 2012 and data collection is ongoing. At the time of analysis, 95 centers were included in the Amyloid Biomarker Study. The study included 9746 individuals with normal cognition (NC) and 3023 participants with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) aged between 34 and 100 years for whom data on amyloid biomarkers, presence of depressive symptoms, and age were available. Data were analyzed from December 2022 to February 2024.

The authors present an interpretable, hybrid method called Neurosymodal Data Fusion for predicting incident AD in the ADNI dataset. They encode the A/T/N framework (amyloid/tau/neurodegeneration) as a logic program with biomarker features extracted by neural networks. The pipeline predicted four-year incident AD with sensitivity up to 0.84. The models learned scores for each A/T/N profile indicating relative importances to predictions, and revealed that empirically-derived cut-off values for A and T criteria might be uninformative for the ADNI data.

dataset_identifier: RADC Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center Cohort
dataset_context_from_paper: Longitudinal study data from 224 Latino participants with geocoded baseline addresses collected from 1997 through 2019. Addresses were reviewed and clerical errors corrected prior to geocoding using internal Geographic Information Systems (GIS) mapping via ESRI ArchMap (v10.8) and ArcGIS Pro (v 3.6.2). Geocoded baseline address data were used to derive Census tract determinations with the 2000 Census covering study visit years 1997 through 2009 and the 2010 Census covering study visit years 2010 through 2019. Dataset includes subjective and objective neighborhood health metrics linked to cognitive outcomes measured through annual study visits. 172 of 224 Latino participants (77%) never moved from their geocoded baseline address during the analysis period.

US Census TigerLine data used in conjunction with geocoded participant addresses for Geographic Information Systems (GIS) mapping to derive Census tract determinations. The 2000 Census covered study visit years 1997 through 2009 and the 2010 Census covered study visit years 2010 through 2019.

The study examined the relationship between imaging measures (GMV, WBD) and biomarkers (log(NfL), C1q, C3b, YBOCS-total score) in asymptomatic GRN carriers (asympGRN), symptomatic GRN carriers (sympGRN), and healthy controls (HC). Sample sizes included: NfL analysis with asympGRN (30), asympGRN-matched HCs (47), sympGRN (13), sympGRN-matched HCs (33); complement analysis with asympGRN (17), asympGRN-matched HCs (20), sympGRN (13), sympGRN-matched HCs (13); and YBOCS analysis with asympGRN (11), sympGRN (9), HCs (12). Voxel-wise correlations and biomarker by gene status interaction analyses were performed using SPM12.

dataset_identifier: Longitudinal Early Onset Alzheimer's Disease Study
dataset_context_from_paper: Multisite study examining associations of the UCSF Tablet-based Cognitive Assessment Tool (TabCAT) tests with clinical and pathophysiologic markers of AD. The cohort included 83 cognitively unimpaired controls and 392 patients with a clinical diagnosis of EOAD (MCI or mild dementia). Participants underwent TabCAT testing including 2 tests of executive function/attention (Match, Flanker) and 2 visuospatial tests (Line Length and Line Orientation). Aβ-PET imaging was performed using Florbetaben-PET with quantification-aided visual read to classify patients as Aβ- (n=95) or Aβ+ (n=297). dataset_context_from_paper: The Queen Square dataset that supports the findings of this study is available from the corresponding author, upon reasonable request. This was used as the discovery dataset for identifying four data-driven subtypes of primary progressive aphasia (PPA) using SuStaIn analysis. The dataset was divided into three smaller datasets representing single phenotypes (svPPA, nfvPPA, and lvPPA) to analyze correspondence between data-driven subtypes and expected disease progression sequences. The greatest phenotype subtype concordance was between svPPA and S1 (left temporal) at 54.1%.

The ALLFTD dataset is available upon reasonable request from https://www.allftd.org/data. The findings in the ALLFTD dataset replicated the Queen Square discovery dataset. As in the Queen Square discovery dataset, the greatest phenotype subtype concordance was between svPPA and S1 (left temporal) (54.1% of svPPA were assigned to S1). Subtypes and stages were stable at follow-up clinic visits, with >90% of individuals remaining in the same stage or advancing to a later stage at first follow-up. The 1958 National Child Development Study (NCDS) was used to identify and categorise early-life variables that fit into 12 previously conceptualised domains of early-life determinants of multimorbidity. Ten domains were characterised by 143 variables in the NCDS. PCA analysis reduced the dimensionality of NCDS variables from 143 to 73. Important PCA components included maternal fertility histories, long-term illnesses, educational ability, ethnicity, housing status and parental-child interactions.

The 1970 British Cohort Study (BCS70) was used to identify and categorise early-life variables that fit into 12 previously conceptualised domains of early-life determinants of multimorbidity. Twelve domains were characterised by 289 variables in the BCS70. PCA analysis reduced the dimensionality of BCS70 variables from 289 to 149. Important PCA components included maternal fertility histories, long-term illnesses, educational ability, ethnicity, housing status and parental-child interactions.

The Aberdeen Children of the 1950s Study (ACONF) was used to identify and categorise early-life variables that fit into 12 previously conceptualised domains of early-life determinants of multimorbidity. Seven domains were characterised by 74 variables in ACONF. PCA analysis reduced the dimensionality of ACONF variables from 74 to 41. Important PCA components included maternal fertility histories, long-term illnesses, educational ability, ethnicity, housing status and parental-child interactions.

Our datasets included 63 variables, with each variable measured separately at multiple time points. Variables were binary (e.g., whether a comorbidity or NPS exists) or categorical (e.g., age groups). The dataset contained information on neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS), comorbidities, and demographic variables in what appears to be a clinical dementia/Alzheimer's disease study population. Authors applied the FCI algorithm to discover causal relationships, generated 100 causal diagrams from bootstrapped samples, and retained relationships appearing in at least 50 out of 100 bootstrapped diagrams. Several unmeasurable or unobserved variables may have influenced relationships among observed variables.

data_repository: Banner Health Brain and Body Donation Program
dataset_context_from_paper: We selected 251 participants (age: 85±8.2) from the BBDP cohort with a plasma sample taken < 5 years (1.45±1.26) prior to death. At post‐mortem each case was classified as CAA+ (n = 140) or CAA‐ (n = 111). We employed the Nucleic Acid‐Linked Immuno‐Sandwich Assay (NULISA™) central nervous system panel for an exploratory biomarker quantification in plasma of patients with CAA or no‐CAA utilizing samples from the Banner Health Brain and Body Donation Program (BBDP). We evaluated the differential protein expression between groups using a linear model adjusted for age, sex, APOE e4 carrier status and the presence of Alzheimer's amyloid plaque load (AD‐status). NULISA™ identified several novel proteomic biomarkers which were up‐regulated (CRP, IL4, SAA1), and down‐regulated (CCL11, PDLIM5, NPY and GDNF) in CAA pathology carriers.

Clinical protocol associated with data published in the current paper. The study participants were drawn from the first 500 individuals who completed the baseline assessments in the Tulsa-1000 study (T-1000). Participants included those diagnosed with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD, n=176, with 122 having anxiety and 54 without anxiety) and healthy controls (HC, n=52), for a total of 228 participants after exclusion of 9 participants due to excessive head motion and imaging quality. The Mini International Neuropsychiatric Inventory (MINI) was used for MDD diagnosis. The study examined rumination in depression using fMRI during a stop-signal task with Easy-stop and Hard-stop conditions, measuring neural activity in relation to Ruminative Response Scale (RRS) scores.

Clinical and genetic data shared by the ARTFL-LEFFTDS Longitudinal Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration consortium (ALLFTD), a nationwide consortium of FTD research centers in the United States. The dataset was queried to identify participants with the TARDBP I383V variant. Five individuals were identified who performed standardized comprehensive neuropsychological evaluations, with four participants completing annual evaluations over 1.0 to 3.9 years. Subsequent changes were evaluated in the Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration Modified Clinical Dementia Rating Scale (FTLD-CDR), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), and neuropsychological measures.

Cohort study data from multiple longitudinal studies including Religious Orders Study (ROS), Memory and Aging Project (MAP), Memory and Resilience in Aging Study (MARS), Clinical Core, and Late-Life Aging and Cognitive Health (LATC). The authors linked Medicare claims data to these cohorts to examine healthcare diagnoses in relation to underlying neuropathologies. 82% of cohort participants provided consent for Medicare records access (87% in ROS, 95% in MAP, 49% in MARS, 66% in Clinical Core, 73% in LATC). Linked Medicare data were available through 1991-2022, with analysis restricted to end of 2019. The dataset includes multiple and granular measures of neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular pathologies linked to administrative claims records and electronic health records with timing of clinical dementia diagnosis.

Medicare claims data linked to cohort participants through a Data Use Agreement between Rush University Medical Center and the NIH. Only named persons on the Data Use Agreement are granted permission to access these Medicare records files. The linked Medicare data were available through 1991-2022, with analysis restricted to the end of 2019 to rule out potential impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on healthcare practice.

Data from 421 participants in the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network (DIAN) across 10 countries was analyzed, including 158 non-mutation carriers (nMC), 170 asymptomatic mutation carriers (aMC), and 93 symptomatic mutation carriers (sMC). Using hierarchical linear mixed models, we evaluated the longitudinal effects of SES, measured by the Hollingshead Social Class Index (SC), on cognition (DIAN Cognitive Composite) and function (Clinical Dementia Rating Scale Sum of Boxes, CDR-SB). We identified an optimal change point (CP) near estimated years from onset (EYO) to detect when mutation carriers diverged from non-carriers.

Ferguson et al used an observational and Mendelian randomization (MR) approach in the UK Biobank data and found that cataracts were associated with dementia risk, and higher genetic risk for cataracts was associated with increased risk of vascular dementia (VaD); analysis using 2-sample MR estimators showed cataracts increased VaD risk 2-fold. The study also found that cataracts were associated with increased brain atrophy. Larger cohorts with longer follow-up times, such as cohorts in the UK Biobank, may have increased statistical power and better ability to capture incident dementia cases over time. Larger cohort studies utilizing the UK Biobank relied on administrative data, including hospital inpatient records.

Positive associations observed in larger cohorts with longer follow-up times, such as cohorts in the Cardiovascular Health Study, may have increased statistical power and better ability to capture incident dementia cases over time.

Smaller sample sizes and shorter follow-up durations, such as those seen in the Shanghai Aging Study, may limit the ability to detect modest relationships. The Shanghai Aging Study utilized detailed clinical evaluations and neuropsychological testing to more accurately diagnose dementia and AD.
The cohort study in Hong Kong utilized detailed clinical evaluations and neuropsychological testing to more accurately diagnose dementia and AD.

The ADNI represents Northern American population. Data were analyzed from July 2022 to January 2025.

dataset_context_from_paper: This cohort study used 3 independent samples: the Anti-Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease study (A4; 2014-2022, mean follow-up: 4.7 years). A4 is a multicenter trial. Participants with amyloid β (Aβ) and subsequent tau PET were included from A4, and a subset had plasma phosphorylated tau (p-tau) 217 (p-tau217) and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (RS-fMRI) data. Aβ-targeting treatment appeared to mitigate plasma p-tau217–associated tau accumulation in patients with AD and higher EA.

Neural Mechanisms of Community Mobility (NMCM) study with n=29 community dwelling older adults based in Pittsburgh, USA. The study aims to study brain function with relation to navigating challenges experienced while walking in the community. Baseline data from this study were utilized in the analysis. Participants were greater than 65 years old and able to walk without assistance, with exclusion of those with history of stroke, dementia, mild cognitive impairment, or major motor and neurological diseases.

Program to Improve Mobility in Aging – Near Infrared Spectroscopy sub-study (PRIMA-NIRS) with n=42 community dwelling older adults based in Pittsburgh, USA. The study aims to assess the effects of motor skill training on central motor control in older adults with walking difficulties. Baseline data from this sub-study were utilized in the analysis. Neuroimaging assessments from functional near-infrared spectroscopy were used to examine cortical activation of frontal areas during walking.

Move Monogahela-Youghiogheny Healthy Aging Team (MoveMYHAT) study with first n=46 enrolled participants, community dwelling older adults based in Pittsburgh, USA. The study aims to understand walking and attention, especially the role of dopamine and sensorimotor brain network connectivity in building resilience to age-related impairments. Baseline data from this study were utilized in the analysis. Accelerometry signals were used to measure changes during dual-task gait.

Pseudonymized data from BioFINDER (Principal Investigator: O.H.) can be shared with qualified academic researchers after a request for the purpose of replicating procedures and results presented in the present study. A data transfer agreement must be established with Skåne University Hospital (Region Skåne) to share data. The study validated differential abundant proteins (DAPs) in an independent cohort of 631 participants from the BioFINDER-1 study, in which a smaller set of CSF proteins was quantified with Olink. From all proteins analyzed in BioFINDER-2, 202 overlapped in BioFINDER-1. In the validation cohort, participants were compared based on their Aβ status (213 A+ versus 418 A−), with 92% consistency in differential abundance analyses.

ADNI data used in this manuscript are publicly available from the ADNI database (adni.loni.usc.edu) on registration and compliance with the data use agreement. The authors replicated many of the main DAPs using 463 ADNI participants who had CSF proteomics quantified with SomaLogic (251 A+ and 212 A−). Analysis of SomaLogic proteins that matched the ones analyzed in BioFINDER-2 yielded an overall 90% consistency in significant DAPs between cohorts.

SnRNA-seq data from ROSMAP are available at https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn52293433 on data use agreement. These data were used in the study to investigate relationships between key differentially abundant proteins and Alzheimer's disease pathology.

SnRNA-seq from the Allen Brain Institute is openly available at https://portal.brain-map.org/atlases-and-data/rnaseq. These data were used alongside other datasets to investigate relationships between key differentially abundant proteins and Alzheimer's disease pathology.

Regional microarray expression data were obtained from six postmortem brains provided by the AHBA (https://human.brain-map.org). Data were processed with the abagen toolbox v.0.1.3 to access and work with the Allen Brain data microarray expression data. Processing steps involved collapsing data into ROIs (parcels of a specified brain atlas) and combining across donors. Regional microarray expression data were generated for two brain atlases—the Desikan–Killiany atlas and the Schaefer 200 parcels—both in MNI (Montreal Neurological Institute) space. Higher NPTX2 and VGF levels were associated with less decline in the global and episodic memory scores.

dataset_context_from_paper: The PAC data set combines data from five different cohort studies, thereby increasing the sample size and allowing examination of brain volumetric change during the preclinical phase of AD with improved statistical power. The dataset was used to evaluate a distance-based method for predicting future diagnostic status in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). The study employed fivefold cross-validation with group-wise division aligned with two diagnostic groups, using historical brain imaging data to predict future diagnostic outcomes. The distance-based method demonstrated significantly superior performance compared to a 'no change' benchmark across all aggregation methods, with ROC-AUC differences showing p values of 0.02 for WOC and 0.04 for both BOC and MOC.

dataset_identifier: Eight well-characterized cohort studies of ageing
dataset_context_from_paper: Leveraging 20,513 participants from eight well-characterized cohort studies of ageing, we determined the effects of genetic variants on resilience metrics using mixed-effects regressions. The outcome of interest was residual cognitive resilience, quantified from residuals in three cognitive domains (memory, executive function and language) and built within two frameworks: 'silver' models, which obviate the requirement for neuropathological data (n = 17,241), and 'gold' models, which include post-mortem neuropathological assessments (n = 3,272). Cross-ancestry genome-wide association studies were conducted with European ancestry (n = 18,269) and African ancestry (n = 2,244) participants.

dataset_identifier: Cognitive domain assessments and neuropathological data
dataset_context_from_paper: Residual cognitive resilience was quantified from residuals in three cognitive domains (memory, executive function and language). Silver models obviated the requirement for neuropathological data (n = 17,241), while gold models included post-mortem neuropathological assessments (n = 3,272). The silver and gold phenotypes were highly correlated (R = 0.77–0.88) and displayed comparable performance in quantifying better- or worse-than-expected cognition.

The top variant at this locus (rs757022) was significantly associated with expression of numerous ATP-binding cassette genes in brain.

Prospective, longitudinal cohort study with participants aged 65 years and older (n = 708). Data collection was suspended between March 13 and April 15, 2020 due to COVID-19 mandates. From April 16, 2020 through April 4, 2021, assessments were modified from full in-person interviews to condensed telephone interviews. Beginning April 5, 2021, participants were offered the option to continue with telephone-only assessments or resume in-person visits. Interrupted time series (ITS) analyses were used to measure the long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on symptoms of depression (mCES-D) and anxiety (GAD-7). Single and multi-group ITS models compared immediate differences in severity levels during the first two months of the pandemic versus the last two months before the pandemic, and examined long-term trends over 17 months of pandemic data compared to 26 months of pre-pandemic data.

dataset_context_from_paper: Participants in the ALLFTD study underwent genetic testing at the University of California, Los Angeles. DNA samples were screened using targeted sequencing of a custom panel of genes previously implicated in neurodegenerative diseases, including GRN (138945) and MAPT (157140). Hexanucleotide repeat expansions in C9orf72 (614260) were detected using both fluorescent and repeat-primed polymerase chain reaction analysis. Identified rare pathogenic variants were documented with specific variations not provided to protect participant anonymity.

NITROGEN was trained on ADNI (N=7858 scans). The dataset contains multimodal clinical data including cortical thickness measurements, age, APOE genotype, and cognitive scores. Authors used this dataset to develop an imputation-free transformer model for Alzheimer's disease diagnostic classification and disease-severity prediction, addressing challenges of incomplete and heterogeneous real-world clinical data.

NITROGEN was evaluated on OASIS-3 (N=2675 scans) as one of two independent cohorts. The dataset was used to assess model performance on diagnostic and cognitive score prediction tasks, demonstrating robust calibration and uncertainty quantification advantages across cohorts and showing expected degradation on more distributionally different cohorts.

NITROGEN was evaluated on AIBL (N=1286 scans) as the second independent cohort. Authors used this dataset to validate model performance across different cohorts, with cross-cohort analyses identifying cortical thickness in the temporal pole, age, and APOE genotype as important features for AD classification.

The ADC training samples were analyzed at the Neurochemistry Laboratory Amsterdam. The training set comprised 495 ADC cases (45% MCI, 55% AD dementia). The validation set included 274 ADC cases (65% MCI, 35% AD dementia). ADC samples were used to develop and validate a multi-analyte algorithm (LucentAD Complete test) consisting of a locked logistic regression formula. Biomarkers measured included NfL, p-tau 217, Aβ42/40, and GFAP. Training and validation sets from ADC had similar demographics due to blinded randomization.

Bio-Hermes training samples were analyzed at the Quanterix CLIA laboratory with a different reagent lot. The training set comprised 235 Bio-Hermes cases (58% MCI, 42% mild AD). The validation set included 271 Bio-Hermes cases (55% MCI, 45% mild AD). A bridging process involving testing a crossover set of 100 samples at both sites was used to normalize biomarker values across laboratories. Biomarkers measured included NfL, p-tau 217, Aβ42/40, and GFAP.

The validation set included 545 ADNI cases (83% MCI, 17% AD dementia). ADNI was an additional independent cohort used for validation of the LucentAD Complete test configuration that was developed and initially validated in ADC and Bio-Hermes cohorts. ADNI validation cases were assessed individually and with the validation cohorts combined.

We examined 394 genetic FTD patients and 279 controls from the ALLFTD consortium, evaluating annual neuropsychological performance and MRI‐derived cortical thickness. Residuals from linear regression models served as proxies for cognitive reserve, and sex differences in longitudinal trajectories were analyzed using linear mixed‐effects models.

dataset_context_from_paper: A publicly available bulk RNAseq dataset from the Allen Institute for Brain Science was analyzed, containing frontal cerebral white matter samples relative to both parietal and temporal gray matter, providing expression data for 25,434 genes from each of 110 cases diagnosed with a spectrum of ADNC and VBI. The dataset was used to identify ferroptosis genes enriched and significantly upregulated in white matter in association with myelination-linked genes. Volcano plot analysis and pathway analysis demonstrated that white matter injury was associated with a distinctly different group of ferroptosis-related genes (FRGs) compared to gray matter, including genes regulating lipid metabolism, iron transport/metabolism, and glutamine and cysteine uptake.

The analysis revealed that reduced amyloid accumulation with treatment may have been associated with worse cognition.

ROSMAP was used to develop and validate lifetime risk prediction models for Alzheimer's disease. The study incorporated longitudinal cognitive data across five domains (episodic memory, visuospatial ability, semantic memory, and others) collected over multiple visits. For ROS cohort, AUC increased from 0.591 at baseline to 0.753 with 10 years of data. For MAP cohort, AUC rose from 0.616 at baseline to 0.796 with 10 years of data. Models were constructed separately for ROS and MAP cohorts, with consistent performance improvements demonstrated across 3, 4, and 5 visits, and for both 5-year and 10-year incident risk predictions.

The study analyzed 56 PSEN1 variants included in the DIAN-Obs cohort and used these variants to predict age of onset (AAO) using a γ-secretase activity-based scoring system (GSC). Proteomic data were sourced from two separate versions of the platform: a proprietary version that captured >4k proteins including AXL, and a commercially-available version that captured >7k proteins including MERTK. CSF AXL data from the 4k platform were available in 31 GRN carriers and 39 controls. Individual protein levels were Log2-transformed and regressed for age and sex based on control sample data. The discovery ADC cohort used 1000 repeats of fivefold cross-validation. CSF proteins within the preAD panel were modelled along CSF Aβ42 as an early proxy of AD pathology progression.

Original dataset from Smith et al. that reported Bonferroni-significant findings for YKL-40 and NfL. All DMPs were located in a region around exon 1 of CHI3L1. A differentially methylated region (DMR) on chromosome 1 around exon 1 of CHI3L1 (chr1:203186609-203187657) overlapped with the region reported by Smith et al.

The ADNI cohort began in 2003 as a public-private partnership, led by Principal Investigator, Michael W. Weiner, MD. The study used diverse datasets obtained from different scanners with different resolutions and different field strengths to train a neural network model approximating N4ITK. ADNI contributed T1w images that were part of the total 10,424 T1w images randomly split into 90/5/5% as training, validation, and testing cohorts respectively. Images were down-sampled to 2 × 2 × 2 mm, padded to 128 × 128 × 128 dimensions, and normalized with min-max normalization.

The NACC cohort began in 1999 and is comprised of dozens of Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers that collect multimodal AD data. The overall intention of the NACC cohort is to collate a large database of standardized clinical/neuropathological data. NACC data are funded by NIA/NIH Grant U24 AG072122 and contributed by multiple NIA-funded ADRCs. The study used de-identified data from NACC as one of eight distinct datasets for training a neural network model with diverse datasets obtained from different scanners with different resolutions and different field strengths.

The BIOCARD Study consists of 7 Cores and 2 projects studying diffusion MRI (dMRI) data from multiple sites. The research objective is to 'deepen understanding of the differences between datasets at the level of connectivity matrices and to evaluate the effectiveness of current tools in harmonizing these differences.' The study examines acquisition-related differences such as variations in scanners, scanning protocols, and reconstruction algorithms that create inconsistencies among dMRI data from various sites. Connectivity matrices weighted by mean streamline length were analyzed from age-matched, sex-matched, and normal cohorts to demonstrate substantial differences between sites.

Published snRNA-seq dataset profiled from flash-frozen cortical tissue acquired during surgical treatment of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus. Data from 983 participants in the Bio-Hermes-001 multi-site study (age mean±SD=72±6.7; 56% female; years of education mean±SD=15±2.7; primary language English), a priori classified as cognitively unimpaired (CU; n=417), mild cognitively impaired (n=309), or probable Alzheimer's dementia (n=257) based on expert consensus clinical diagnosis and neuropsychological evaluation were analyzed. A random forest model was trained on DCTclock and word recall data to classify cognitive impairment using a binary (CI and CU) and 3-tier (CI, Indeterminate, and CU) prediction thresholding schemes. The 3-tier model predictions performed well (AUC=0.887; accuracy=0.834; NPV=0.801; PPV=0.859) when measured on Biohermes' cohort diagnosis.

The first clinically indicated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan from each participant in the Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) Study—a prospective cohort study within Kaiser Permanente Washington (KPWA)—collected between January 2003 and March 2020 from participants ≥65 years old and with ≥10 years of continuous KPWA enrollment prior to the scan. Of the 1,043 individuals included in analyses, 28% had no use, 33% had 1‐90 TSDD, 15% had 91‐365 TSDD, 7% had 366‐1095 TSDD, and 17% had ≥1096 TSDD. The mean age at the time of the scan was 81 years among a group that was majority female (58%) and White (88%). Neuroimaging outcomes were common data elements (CDEs) for WMH on MRI scans (Fazekas, Scheltens, Age‐Related White Matter Changes [ARWMC]). Authors used separate linear regression models for each outcome to estimate adjusted mean values of CDEs in each exposure group and test for differences in mean values.

Participants were recruited from memory clinics or research cohorts at LEADS sites in the United States. The study combined PPA subtypes (semantic variant [svPPA], non-fluent/agrammatical variant [nfvPPA], and logopenic variant [lvPPA]), and unclassified PPA into a single PPA group. The PPA group consisted of three clinical subtypes: semantic variant (svPPA, n = 19), non-fluent/agrammatical variant (nfvPPA, n = 3), and logopenic variant (lvPPA, n = 14). Two participants did not meet criteria for any clinical subtype and were diagnosed with unclassified PPA (n = 2). Diagnostic groups did not differ with respect to years after onset, suggesting comparable disease progression stages at baseline visit.

dataset_context_from_paper: CSF and MRI data were collected from 213 BIOCARD Study participants (M baseline age = 57.2y, mean MRI follow‐up=13.9y), including 41 who have since progressed to MCI/dementia. Atrophy on volumetric MRI scans was quantified with MUSE and assessed as three composites including: (1) AD vulnerable regions (SPARE‐AD), (2) medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions, and (3) regions indexing advanced non‐AD related brain aging (SPARE‐BA). Participants included 15 bvFTD (mean age = 64.3, SD = 9.1 years) and 19 HC (mean = 55.8, SD = 14.2) from the ALLFTD Consortium. Features were selected for classification analysis if they differed between groups based on a MANCOVA adjusted for age, sex/gender, and education. Three features were selected: average seconds of non-speech (silence), ratio of number of complex nominal clauses to total clauses, and number of restarts (disfluency). The logistic model showed ROC-AUC score of 84.8% accuracy for distinguishing between bvFTD and healthy controls.

Hundreds of geographic covariates including land use, roadway proximity, and population density used to develop universal kriging–partial least squares (UK-PLS) models to predict PNC from geographic features. Authors collected and uniformly processed all publicly available metadata on 27 other studies (36 datasets total across 28 studies including their biopsy cohort). The authors developed an optimized single-cell integration framework to combine these datasets with their biopsy cohort, handling substantial technical variation (sample preparation, sequencing platforms and depth) and biological variation (human vs mouse). A random walk method transferred cell type annotations from the biopsy cohort to each of 27 other studies, uniformly annotating 2,406,980 cells with 82 cell type labels.

This study builds on prior WRAP findings on [11C]PiB PET amyloid biomarkers and validated them in the BIOCARD cohort using CSF amyloid and pTau biomarkers. CSF samples were collected via lumbar puncture after an overnight fast at the NIH (1995–2005) and JHU (since 2015). Samples were aliquoted into polypropylene cryotubes kept on dry ice and transferred to −80°C freezer for long-term storage. Samples were analyzed to measure Aβ40, Aβ42, t-tau, and pTau181 levels using fully automated electrochemiluminescence assays on the Lumipulse G1200 platform. Binary outcomes included amyloid (Aβ42/Aβ40; A+/−) and pTau181 (T+/−) status.

This study builds on prior WRAP findings on [11C]PiB PET amyloid biomarkers. WRAP data combined stories A and B (range = 0-9) for delayed recall assessment. Findings from WRAP using combined story recall measures were consistent with BIOCARD findings using Story A alone (range = 0-4), confirming that baseline delayed proper name recall predicted biomarker positivity.

Python codes have been deposited to Github (https://github.com/Wyss/chip-extract). The codes support the digital SAA (seed amplification assay) for quantifying TDP-43 aggregates in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples, including programmed image analysis for processing microwell data.

40 CSF samples from the ALLFTD cohort were tested, representing three groups of different FTLD-TDP subtypes: GRN mutation carriers, C9ORF72 repeat expansion carriers, patients without mutations but with a clinical diagnosis of svPPA, and a control group (CN). Patient characteristics are summarized in Table 1. In total, 30 out of 40 samples were successfully detected above the assay's LOD. Each calibrator and sample was tested in triplicate chips. Mean seed concentrations of triplicate chips per sample were grouped by FTLD-TDP subtype.

The study involves ICICLE-Gait and ICICLE-PD cohorts with Parkinson's disease patients, including measurements such as Movement Disorders Society Unified Parkinson's disease rating scale (MDS-UPDRS), Mini mental state examination (MMSE), and body mass index (BMI).

The study included 192 participants without dementia (14 with mild cognitive impairment [MCI]) from the BIOCARD cohort (mean age = 68), of which 52 (27%) were Aβ positive. Multiple linear regression analyses tested whether Aβ status moderated associations between hippocampal mean diffusivity (MD), Braak-staged tau accumulation on PET, and an episodic memory composite score. Participants underwent diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) to assess hippocampal microstructure, tau PET imaging, amyloid-beta PET imaging, and episodic memory testing. The study assessed relationships between hippocampal microstructure, tau pathology, and episodic memory performance, focusing on the moderating role of Aβ status.

From the EMIF-AD PreclinAD study we selected individuals with normal cognition and longitudinal plasma, PET and cognitive data available (n baseline=200). Amyloid-status was determined using visual assessment of dynamic [18F]flutemetamol-PET scans. Plasma levels of amyloid-β1-40, amyloid-β1-42, neurofilament light (NfL), and GFAP were measured using the neurology 4-plex E Simoa assay (Quanterix). Linear mixed models were applied to examine longitudinal changes in plasma biomarker levels, and their association with longitudinal changes in amyloid-status and cognition. Baseline and up to 6-year follow-up plasma, positron emission tomography (PET) and cognitive data from cognitively unimpaired individuals were utilized.

The datasets analyzed during the current study are available on AMP-AD knowledge portal with synapse accession ID included in the main text. All the clinical and pathological data for the ROSMAP cohort were obtained from the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center Research Resource Sharing Hub. The framework utilized datasets from three different brain regions (DLPFC, PCC, and HCN) of the ROSMAP cohort to train three deep neural network classification models separately for distinguishing AD, OTHER, and CN subjects. RNA-seq data from ROSMAP was used as the reference dataset for batch correction and training of the deep learning models.

The harmonized, uniformly processed RNA-seq data sets from MAYO were first sorted by the same gene order as the input data set of ROSMAP. Batch effects were then removed by the ComBat function using empirical Bayes methods. The MAYO cohort was used as an independent external validation cohort for the models trained on ROSMAP data.

The harmonized, uniformly processed RNA-seq data sets from MSBB were first sorted by the same gene order as the input data set of ROSMAP. Batch effects were then removed by the ComBat function using empirical Bayes methods. The MSBB cohort was used as an independent external validation cohort for the models trained on ROSMAP data.

Publicly available datasets were analyzed in this study from ADNI. The study used biomarker-confirmed sporadic Alzheimer's disease (sAD) subjects with genomic and clinical data. Authors applied unsupervised clustering algorithms to genotype data using curated SNP panels (9-25 SNPs) to investigate genetic-only subgroups in AD. The analysis prioritized diagnostic quality with gold-standard neuropathological diagnosis uniformly guaranteed across subjects. Key SNPs analyzed included rs2421847, rs7245858, rs11154851, and rs4296166. The study maintained rigorous sAD standards with biomarker confirmation per updated guidelines and focused on multimodal integration combining genetic data with phenotypic/clinical data.

Whole genome sequencing (WGS) data from the ADSP cohort. Comprehensive QC procedures were applied including initial filtering with VFLAG = 0 annotation, depth (DP) < 8 and genotype quality (GQ) < 10 exclusion. Key genetic variants including APOE (rs7412, rs429358) and ABCA7 44-bp deletion (rs142076058) were extracted from WGS. Correlation analysis was conducted on NPH (n = 106) dataset to examine relationships among RNA quality metrics including RNA Integrity Number (RIN), Post-Mortem Interval (PMI), proportion of top 10 gene counts (PTT), DV200, and 5' and 3' bias measurements. Spearman's correlation analysis was performed using the corr.test function from the psych library in R, with p-values adjusted for false discovery rate (FDR) at a threshold of 0.05.

Correlation analysis was conducted on NYBB (n = 513) dataset to examine relationships among RNA quality metrics. Spearman's correlation analysis was performed on NYBB samples for RIN and PMI relationships. Genes with fewer than 5 counts in at least 90% of samples were filtered out, then normalized using variance stabilizing transformation (VST) with DESeq2. RIN and PMI for each sample were correlated with normalized gene counts across all samples. RIN does not correlate with Braak stage in the NYBB dataset (r = −0.052, p = 0.318).

Correlation analysis was conducted on ROSMAP (n = 534, 365) datasets with both poly-A and ribosomal RNA depletion library preparation protocols. Spearman's correlation analysis examined relationships among RNA quality metrics including RIN, PMI, PTT, DV200, and 5' and 3' bias. RIN mildly correlates with Braak stage in the ROSMAP poly-A dataset (r = −0.11, p = 0.01), but RIN does not correlate with Braak stage in the ROSMAP ribosomal RNA depletion dataset (r = −0.091, p = 0.15). Analysis identified 2,512 genes that positively correlate with RIN and 1,421 genes that negatively correlate with RIN across datasets.

The ASPERA study analysed 1649 patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) who had neuroimaging-confirmed ischemic stroke despite ongoing therapeutic oral anticoagulation (OAC) between 2020 and 2025. Causal factors for breakthrough ischemic stroke included drug-to-drug interactions potentially affecting OAC efficacy (26.4%), competing aetiologies (24.3%), and active cancer (4.4%). 724 patients (43.9%) had at least one of those factors. The findings suggest that improved recognition and management of these factors may help reduce the risk of breakthrough stroke in patients with AF receiving OAC.

A previously established and publicly available AD Common Data Model (CDM) that defines 1300 core variables commonly collected in AD studies, including demographics, clinical assessments, biomarkers, and imaging data. The AD-Mapper CDM comprises the variable naming conventions of 23 distinct cohort studies that were harmonized against one another. The CDM includes reference terms to which all variables were mapped, along with definitions for each reference term extracted from well-established ontologies, such as SNOMED-CT or LOINC. This CDM was used as ground-truth for benchmarking language models' ability to automatically match cohort variable descriptions based on semantic similarity.

Metadata consisting of variable names and variable descriptions collected from seven different cohort datasets in the context of Alzheimer's disease. These data dictionaries were used to assess the feasibility of harmonizing variables across cohorts and to evaluate five language models' ability to automatically match cohort variable descriptions to ground-truth descriptions in the manually curated CDM based on semantic similarity.

Participants were from the Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) cohort study. We included 611 ACT participants who wore accelerometers and had 3+ measures of cognition in the 10 years prior to accelerometer wear. The Cognitive Assessment Screening Instrument (CASI) measured cognition and was scored using item-response theory (IRT). activPAL and ActiGraph accelerometers worn over 7 days measured ST and PA outcomes. Self-reported time in bed and sleep quality measured sleep outcomes.

The objective of this report is to provide a detailed illustration of three additional statistical models that have been implemented on the DIAN-TU platform. These models are employed to better handle the complexity of the data generated from both the double-blind and the open-label extension periods of the DIAN-TU trials.

161 participants from the BIOCARD study, who were cognitively unimpaired at baseline, with the first biofluid collection at mean age of 59.3 years (SD = 6.2), median of 3 samples (range 2–5) over 19.5 years on average. Linear mixed-effects models related baseline systemic inflammatory levels, within-person change in each systemic inflammatory marker, and interactions between baseline systemic inflammation and Aβ, ptau181, or GFAP to change in a general cognitive factor score, adjusting for age, sex, education, and vascular risk.

Proteomic profiling dataset from human substantia nigra (SN) tissue samples across different age groups (young, middle-aged, and elderly individuals). Group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) identified latent subgroups for CSF p-tau181, CSF Aβ1-42, PiB PET, and FDG PET. Baseline [18F]Flortaucipir‐PET scans from 365 amyloid‐PET‐positive participants with sporadic EOAD were quantified in 10 regions: left and right medial temporal, lateral temporal, occipital, parietal, and frontal. Tau‐PET values were z‐scored against 85 amyloid‐PET‐negative cognitively normal age‐matched controls and fitted into Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn), an unsupervised clustering algorithm that simultaneously models subtypes and progression from cross‐sectional data. Follow‐up Flortaucipir‐PET scans were also collected, with 85.6% participants clustered within the same subtype as their baseline scans; SustaIn stage increased by 0.56/year on average.

dataset_identifier: Mayo Clinic Alzheimer's Disease Research Center
dataset_context_from_paper: MRI, PET, and other data from the Mayo Clinic Alzheimer's Disease Research Center (MCADRC) are available to qualified academic and industry researchers by request to the MCADRC Executive Committee. The dataset was used in this study to analyze amyloid-beta (PiB PET) and tau (FTP PET) pathology in Alzheimer's disease dementia (aDem) patients compared to healthy controls (HC). ROI correlation analysis was performed on 48 β-amyloid and τ positive aDem patients, examining deep gray matter regions including caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus, as well as frontal and paracentral gyri regions. Statistical analysis included linear regression and Pearson's correlation coefficient with multiple comparison corrections using 5000 permutations.

Eye ACT retrospective medical record data collection protocol includes extraction of eye-related data from all ACT study participants including from paper charts dating to the 1940s, diagnosis and procedure codes since 1993, electronic pharmacy records since 1978, and laboratory data since 1988. Manual abstraction of paper medical records dating from 1950 to 2005 is performed by trained abstractors extracting up to 338 data fields per encounter, including 44 age-related macular degeneration (AMD)-related, 66 diabetic retinopathy (DR)-related, and 86 glaucoma-related fields. Eye clinical data from EHR is obtained on all participants using an in-house natural language processing (NLP) algorithm, with International Classification of Disease (ICD) and Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes of eye diseases and procedures, and eye medication history from electronic pharmacy records. Visual impairment was defined as any clinical encounter with Snellen VA worse than 20/40.

The MYHAT cohort study was used to calculate LIBRA (Lifestyle for Brain health) index using cohort-specific hazard ratio estimates. Authors calculated LIBRA using factor weights based on MYHAT-specific data to compare with reference factor weights derived from meta-analyses. The study examined associations between LIBRA indexes and incident mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and incident dementia risk. The 14-factor LIBRA2[MCI] using MYHAT-specific HR estimates for MCI risk and both the 11-factor LIBRA[Dementia] and 14-factor LIBRA2[Dementia] using MYHAT-specific HR estimates for dementia risk consistently demonstrated strong associations with incident MCI and dementia risk respectively.

1,347 abstracts screened using a validated prompt engineering system, extracting structured biomedical triples from 823 relevant studies. Semantic path analysis was performed using SapBERT embeddings, dimensionality reduction (PCA‐UMAP), and hierarchical clustering (HDBSCAN) to construct directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of causal evidence.

Retrospective cohort of 32 GBM patients using spatial transcriptomics. All patients had confirmed GBM, and complete clinical and molecular data. Molecular profiling, including IDH mutation and MGMT promoter methylation status, was performed by next‐generation sequencing. Spatial transcriptomic analyses were conducted using the GeoMx DSP® platform.

Valproate trial dataset (VALID) used as training data for generative AI model that creates digital twins. The model is 'a system of neural networks trained on data from historical clinical trials and observational studies' and uses this dataset to forecast placebo outcomes from participant baseline information for prognostic covariate adjustment (PROCOVA) in clinical trials.

Resveratrol trial dataset (RN) used as training data for the generative AI model that creates digital twins. Part of the historical clinical trials and observational studies data used to train the neural network system for forecasting participant health outcomes and enabling prognostic covariate adjustment in clinical trials.

Longitudinal Mayo Clinic Study of Aging (MCSA) from two sites (Mississippi-MS and Minnesota-MN). Participants scanned using standardized protocols with N_MN-MCSA = 204 and N_MS-MCSA = 52. Diffusion MRI (dMRI) measures including DTI and NODDI metrics were acquired and analyzed for whole-brain densities and regional measurements in the genu of the corpus callosum (GCC). The study tested whether protocol standardization could minimize machine-origin differences in dMRI biomarkers for aging and dementia across multi-center acquisitions on different scanner systems (GE and Siemens).

dataset_context_from_paper: Crossover dataset with 80 participants scanned within 2 days bridging two different protocols on GE and Siemens scanners. For analysis, GE data were resampled to 2-mm isotropic resolution and Siemens-only b-shells were discarded to artificially reduce protocol disparities. Whole-brain masks were used to obtain subjectwise histogram-derived densities for dMRI measures, and median dMRI measures were extracted from the genu of the corpus callosum (GCC) with both DTI and NODDI measures compared.

Proteome-wide association (PWAS) was performed, which integrates GWAS summary statistics and pQTL data to resolve causal protein in GWAS loci. Variant weights were calculated for each protein and for each association separately for those aptamers with at least one study-wide pQTL. Protein levels were estimated based on these weights and correlated with EOAD using NHW summary statistic on chromosomes where genome wide significant EOAD GWAS loci were identified. Finally, colocalization between EOAD and trans-pQTLs was performed to see if there was potential evidence of co-regulation of genes in EOAD loci.

It is accessible through the Accelerating Medicines Partnership program for Parkinson's disease and through the BWH Parkinson's Center Biobank. This research population was used as one of two research cohorts in the study examining Parkinson's disease progression.

Fox Insights (N = 36,660) is an online self-survey-based research study of the Michael J. Fox Foundation. This research population was used as one of two research cohorts in the study examining Parkinson's disease progression and patient-reported outcomes.

Optum Integrated Claims-electronic health records (N = 157,475) represents wide-scale linked medical and claims data used as a real-world data derived (RWD) population in the study. This dataset provided real-world evidence for Parkinson's disease progression analysis.

De-identified data from Mass General Brigham (MGB, N = 22,949) is an academic hospital system real-world cohort. The MGB EMR includes > 6.8 million total active records from 1990 to 2020 with available data including encounters, diagnoses, medications, procedures, observations, and labs. Structured, de-identified electronic health records data at MGB are supplemented using natural language processing with a large language model to extract measurements of PD progression, with manual validation for accuracy. The MGB EMR also includes a biobank with >36,000 patients genotyped with Illumina Multi-Ethnic Global Array (MEGA) microarray chip.

Clinical dataset presented in the study is available upon request and after approval of each data provider, via the EMIF-AD platform. This study examined 3 core CSF AD biomarkers: Aβ42, p-tau, and total tau. The CSF biomarker protein levels from the 20 cohorts were obtained using different platforms in each cohort. From 20 cohorts, 4630 individuals with and without AD were considered. After excluding individuals with missing data on biomarkers, sex, age, or APOE genotype, 4592 remained. The CSF biomarker levels were log10 transformed and z score normalized in each cohort. Any biomarker values outside 3 SDs from the mean were considered outliers and excluded from the analysis. Individuals were classified into ancestry groups: European ancestry (n = 4421), African ancestry (n = 119), or Asian ancestry (n = 52) based on principal component analysis combining genomic data and HapMap data.

Regions of interest (ROI) included the following bilaterally: NAc (ROIs:223, 224), Globus Pallidus (GP; [ROIs: 21, 222]), Ca (ventral [ROIs:219, 220] and dorsal [ROIs:27, 228]), and ventral medial (ROIs:225, 226) and dorsal lateral (ROIs:229, 230) PUT. ROIs were defined by the Brainnetome Atlas, in which allows the correlation of brain anatomy and psychological/cognitive functions.

Cross-sectional data from 964 participants in the Bio-Hermes study, comprising cognitively normal (CN=404), mild cognitive impairment (MCI=302), and mild AD dementia (AD=258) groups. Serum concentrations of 32 cytokines, NfL, GFAP, and AD biomarkers (Aβ40, Aβ42, Aβ42/Aβ40, total tau, p-tau181, and p-tau217) were measured. Age/sex-adjusted ANCOVA compared cytokine, NfL, and GFAP levels across cognitive groups, stratified by amyloid and APOEε4 status. Pearson correlations assessed relationships between significant cytokines and AD plasma biomarkers. Linear regressions assessed associations with clinical scores (MMSE, FAQ, RAVLT, GDS), adjusted for age, sex, education, and APOEε4.
