Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP) dataset. RNA-seq data analyzed for quality metrics including RIN, PMI, DV200, PTT, 3′ bias, 5′ bias, and 5′/3′ ratio. The metrics were calculated on datasets that underwent oligo-dT priming. 3′ bias for a sample was the average value over the 1000 highest expressed transcripts. 5′ bias was defined similarly (reads over the 500 base pairs at the 5′ end divided by total counts over the entire transcript, averaged over the 1000 highest expressed transcripts). Authors examined correlations between RIN, PMI, and other quality metrics.

The New York Brain Bank (NYBB) set of RNA-seq data. Measurements of 5′ and 3′ bias are irrelevant in this dataset given the fact that poly-A selection was not used. For postsequencing measurements, PTT was recorded. For presequencing measurements, DV200 was also recorded for these samples. RIN negatively correlated with PTT (r = −0.53, adjusted P-value = 7.35×10−39). RNA integrity number and DV200 are closely aligned (r = 0.72, adjusted P-value = 6.06×10−82), and RIN has a weak negative correlation with PMI (r = −0.11, adjusted P-value = .017).

Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) dataset. RNA-seq data analyzed for quality metrics including RIN, PMI, DV200, PTT, 3′ bias, 5′ bias, and 5′/3′ ratio on datasets that underwent oligo-dT priming. RIN negatively correlated with PTT in this dataset. Ontology categories of commonly correlating genes were examined across NPH, NYBB, and ROSMAP datasets.

Longitudinal Early-Onset Alzheimer's Disease Study (LEADS) cohort. Data from 20 participants with early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD) treated with Aducanumab (n=4), Lecanemab (n=15), or both (one transitioning from Aducanumab to Lecanemab). All participants had MCI or mild dementia at baseline with longitudinal Aβ and tau PET imaging, as well as cognitive assessments, with at least one observation before and after treatment initiation. Piecewise regression with a knot at treatment start was applied to evaluate changes in Aβ and tau PET burden and Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores. An untreated comparison group from LEADS was matched 1:3 for age, sex, APOE ε4 genotype, pretreatment Aβ and tau PET load, CDR-SB, and follow-up duration. Median treatment duration was 8 months (IQR=5-10). Treated group showed significant decreases in Aβ burden post-treatment (Δ=-52 Centiloids/yr, p<0.001) with widespread neocortical involvement, but no significant inflection in tau burden or CDR-SB trajectories.

We examined the associations between regional Aβ and tau burden measured by positron emission tomography (PET) in 192 participants without dementia (14 with mild cognitive impairment [MCI]) in the BIOCARD cohort, of whom 52 (27%) were Aβ positive. Amyloid status was assessed using standardized uptake value ratios (SUVR) obtained from the medial orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), lateral OFC, precuneus, posterior cingulate, anterior cingulate, parietal, temporal, and superior frontal regions using 11C‐PIB PET. Tau burden was quantified using 18F‐MK6240 PET across 29 brain regions, assigned to each of the Braak stages. Associations were examined with stepwise and hierarchical regressions, covarying for age, sex, education, and ApoE4 status.

The McGill cohorts are partially available through The Canadian Open Parkinson Network (C-OPN). Access, including genetic data, can be requested through the C-OPN data access committee. Targeted capture was performed using molecular inversion probes (MIPs), libraries were sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform (paired-end 100 bp), sequence reads were aligned to hg19 using BWA, with base-quality recalibration and variant calling conducted using GATK v3.8, and variants were subsequently mapped from hg19 to hg38 using CrossMap.

The AMP-PD data was assessed using the Terra platform. For external datasets, the same 36 genes were extracted from the AMP-PD genome sequencing data (hg38). The data was used for meta-analysis of rare variants associated with Parkinson's disease.

The UKBB was acquired using WGS data from the UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform under application number 45551. The same 36 genes were extracted from the UKBB genome sequencing data (hg38) for analysis of rare variants associated with Parkinson's disease.

Clinical data and biosamples were obtained from the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research (MJFF) and National Institutes of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) BioFIND study. BioFIND is sponsored by The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research (MJFF) with support from the National Institute for Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS).

Clinical data and biosamples were obtained from the National Institute on Aging (NIA) International Lewy Body Dementia Genetics Consortium Genome Sequencing in Lewy Body Dementia Case-control Cohort (LBD). Genome sequence data for the Lewy body dementia case-control cohort were generated at the Intramural Research Program of the U.S. National Institutes of Health.

Clinical data and biosamples were obtained from the Harvard Biomarkers Study (HBS). The Harvard Biomarker Study (HBS) is a collaboration of HBS investigators and funded through philanthropy and NIH and Non-NIH funding sources.
Clinical data and biosamples were obtained from the MJFF Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). Data was used for meta-analysis of rare variants associated with Parkinson's disease.

The datasets from this study are available upon reasonable request. The study involved analysis of biomarkers including amyloid beta 42/amyloid beta 40 ratios and phosphorylated tau forms in a cohort with Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal lobar degeneration. The study population consisted mainly of White and well-educated participants without major comorbidities. Clinical assessments included Clinical Dementia Rating, Montreal Cognitive Assessment, California Verbal Learning Test, and Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale measurements.

Raw sequencing data are available in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession number PRJNA1182356. This dataset includes snRNA-seq data from donor samples used in the study, with donor metadata provided in Table S1.

snRNA-seq data are also available to browse at https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/e/203025fe-fa99-4d57-81da-458ed8f0c334.cxg/. This provides an interactive web browser for exploring the single nucleus RNA sequencing data.

The eQTL data for COL4A2, LAMC1, CASS4, CER1G, and SCIMP loci was obtained from the GTex portal GTEx Analysis Release V8 (dbGaP Accession phs000424.v8.p2). This data was used for overlap analysis with variants identified in the study.
HiChIP data was obtained from HiChIPdb. This dataset was used in the study for chromatin interaction analysis.

The single nucleus data from the Knight ADRC accessed in this study are found in the National Institute on Aging Genetics of Alzheimer's Disease Data Storage Site (NIAGADS) with accession number NG00108. These single nucleus data were used for transcriptomic analysis in the study.

dataset_identifier: DIAN brain bank single nucleus data
dataset_context_from_paper: The raw single nucleus data from the DIAN brain bank accessed in this study are available under restricted access to maintain individual and family confidentiality. These samples contain rare disease-causing variants that could be used to identify the participating individuals and families. Access can be obtained by request through the online resource request system on the DIAN Website.
The ROSMAP single nucleus RNA sequencing data used in this study are available at Synapse under Synapse ID syn21125841. These data were used for single nucleus transcriptomic analysis.

The pySCENIC default reference data was downloaded from https://resources.aertslab.org/cistarget/. Database file hg38_500bp_up_100bp_down_full_tx_v10_clust.genes_vs_motifs.rankings was used for transcription factor analysis with default parameters.

The pySCENIC default reference data was downloaded from https://resources.aertslab.org/cistarget/. Database file hg38_10kbp_up_10kbp_down_full_tx_v10_clust.genes_vs_motifs.rankings was used for transcription factor analysis with extended regulatory regions.

The pySCENIC default reference data included a motif-to-transcription factor mapping table (motifs-v10nr_clust-nr.hgnc-m0.001-o0.0.tbl) downloaded from https://resources.aertslab.org/cistarget/ for transcription factor identification.
The pySCENIC default reference data included a transcription factor list (allTFs_hg38.txt) downloaded from https://resources.aertslab.org/cistarget/ for use in regulatory network analysis.

An additional TF list was downloaded from http://humantfs.ccbr.utoronto.ca/download/v_1.01/TF_names_v_1.01.txt and the two lists were merged totaling 2093 TFs for comprehensive transcription factor analysis.

A population of patients in the early AD stage was selected for the base-case analysis. In total, ADNI included 1735 patient profiles, of which 260 were selected as inputs for AD ACE. This subgroup of patients was matched based on the inclusion criteria of the CLARITY AD trial as follows: an age of 50–85 years, an MMSE score greater than or equal to 22, and an amyloid PET standardized uptake value ratio (SUVr) of 1.1. To simulate the effects of DMTs and interventions on disease progression in early AD, AD ACE estimates disease progression using interconnected predictive equations based on longitudinal clinical and biomarker data derived from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). The biomarkers extracted from the longitudinal ADNI dataset include CSF protein levels (Aβ1-42 and total tau), fluorodeoxyglucose-PET (assessing brain cell metabolic activity), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (assessing hippocampal volume).

data_repository: Assessment of Health Economics in Alzheimer's Disease II
dataset_context_from_paper: Because the ADNI dataset does not effectively capture the more severe stages of AD, to simulate AD progression in more severe stages of AD, AD ACE relies on equations based on cognitive and behavioral scales derived from the Assessment of Health Economics in Alzheimer's Disease II (AHEAD) study. This adjustment enhances the accuracy of the model and makes it more representative across the entire AD continuum and its varying levels of disease severity.

231 adults with FTD (24.35% sporadic FTD syndromes; 19.19% MAPT; 19.56% GRN; 22.14% C9orf72 pathogenic carriers) and 40 normal controls from the ALLFTD Consortium completed longitudinal neuropsychological testing and a blood draw with plasma analyzed on SomaScan V4.0 (baseline only: GDF15, CRP, and IL6) and Simoa (longitudinal: NfL). Linear mixed effects models separately examined longitudinal cognition (global, executive functioning, memory, and language z-scores) and plasma NfL levels as a function of baseline plasma GDF15, time, and their interaction, controlling for baseline age, sex, and education.

dataset_identifier: Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center - MAP and MARS cohorts
dataset_context_from_paper: Secondary data analysis using merged Memory and Aging Project (MAP) and Memory and Aging Research Study (MARS) cohorts. Recruitment targeted adults at least 65 years old, free of known dementia at enrollment, with annual clinical evaluation and blood draw. MARS participants required to identify as Black/African American. Combined dataset of 3,118 participants with 97% at least 65 at analytic baseline. Data collection began in 1997 for MAP and 2004 for MARS. Participants' DNA were extracted and sequenced for Apolipoprotein E alleles by Polymorphic DNA technologies. Data are not publicly available due to ethical concerns about de-identification but can be requested through review process for specific variables.

Preregistration, R scripts, complete model output, and supplementary materials deposited on Open Science Framework. Supplementary Table 1 reports preregistration deviations. All analyses were performed using R software, version 4.4.1.

The authors acknowledge access to data from Global Alzheimer's Platform (GAP) and the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative (ADDI) for this project. The dataset includes whole-blood samples processed for plasma separation and stored at -80°C within 4 hours of blood draw. Plasma cytokine levels were quantified using the 65-Plex Luminex xMAP immunoassay (Merck Millipore). Twenty-eight of 65 analytes were excluded due to low detectability (>75% missingness), leaving 37 markers for analysis. The dataset includes demographics, clinical, and biological information from participants with Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and controls, with measurements including Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores and biomarkers such as neurofilament light (NfL) and phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217).

The Bio-Hermes Data Challenge dataset was conceived by the Brain Health Alliance for Research Challenges (ARC) team. The dataset includes biological and clinical data from volunteers who participated in the challenge, with data collection and curation performed by the involved teams. This dataset was used as the basis for the research challenge and analysis project.

For MYHAT-NI and HCP cohorts diagnostic potential was examined using receiver operating characteristic curves and area under the curve (AUC-ROC). The reported AUC is the average of the test set AUCs across folds. Three data points, one from the ADAD study and two from the HCP cohort, that fell outside the calibration curve range were excluded from the final analysis.

For MYHAT-NI and HCP cohorts diagnostic potential was examined using receiver operating characteristic curves and area under the curve (AUC-ROC). The reported AUC is the average of the test set AUCs across folds. Three data points, one from the ADAD study and two from the HCP cohort, that fell outside the calibration curve range were excluded from the final analysis.

Python (version 3.12) was used to measure AUC-ROC for ADAD study. Three data points, one from the ADAD study and two from the HCP cohort, that fell outside the calibration curve range were excluded from the final analysis.

Covariates were ascertained from ACT study visits (age, sex, self-reported race and ethnicity, education level, BMI, self-rated health, smoking status, self-reported exercise). The ACT study provided longitudinal data on participants including demographic information and health-related variables collected at multiple study visits.

Covariates were ascertained from KPWA electronic health records and health plan administrative data (eg, ICD codes, Charlson Comorbidity Index). The dataset included comorbidities defined as coronary heart disease (CHD), anxiety, Parkinson disease, insomnia, depression, and stroke.

NACC data are contributed by the NIA-funded ADRCs. The NACC database is funded by NIA/NIH Grant U24 AG072122. APOE haplotypes were determined from single nucleotide variants rs7412 and rs429358 for NACC. The study used NACC as part of a large, harmonized multicohort dataset to explore APOE-ε4 and -ε2 allele frequency in SuperAgers compared to AD dementia cases and controls, using harmonized clinical diagnoses and cognitive domain scores.

ADNI data are disseminated by the Laboratory for Neuro Imaging at the University of Southern California. APOE haplotypes were determined from pyrosequencing of APOE codons 112 and 158 for ADNI. The study included ADNI as part of the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project Phenotype Harmonization Consortium (ADSP-PHC) multicohort dataset for comparing APOE allele frequencies across SuperAgers, AD dementia cases, and controls.

Data contributed from MAP/ROS/MARS was supported by NIA R01 AG017917, P30 AG10161, P30 AG072975, R01 AG022018, R01 AG056405, UH2 NS100599, UH3 NS100599, R01 AG064233, R01 AG15819 and R01 AG067482. Data can be accessed at www.radc.rush.edu. APOE haplotypes were determined from pyrosequencing of APOE codons 112 and 158 for ROS/MAP/MARS. The dataset was included in the ADSP-PHC harmonized multicohort analysis of APOE allele frequency in SuperAgers.

APOE haplotypes were determined from single nucleotide variants rs7412 and rs429358 for WRAP. The Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention data were supported by R01 AG027161 and included in the ADSP-PHC multicohort dataset for analyzing APOE-ε4 and -ε2 allele frequency in SuperAgers compared to AD dementia cases and controls.

APOE haplotypes were determined from single nucleotide variants rs7412 and rs429358 for BIOCARD. The dataset was part of the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project Phenotype Harmonization Consortium (ADSP-PHC) harmonized multicohort dataset used to explore APOE allele frequency in SuperAgers, AD dementia cases, and controls with harmonized clinical diagnoses and cognitive domain scores.

APOE haplotypes were determined from single nucleotide variants rs7412 and rs429358 for ACT. The Adult Changes in Thought study data were included in the ADSP-PHC multicohort analysis comparing APOE-ε4 and -ε2 allele frequency across SuperAgers, AD dementia cases, and controls by age bin.

APOE haplotypes were determined from single nucleotide variants rs7412 and rs429358 for Knight ADRC. The Knight Alzheimer's Disease Research Center data were included in the ADSP-PHC harmonized multicohort dataset for analyzing APOE allele frequency in SuperAgers compared to AD dementia cases and controls.

APOE haplotypes were determined from single nucleotide variants rs7412 and rs429358 for NIA-AD FBS. The NIA Alzheimer's Disease Family Based Study data were part of the ADSP-PHC multicohort dataset used to explore APOE-ε4 and -ε2 allele frequency in SuperAgers, AD dementia cases, and controls.

The challenge data has been deposited at Synapse and is publicly available. This dataset contains single-cell transcriptomic profiles from human cortical tissue used in a DREAM challenge for predicting disease-related transcriptomic features. The dataset includes donor metadata variables (age, post-mortem interval, sex, years of education) and cell-type annotations. Training and test sets contained overlapping donors. Participants developed machine learning models to predict donor-level outcomes from cell-type-stratified expression features, with some models leveraging donor metadata correlations rather than purely transcriptomic disease signals.

All original code has been deposited at Synapse and is publicly available. This includes code from challenge submissions (Team BioICAR, Team CMC-TJU, Team gisl7) implementing two-stage modeling frameworks, PCA-based feature compression, cell-type stratification, and donor-level prediction models. Code repositories document the methods used for interpreting feature contributions through model weights and PCA back-projection to gene space.

Challenge data publicly available through AWS S3 bucket. Contains single-cell expression profiles used in the SEA-AD DREAM challenge, including transcriptomic measurements across multiple cell supertypes and broad cellular classes (GABAergic neurons, glutamatergic neurons, non-neuronal cells) from human cortical tissue.

The data used for these analyses are all publicly available at http://ghdx.healthdata.org/gbd-results-tool. The GBD estimates have limitations, as detailed in the 'strengths and limitations' section. Given the importance of evidence-based health policies, a core concept of the GBD Study is that 'some data is better than no data'. The quality and accuracy of data collection depend on the disease type and local data collection policies, both of which might affect the analysis.

The datasets supporting the conclusions of this article are available in the publicly available ADNI database. The datasets used and/or analyzed during the current study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. PCA analysis was performed on NTB (Neuropsychological Test Battery) assessments from MCI (mild cognitive impairment) patients. The study examined 13 cognitive assessments including memory-related measures (Logical Memory Immediate Recall) and non-memory measures to distinguish cognitive profiles within the prodromal AD spectrum. Factor loadings for principal components were validated across 100 bootstrap iterations.

RNAseq datasets were referenced to establish that SMOC1 expression is highest in oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs). The authors state: 'Co-localization of SMOC1 and PDGFRα was frequently observed indicating that SMOC1 expression is highest in OPCs, as expected from RNAseq datasets [23, 40, 47, 61, 83–85, 105].' These datasets provided the baseline gene expression evidence supporting their immunofluorescence findings in temporal cortex sections.

dataset_identifier: Banner Sun Health Research Institute Brain and Body Donation Program
dataset_context_from_paper: Biospecimens from the Banner Sun Health Research Institute Brain and Body Donation Program, including those presented in this report, are available to qualified researchers upon request. The study collected autopsy samples from COVID-19 subjects including multiple tissue types: femoral nerve, quadriceps muscle, carotid artery, trachea, aortic arch, cardiac apex, interventricular septum, left and right ventricular walls, and lung samples from upper and lower lobes. Enhanced PPE and safety procedures were used for all autopsies regardless of COVID-19 status.

All data included in these analyses are available at the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center Resource Sharing Hub. The study analyzed data from MAP participants, examining associations between lifetime cognitive enrichment and risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease pathology. The postmortem subset included N = 948 participants with brain donation data. The analysis examined multiple pathologic indices across different life periods (early-, mid-, and late-life enrichment) and their associations with hazard of developing MCI. Qualified investigators may create an account and submit requests for deidentified data through radc.rush.edu/.

Participant data from open access cohort ADNI used in multi-cohort dataset. Automated quality control procedures were performed on imaging data to identify and exclude scans with evident technical flaws or misalignments. ADNI data are disseminated by the Laboratory for Neuro Imaging at the University of Southern California. The study is coordinated by the Alzheimer's Therapeutic Research Institute at the University of Southern California.

Participant data from open access cohort A4 used in multi-cohort dataset. The A4 Study was a secondary prevention trial in preclinical Alzheimer's disease, aiming to slow cognitive decline associated with brain amyloid accumulation in clinically normal older individuals. Automated quality control procedures were performed on imaging data.

Participant data from open access cohort OASIS used in multi-cohort dataset. Automated quality control procedures were performed on imaging data to identify and exclude scans with evident technical flaws or misalignments. Detailed demographics are presented by cohort.

Participant data from open access cohort PREVENT-AD used in multi-cohort dataset. Automated quality control procedures were performed on imaging data to identify and exclude scans with evident technical flaws or misalignments.

dataset_identifier: BF1, BF2, Avid studies, BACS, UCSF
dataset_context_from_paper: Pseudonymized data from cohorts BF1, BF2, Avid studies, BACS, and UCSF can be shared with qualified academic researchers upon request to respective principal investigator for the purpose of replicating procedures and results presented in the study. Data transfer must be in agreement with data protection regulation and local ethics review board decisions.
The structural and functional connectomes used in this study are openly available and can be accessed via GitHub. These connectome datasets were utilized as core brain mapping data for the analyses.

The neuromaps software toolbox, utilized for brain mapping analyses, is available at https://github.com/netneurolab/neuromaps, with documentation provided on GitHub Pages. The neuromaps toolbox was used to obtain regional maps for all factors except the AD-related factors.
Cortical layer thickness data are publicly available through BigBrainWarp. This resource provided cortical layer thickness measurements used in the study.

Gene expression data used in this study were obtained from the Allen Human Brain Atlas and are openly accessible. To extract AD-related gene clusters, 79 genes from three recent large GWAS studies were identified and available in the AHBA dataset. Regional expression maps of the available 79 genes were processed using the abagen toolbox.

The BioFINDER data are not publicly available, but access requests of anonymized data can be made to the study's steering group bf_executive@med.lu.se. Access to the data will be granted in compliance with European Union legislation on the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and decisions by the Ethical Review Board of Sweden and Region Skåne. Data transfer will be regulated under a material transfer agreement.

Mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD056614. Raw mass spectrometry data were processed into peak list files using Proteome Discoverer (ThermoScientific; v2.5). The raw data file was searched using the Sequest search algorithm against the Uniprot Human Taxonomy database (51,829 entries) and a bespoke database containing 6 tau isoforms of the human CNS. Database searching was performed at a stringency of 1% FDR including a decoy search. Posttranslational modifications for carbamidomethylation (C, static), oxidation (M, variable) and phosphorylation (S, T & Y; variable) were included in the database search.

Raw FASTQ files have been deposited at the National Center for Biotechnology Information (nih.gov) Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database with Bioproject ID: PRJNA1171874. Azenta provided a basic analysis package which included QC report, FASTQ files, data QC, trimming, mapping, differential gene expression, alternative splicing and gene ontology analysis. RNA integrity was further validated by Genewiz (Azenta) using Bioanalyzer/TapeStation QC before sequencing. No RNA degradation was observed in any samples.

Summary data for main and supplementary figures is available on FigShare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28955612). All data generated or analyzed during this study are included in this published article and its supplementary files 1 and 2.

Data abstracted from medical charts from KPWA (formerly GHC) healthcare system providing comprehensive, longitudinal care. Chart abstractors utilize a 200+ page manual of operations to systematically review paper and electronic medical records and abstract specific information. Data are abstracted for one time point only (e.g., first adult height, initial diagnoses of chronic conditions such as CHF, COPD, diabetes, AFib), yearly (e.g., weight, angina, edema, hearing difficulties, hypertension, memory complaints, stroke), or three times per year (e.g., blood pressure, insulin usage, laboratory results including cholesterol and glucose). The dataset includes personal health identifiers (PHI) such as dates of birth and death, dates of diagnoses, and ages. Data complement other sources including computerized pharmacy and laboratory data, and research data collected at in-person ACT study visits. Medical records abstraction transforms decades' worth of medical record information into standardized variables for aging research with careful attention to quality.

718 participants (cognitively unimpaired (CU) or Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI)) from the Swedish BioFINDER-1 cohort who were followed up to 8 years. Plasma samples were analyzed for p-tau217 (Lilly immunoassay), NfL, GFAP, p-tau181 (Roche Prototype immunoassay), N-terminal tau (NTA-tau; Simoa immunoassay) and Aβ42/Aβ40 (mass spectrometry). Changes in individual plasma biomarker levels were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, incorporating Aβ status*time interaction. Associations between biomarker slopes and cognitive decline (assessed with mini-mental state examination [MMSE] and modified Preclinical Alzheimer's Cognitive Composite [mPACC]) were assessed.

CODES was a clinical trial developed over a succession of studies in a condition that remains only partially understood. The trial compared cognitive behavioural therapy versus standardised medical care for adults with Dissociative non-Epileptic Seizures. Key data from the CODES trial included measurements using Clinical Global Impression of Change (CGI), Clinical Outcomes in Routine Evaluation 10 (CORE-10), European Quality of Life 5 Dimensions 5 Levels (EQ-5D-5L), 7-item Generalised Anxiety Disorder Assessment (GAD-7), Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ), quality adjusted life years (QALY), 12-item Short Form Survey version 2 Mental Component Summary score (SF-12v2 MCS), 12-item Short Form Survey version 2 Physical Component Summary score (SF-12v2 PCS), and Work and Social Adjustment Scale (WSAS).

dataset_identifier: Not publicly available - contact corresponding author
data_repository: Available on request from corresponding author
dataset_context_from_paper: The data supporting the findings of this study are available on request from the corresponding author. The data is not publicly available due to privacy or ethical restrictions. The study developed a predictive model using FDG-PET imaging to identify brain regions associated with TDP-43 pathology in Alzheimer's disease patients. The predictive model achieved 68% prediction accuracy (95% bootstrap CI, 54–82%) and an AUC of 0.70 (95% bootstrap CI, 0.52–0.87) for distinguishing TDP-43-positive from TDP-43-negative cases based on FDG-PET-derived metabolic patterns adjusted for age.

De-identified human tissue samples collected under approved protocols by the University of Washington (UW) BioRepository and Integrated Neuropathology laboratory (BraIN). Tissue samples were used for histological analysis and microRNA expression studies in hippocampal regions (CA1, DG, subiculum) and entorhinal cortex from control, MCI, and AD subjects.

De-identified human tissue samples collected under approved protocols by the Arizona Study of Aging and Neurodegenerative Disorders and Brain and Body Donation Program (BBDP). Tissue samples were used for histological analysis and microRNA expression studies in hippocampal regions (CA1, DG, subiculum) and entorhinal cortex from control, MCI, and AD subjects.

data_repository: Arizona Study of Aging and Neurodegenerative Disorders / Banner Brain and Body Donation Program
dataset_context_from_paper: The dataset included 88 PD and 204 Control subjects, 225 subjects neuropathologically diagnosed with AD, 47 with vascular dementia, 31 with dementia with Lewy bodies, 18 with incidental Lewy body disease, 31 with progressive supranuclear palsy, 7 with multiple system atrophy, and 11 with FTLD-TDP. Cerebrovascular-related neuropathological variables included total cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) score, cerebral white matter rarefaction (WMR) score, circle of Willis atherosclerosis score, and presence or absence of brain infarcts. Pathological TDP-43 deposits were immunohistochemically detected and semi-quantitatively assessed in amygdala, hippocampal CA1, entorhinal/transentorhinal area, middle temporal gyrus and middle frontal gyrus. All subjects had at least one, and in most cases annual, standardized research-dedicated clinical evaluations using standardized assessment batteries including MMSE, NACC Uniform Data Set (UDS) and UPDRS. Case IDs and Donor IDs are known only to researchers of AZSAND/BBDP and are not accessible to hospital or healthcare staff.
dataset_keywords: ['neuropathological assessment', 'neurodegenerative disease', 'clinical cognitive and motor scores']

dataset_context_from_paper: Epigenetic data generated from BSHRI-BBDP samples analyzed in the current study. The datasets are available in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) repository under GEO accession number GSE109627 for the epigenetic data.

Gene expression data generated from BSHRI-BBDP samples analyzed in the current study. Available in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) repository under GEO accession number GSE109887 for the expression data. Microarray data were analyzed for 56 TRP pathway-associated genes and 52 NAD pathway-associated genes, with 12 TRP genes showing significant differential mRNA expression in Alzheimer's disease patients versus controls after FDR correction.

Sequencing and SIMOA expression data for the subjects within this study, as well as qPCR data for antibody versus isotype control experiments, have been deposited in Dryad. Python code developed for LASSO feature selection and MATLAB code for ensemble learning can be found in Dryad. Individual identifiers and demographic information have been removed to protect patient privacy.

RNA sequencing data was demultiplexed using Illumina BCL Convert before alignment, counting, and counts-per-million (CPM) normalization using the Qiagen RNA-seq Analysis Portal.

GO and KEGG pathway analyses were performed on differentially expressed miRNAs using DIANA miRPath v4.0 using the TarBase v8.0 database (accessed September 2024). FDR P values for identified GO terms and KEGG pathways were calculated using a one-sided Fisher's exact test and considered significant at P value < 0.05.

dataset_identifier: Alzheimer's Prevention Initiative ADAD Colombia Trial
dataset_context_from_paper: A placebo-controlled clinical trial of crenezumab in 252 cognitively unimpaired Presenilin 1 (PSEN1) E280A kindred members. The study evaluates regional tau accumulation patterns in ADAD compared to sporadic AD and estimates the association between changes in regional tau and amyloid PET. Linear mixed effect models were used to evaluate longitudinal outcomes with fixed effects for mutation status, time, and interaction terms, revealing distinct tau accumulation patterns in carriers compared to non-carriers with regional variations in baseline amyloid-related dynamics.

The CPAD consortium integrates clinical trial and observational data to develop tools to accelerate drug development for ADAD. The consortium aims to create a comprehensive drug-disease-trial model for ADAD using data from multiple sources to address critical questions on tau and amyloid pathologies, biomarker-cognition relationships, and disease progression.

The Monongahela Youghiogheny Healthy Aging Team–Neuroimaging (MYHAT-NI) cohort comprised 113 participants with Aβ-PET positivity of 24.8%. The study assessed the Janssen plasma p-tau217+ assay in this community-based cohort, employing [11C] Pittsburgh Compound B (PiB) positron emission tomography (PET) imaging for brain Aβ load. The Janssen p-tau217+ assay exhibited high performance with AUC of 91% for identifying Aβ PET positivity, with specificity of 57% and sensitivity of 75%. p-tau217+ was strongly correlated with Aβ-PET SUVR (r = -0.1292; p = 0.2443), with strongest correlation in this cohort which had the highest proportion of Aβ-PET-positive participants.

The Human Connectome Project (HCP) comprised 234 participants with Aβ-PET positivity of 15.0%. The study assessed the Janssen plasma p-tau217+ assay in this community-based cohort, employing [11C] Pittsburgh Compound B (PiB) positron emission tomography (PET) imaging for brain Aβ load. The Janssen p-tau217+ assay exhibited high performance with AUC of 93% for identifying Aβ PET positivity, with specificity of 81% and sensitivity of 70%. p-tau217+ was strongly correlated with Aβ-PET SUVR (r = -0.1617; p = 0.0347).

The Heart Strategies Concentrating on Risk Evaluation study (Heart SCORE) comprised 154 participants with Aβ-PET positivity of 18.2%, all recruited from southwestern Pennsylvania, USA. The study assessed the Janssen plasma p-tau217+ assay in this community-based cohort, employing [11C] Pittsburgh Compound B (PiB) positron emission tomography (PET) imaging for brain Aβ load. Multi-centre amyloid PET imaging dataset created through collaboration across six centres (University of Geneva, BioFINDER, AMPLE, AMYPAD PNHS, MCSA, GEHC). The dataset includes amyloid PET scans acquired using [11C]PiB, [18F]Flutemetamol or [18F]Florbetapir, and MRI scans from approximately 130 DLB patients, along with approximately 150 AD patients and approximately 150 controls. Additionally, 99 patients positive for the CSF α-Synuclein Seeding Amplification Assay were included. The processing workflow includes rigorous quality control, formatting, normalisation to MNI space, harmonisation with differential smoothing, and MRI-based segmentation. Patient data were anonymized, and a harmonised database was created including demographic characteristics, clinical history, and results from neuropsychological assessments. The dataset enables study of amyloid PET patterns at global, regional and voxel level for investigating neuropathological underpinnings of DLB, improving diagnostic accuracy, and guiding patient stratification in anti-amyloid trials.

Lipidomics mass spectrometry data acquired in full-scan/data-dependent MS2 mode from FTD patients with different genetic mutations (FTD-GRN, FTD-C9orf72, FTD-MAPT) and controls. The Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) study provided the primary data for this research. The Kaiser Permanente Interregional Institutional Review Board approved the study and data sharing (IRBNet Protocols: 821300 and 278254). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants including permission to examine medical records and brain autopsy upon death. Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to evaluate the association between number of children and risk of dementia, with age as the time scale and multiple imputation (5 imputations) applied to account for missing covariate data.

ROSMAP study data, including the miRNA data, can be requested at https://www.radc.rush.edu. miRNA sequencing data underwent quality control filtering with samples iteratively removed if their total raw read counts, trimmed read counts, or mapped read counts were larger than 5 standard deviations from the means. Raw counts of miRNAs were normalized for sequencing depth and transformed to log2 counts per million using edgeR. Principal component analysis was performed on normalized counts, and samples with counts larger than 4 SD from the mean for the first two PCs were removed. KING was used to estimate and remove cryptic relatedness. A total of 648 samples passed QC filtering. The miRNA data was used for differential expression analysis across multiple cerebral pathologies including AD pathology, Lewy body pathology, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, arteriolosclerosis, and LATE-NC.

RNA-sequencing data from dlPFC of ROS/MAP donors have been described previously. Transcriptome-wide differential expression analysis was performed using voom-limma, with models adjusted for RNA sequencing batch, PMI, RIN, sex, age at death, education, surrogate variables, and pathology covariates. In a subset of 55 PSEN1 variants with available data from DIAN, variant-level Aβ production profiles correlated with all clinical (CDR), cognitive (Logical Memory; MMSE), and biomarker (Amyloid PET, structural MRI, CSF ptau) measures examined, as well as with observed longitudinal rates of biomarker and clinical progression of ADAD. Expression of mutant or wild-type PSEN1/2 in cell culture and measurement of Aβ production, coupled with literature-derived AAO and in vivo clinical, cognitive, and biomarker data from the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer's Network Observational Study (DIAN).

Aβ peptide production from 161 known pathogenic mutations in PSEN1 and 70 variants in PSEN2 were assessed in vitro. Aβ production (particularly the Aβ42/40 and Aβ37/42 ratios) by individual PSEN1 variants was strongly correlated with AAO, with more abnormal γ-secretase function associated with earlier AAO. Aβ production among PSEN2 variants with known homologs in PSEN1 showed strong associations with AAO.

The data for these analyses come from the ongoing prospective, longitudinal Biomarkers for Older Controls at Risk of Dementia (BIOCARD) study, which was started in 1995 at the National Institute of Health (NIH), to examine the early phases of AD. The participants were primarily middle aged at enrollment (mean 56.7 years) and approximately 75% had a family history of dementia. The study was stopped in 2005 for administrative reasons and was re-established in 2009 by an investigative team at the Johns Hopkins University (JHU) School of Medicine. APOE genotyping was performed using restriction endonuclease digestion of polymerase chain reaction amplified genomic DNA. APOE genotypes were included as covariates because the APOE-e4 allele is the major genetic risk factor for late onset AD and has been related to greater cognitive decline among older adults free of dementia.

The HCP cohort was used to examine diagnostic potential of p-tau217 assays using receiver operating curves and area under the curve (AUC-ROC). Two data points from the HCP cohort that fell outside the calibration curve range were excluded from the final analysis. The study assessed the performance of p-tau217 assay in predicting Aβ-PET and Tau PET status using multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for age, sex, and APOE ε4 carrier status, with three-fold cross validation.

The MYHAT-NI cohort was used to examine diagnostic potential using receiver operating curves and area under the curve (AUC-ROC). Multivariable logistic regression models were built to assess the performance of p-tau217 assay in predicting Aβ-PET and Tau PET status, adjusted for age, sex, and APOE ε4 carrier status, with three-fold cross validation applied.

The ADAD study was used to assess p-tau217 assay performance in predicting Aβ-PET and Tau PET status using multivariable logistic regression models. Python was used to measure AUC-ROC for this study. One data point from the ADAD study that fell outside the calibration curve range was excluded from the final analysis.

The Pittsburgh ADRC (Alzheimer's Disease Research Center) was one of the cohorts used in this study examining p-tau217 assay performance. Biomarker associations were assessed using Spearman correlation, and multivariable logistic regression models were built to assess performance in predicting Aβ-PET and Tau PET status.

The EMIF-AD Multimodal Biomarker Discovery study harmonized and pooled clinical data from 11 cohort studies and samples from CSF, plasma, DNA, and MRI scans were centrally analyzed using different omics techniques (proteomics, metabolomics, and genomics) and integrated analysis has demonstrated the power of such approaches.

The Accelerating Medicines Partnership - Alzheimer's Disease (AMP-AD) allows researchers to access multiple cohorts via a single platform. It is a partnership between government, industry, and nonprofit organizations to transform the current model for developing new diagnostics and treatments for AD. The sharing of multi-omics datasets through this centralized data infrastructure, the AD Knowledge Portal, enables integrative and collaborative analyses to more easily and effectively advance biomarker identification and replication.

Monongahela-Youghiogheny Health Aging Team (MYHAT, n=87, median age 83 [IQR: 78-87.5], 74% female), an ongoing population-based cohort drawn from a medically and economically underserved Rust Belt region in southwestern Pennsylvania, USA. In MYHAT, the UGOT and ALZpath assays separated CDR=0 and CDR=0.5 participants with equivalent AUCs (0.79 vs. 0.81).

MYHAT-NI sub-study (n=111, median age 76 [IQR: 72-80], 54% female), which performed two-year longitudinal follow-up neuroimaging assessments of Aβ, tau, and neurodegeneration by structural MRI. Three p-tau217 assays—UPitt, ALZpath, and NULISA—were employed in the MYHAT-NI cohort. The assays demonstrated equivalent AUCs for determining Aβ positivity, ranging from 0.84 to 0.90.

Human Connectome Project (HCP, n=229, median age 62 [IQR: 56-70], 65% female) which targeted a 50:50 split of self-identified Black and non-Hispanic White individuals. UPitt and ALZpath assays showed similar AUCs in the HCP cohorts, with values of 0.87 and 0.90, respectively.

Harvard Biomarkers Study is a longitudinal biomarkers study with structured study visits. HBS has strengths in terms of the quality of targeted data (e.g., environmental exposures, clinical rating scales, genetics) but is comparatively small in participant numbers with 935 participants. As it is based at a single site in Boston, it may not be representative of the diversity of PD across the nation. Patients at HBS are predominantly of European descent.

Mass General Brigham electronic medical records dataset includes data extracted from typical clinical care records for PD (i.e., real-world data). MGB has approximately 25 times as many participants as HBS with 22,949 participants. Subjects at MGB were only included if they had at least two years of data coverage prior to initial PD diagnosis to filter for de novo diagnoses. Patients at MGB are predominantly of European descent.

Optum Claims-EHR dataset is a large real-world data source used in this study. Subjects at Optum were only included if they had at least two years of data coverage prior to initial PD diagnosis to filter for de novo diagnoses. Ethnicity data were not available in the licensed Optum dataset, limiting the ability to subset people with PD according to race or ethnicity in search of different progression patterns.

The insoluble fraction from NDD brain samples investigated in this study has also been analyzed using mass spectrometry (MS) to identify AD-associated proteins that correlate with disease onset and progression, and to identify proteins that are not present in other NDDs such as frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD). MS signatures of the insoluble proteome from AD brain and other NDDs are distinct from that of control patients and from each other. The study utilized MX-Raman spectroscopy on NDD tissue samples with N = 15, n = 3 (limited sample size). Each spectral data set contained 30 spectra for each of the 15 patients, resulting in 450 spectra total, of which 405 were used for training and 45 for testing using LDA with 5-fold cross-validation for classification.

Translational research has also been performed to demonstrate that MS is an effective tool for biomarker discovery in CSF from heterogeneous AD cohorts, as well as from blood plasma at early stages of AD. MS excels at molecular identification and sample classification for distinguishing Alzheimer's disease from other neurodegenerative diseases and control patients.

The Aberdeen Child Development Survey provided the foundational data for the Children of the 1950s cohort study. The cohort comprised 12,150 individuals (males 51.7%) born in Aberdeen who were successfully linked to obstetric records from the Aberdeen Maternity and Neonatal Databank. The cohort was revitalized beginning in 1998 with tracing of vital status and area of residence. A 21-page questionnaire was mailed to subjects believed to be resident in the UK, covering living conditions, occupation, education, income, height and weight, health, health-related behaviours, and parental vital status. The analysis was restricted to 8,452 subjects due to missing data for some variables.

Obstetric records from the Aberdeen Maternity and Neonatal Databank were linked to the Aberdeen Child Development Survey cohort members. The 12,150 individuals in the Children of the 1950s cohort had been successfully linked to information from obstetric records held in this databank.

A small subgroup of cohort members (less than 1 in 5) had been followed up in various investigations of respiratory function since the mid-1980s, known collectively as the WHEASE study. This represented the only prior direct contact with cohort members before the 1998 revitalization effort.

UK Biobank (UKBB) datasets were used in multiple GWAS studies on Alzheimer's disease. SNP-level fine-mapping and functional annotation suggest that these four genes are likely causal genes for AD. UKBB was also used as a source for patient cohorts in PRS calculation studies.

The data used in this study were obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. Protein co-abundance modules were identified from CSF proteomics data using WGCNA. Among the 7008 aptamers measured across 229 participants, proteins exhibiting low variability were removed by excluding those within the lowest quartile (Q1) of standard deviation. This filtering step resulted in 5256 aptamers, which were retained for network construction. Network modules were detected using the blockwiseModules function, with a soft-thresholding power set to 7 and a minimum module size of 30. Associations between module eigenproteins and DNA methylation-based epigenetic age measures were evaluated using linear regression models adjusted for chronological age, sex, APOE ε4 carrier status, and blood cell composition.

dataset_context_from_paper: Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) is a prospective cohort study, enrolling dementia-free individuals age 65 and following them with biennial cognitive testing. ACT participants diagnosed with AD (ACT AD) were divided into subgroups with greater deficits in memory (AD-Memory), executive function (AD-Executive), language (AD-Language), or visuospatial (AD-Visuospatial) scores on an extensive battery of cognitive tests. MRI within 4 years of diagnosis were available for 220 ACT AD participants (35 AD-Memory, 31 AD-Visuospatial, 26 AD-Language, 18 AD-Executive, and 110 AD-no specific subdomain), as well as 516 no-dementia controls. Neuroradiologists rated each patient's MRI using NIH neuroimaging common data elements (CDE).

Data used in this study are available here: https://www.radc.rush.edu/. Longitudinal Early-Onset Alzheimer's Disease Study (LEADS) cohort. All participants had MCI or mild dementia at baseline with longitudinal Aβ and tau PET imaging, as well as cognitive assessments, with at least one observation before and after treatment initiation. Piecewise regression with a knot at treatment start was applied to evaluate changes in Aβ and tau PET burden and Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores. An untreated comparison group from LEADS was matched for age, sex, APOE ε4 genotype, pretreatment Aβ and tau PET load, CDR-SB, and follow-up duration using a 1:3 matching design. Median treatment duration was 8 months (IQR=5-10).

Plasma analytes in the ADNI cohort (ptau181, ptau217, ptau231, Aβ42/40, NfL, GFAP) were quantified using a multiplex NULISA assay. Johnson-Neyman analysis revealed that slope differences between ADP and AD were significant for ptau181 at low biomarker levels across all three non-memory domains: language, visuospatial, and executive function. For ptau217, significance emerged at higher thresholds than ptau181 for language and visuospatial function. Ptau231 was elevated at baseline but was not predictive of decline in ADP in the ADNI cohort.

Plasma analytes in the LZ cohort were quantified using the Quanterix Simoa® platform at Quanterix Corporation's Accelerator Lab (Bedford, MA) using the Simoa® HD-X analyzer. Plasma Aβ1–40, Aβ1–42, GFAP and NfL were measured using the Simoa® Neurology 4-Plex E Advantage kit. Plasma phospho-Tau 181 (pTau-181) was measured with the Simoa® pTau-181 Advantage V2 kit. Baseline levels of ptau212 were elevated in AD and ADP relative to CU in the LZ cohort, though ptau212 did not predict decline in ADP relative to AD.

The raw 16S and ITS sequence data were deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database (BioProject accession number: PRJNA1234023). DNA was extracted from 54 transverse colon samples using the DNeasy PowerSoil Pro Kit (QIAGEN). The V4 region of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene was amplified with the primers 515F (5′‐GTGCCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA) and 806R (5′‐GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT), and sequenced using the Illumina MiSeq platform (2 × 250). QIIME 2 (version 2023.5) was used for sequence quality control, feature table and representative sequence construction, and phylogenetic tree generation. Sequences were then mapped to the Silva 138 SSURef NR99 database for the microbiome composition analysis.

Quality-controlled data were merged with clinical metadata (diagnosis, Braak stage, age at death, APOE genotype) by project ID. Differential expression between AD and NC cells was conducted using Seurat's Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

Processed scRNA-seq data by cluster were downloaded under synapse ID syn52293433 from the ROSMAP cohort and used for differential expression analysis between Alzheimer's disease and normal control conditions.
Bulk RNA-seq data from the ROSMAP cohort used in conjunction with single-cell RNA-seq data for comprehensive transcriptomic analysis of Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis.
Cortex-specific eQTL data from the MetaBrain consortium used for GWAS-eQTL integration analysis to identify pathways associated with methylation changes and Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis.
AD GWAS summary statistics were obtained from the GWAS Catalog and used for GWAS-eQTL integration analysis to identify genetic associations with Alzheimer's disease.

Processed DNA methylation data, including normalized methylation values, count matrices, and associated sample metadata, are provided in the Supplementary Materials and deposited in GEO under accession GSE328184. DMRs with p-value < 0.05 were retained and used for pathway enrichment analysis focusing on GO molecular function database.

Heart rate was continuously collected during the sensorimotor task using BIOPAC ECG instrumentation (MP150 system). For analysis, instantaneous heart rate was sampled at 1 second intervals throughout the task (heart rate was computed based on ECG trace using BIOPAC AcqKnowledge software). Study included 40 individuals with PTSD, 40 individuals with mood and anxiety complaints (MA), and 40 matched healthy controls (HC), with matching performed using propensity matching on gender, age, negative affect, and fear measures.

Electronic health records (EHRs) data provided with permission from ACT. The study used ACT data to estimate the average treatment effect (ATE) of hypertension on developing Alzheimer's disease (AD). The analysis involved integrating gold-standard validation measures with EHR-derived outcomes from a non-probability sample. Authors excluded individuals with missing covariate information and applied propensity score-based weighting and calibration weighting methods to address selection bias and improve inference. The dataset represents patient information from a regional healthcare system including clinical outcomes, treatment information, and covariate data.

We analyzed 3,635 plasma proteins using SOMAscan assay platform from 973 participants in European Medical Information Framework (EMIF)‐AD Multimodal Biomarker Discovery (MBD) study. By integrating CSF amyloid β (A) and phosphorylated tau (T) profiles, we performed linear regression analysis to identify differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) in A+T+ patients (n = 335) versus A‐T‐ controls (n = 297). Using 201 DAPs in A+T+ patients, we classified biologically defined AD into four distinct molecular subtypes, each enriched in different biological pathways, including complement activation, lipid storage regulation, glucose metabolism, and cytokine production.

Raw and processed DNAm data are available from GEO under accession number GSE279509. GSE279509 DNAm data was loaded into R (version 3.6.3) from IDAT files using the package bigmelon. These data were processed through a bespoke quality control pipeline developed for cell-specific DNAm data. The dataset includes five different purified cell populations isolated from PFC (prefrontal cortex). The authors used this large DNAm dataset to evaluate the effects on study design, data preprocessing, and statistical analysis for cell-specific studies of DNAm, particularly where multiple cell types are considered. The study assessed quality control procedures for confirming successful isolation of purified cell populations, investigated statistical power of association studies using cell-specific DNAm data, assessed the impact of data normalization on DNAm variance, and evaluated multiple statistical frameworks for analyzing cell-specific DNAm data using simulation scenarios.

Through the application of the European Medical Information Framework (EMIF)-AD cohort, researchers analysed a set of proteins in plasma samples from controls (n = 220), individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) (n = 382) and AD (n = 183) patients, obtained via aptamer capture array (SomaScan). The study found that some proteins involved in synaptic plasticity and mitochondrial homeostasis changed in concentration in at least one of the comparison groups. Proteins analysed included autophagy proteins such as PINK1, BNIP3L, TFEB and REST as potential biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis and staging.

dataset_identifier: P301S RNA dataset treated with NR
dataset_context_from_paper: Dr. (Alice) Ruixue Ai (UiO) shared the RNA dataset from P301S treated with NR, which was used in this study for analysis of gene expression changes related to neurodegeneration and REST signaling.

The Harvard Biomarkers Study represents a transformative resource for holistically decoding the environmental, genetic, biological and clinical features of PD. As one of the few patient cohorts with this extensive collection of environmental exposure data combined with whole genome sequencing, the HBS provides comprehensive clinical characterization of PD patients with extensive environmental exposure data and whole genome sequencing data.

The DIAN‐TU‐001 Tau NexGen Trial (NCT05269394) is a phase II/III randomized, double blinded, placebo‐controlled trial in participants with DIAD. Eligible mutation‐positive participants were enrolled in 2 cohorts (Cohort 1: Symptomatic Population (CDR=0.5‐1), n=97; Cohort 2: Asymptomatic Population (CDR=0), n=100). Preliminary Week 24 amyloid PET data was available from 62 symptomatic participants receiving lecanemab (avg EYO=1.51 and avg age=47.4). Baseline mean amyloid PET SUVr was 2.06 (SD=0.38) and change from baseline at 24 weeks was ‐0.18 (SD=0.17). Change on amyloid PET from Week 0 to Week 24 is a secondary endpoint for Cohort 1.

dataset_context_from_paper: Gene Ontology (GO) terms and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways from the Molecular Signature Database were used for the pathway analysis. Gene sets were considered significant if they surpassed the adjusted false discovery rate of 0.05 after Benjamini–Hochberg multiple testing correction.
GWAS Catalog was used for the pathway analysis alongside Gene Ontology terms and KEGG pathways from the Molecular Signature Database.

Three cohort studies were referenced: Gingko Evaluation of Memory (GEM), Monongahela Valley Independent Elders Survey (MoVIES), and Monongahela-Youghiogheny Healthy Aging Team (MYHAT). These appear to be the source populations for genetic variants and cognitive assessments including Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores used in the analysis.

Anonymized data from the MELD-B project can be requested by accredited researchers with appropriate research governance and ethics approvals via the Grampian Data Safe Haven. The dataset was used to investigate the relationship between early-life education and academic ability with healthcare utilization (hospital admissions and outpatient appointments) in adulthood. The research examined whether this relationship is explained by multiple long-term conditions and other adult factors. Ethics approval was obtained from the University of Southampton Faculty of Medicine Ethics committee (ERGO II Reference 66810).

Participants of the ACONF study contributed data that was used in the MELD-B project analysis. The study data were accessed through the Grampian Data Safe Haven and used to examine relationships between early-life factors and later healthcare burden.

The DIAN Obs dataset is a longitudinal cohort study of autosomal dominant Alzheimer's disease (ADAD). At each in-person initial visit, whole blood is collected for ADAD mutation status, APOE genotype, genome-wide association study (GWAS) genotyping array, and whole genome sequencing (WGS). At initial and follow-up visits, buffy coat blood and PAXgene blood tubes are collected for longitudinal assessment of DNA methylomics and RNA transcriptomics. The dataset includes derived biospecimens including induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) generated from dermal fibroblasts. Data is stripped of identifiers, re-coded with dummy IDs, and transferred with encryption and password protection. As of December 2022, DIAN Obs has received 288 data requests with 231 requests fulfilled.

National Centralized Repository for Alzheimer's Disease (NCRAD) at Indiana University School of Medicine receives whole blood samples from DIAN Obs participants. Four tubes of whole blood are drawn at participant initial visit, with two sent to the Genetics Core and two sent to NCRAD. NCRAD serves as a centralized repository for sample banking and biomarker measurement availability to approved investigators.

Diffusion MRI (dMRI) data from ADNI3/4 cohorts were used to evaluate harmonization approaches for multi-site neuroimaging data. The study applied four harmonization methods to regional fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) measures across different acquisition protocols. The dataset included cognitively normal (CN) participants and those with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), with clinical indicators including CDR-sob scores, Aβ-PET and tau-PET burden measurements. Unharmonized FullWM FA and MD measures in CN participants showed substantial protocol-related differences across acquisition protocols (partial R² ≥0.24, P <0.001). All harmonization approaches reduced protocol-related variability, with residual protocol-attributable variance remaining low after harmonization (partial R² <0.03).

Longitudinal imaging data from the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging (MCSA, n = 1834) were analyzed. Participants were categorized into typical AD and resilient groups using amyloid PiB‐PET (abnormal PiB‐PET≥25 Centiloid units), Flortaucipir (FTP‐PET) (meta‐ROI≥1.29 SUVr, ERC≥1.27 SUVr) and Mini‐Mental State Examination (MMSE). The dataset included imaging biomarkers and cognitive assessments used to validate the THETA machine learning model for distinguishing resilient individuals from those with typical tau pathologies.

Longitudinal imaging data from ADRC (n = 246) were analyzed alongside MCSA data. Participants were categorized into typical AD and resilient groups using amyloid PiB‐PET, Flortaucipir (FTP‐PET), and Mini‐Mental State Examination (MMSE) assessments. This dataset was used for validation of the THETA machine learning model.

Data were collected from 192 individuals (mean age = 62.4, SD = 8.4, 37% female) with bvFTD from the ARTFL-LEFFTDS Longitudinal Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration study. Participants were classified into 'fast' (n = 71) and 'slow' (n = 121) progressors based on a >4 point increase in the FTLD-modified Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes. Random forest modeling identified the top 7, 5, and 3 most important neuropsychiatric, motor, and cognitive features (out of 43) linked to fast disease progression. The top 7 features associated with fast progression included impaired verbal memory (encoding then delayed recall), impaired working memory, compulsive behaviors, irritability, impaired letter fluency, and impaired mental flexibility.

Plasma proteomic data for the Knight ADRC participants are available from the Knight ADRC. Requests for clinical or proteomic data from individual investigators will be reviewed to ensure compliance with patient confidentiality.
Stanford ADRC data can be requested through the Stanford ADRC data release committee. Data includes proteomic and clinical information from Alzheimer's Disease Research Center participants.
ROSMAP resources can be requested through the RADC and Synapse. Dataset used for proteomic analysis in neurodegenerative disease research.

GNPC is an initiative aimed at discovering biomarkers by integrating and expanding proteomic data from thousands of patient samples across global dementia cohorts. The GNPC successfully brought together >40,000 samples from more than 23 different international cohorts, creating a harmonized dataset that covers multiple neurodegenerative disorders and includes approximately 300 million protein measurements. Cross-sectional and longitudinal SomaScan proteomic data were incorporated. GNPC neurodegenerative disorders include AD, Parkinson's disease, FTD and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

ACE cohort data are available upon reasonable request. The largest preprocessed SomaScan proteomic dataset from the ACE cohort has been uploaded and is publicly accessible through the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative (ADDI) community. The discovery dataset was divided into a training set (70%, 967 controls and 525 AD cases) and testing set (30%, 414 controls and 225 AD cases). The replication dataset consisted of 715 controls and 520 AD cases.

As of November 2023, CPAD's clinical trial repository contains 73 studies with over 100,000 individual de-identified patient records, with a rich source of key AD biomarkers (biofluids and imaging). Clinical data are curated, standardized, and aggregated into analysis subsets, which are used to develop disease progression models that form the basis for clinical trial simulation (CTS) tools. Different linear and non-linear mixed effects models have been fit based on relevant biomarker combinations, characterizing the time course of clinically relevant outcome measures.

CPAD's database includes raw neuroimages from contemporary datasets, which are used to lead two pre-competitive efforts, in collaboration with leading academic and industry experts, to 1) test and validate a tau-PET quantification method that harmonizes derived measures across tracers and cohorts, and 2) explore and evaluate the readiness of tau-PET as a surrogate marker in AD drug development to support accelerated drug approval. To harmonize tau-PET quantification, two different methods (a Centiloid-like approach and a Joint Propagation model) were tested and validated across multiple tracers, cohorts and studies.

Participants with mild cognitive impairment or probable AD (CI group), versus cognitively normal comparators (CN) from the Bio-Hermes study. Study included 661 participants (n = 266 CN, n = 395 CI; mean age 72.4 years; 55% male). Blood-based biomarkers measured included plasma amyloid beta (Aβ) 42/Aβ40, phosphorylated tau (p-tau)181, p-tau217, and apolipoprotein E ε4 allele (Apoε4) status. CVD risk was calculated using the Atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD) risk score calculator. Logistic regression analyses evaluated the association of AD biomarkers and CVD risk with cognitive impairment.

data_repository: Adult Changes in Thought Study, University of Washington
dataset_context_from_paper: We identified a cohort of adults aged ≥ 65 years diagnosed with dementia from the Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) Study, a prospective cohort study of older adults in Seattle, WA. We compiled a corpus of secure messages sent from participants' patient portals in the period spanning 5 years before until 5 years after dementia onset. We used Natural Language Processing (NLP) to select messages focused on patients' lived experiences. We qualitatively analyzed 1023 secure messages between patients or caregivers and healthcare providers to identify themes.

All omics data of ROS/MAP samples are available from Synapse. These include individual-level snRNA-seq, TMT proteomics, and whole genome sequencing data of ROS/MAP samples used to generate xQTL summary data and corresponding LD matrices for the xWAS-O framework integrating multi-omics data with GWAS summary data.

GWAS summary data of PD by the Nalls et. al. 2019 excluding the 23andMe cohort are available from google drive. These GWAS summary statistics were integrated with xQTL weights through the xWAS-O framework for gene-based association testing.

Trained bulk cis-eQTL weights, cell-type-aware cis-eQTL weights, and cis-pQTL weights are available from SYNAPSE. These xQTL imputation models were trained in Stage I of the xWAS-O pipeline using individual-level genotype and transcriptomic/proteomic expression data from ROS/MAP samples.

GWAS LD derived from the UK Biobank reference panel was used for the xWAS-O framework analysis. Reference LD from different reference panels are recommended by GIFT developers for resolving potential computational issues.

Cognitively unimpaired participants from BIOCARD (N = 133) who completed accelerometer-measured physical activity monitoring over 7 days and underwent 11C-Pittsburgh compound B PET imaging were included. The study used BIOCARD (Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline among Normal Individuals) study data to investigate if higher levels of physical activity are associated with later estimated amyloid onset age (EAOA) across three cohort studies. Total daily physical activity was measured through wrist-worn accelerometers and EAOA was estimated using sampled Iterative Local Approximation. Proportional Hazard Cox regression models assessed whether physical activity is associated with EAOA, adjusting for sex and APOE status.

Cognitively unimpaired participants from BLSA (N = 117) who completed accelerometer-measured physical activity monitoring over 7 days and underwent 11C-Pittsburgh compound B PET imaging were included. The Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA) provided data on community-dwelling middle-age and older adults. Total daily physical activity was measured through wrist-worn accelerometers and EAOA was estimated using sampled Iterative Local Approximation. No significant association between physical activity and EAOA was observed (z-score HR = 1.01, p = 0.97).

Cognitively unimpaired participants from WRAP (N = 115) who completed accelerometer-measured physical activity monitoring over 7 days and underwent 11C-Pittsburgh compound B PET imaging were included. The Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (WRAP) study contributed data on community-dwelling middle-age and older adults. Total daily physical activity was measured through waist-worn accelerometers and EAOA was estimated using sampled Iterative Local Approximation. No significant association between physical activity and EAOA was observed (z-score HR = 0.96, p = 0.85).

Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC) ID1000 dataset containing multimodal (3T) MRI data including structural (T1-weighted), diffusion-weighted, and resting-state and task-based functional BOLD MRI data, as well as detailed demographics and psychometric variables from a large set of healthy participants. Version 1.2.1 used in this research.

Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC) PIOP1 dataset containing multimodal (3T) MRI data including structural (T1-weighted), diffusion-weighted, and resting-state and task-based functional BOLD MRI data, as well as detailed demographics and psychometric variables from a large set of healthy participants. Version 2.0.0 used in this research.

Version 2.0.0 used in this research.

Southwestern University (SWU) dataset from the Consortium for Reliability and Reproducibility (CoRR), downloaded via NITRC-IR from the 1000 Functional Connectomes Project. Emotion and Creativity One Year Retest Dataset subset comprised of 235 college student subjects. Each subject underwent two sessions of anatomical, resting state fMRI, and DTI scans, spaced one year apart.

Memory performance and decline GWAS summary statistics. The authors conducted genome-wide association studies on memory performance and decline phenotypes, which are highly heritable traits associated with Alzheimer's disease. These summary statistics were made publicly available through NIAGADS.

UK Biobank brain-imaging derived phenotype GWAS summary statistics. The study utilized large-scale biometric data from UK Biobank, revealing that neuroimaging phenotypes, particularly structural and diffusion imaging measures, are highly heritable. Top imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) for each modality that survived FDR correction included diffusion measures highlighting regions such as the fornix, cingulum, and posterior thalamic radiation, and structural measures highlighting regions such as the pars orbitalis, posterior cingulate gyrus, superior occipital gyrus and sulcus, and insula.

Longitudinal cohort study conducted in tertiary and community-based medical centers from February 2010 to March 2020. Data from 252 pathogenic variant carriers (mean age 38.4 years, 54% female) with 3960 MRI sessions among 1141 participants total. Used to assess associations between neurodegeneration, amyloidosis, cerebral microbleeds, and white matter hyperintensity volume in autosomal dominant Alzheimer disease.

Longitudinal cohort study conducted in tertiary and community-based medical centers from July 2007 to September 2021. Data from 571 older adults (mean age 72.8 years, 48% female) with 3960 MRI sessions among 1141 participants total. Used to examine longitudinal increases in white matter hyperintensity volume in individuals with cerebral microbleeds and associations with gray matter volume decline and amyloid burden in late-onset Alzheimer disease.

Longitudinal cohort study conducted in tertiary and community-based medical centers from September 2010 to December 2019. Data from 318 older adults (mean age 72.4 years, 61% female) with 3960 MRI sessions among 1141 participants total. Used to assess relationships between white matter hyperintensity volume, gray matter volume changes, cerebral microbleeds, and amyloid positron emission tomography in aging populations.

The Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) study provided the primary dataset for this research. Study participants underwent brain autopsy after death as part of a brain donation program, having provided consent for autopsy during the study. Detailed data on blood pressure and medical history from midlife to late life were retrospectively collected from Kaiser Permanente Washington (KPW) medical archives, complementing the ACT study's prospective data. Data were collected from 1994 (ACT study enrollment) through November 2019 (dataset freeze). Extensively trained research staff manually extracted data following strict protocols with regular supervision meetings to ensure high data quality.

199 adults enrolled in the ALLFTD Mobile App study (mean age = 53.4 [SD = 15.2]; 58% women) completed up to 6 months of passive smartphone monitoring via the ALLFTD Mobile App. 55% were unimpaired [CDR®+NACC FTLD = 0], 22% had prodromal FTD [CDR®+NACC FTLD = 0.5], and 23% had symptomatic FTD [CDR®+NACC FTLD≥1]. Battery percentage was collected frequently (median interval = 45 min), and total daily battery usage was calculated as a proxy for smartphone use. Daily step counts were also passively collected. Logistic regression classified prodromal or symptomatic FTD vs. unimpaired as a function of MoCA score, 7 passive features characterizing average, inter-day variability, and changes over time in smartphone use and movement, or passive smartphone features and MoCA combined.

dataset_context_from_paper: GNPC is open access. The dataset was used to train and validate the ProtAIDe-Dx machine learning model for proteomics analysis. Leave-one-site-out cross-validation was performed across 14 test sites. Each participant's proteomics values were normalized by their averaged protein levels, missing protein entries were imputed using a 10-nearest neighbor data imputer, and a Gaussian rank normalizer was applied to ensure normalized proteomics followed a normal distribution.

Pseudoanonymized BioFINDER-2 data will be shared by request from a qualified academic investigator for the sole purpose of replicating procedures and results presented in this article and as long as data transfer is in agreement with European Union legislation on the general data protection regulation and decisions by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority and Region Skåne. Model generalization performance was evaluated in the BioFINDER-2 cohort across 20 random K-shot repeats, measuring both balanced classification accuracy (BCA) and area under the curve (AUC).

A total of 5,154 neuroimages from the ADNI dataset were utilized in this study, comprising 2,590 MCI, 1,124 AD, and 1,440 cognitively normal (CN) samples. The neuroimages were processed through image enhancement via an Adaptive Self-Guided Loop Filter, followed by precise brain region segmentation with GoogLeNet Inception-v3, and advanced feature extraction using a new Discrete Cosine-Krawtchouk-Tchebichef Transform (DCKTT). Classification was performed using the SQPHGM model to diagnose Alzheimer's Disease, achieving 99.9% accuracy and 99.8% precision.
