The snRNA-seq dataset from the Allen Brain Institute is openly accessible at https://portal.brain-map.org/atlases-and-data/rnaseq. This dataset was used for cell-type enrichment analysis across protein co-abundance modules.

The snRNA-seq dataset from the Human Brain Vascular Atlas can be found in the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession code GSE163577. This dataset was used for cell-type enrichment analysis across protein co-abundance modules in the study.

568 LEADS participants with baseline [18F]florbetaben and [18F]flortaucipir PET imaging were analyzed, including 483 cognitively-impaired (CI) participants with clinical diagnosis of MCI or dementia and 85 cognitively unimpaired (CU) participants. Amyloid positivity was determined using [18F]florbetaben-PET quantification with a 25 Centiloid threshold. Tau-PET status was determined through expert visual reads following FDA-approved guidelines and quantitative approaches using Flortaucipir-SUVR from various regions of interest. Longitudinal clinical decline was assessed using CDR-SB scores with linear mixed effect models.

The GNPC Harmonized Dataset v1.3 includes plasma proteomic data from 19 cohorts generated on the SomaLogic SomaScan platform, providing 7,274 protein measurements encompassing 6,391 unique protein gene symbols across 17,484 individuals and 22,392 samples. The dataset was used for weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) applied to a 7,333 × 22,392 log2(abundance) matrix, yielding 12 co-expression modules. Trait and proteomic data were downloaded on March 27, 2025, with quality control pipeline applied including removal of outliers, harmonization of APOE genotype coding, and restriction to blood plasma samples. The dataset was used to develop a machine learning model to impute APOE genotypes with 94% accuracy and to perform gene ontology enrichment analyses across 5-year bins of significant proteins.

Demographics and BDP status were extracted from the CADRC database and analyzed based on initial and current BDP enrollment status. Key variables included in the analyses were: age, sex, race/ethnicity, years of education, marital status, study partner relationship (defined as a relative, including spouse/partner, or non‐relative), diagnostic cohort at baseline and most recent visit, most recent biomarker results, and total number of completed study visits.

Processed snRNA-seq data and metadata from Leng et al. are available for download at the Synapse portal under ID syn21788402, under controlled use conditions. This dataset was used for cell type-specific differential gene expression analysis between control and Alzheimer's disease groups across multiple brain regions (MTG, STG, ETC) using DESeq2 with pseudo-bulk aggregation of unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts from cells belonging to the same individual and specific cell type.

Processed data from Gabitto et al. can be freely downloaded without registration from the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease (SEA-AD) Brain Cell portal and a public AWS bucket. This processed snRNA-seq data was used for differential gene expression analysis and co-expression module analysis across brain regions and cell types in Alzheimer's disease research.

The overlap of co-expression modules with DEGs or AD-associated genes from the Open Targets Platform was calculated using the R package GeneOverlap via Fisher's exact test to identify genes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The overlap of co-expression modules with KEGG Alzheimer's disease pathways was calculated using the R package GeneOverlap via Fisher's exact test to identify dysregulated pathways in different cell types across brain regions.
The overlap of co-expression modules with genes from Harmonizome was calculated using the R package GeneOverlap via Fisher's exact test as part of the functional enrichment analysis.

The compendium of Gene Ontology biological processes (2018 edition) was retrieved from the Mayaan laboratory repository and used for functional enrichment analysis on hdWGCNA modules using the R package enrichR, focusing on Gene Ontology processes exhibiting differential expression in specific cell types.

Alzheimer's disease and control BA9 brain tissue samples obtained from the London Neurodegenerative Diseases Brain Bank. These biological samples were used in the study for analyzing synaptic dysfunction and protein interactions in Alzheimer's disease pathology.

Plasmid SypHy from Granseth et al. obtained from Addgene (plasmid# 24478). This recombinant DNA construct was used as a fluorescent reporter for synaptic vesicle dynamics and pH-dependent imaging in neuronal experiments.
Plasmid SypH 2x from Zhu et al. obtained from Addgene (plasmid# 37004). This recombinant DNA construct was used for enhanced synaptic vesicle pH imaging in neuronal studies.

B6.Cg-Zbtb20 Tg(PDGFB-APPSwInd)20Lms/2Mmjax (J20) transgenic mice from Jackson Laboratory. These experimental model organisms expressing Alzheimer's disease-related APP mutations were used to study synaptic dysfunction and neurodegeneration.

B6.Cg-Tg(tetO-APPSwInd)102Dbo/Mmjax transgenic mice from Jackson Laboratory. These inducible transgenic mice expressing Alzheimer's disease-related APP mutations were used as experimental models for studying neurodegeneration.

The microarray gene expression profile used in this work is publicly available on NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GSE53890). After data preprocessing and quality control, the final dataset was composed of 41 PFC samples covering 14,844 unique genes. Samples were divided into three age groups: the young old (YO) group, the middle-old (MO) group, and the oldest old (OO) group to study the transcriptome changes across these populations. Probes were annotated with the Affymetrix Human Genome U133 Plus 2.0 Array annotation data (chip hgu133plus2).

The RNAseq data used in this work were developed through the Religious Orders Study and Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP) study and are available via the AD Knowledge Portal (https://adknowledgeportal.synapse.org). The AD Knowledge Portal is a platform for accessing data, analyses, and tools generated by the Accelerating Medicines Partnership (AMP-AD) Target Discovery Program and other National Institute on Aging (NIA)-supported programs. Authors kept only the common genes between the microarray dataset and the RNAseq dataset from ROSMAP for cross-study comparison, resulting in 14,844 unique genes analyzed across age groups.
The Mathys et al. dataset is accessible at https://doi.org/10.7303/syn2580853. This dataset was used as part of the multi-study integration for transcriptomic analysis in the research.
The Zhou et al. dataset is accessible at https://doi.org/10.7303/syn21125841. This dataset was incorporated into the multi-study integration for transcriptomic analysis.
The Lau et al. dataset is available at GEO under GSE157827. This dataset was used as part of the multi-study integration for transcriptomic analysis.

The integrated human snRNA-seq dataset and the snRNA-seq data in combination with vehicle-treated mice were uploaded to Mendeley Data, V1, doi: 10.17632/f5kx9k264n.1. This represents the authors' primary single-cell RNA sequencing data generated for this study.

The computational drug repurposing algorithm was applied using the publicly available Connectivity Map (CMap) database, consisting of treatment profiles of more than 1300 FDA-approved drugs or previously investigated compounds. The pipeline overlaid cell-type-specific DEG signature sets with 6100 drug profiles on the 1300 drugs provided by CMap, assessing disease-drug relationships using CMap scores derived from Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests.

Population-based cohort from USA including 51 Cognitively Unimpaired (CU) individuals with available plasma p-tau217 measurements at two time points (24 months follow-up) and baseline Aß-PET imaging. Plasma p-tau217 was quantified using the ALZpath assay. Linear regression was used to investigate p-tau217 association with cognitive decline.

Memory clinic-based cohort from South Korea including 135 Cognitively Impaired (CI) individuals with available plasma p-tau217 measurements at two time points (24 months follow-up) and baseline Aß-PET imaging. Plasma p-tau217 was quantified using the ALZpath assay. Data were used to investigate p-tau217 association with cognitive decline and determine sample sizes required for clinical trials.

Data from the Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) study used for analysis of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD). The dataset includes personal health identifiers (PHI) such as dates of birth and death, dates of diagnoses, and ages over 89. Data cannot be made publicly available for ethical and legal reasons but are available upon reasonable request and execution of appropriate human subjects review and data sharing agreements. The analysis required these PHI variables to replicate findings. Covariates were calculated using self-reports, except for APOE genotype.

Human brain sequencing datasets are under controlled access and require a dbGap application (phs001300.v4). Afterwards, the data will be available through the restricted AnVIL workspace. Long-read sequencing data from two post-mortem brain cohorts (NABEC and HBCC, n = 351 total) with reads basecalled, aligned to GRCh38, and provided as mapped BAM files. These were input into GraffiTE pipeline for detecting, annotating, and genotyping polymorphic transposable elements from long-read sequencing data.
Human brain sequencing datasets are under controlled access and require a dbGap application (phs000979.v4). Afterwards, the data will be available through the restricted AnVIL workspace.

Short-read Illumina WGS data (dbGaP accession phs002636.v3.p1) was used for NABEC to supplement variant calling due to lower basecalling accuracy for SNVs from R9 flow cells. Additional Illumina data for NABEC was accessed via dbGaP accession phs002636.v3.p1.

A custom TE library derived from Dfam was used to annotate transposable elements. This library was converted into FASTA format using the FAMDB tool (v2.0.2) and provided as input to RepeatMasker (v4.1.3) for TE annotation of structural variants.

All data analyzed from the full LBP cohort are available via the AD Knowledge Portal. The data includes gene expression data from the LBP cohort used for differential gene expression analysis, network analysis, and gene set enrichment testing. The dataset contains expression data for 21,635 genes across the cohort, with 11,747 probe sets representing unique genes retained for analysis after mapping and filtering.

The htext-formatted hsa00001 KEGG database was downloaded on October 4th, 2021 via the KEGG web server and parsed into structured data tables in Python. All KEGG gene sets with the top-level string 'Human' were excluded from analysis. A total of 278 KEGG gene sets with at least 10 member genes were tested for enrichment in 26 separate LBP gene sets using Fisher's exact test.

PD GWAS genes were defined using the default list provided on the PD GWASbrowser accessed on September 12th, 2021, which comprised the nearest genes to the 78 risk loci discovered in a PD GWAS of over one million individuals. Gene symbols were converted to Ensembl identifiers using the HUGO web server mapping file generated on June 10th, 2020. These PD GWAS genes were tested for enrichment in conserved network structures using Fisher's exact test.

For the imputation, the 1000 Genomes (publicly available) reference panel was used as the DPUK data sharing policy does not allow any data to leave the platform. This reference panel was used for genetic imputation as part of the standardized processing pipelines for harmonizing genome-wide data across five studies approved for the project.

Imputation with the TOPMED panel was only possible when the data moves to the Imputation Server provided by the University of Michigan (USA). The authors used the same software and similar pipeline as implemented at the Michigan server for genetic imputation of their harmonized genome-wide data.

The data processing pipelines, research-ready imputed genetic data, and PRS scores are now available on the DPUK platform and can be accessed upon request through the DPUK application process. The authors combined genetic data across five studies and provide research-ready datasets to the wider community that can be compared and/or analyzed together. All generated and QC-ed data are provided in PLINK format with standardized processing pipelines including quality control steps, genetic imputation, and calculation of standardized PRSs with six latest GWAS summary statistics related to neurodegeneration diseases (AD, AD-by-proxy, PD, frontotemporal dementia, ALS, and Lewy body dementia).

We utilize data from the Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) study (1994 – 2020), a population‐based longitudinal study of aging and the incidence of and risk factors for dementia. We focus our study on individuals who developed incident AD and classify these individuals into one of six cognitively‐defined AD subgroups using previously described methods. We identify a sex‐ and birth year‐matched set of controls using a many‐to‐one matching method. Controls are assigned an index date equal to the AD onset date for their matched AD case. We examine utilization and costs in the year preceding AD onset and in the three years following. Our utilization outcomes include number of days in a month spent in a hospital inpatient, intensive care unit, or skilled nursing facility setting, and number of emergency department visits. We also examine monthly total health care costs and component costs, including outpatient, hospital inpatient, skilled nursing facility, and pharmacy costs.
dataset_keywords: ["Alzheimer's disease", 'longitudinal aging study', 'healthcare utilization and costs']

data_repository: Douglas Bell Brain Bank (contact for access)
dataset_context_from_paper: Tissue was supplied by the Douglas Bell Brain Bank from individuals with depression, early AD and controls. The Douglas Bell Brain Bank has a long-standing arrangement with the Quebec coroner's office which allows collection of brain tissue from individuals who have died by suicide, with next-of-kin consent. Approximately 4 months after donation, a trained researcher visits relatives, with permission, to perform a psychological autopsy with 2 different informants. The study included 28 early life MDD cases and 30 later life MDD cases who died by suicide. As this dataset contains potentially identifiable clinical information on rare events (suicide), it has not been made publicly available. Phenotypic information on individuals who donated tissue to the Douglas Bell brain bank is available on request by bona fide researchers.

data_repository: South West Dementia Brain Bank (contact for access)
dataset_context_from_paper: Tissue was supplied by the South West Dementia Brain Bank (SWDBB) from individuals with early AD and older controls. Comprehensive clinical summaries are recorded in the SWDBB database for all brain donors. The summaries are generated from the patient medical notes and from any additional information collected as part of the Brains for Dementia Research Programme. The study included 19 AD controls and 28 early AD cases. As far as practicable, cases and controls were matched for age, gender and post-mortem interval.

data_repository: Available upon request from corresponding or senior author
dataset_context_from_paper: Clinic Barcelona cohort anonymised data can be shared upon request to the corresponding or senior author. However, data is likely to be subject to a data transfer agreement with restrictions required to comply with participant consent and data protection regulations. The cohort was used to study cortical asymmetry index (CAI) values across diagnostic groups including SMC-AD, SMC-MCI, CTR, and AMC, with analysis of PSEN1 and APP genes showing significant differences between clinical groups.

DIAN data can be obtained following the DIAN data-sharing agreement, subject to review by the DIAN data access committee, with final approval granted by the DIAN steering committee. The DIAN-OBS cohort was used to study differences between APOE genotypes for mutation carriers, examining CAI values across APOE3/3 and other genotypes in clinical groups (SMC, AMC, CTR), with analysis of PSEN1 and APP genes.

Code for the cortical asymmetry index is available at the following GitHub link: https://github.com/Agnes2/CAI. This computational resource was used to calculate CAI values across the study cohorts for tracking disease progression along the disease continuum.

NACC data are contributed by the NIA-funded ADRCs. The NACC database is funded by NIA/NIH Grant U24 AG072122. The study used NACC data to identify and characterize frontotemporal dementia (FTD) syndrome participants. Clinical diagnoses were established through consensus following established diagnostic criteria and research protocols. The dataset includes cognitive assessments (MMSE, MoCA), clinical diagnostic information for FTD subtypes including lvPPA, and limited biomarker data (31.1% with genetic testing, 0.02% with fluid biomarkers).

SCAN is a multi-institutional project that was funded as a U24 grant (AG067418) by the National Institute on Aging in May 2020. The dataset contributes to the study of frontotemporal dementia research through multi-institutional collaboration.

Advancing Research and Treatment in Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration–Longitudinal Evaluation of Familial Frontotemporal Dementia Subjects (ALLFTD) is a longitudinal study of FTD. The dataset includes participants with familial frontotemporal dementia and longitudinal follow-up data.

dataset_identifier: UCSF and ALLFTD Consortia C9orf72+ Longitudinal Neuroimaging and Biomarker Study
dataset_context_from_paper: Longitudinal structural and task-free fMRI data and plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) concentrations collected from C9orf72 expansion carriers recruited from UCSF and the ALLFTD Consortia. Mean time from first to last scan was 2.4±1.3 years. Participants included 36 asymptomatic (aSx-C9), 17 prodromal (prodromal-C9), 29 symptomatic (Sx-C9) carriers, and 107 healthy controls (HC). Structural MRI analyses used smoothed gray matter maps parcellated into 246 regions-of-interest based on the Brainnetome atlas. Voxelwise seed-based task-free fMRI analyses examined intrinsic connectivity networks (ICNs) including salience network (SN), sensorimotor network (SMN), default mode network (DMN), and medial pulvinar thalamus network. General linear models and linear mixed models compared groups at baseline and longitudinally, and examined associations between longitudinal functional connectivity changes and baseline NfL concentrations.

This two-step, individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis used data from eight Dutch cohorts. In the Rotterdam Study, plasma biomarkers of endothelial dysfunction (ED) were measured in two different ways. In the RS-I cohort, sICAM-1 and sVCAM-1 were determined using a commercially available ELISA (R&D Systems Europe). Plasma samples had been stored at -80°C. In the RS-III cohort, sICAM-1 and sVCAM-1 were measured using the Olink Target 96 Cardiometabolic panel. Blood samples were obtained and plasma was stored at -80°C. Mean ED plasma biomarkers levels in RS-I cohort exhibited lower average sICAM-1 levels (144.0 ± 38.7), whereas VCAM-1 levels were within the same range. In RS-III, ED biomarker levels were expressed in z-transformed normalized protein expression (NPX) values.

In the Leiden Longevity Study, fasting EDTA plasma was obtained in 2009 and stored for 18 years at -80°C. This cohort was included in the two-step, individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis using data from eight Dutch cohorts to measure plasma biomarkers of endothelial dysfunction.

In LASA, fasting blood samples were obtained in Amsterdam, Zwolle Oss, and the surrounding areas. The samples were centrifuged and stored at -80°C. This cohort was included in the two-step, individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis using data from eight Dutch cohorts to measure plasma biomarkers of endothelial dysfunction.

The Maastricht Study was one of eight Dutch cohorts included in the two-step, individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis. For this cohort, the ED Z-score was calculated using sICAM-1, sVCAM-1, sE-selectin, and von Willebrand factor as plasma biomarkers of endothelial dysfunction.

The BCS70 dataset was generated and analysed in the current study and is available from the UK Data Archive repository. The dataset was obtained by the authors and used for statistical analysis as part of the MELD-B project. A data landscape audit was performed mapping the available and relevant variables in BCS70 to the conceptualised domains.

The NCDS dataset was generated and analysed in the current study and is available from the UK Data Archive repository. The dataset was obtained by the authors and used for statistical analysis as part of the MELD-B project. The authors acknowledge the participants of the NCDS cohort study.

ACONF data can be accessed via the Grampian Data Safe Haven by accredited researchers with appropriate research governance approvals. The dataset was obtained by the authors and used as part of the MELD-B project analysis. The authors acknowledge the participants of the ACONF cohort study.

All the raw and processed WGS, snRNA-seq, and metadata are available from Synapse with accession syn51753326. The dataset includes whole genome sequencing and single nucleus RNA-seq data from 436 subjects that were integrated in multiple batches using reference-based integration with Seurat, RPCA, and SCTransform methods. The resulting integrated object was used for dimensionality reduction, clustering, and cell type annotation.

snRNA-seq reference dataset published earlier and leveraged for cell type annotation. Authors used this dataset as a reference for cell type label transfer using the 'FindTransferAnchors' and 'TransferData' functions in Seurat to annotate cell clusters and project query cells onto reference UMAPs.

The study used longitudinal data from the NIFD team. The authors analyzed rsfMRI-based topological data analysis (TDA) and structure-based atrophy analysis on subjects from this dataset. The dataset had decreasing sample size over the course of the disease with missing behavioral scores. Access to the data was provided through the Laboratory of Neuroimaging (LONI). The authors note that finer details such as information about genetics that are important in PPA were not available in the dataset. The study focused on primary progressive aphasia (PPA) variants, though other variants of PPA could not be included due to unavailability of data in the NIFD dataset.

DIAN-Obs data that was used in this study can be accessed upon review and approval of both the pertinent DIAN Core leaders and the Principal Investigator overseeing the grant. The dataset includes biospecimens and observational data from participants in the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network study, which was established in 2008 with grant U19AG032438 to Washington University from the National Institute on Aging. The study involves participants with genetic mutations (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) associated with early-onset Alzheimer's disease, with clinical assessments including Clinical Dementia Rating Scale and estimated years to symptom onset (DIAN-EYO).

Individual-participant data meta-analysis using data from 21 cohorts drawn from 17 countries across six continents. All cohorts are part of the Cohort Studies of Memory in an International Consortium (COSMIC) collaboration. Data were provided by the contributing studies on the understanding that relevant study leaders be contacted for further use of their data and additional formal data sharing agreements be made. Researchers can apply to use COSMIC data by completing a COSMIC Research Proposal Form.

dataset_identifier: Not specified - available from corresponding author
dataset_context_from_paper: The datasets analyzed during the current study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. The study tested whether a quantitative approach using cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples is feasible and reliable for seed quantification based on endpoint dilution RT-QuIC. Results demonstrate that SD50 values showed a strong positive association with brain LB-density score, a measure of Lewy Body Disease (LBD) burden detected by immunohistochemistry, and with LBD stages. The research involved CSF samples and brain homogenates analyzed through α-syn RT-QuIC methodology to estimate α-syn seed concentration and predict the burden and extent of underlying LBD pathology.

Multicohort study examined data from US adults aged 65 and older enrolled in the Health and Retirement Study (2013). Data were analyzed from May 27 to September 24, 2024. Of 10,974 participants (60.0% female, mean age: 73.2 years), 2,445 developed incident all-cause dementia over 116,067 person-years of follow-up. The primary outcome was all-cause dementia ascertained at least 2 years after baseline from active research follow-ups and passive surveillance.

Multicohort study examined data from US adults aged 65 and older enrolled in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study (1987-1995). Participants were followed for a mean of 10.7 years to assess associations of sugar-sweetened beverages (SSB) and artificially sweetened beverages (ASB) with incident dementia using Cox proportional hazard regression models.

Multicohort study examined data from US adults aged 65 and older enrolled in the Chicago Healthy and Aging Project (1993-2012). Data contributed to the pooled analysis of 10,974 older adults examining consumption of SSB and ASB in relation to all-cause dementia risk.

Multicohort study examined data from US adults aged 65 and older enrolled in the Rush Memory and Aging Project (1997-2005). Participants were included in the pooled analysis of 10,974 older adults to assess whether consumption of SSB and ASB is associated with the risk of all-cause dementia.

Multicohort study examined data from US adults aged 65 and older enrolled in the Framingham Heart Study original cohort (1986-1994). Data were included in the pooled analysis examining associations of SSB and ASB with incident dementia over a mean follow-up of 10.7 years.

Multicohort study examined data from US adults aged 65 and older enrolled in the Framingham Heart Study offspring cohort (1991-2001). This cohort contributed to the pooled analysis of 10,974 participants with 2,445 incident dementia cases over 116,067 person-years of follow-up.

dataset_identifier: In-house Dazhou Central Hospital MRI-text dataset

dataset_context_from_paper: Self-constructed dataset included 10 de-identified clinical text samples provided by Dazhou Central Hospital and additional data collected from publicly available platforms such as Kaggle, comprising 2,106 paired samples of structural MRI scans and clinical text. Samples were categorized into four diagnostic groups: Non-dementia, Very Mild dementia, Mild dementia, and Moderate dementia. Clinical text was extracted from de-identified electronic medical records with chief complaints summarized by clinical staff into symptom-level phrases. The in-house cohort was jointly used with ADNI1, ADNI GO, and ADNI2 for model development.

Public Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort was incorporated as a multi-center public validation source. Only T1-weighted structural MRI and baseline demographic/clinical variables were used, without introducing additional modalities such as PET, CSF, or APOE genotype. ADNI1, ADNI GO, ADNI2, and the in-house cohort were jointly used for model development, whereas ADNI3 was reserved as an independent external validation cohort. Demographic information was obtained from baseline records. The validation set, internal test set, and ADNI3 external validation set retained their original class distributions without resampling or augmentation.

Additional data collected from publicly available platforms such as Kaggle, comprising 2,106 paired samples of structural MRI scans and clinical text as part of the self-constructed dataset. These samples were categorized into four diagnostic groups: Non-dementia, Very Mild dementia, Mild dementia, and Moderate dementia.

HRS data are publicly available and were used for this study. The study involved dataset construction and analysis of HRS data to examine loneliness intervention outcomes. HRS data collection was approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Review Board. All HRS participants provided informed consent. The proposed study used publicly available de-identified data.

dataset_context_from_paper: Data from 944 participants enrolled in the Global Alzheimer's Platform (GAP) Bio-Hermes trial. After exclusion of technical failures (N=9), subgroups in the 'Non-Hispanic or Latino' population were defined as Group 1 ('Black or African American') and Group 2 ('White'). Amyloid status was defined qualitatively through expert neuroradiologist visual read and quantitatively through SUVR analysis. The study investigated differences in amyloid status classification between racial groups, examining GCA SUVR values and Grothe Stages 2, 3, and 4 across groups. Findings suggest potential differences in patterns of amyloid deposition between racial groups that may confound quantitative and visual classification of amyloid status.

The data used in this study were obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. ADNI was launched in 2003 as a public–private partnership, led by Principal Investigator Michael W. Weiner, MD. The primary goal of ADNI has been to test whether serial MRI, PET, other biological markers, and clinical and neuropsychological assessment can be combined to measure the progression of MCI and early AD. The study utilized MRI scans from ADNI subjects for classification of Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), early MCI (EMCI), late MCI (LMCI), and cognitively normal (CN) groups. MRI scans in ADNI originate from multiple vendors and protocols. Previous studies referenced in this work used 202, 660, and other numbers of ADNI subjects for various classification tasks achieving accuracies ranging from 85.71% to 91.2%.

The LOAD dataset was developed from multiple brain banks representing large independent research efforts within AMP‐AD and TREAT‐AD. The transcriptomic dataset was drawn from the Religious Orders Study/Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP), Mayo, and Mount Sinai brain banks, comprising over 1700 individual brains across genders, ethnicities, and age brackets. The compiled datasets are currently available on the AD Knowledge Portal. The transcriptomic dataset was analyzed and compared to the Kat5 cKO model.

To assess the similarity of the Kat5 cKO transcriptomic profile across neurodegenerative disease states, we examined the TREAT‐AD LOAD transcriptomic data, the LOAD diversity cohort (LOAD_DC). Correlation mapping was performed with LOAD_DC also correlating in epigenetics.

The upregulated and downregulated DEGs within the Kat5 cKO model at each tier (1.2, 1.5, and 2‐fold) were compared to the 2023 GWAS Catalogue (which incorporates both TopMed and UK Biobanks data) to assess enrichment of genetic trait linkage using the Enrichr tool.

Periodically a checked and approved copy of the live DIAN database is frozen and a copy is saved (referred to as a data freeze), no further data is entered into the frozen copy and it is subsequently made available for analysis. The first analytical sample encompassed all participants available at the DIAN study data freeze 13, where data were deemed useable, approved by study monitors, and passed all quality control measures. The second sample was a subset of the full sample and included only participants who had at least one follow-up visit after baseline, at least two blood pressure measures and who had a baseline CDR <0.5. CSF biomarkers for AD-related amyloid at baseline were available for 420 participants, with measurements of Aβ42/40 ratio, Aβ42, and Aβ40 differing between mutation carrier (MC) and non-carrier (NC) groups.

ADNI dataset used for training, validating, and testing RAVEN, a deep learning method for super-resolution of neuroimaging data. The dataset was used across multiple experiments with different degradation modes and upsampling factors (2×2×2, 3×, and 4×).

AHEAD (Amsterdam Ultra-high field adult lifespan database) used for training, validating, and testing RAVEN super-resolution method. Multimodal 7 Tesla MRI database used across multiple upsampling experiments.
AOMIC dataset used for training, validating, and testing RAVEN with different degradation modes and upsampling factors in neuroimaging super-resolution experiments.

UNC Paired 3T-7T Dataset used for training, validating, and testing RAVEN super-resolution method. Dataset contains paired MRI acquisitions at different field strengths used across multiple upsampling experiments.
HBA dataset used for training, validating, and testing RAVEN with different degradation modes and upsampling factors in neuroimaging super-resolution experiments.

Human Connectome Project (HCP) data used for training, validating, and testing RAVEN. The paper notes that alternative deep learning methods (ArSSR-RDN and SuperFormer) were trained on HCP data but were outperformed by traditional methods (Lanczos, Trilinear, NLMUPSAMPLE) at 2×2×2 upsampling factor, while showing improved performance at upsampling factors of 3 and above.
OSCBS 7T quantitative dataset used for training, validating, and testing RAVEN super-resolution method across multiple degradation modes and upsampling factors.
LUSEBRINK dataset (ds003563) used for training, validating, and testing RAVEN with different degradation modes and upsampling factors in neuroimaging super-resolution experiments.

All data from this study are available on request from the DIAN at dian.wustl.edu/our-research/observational-study/dianobservationalstudy-investigator-resources/. The dataset involves acquisition of data by multiple researchers across international neurology and neuroscience institutions including Washington University, University of Tübingen, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, University of Ulsan, Mayo Clinic, Massachusetts General Hospital, University of Pittsburgh, and Brown University, indicating a multi-site observational study of neurodegenerative disease.

The MRI, PET, and associated clinical data from the MCSA are available under restricted access due to institutional review board (IRB) requirements and participant consent limitations. Access is limited to qualified academic and industry researchers for research purposes. Requests for access must be submitted to the MCSA Executive Committee via the Global Alzheimer's Association Interactive Network (GAAIN) portal. The study utilized available NODDI data in MCSA-CU participants (n = 235) to extract regional NDI values for the major white matter fibers within two predefined regions of interest, with higher NDI values indicating greater microstructural integrity. Associations between regional white matter NDIs and FDG-PET SUVR were assessed using partial correlation analyses.

The imaging and demographic data used in this study from the ADNI are publicly available in the ADNI database to qualified researchers upon registration. All analyses were conducted separately in MCSA and ADNI using all available data for each biomarker; sample sizes varied by biomarker and are reported in the figure legends.

Reference panel of 15,958 whole-genome sequenced genomes from ADSP R3 with diverse populations, including NHW, AA, Asian, and Hispanic, constructed to provide high-quality reference panels for ADRD research. Final dataset contained 43,735,105 SNVs and 3,199,390 indels after stringent filtering. Panel was used for genotype imputation and compared against TOPMed-r2 reference panel, capturing rare but potentially causal indels and high-quality structural variants missed by TOPMed-r2.
ADGC datasets were used to assess the performance of the ADSP R3 reference panels through imputation analysis and comparison to the public reference panel TOPMed-r2.

Public reference panel including 97,256 WGS samples, the largest reference panel for genotype imputation available at the time of study. Used as comparison benchmark for the ADSP-Short-Var panel. Imputation results showed that TOPMed-r2 was missing 10 out of 55 indels identified by ADSP panel in genes including TMDD1, TOMM20L, FAM174B, NTN3, RGL3, PNKP, PPDPF, and PCDHB13.

dataset_context_from_paper: Baseline/longitudinal amyloid/tau positron emission tomography (PET) data across two independent AD cohorts (N = 490) combined with multimodal connectomics data. Authors quantified epicenter broadcast capacity (EBC) to determine whether tau epicenters preferentially access regions supporting cross-network communication or within-network communication.

The paper references DIAN (Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network) in the context of studying autosomal-dominant Alzheimer's disease (ADAD). The research involves biomarker analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) using seed amplification assay (SAA) to evaluate pathological burden in patients with AD-LBD (Alzheimer's disease with Lewy body disease co-pathology). The study aims to develop precision medicine approaches for estimating relative burden of pathology in preclinical stages using CSF biomarkers.

The EMIF-AD MBD study was conducted as part of the EMIF-AD project. Proteomics was performed with tandem mass tag mass spectrometry (TMT-MS) with 10+1 plexing using high pH reverse phase high-performance liquid chromatography for peptide prefractionation. CSF samples were analyzed and protein concentrations were log-transformed and scaled according to control group values. Proteins were selected when detected in both cohorts with at least 70% of individuals having observations, resulting in 978 proteins. Data was pooled with ADC cohort to increase subgroup sample sizes for different APOE alleles.

Proteomics was performed with tandem mass tag mass spectrometry (TMT-MS) with 16-plexing using high pH reverse phase high-performance liquid chromatography for peptide prefractionation. Reference channels were used to normalize peptide relative abundances between TMT experiments. Protein concentrations were log-transformed and scaled according to control group values (A−T− individuals with APOE ε3/ε3 genotype). Proteins were selected when detected in both cohorts with at least 70% of individuals having observations, resulting in 978 proteins. Data was pooled with EMIF-AD MBD cohort.

The KHHP cohort was used to study gene-environment interactions between FOXO3 genotype and chronic hypertension. Participants with autopsy and genotyping data were included in the analysis. Genotyping of FOXO3 and apolipoprotein E (APOE) variants was performed on blood samples that had been frozen at –70ºC. For men who participated in Examination 4 (1991–1993), DNA for genotyping was obtained from the blood sample buffy coat. Brain autopsy data were coded in two distinct periods (1992–2003 and 2003–2012) with microscopic neuropathologic assessments performed by senior neuropathologists who were blind to clinical features. The study examined how FOXO3 G-allele carriage attenuates the impact of chronic hypertension on cerebral microinfarcts (CMI), with standardized brain locations assessed including caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, thalamus, frontal lobe, temporal lobe, parietal lobe, occipital lobe, hippocampus, and brainstem.

Monongahela-Youghiogheny Healthy Aging Team (MYHAT), whose data was used in this manuscript, has been approved by University of Pittsburgh Institutional Review Board. The IRB approval number is STUDY19040058. The dataset includes depressive symptoms measured using mCES-D (with the 'I felt lonely' item omitted to avoid overlap with loneliness measures), general health status (self-rated health on a 1-5 scale), physical functional status (number of prescription medications, dichotomized at 4 or more medications), and IADL scores ranging from 0 to 7 measuring instrumental activities of daily living.

Clinical trial dataset examining cognitively unimpaired participants (N = 182, age mean±SD = 64.8±7.5; 60% female; years of education mean±SD = 14.4±2.5; 20% Hispanic; 3-5 weeks between tests). Used to assess test-retest reliability of digital Trail Making Test Part B (dTMT-B) via intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC 3, k). Reliability was assessed for time to complete (TTC) showing ICC of 0.87 (95% CI = 0.83-0.90, p < 0.0001) and total errors (TE) showing ICC of 0.65 (95% CI = 0.53-0.74, p < 0.0001).

Clinical trial dataset with cognitively unimpaired participants (N = 342, age mean±SD = 70.5±6.4; 63% female; years of education mean[IQR] = 16[14-23]; 6% Hispanic). Visit 1 data combined with DCT216 visit 1 data to assess validity of dTMT-B through multiple linear regression predicting time to complete (TTC) using predictors for study, age, sex, education, ethnicity, and interactions. Found significant main effect of age (T = 7.48, p < 0.001) with no significant interactions (p > 0.05), suggesting consistent performance trends across studies.

Cryo-EM map for Type I amyloid filament structure. Cryo-EM maps and atomic coordinates have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB with accession codes: EMD-75195 (Type I) and EMD-75196 (Type II), and PDB 10IJ (Type I) and 10IK (Type II).

Atomic coordinates for Type I amyloid filament structure. Cryo-EM maps and atomic coordinates have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB with accession codes: EMD-75195 (Type I) and EMD-75196 (Type II), and PDB 10IJ (Type I) and 10IK (Type II).

Atomic coordinates for Type II amyloid filament structure. Cryo-EM maps and atomic coordinates have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB with accession codes: EMD-75195 (Type I) and EMD-75196 (Type II), and PDB 10IJ (Type I) and 10IK (Type II).

Poly(A) RNA ligand structure obtained from PDB entry 8ZWJ. The poly(A) RNA ligand was obtained from PDB entry 8ZWJ. A poly(G) RNA model was generated by modifying the purine base of the poly(A) RNA structure.

Inositol diphosphate structure obtained from PDB entry 1I9Z. The inositol diphosphate structure was obtained from PDB entry 1I9Z. Inositol diphosphate fits well in an arrangement in which the phosphate groups interact with K290, K294, Y310, and K311.

Filament fold comparison code is available at https://github.com/degrado-lab/amyloid_analysis. The code is used for comparing amyloid filament folds across different structural types including AGD Type I, P301T Type I, and CBD folds.

All data analyzed from the full LBP cohort are available via the AD Knowledge Portal. The data, analyses and tools are shared early in the research cycle without a publication embargo on secondary use. Data is available for general research use according to the following requirements for data access and data attribution. For access to content described in this manuscript see: https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn51622714/datasets/

All data analyzed from the full LBP cohort are available via the AD Knowledge Portal (https://adknowledgeportal.org). The AD Knowledge Portal is a platform for accessing data, analyses, and tools generated by the Accelerating Medicines Partnership (AMP-AD) Target Discovery Program and other National Institute on Aging (NIA)-supported programs to enable open-science practices and accelerate translational learning.

Gene set enrichment analyses were performed using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database. The htext-formatted hsa00001 KEGG database was downloaded on October 4th, 2021, via the KEGG web server and parsed into structured data tables in python. All KEGG gene sets with the top-level string 'Human' were excluded from analysis since these gene sets may be derived from studies of postmortem human tissues. Sets with less than 10 member genes were excluded from analysis, leaving 278 KEGG gene sets tested for enrichment.

Genetic and clinical data from the Mount Sinai Million Health Discoveries Program (MSM-HDP; formerly, the BioMe Biobank Program; N = 29,064) were analyzed to test the effects of rare PTVs in the genes encoding RNA transcripts in TPAWN on illnesses of brain functions. The genetic data was comprised of whole-exome sequencing (for identifying rare PTVs) and microarray (for calculating genetic principal components); the clinical data was comprised of billing codes from the electronic medical records that had been mapped to phecodes.

ADNI data used for analysis of infarct availability and APOE ε4 availability across cognitive groups. Dataset includes cognitively unimpaired (CU) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) participants stratified by amyloid (A) and tau (T) biomarker status. Infarct availability in ADNI: CU A−T−: 225/268, CU A+T− 100/112, AD A+T− 14/18, AD A+T+ 45/58. APOE ε4 availability ADNI: CU A−T−: 235/268, CU A+T− 100/112, AD A+T− 15/18, AD A+T+ 54/58. Hippocampal volume availability in ADNI: CU A−T−: 200/268, CU A+T− 89/112, AD A+T− 14/18, AD A+T+ 44/58. ADNI data are disseminated by the Laboratory for Neuro Imaging at the University of Southern California.

Amsterdam-based cohort used for validation of infarct and APOE ε4 analysis. Infarct availability in Amsterdam-based cohort: CU A−T−: 38/92, CU A+T− 15/39, AD A+T− 10/10, AD A+T+ 75/75. APOE ε4 availability in Amsterdam-based cohort: CU A−T−: 86/92, CU A+T− 38/39, AD A+T− 10/10, AD A+T+ 71/75.

123 I-FP-CIT SPECT scans of three familial frontotemporal dementia (fFTD) individuals with MAPT N279K mutation and similar autopsy findings of frontotemporal degeneration with severe neuronal loss in the substantia nigra. The study found prominent decrease of dopamine transporter binding (z-score < −5.0) was present at prodromal fFTD without parkinsonism.

Peak calls, ChromBPNet models, ChromBPNet variant scores, and FLARE variant scores made available for the study. These outputs represent the computational predictions and variant scoring results generated as part of the research.

Adult heart data and cell-type annotations from the latest ENCODE release. The data includes human left ventricle snATAC-seq experiments from the Michael Snyder lab at Stanford, representing single-nucleus ATAC-seq chromatin accessibility data.
DOI-minted repository containing replicated neuro-variants code and models for variant analysis and functional prediction in neurological contexts.

Short read WGS from the ADSP is available via NIAGADS (ADSP R4: ng00067.v10). This dataset was used for whole genome sequencing analysis and variant calling in the study.

dataset_context_from_paper: Long read sequencing is available upon request from the corresponding author. DNA was extracted in the HIHG biorepository using the AutoGen FlexSTAR. Libraries were constructed using the SQK-LSK109 ligation kit from Oxford Nanopore Technology (ONT). Samples were loaded onto PromethION R9.4.1 flow cells and sequenced in 72-hour data acquisition runs on the PromethION24 device. Base calling was performed with Guppy version 3.3.2. Resulting FASTQs were aligned to GRCh38 using minimap2 v2.17-r941. Small variant calling was performed with Clair3 (v1.0.3). Sniffles2 (v2.0.7) was used for structural variant calling.

Participants were part of the BIOCARD study including 136 cognitively normal individuals and 21 participants with mild cognitive impairment (mean age = 71.7 years). The study investigated cross-sectional relationships between actigraphy-estimated total volume of physical activity (TVPA) and sleep patterns [total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency (SE)] with cognitive performance (n = 157). In a subset of participants (n = 135), physical activity and sleep measures were evaluated in relationship to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) measures of large-scale network connectivity and positron emission tomography (PET) measures of amyloid-β. Linear regression analyses assessed associations between TVPA, TST, and SE with cognition, connectivity within default-mode, salience, and fronto-parietal control networks, and network modularity.

The Phenoverse framework is implemented as a Python PyPI package, and the source code is available at https://github.com/KellisLab/Phenoverse. Documentation for using the tool is available at https://kellislab.github.io/Phenoverse/. The framework was used to translate high-resolution single-cell transcriptomic disease cohorts into sample-level disease continua and cell type-specific molecular programs.

Using the single-cell transcriptomic PBMC dataset, we investigated whether Phenoverse can identify cell type-specific disease states by learning from binary sample phenotype labels. We trained Phenoverse and applied it to held-out samples comprising approximately 600,000 cells across 131 samples spanning nine cell types. The dataset was used to study Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by dysregulation of interferon signaling in circulating immune cell compartments. The representation space exhibited a clear separation of samples between SLE and healthy groups.

The pathway activity along the Phenoverse inferred trajectory was computed per cell type by performing single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) against hallmark gene sets from the molecular signatures database (MSigDB). Gene set enrichment analysis was performed against MSigDB Hallmark gene sets for the top 200 positively correlated genes per prototype.

Qualitative research study involving systematic stakeholder engagement for breast cancer screening programme reform in Scotland. Data collection included interviews and focus group meetings with stakeholders across three geographical areas of Scotland (urban and rural populations). All data generated during this study are included in the published article and its supplementary information files. Interviews and focus group meetings were transcribed verbatim by an external transcriber company and double-checked by researchers. Two researchers double-coded 10% of transcripts to ensure consistency. Study registered on 16/02/2021.

Summary statistics from the main meta-analysis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) genome-wide association study. The meta-analysis included 72,721 AD cases, 55,960 proxy ADRD cases, 614,267 controls and 235,566 proxy controls from 52 studies, with an effective sample size of 230,631. After quality control, associations for 20,045,120 variants were considered. The analysis identified 91 genome-wide significant loci (P ≤ 5 × 10−8), including 16 new loci in European-ancestry samples.

Summary statistics from the no-proxy meta-analysis of Alzheimer's disease GWAS, a sensitivity analysis excluding proxy ADRD cases. This analysis identified new loci including UBFD1 and LRRC25 as genome-wide significant, and 12 known ADRD loci became genome-wide significant after focusing on clinically diagnosed AD cases.

Summary statistics from the no-biobank meta-analysis of Alzheimer's disease GWAS, excluding large biobanks (UKBB, FinnGen, deCODE and HUNT studies) that used International Classification of Diseases codes to identify AD cases. This sensitivity analysis identified UBFD1 and LRRC25 as genome-wide significant loci and four additional tier 2 loci.

Polygenic score derived from the main Alzheimer's disease meta-analysis GWAS results. Genetic scores are available in Supplementary Table 15 and through the PGS Catalog for use in predicting genetic risk for Alzheimer's disease.

High-quality imputed genotypes dataset (imputation quality >0.8) used for computing linkage disequilibrium (LD) in pathway analyses. LD was computed from the EADB-core dataset with genotypes having genotype probability of ≥0.9 included in the analysis.

Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) is a prospective cohort study of older adults. Dementia free individuals age 65 are evaluated every two years with the Cognitive Abilities Screening Instrument (CASI). Those with low scores receive a clinical evaluation with an extensive neurocognitive battery; all data are reviewed at a multidisciplinary consensus conference. CASI and neurocognitive battery data are processed for composite memory, executive functioning, language, and visuospatial scores. At death, consenting participants receive a standardized postmortem evaluation including guideline-based assessments of Alzheimer's type pathology (CERAD score, Braak stage, Thal phase, and ADNC score) and cerebral amyloid angiopathy, LATE, Lewy bodies, hippocampal sclerosis, atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis, deep and cerebral microinfarcts, and gross infarcts. The analysis included 864 people with autopsy data: 432 cognitively normal, 74 with other dementia forms, and 358 with AD dementia subdivided into cognitive phenotypes (AD-No Domain, AD-Visuospatial, AD-Memory, AD-Language, AD-Executive).

As of a data cutoff of December 3, 2024, 243 participants were screened and 197 randomized in DIAN‐TU‐001 Tau NexGen trial (Cohort 1: 97; Cohort 2: 100). DIAN‐TU‐001 is a phase II/III multicenter randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled platform trial of potential disease modifying therapies utilizing biomarker, cognitive, and clinical endpoints in DIAD. The purpose of this study is to assess the safety, tolerability, biomarker, cognitive and clinical efficacy of investigational products in participants with an AD‐causing mutation by determining if treatment with the anti‐tau antibody (etalanetug) slows the rate of progression of cognitive/clinical impairment or improves disease‐related biomarkers. Cohort 1 represents Symptomatic Population (CDR=0.5‐1) with mean age 47.8 years and mean CDR‐SB 3.7; Cohort 2 represents Asymptomatic Population (CDR=0) with mean age 43.4 years and mean CDR‐SB 0.1. APOE4 carrier frequency was 25.8% in Cohort 1 and 21.0% in Cohort 2. The most common gene type was PSEN1 (78.4% in Cohort 1; 85.0% in Cohort 2).

dataset_context_from_paper: Limited datasets provided by the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center (RADC) through a data use agreement request. These datasets were selected for analysis due to their extensive information on HRT and associated neuropathological changes. Inclusion criteria were information about HRT and neuropathological data available. Missing data included age at menarche (18 non-HRT, 10 HRT), menopause type (six non-HRT, five HRT), age at menopause (38 non-HRT, 22 HRT), and reproductive duration (44 non-HRT, 24 HRT).

The CEPAC model is a validated microsimulation of HIV disease and treatment. Upon entry into the model, simulated individuals draw for CD4 count and HIV RNA from user-defined initial distributions. Simulated PWH in care are treated with ART and transition monthly between health states defined by CD4 count, HIV RNA, history of opportunistic infection (OI), and ART use. They can disengage from HIV care, stop ART, and subsequently return to care and reinitiate ART. Death among PWH can occur from HIV-related causes (OI or chronic HIV-related mortality), AAD, or other non-HIV-/non-AAD-related causes (e.g., cancers, suicide).

The Age-associated Dementia Policy (AgeD-Pol) model is a computer microsimulation model that projects age- and sex-specific prevalence, incidence, and mortality of AAD in the US. The CEPAC model was expanded to incorporate features of the AgeD-Pol model. AAD-associated input parameters (i.e., AAD incidence, progression, and mortality) were parameterized with data from the general US population; for AAD incidence in PWH, age-/sex-stratified AAD incidence was increased as recently reported.

Genomic DNA was extracted from frozen brain tissue. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed using the SureSelectTX Human All-Exon library (v6; Agilent). A HiSeq 4000 (Illumina) was used for sequencing with 75-bp paired-end reads. WES data were analyzed for variants in ALS/FTD-associated genes, including ANXA11, SOD1, SETX, FUS, PGRN, VAPB, ANG, TARDBP, FIG4, OPTN, VCP, UBQLN2, SQSTM1, PFN1. No pathogenic variants were identified in any gene.

Systematic review protocol examining therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) and pharmacogenomics (PGx) implementation. A comprehensive search of eight scientific databases and grey literature sources revealed 10,341 relevant papers. Title and abstract screening and full-text screening were performed, requiring consensus between two independent reviewers. Of the screened articles, 35 qualified for and had data extraction performed.

Healthcare database used by Ontario Health Teams (OHTs) to measure frailty using the Johns Hopkins Adjusted Clinical Groups indicator. The study aimed to identify validated clinical and machine learning methods of measuring frailty using healthcare databases and recommend the most effective frailty indicator to the OHTs. The EMR was also used to document Goals of Care (GCD) and dementia diagnoses for persons living with dementia (PLWD).

dataset_identifier: MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, CINAHL, PsycINFO systematic review search
data_repository: Multiple databases (MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, CINAHL, PsycINFO)
dataset_context_from_paper: Systematic review searched MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and grey literature from inception until June 13, 2024, for randomized trials (RCTs) comparing any intervention's efficacy to usual care or any other intervention for reducing depressive symptoms or burden in persons living with dementia's family or friend caregivers. Independent reviewer pairs conducted study screening, data abstraction, risk of bias appraisal, and GRADE assessments.

MRI scans were obtained from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA) which contributed 1,032 scans from 1,032 participants (mean age, 73.32 ± 13.36 years; 45.6% male, 54.4% female). Data from this cohort was used for model training and internal validation. After training the nnU-Net V2 model for nearly 1,000 epochs on MRI data from BLSA, BIOCARD, and Johns Hopkins cohorts, it achieved a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.98 during internal validation.

The BIOCARD study contributed 395 scans from 395 participants (mean age, 64.22 ± 11.02 years; 40.8% male, 59.2% female). Data from this cohort was used for model training and internal validation. The nnU-Net V2 model was trained on MRI data from BLSA, BIOCARD, and Johns Hopkins cohorts, achieving a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.98 during internal validation.

The Johns Hopkins Hydrocephalus Clinic provided 195 scans from 195 patients (mean age, 71.54 ± 8.30 years; 53.8% male, 46.2% female). Data from this cohort was used for model training and internal validation. The nnU-Net V2 model was trained on MRI data from BLSA, BIOCARD, and Johns Hopkins cohorts, achieving a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.98 during internal validation.

The PENS cohort contributed 190 scans from 99 participants (mean age, 75.00 ± 5.70 years; 51.5% male, 48.5% female) and served as the external validation dataset. When the trained model was applied to all scans from the PENS trial for external validation, it sustained its performance, yielding an overall Dice score of 0.98.

Sample included 50 symptomatic and 70 prodromal, sporadic and familial FTD participants (CDR®+NACC‐FTLD = 1 or 0.5, respectively) with a range of FTD syndromes, and 70 controls (CDR®+NACC‐FTLD = 0, no pathogenic mutation) from the ALLFTD Consortium. Participants completed a two‐minute, 100‐trial digital flanker assessment on the ALLFTD Mobile App. We extracted 301 distribution metrics, based on reaction time and trial type, and 15 traditional metrics using an in‐house pipeline. Random forest models were trained using 5‐fold cross validation to classify controls from prodromal or from symptomatic individuals.

Pre-processed scRNAseq by Schulte-Schrepping et al. was downloaded from (https://beta.fastgenomics.org/datasets/detail-dataset-1ad2967be372494a9fdba621610ad3f3#Files). Pre-processed human scRNA-seq data by Schulte-Schrepping et. al. was re-analyzed using Seurat. High quality neutrophils were selected after high mitochondrial or ribosomal gene expressing cells were removed.

The Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) dataset was used for analyzing plaque burden associations with sex. The study performed group comparisons using Kruskal-Wallis test, Chi-square test, and Fisher's exact test. Multivariable logistic regression was applied to assess sex association with greater presence of plaque burden after adjusting for potential confounders including age at death and ApoE status.

The PPMI is a longitudinal observational study of 1,923 participants with PD, or at risk for PD, and healthy volunteers, thereby contributing comprehensive clinical and imaging data and biological samples from 33 clinical sites around the world. In the PPMI study, patients in the PD cohort have been diagnosed within two years of enrollment. Importantly, they are de novo patients and as such, not yet taking PD medications, which may confound biomarker analyses. The PPMI samples (discovery cohort) were randomly split into a training set (80%) and a validation set (20%). Of the 874 DEGs from discovery dataset, 502 genes were replicated in the replication dataset with a nominal p-value < 0.05.

The PDBP is another PD program that collects standardized longitudinal clinical data and biospecimens across all stages of PD. The program has 1,604 participants and was developed to accelerate the discovery of promising new diagnostic and progression biomarkers for PD. Final models were tested on the independent PDBP/BioFIND samples (replication cohort).

The Fox Investigation for New Discovery of Biomarkers (BioFIND) is an observational clinical study designed to discover and verify biomarkers of PD, which includes blood and cerebrospinal fluid, in 118 well-defined, moderately advanced people with PD and 88 control volunteers. Final models were tested on the independent PDBP/BioFIND samples (replication cohort).

This study used data from the AMP PD program, which includes eight cohorts from the PPMI, PDBP, and BioFIND study, with PAXgene-based total RNA-seq data, whole genome sequences, and clinical data available for 3,274 participants (release v2). The PPMI, PDBP, and BioFIND data can be accessed from the AMP-PD Google Cloud Storage with the approved 'Data Use Approvement'.
The brain neuron data and the NanoString were produced in our own lab.

Large multicenter cohort of individuals with MCI who have longitudinal clinical follow-up and multimodal neuroimaging data available. Study includes discovery cohort and independent external validation cohort with approximately 2 years of follow-up duration. Dataset contains tau PET imaging, MRI data, and clinical outcomes including MMSE scores and APOE ε4 genotype information used to predict progression from stable MCI to dementia.

Analyses included 121 BIOCARD study participants who were cognitively unimpaired at baseline (mean age 57 years). Current tau burden was measured by 18F-MK6240 PET, and prior levels and trajectories of change in CSF AD biomarkers were measured with p-tau181, total tau (t-tau), and Aβ42/Aβ40 (Lumipulse assay), collected approximately bi-annually over a mean of 12.8 years prior to the tau PET scan. Linear mixed-effect models examined how prior CSF biomarker levels and rates of change in these CSF markers relate to current tau PET burden, covarying for age, sex, education, APOE4 genotype, and amyloid positivity.

dataset_context_from_paper: Professor Rohrer introduced the Frontotemporal Dementia Prevention Initiative (FPI), a global endeavor targeting familial forms of FTD, integrating ongoing cohort studies worldwide. The FPI involves over 300 researchers and 3,000 participants worldwide. Key achievements included clinical rating scale development, validation of multimodal biomarkers for trials, and fluid biomarker validation, notably plasma neurofilament light chain. Ongoing studies explored genomics and digital biomarkers, culminating in a global platform trial for testing novel FTD therapies, initially focusing on MAPT gene mutations.

data_repository: Chinese Familial Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration Consortium database
dataset_context_from_paper: Professor Chen presented cross-sectional reports of Chinese FTD patients with gene mutations and updated status of the longitudinal study by the Chinese Familial Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration Consortium (CFFC). The CFFC was initiated in October 2022 with seven top teaching hospitals, and has expanded to over 20 centers. The CFFC has enrolled 26 pedigrees with MAPT mutations, 11 with GRN mutations, and 9 with C9orf72 repeat expansions. The CFFC has also endeavored to create a behavioral assessment scale for Chinese bvFTD patients, to develop voice-based digital biomarkers for various PPA types, and to participate in international phase III clinical trials for familial FTD.

dataset_context_from_paper: Study data from antemortem MRI volumes of amygdala nuclei and hippocampal subfields in 16 PART-TDP-α and 12 FTLD-TDP-A autopsy-confirmed cases. Data includes measurements across 30 hippocampal and amygdala regions of interest (ROIs) including CA1 body, hippocampal tail, lateral amygdala, and central amygdala nuclei. Hippocampal tail and CA1 body volumes were smaller in PART-TDP-α group, which also had smaller lateral and central amygdala nuclei compared to FTLD-TDP-A group. Statistical analysis included Welch's t-tests comparing deviation values between groups and FDR correction for multiple comparisons.

We searched the gene expression omni (GEO) for datasets evaluating the gene expression of obese vs. normal weight and individuals with high peak bone mass (PBM), an important determinant of osteoporosis, versus subjects with low PBM. The datasets were analyzed using affy and limma packages in R. The up-regulated differentially expressed genes (DEGS) in each dataset were retrieved and the community between three lists was obtained through a Venn diagram. The shared genes were enriched in Enrichr and Enrichr-KG.

The final cohort contained 1,200 subjects, including 350 NC, 550 MCI, and 300 AD subjects. The dataset was divided into training, validation, and test sets using a stratified subject-level split with a ratio of 70%/10%/20%. The MCI group was larger than the NC and AD groups, reflecting the common distribution of ADNI-based NC/MCI/AD classification studies. The dataset was used to evaluate the APLG-Net method for disease progression classification using ordinal objectives that encode NC, MCI, and AD as [0, 0], [1, 0], and [1, 1]. Evaluation metrics included Accuracy, Balanced Accuracy, Macro-F1, Macro-AUC, and class-wise precision, recall, and F1 score.

Part of the data were from the ADNI. The study analyzed progression trajectories in MCI subtypes (MCI-A with AD-like perfusion changes and MCI-N with perfusion similar to normal controls) using baseline and longitudinal cerebral blood flow (CBF) measurements. Logistic regression analysis was conducted to assess the association between baseline subtype and the risk of conversion from MCI to AD during the follow-up period.

Part of the data were from the UK Biobank. The study utilized this resource to analyze progression trajectories in MCI subtypes and their progression patterns in deviation scores related to cerebral perfusion metrics.

The Adult Changes in Thought Study (ACT) cohort is referenced as a pharmacoepidemiology study population that reports associations between specific anticholinergic classes – antidepressants and bladder antimuscarinics – and increased dementia incidence. Human induced pluripotent stem cells were generated from ACT participants to directly examine the effects of various anticholinergic classes on dementia-related cellular phenotypes. The authors generated 16 hiPSC lines from ACT participants and differentiated them to cortical neurons (hiPSC-Ns) for drug treatment experiments.

dataset_identifier: hiPSC-derived neuronal dataset from ACT participants
dataset_context_from_paper: 16 hiPSC lines were generated from ACT participants and differentiated to cortical neurons (hiPSC-Ns). These neurons were treated with drugs from anticholinergic classes linked to dementia (antidepressants and bladder antimuscarinics) and those not associated with dementia (antihistamines and antispasmodics) at two concentrations and two timepoints. Molecular hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease were assessed by measuring neurotoxicity, secreted amyloid-beta peptide ratios, and tau phosphorylation. Results showed that antidepressants and bladder antimuscarinic drugs consistently induced neurotoxicity and pathogenic amyloid-beta peptide secretion without affecting tau phosphorylation.

The Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) Study is a prospective cohort study embedded in an integrated health care system of adults aged 65 and older without dementia at enrollment. Among ACT participants enrolled between 1994 and 2020 (n = 5,763, 58% women), women eligible for this study were born in 1940 or later, had evidence of ≥1 child or pregnancy, and had maternal or pregnancy information in their medical record (n = 444). Cognition at ACT enrollment and every two years thereafter was assessed by the Cognitive Abilities Screening Instrument, a 40-item instrument of global cognition, further processed using item-response theory (CASI-IRT). The study examined associations between history of adverse pregnancy outcomes (preterm birth, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, low birth weight, small for gestational age, and stillbirth) with cognition scores and cognitive decline using linear models with generalized estimating equations.

De-identified data made available through the LONI interactive data portal to investigators after IRB approval. Analyses based on frozen, quality-controlled and cleaned datasets. Blood samples processed for serum biomarkers, plasma biomarkers, DNA, RNA, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Samples shipped to NCRAD for banking and distribution. Fixed hemibrain tissue samples collected from cases. DNA extracted at NCRAD for genetic screening and genomic analyses. Custom 96-SNP fingerprint panel used for genotyping and APOE genotype determination (rs429358 and rs7412). De-identified APOE genotypes uploaded to LONI. A 6-month embargo placed on returned data to allow publication of results.

Source code for the Ordinal SuStaIn algorithm is available at https://github.com/ucl-pond/pySuStaIn. The new implementation of SuStaIn was able to accurately capture heterogeneity in disease trajectories of postmortem TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) data and provided biologically plausible subtypes. Ordinal SuStaIn was used to estimate multiple progression patterns with a prespecified number of subtypes (up to 5 subtypes), and 10-fold cross-validation was used to assess the optimal number of patterns/subtypes in the data.

The study used a large dataset of well-characterized postmortem cases with Lewy body pathology data across multiple brain regions. The dataset included spinal cord and peripheral Lewy body measures, with 40 stages modeled across 10 brain regions with 4 score transitions each.

European summary statistics from Bellenguez et al. 2022 were accessed through the National Human Genome Research Institute‐European Bioinformatics Institute using accession number GCST90027158. These summary statistics were used to construct a cross-ancestry AD-PRS model using PRS-CSx methodology, which improves cross-population polygenic prediction by jointly modeling GWAS summary statistics from multiple populations.

data_repository: Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network Trials Unit
dataset_context_from_paper: DIAN-TU-001 is a phase II/III multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled platform trial evaluating various therapies intended to slow or prevent Alzheimer disease progression in Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer's disease (DIAD). The Tau NexGen DIAN-TU-001 arm investigates the anti-tau therapy etalanetug (E2814) with lecanemab as background therapy. Safety evaluations included monitoring of vital signs, physical examinations, adverse events, clinical laboratory parameters, and 12-lead electrocardiograms. ARIA occurrence was monitored throughout the study by MRI, read both locally and centrally. The paper provides 6-month safety results for 97 DIAD participants in the symptomatic cohort (CDR 0.5-1) receiving lecanemab only, with adverse event data including ARIA-H (26.8%), headache (25.8%), ARIA-E (20.6%), and infusion-related reactions (11.3%).

Interview data were collected from study participants and analyzed using template analysis with deductive and inductive codes through six-step thematic analysis process.

An observational study of 1,786 plasma samples from individuals with or without cognitive impairment collected in a longitudinal fashion with data collected on a nearly annual basis. Samples were analyzed using deep LC-MS proteomics with the Proteograph workflow, identifying 4,007 protein groups and 36,259 peptides using the GPF library. Cox regression models were created to determine the association of proteins with disease progression. A logistic regression-based machine learning model was developed to classify AD versus healthy controls using both pTau-181 concentration and LC-MS proteomics features. This represents the largest, deep, unbiased proteomics study of ADRD conducted to date.

Deidentified human/patient clinical, demographic, imaging, and plasma NfL data are available from ALLFTD on request. Investigators are required to complete the Request Clinical Data form on the request portal and to review the data sharing and publication policy. Data that could identify a participant are not provided. Any additional information required to reanalyze the data reported in this paper is available from the lead contact and ALLFTD.

140 Aβ-negative aMCI patients from BioFINDER-1/2 with longitudinal Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), and subsets with longitudinal data on Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB; n = 67) and progression to dementia (n = 134, 43% progressors). Aβ status based on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and positron emission tomography. Predictors included global and regional atrophy measures, CSF Aβ42/40 and p-tau181, hypertension, white matter hyperintensities and global cognition. Individual MMSE and CDR-SB slopes were estimated with linear mixed-effects models to investigate which predictors can best predict cognitive decline and progression to dementia in Aβ-negative aMCI patients.

Data used in this study were obtained from the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network (DIAN). The DIAN cohort included individuals with autosomal dominant Alzheimer's disease (ADAD) with different genetic mutations (APP, PSEN 1, and PSEN 2). Authors analyzed FDG uptake patterns relative to estimated years to symptom onset (EYO) using Generalized Additive Models with cubic regression splines. The ADAD cohort had 54 individuals with the APP mutation, 217 with the PSEN 1 mutation, and 24 with the PSEN 2 mutation. Participant APOE genotype was determined using blood samples and TaqMan assays. Access to DIAN data is restricted and subject to approval by the respective data access committee.

Data used in this study were obtained from the Alzheimer's Biomarkers Consortium–Down Syndrome (ABC-DS). Authors analyzed FDG uptake patterns in individuals with Down syndrome relative to estimated years to symptom onset (EYO) and compared these patterns with ADAD and neurotypical familial controls. Participant APOE genotype was determined using blood samples with KASP assays (LGC Genomics). Access to ABC-DS data is restricted and subject to approval by the respective data access committee.

Bulk tissue RNA-sequencing results were accessed through The Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) Project. One file per tissue type was downloaded and subsequently loaded into and read by RStudio. NORAD and MIR22HG transcripts per million were subset by tissue type and exported as an Excel file using the writexl package. The data used for the analyses described in this manuscript were obtained from the GTEx Portal on 09/25/2025 (V11).

Genomic coordinates for lncRNAs were obtained using the Bioconductor package, biomaRt (v2.60.1), in RStudio (v4.4.1). To account for annotation differences between genome builds, both the GRCh37 (Ensembl archive) and GRCh38 (Ensembl v.114) assemblies were queried, and gene models were reconciled to ensure complete locus representation. For each lncRNA, chromosomal coordinates (chromosome, start position, end position, and strand) were extracted from the Ensembl hsapiens_gene_ensembl dataset.

dataset_identifier: iPSC-derived neurons, astrocytes, and microglia from MAPT IVS10+16
dataset_context_from_paper: Bulk RNAseq was reanalyzed from iPSC-derived neurons, astrocytes, and microglia from MAPT IVS10+16 and isogenic controls using datasets described previously. RNA was isolated using the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen Cat. 74106) followed by ribodepletion (RiboZero). Samples were then sequenced by an Illumina HiSeq 4000 Systems Technology with a read length of 1 × 150 bp and an average library size of 36.5 ± 12.2 million reads per sample. Salmon (v. 0.11.3) was used to quantify the expression of the genes annotated within the human reference genome (GRCh38.p13).

Raw RNA-seq data files, transcript count matrix files and transcript level alternative splicing proportions are available upon reasonable request to the corresponding author. The study investigated differentially expressed transcripts (DET) across brain regions using RNA-seq analysis with edgeR (p < 0.05 threshold). Transcript-level differential expression analysis was performed, and results were converted from Ensembl transcript IDs to UniProt Accession numbers for functional enrichment analysis using DAVID.

Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID) was used to investigate functional implications of identified differentially expressed transcripts. DAVID groups input terms into biological modules and identifies enriched biological processes, molecular functions and Kyoto Encyclopaedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways. Authors combined all nominally significant DET from both brain regions and analyzed them using DAVID for functional enrichment.
Biological database network (bioDBnet) was used to convert Ensembl transcript IDs to UniProt Accession numbers for downstream functional analysis of differentially expressed transcripts.

The SEA-AD dataset provides publicly accessible brain cell atlas data from Alzheimer's disease patients. The database includes de-identified donor information such as age, sex, education years, and diagnosis based on DSM-4. It contains global cognitive performance measurements from CASI and MMSE scores, AD pathology metrics including Thal phase, CERAD, Braak, and ADNC scores, and additional metadata such as APOE genotype, brain pH, fresh brain weight, and postmortem interval (PMI). The dataset also provides publicly accessible code via Jupyter Notebooks and .csv files containing quantitative neuropathology metrics for each donor that can be used to cross-validate analyses.
