The analyses were conducted in 727 participants with both microinfarcts and dementia data available among 850 autopsy participants. The study is based on one of the largest autopsy datasets from a longitudinal community-based cohort. Participants were over 90% non-Hispanic white urban-dwelling individuals enrolled in one of the largest managed care systems. The dataset includes autopsy-based neuropathological data including microinfarct detection via microscopic examination, dementia status, BRAAK staging, and CERAD scores. The Dementia DataHub (DDH), an online data portal with public use files accessible at https://www.dementiadatahub.org/, disseminates data on the prevalence and incidence of diagnosed dementia at the state and county levels. DDH estimates are derived by applying NORC's researcher-consensus and data-driven ICD-10 and National Drug Code case definition to Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) claims and Medicare Advantage (MA) encounter data between 2016 and 2018. The study analyzed Medicare master beneficiary summary files (MBSF); FFS inpatient, outpatient, carrier, hospice, skilled nursing facility (SNF), home health claims data; MA inpatient, outpatient, carrier, home health, SNF encounter data; and part D claims data to investigate how specific ICD-10 codes perform in identifying dementia and to evaluate the accuracy of dementia case definitions.

The study used the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) as a validation benchmark. Because HRS lacks formal dementia ascertainment, the authors determined dementia status using probabilistic algorithms based on collective cognitive, functional, and sociodemographic data. The HRS algorithms were used to evaluate the NORC code-based case definition derived from Medicare claims. The authors note that HRS algorithms over-estimate dementia at the population level, implying an under-estimation of sensitivity and over-estimation of specificity when compared against formal dementia ascertainment.

Validation against the ADAMS sub-study showed that the HRS algorithms over-estimate dementia at the population level, implying an under-estimation of sensitivity and over-estimation of specificity. This sub-study provided formal dementia ascertainment data used to evaluate the accuracy of the code-based case definitions.

A recently published study evaluated NORC's case definition against in-person research-based dementia ascertainment from the Chicago-based Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center (RADC) cohorts, with findings consistent with the HRS validation results regarding sensitivity and specificity of code-based classifications.

Blood sample collection was performed in 22 centres across the UK during the baseline visit in 2007–2010 and then during the imaging visit to the UK Biobank in 2014. Proteomic profiling was done on plasma samples from 53,014 UK Biobank participants from the baseline visit in 2007–2010 and 1173 UK Biobank participants from the imaging visit in 2014. After quality control, a total of 2922 unique proteins in the baseline visit and 1463 unique proteins in the imaging visit were measured across four panels focussing on cardiometabolic, inflammation, neurology, and oncology proteins. Protein levels were represented as Normalised Protein eXpression (NPX) values. The first proteomic analysis examined 2922 proteins in 5021 participants at the baseline visit and 1460 proteins in 1028 participants at the imaging visit.

The Living Brain Project (LBP) generated data to investigate whether prefrontal cortex (PFC) tissue from individuals with intact higher-order brain function has characteristic multiomic foundations. Two complementary strategies were employed: (1) identifying in PFC samples from living study participants a signature of RNA transcript expression associated with neurotransmission measured intracranially at the time of PFC sampling, in some cases while participants performed a task engaging higher-order brain functions; and (2) performing multiomic comparisons between PFC samples from individuals with intact higher-order brain function (living study participants) and PFC samples obtained in the postmortem state. RNA transcript expression within multiple PFC cell types was associated with fluctuations of dopaminergic, serotonergic, and/or noradrenergic neurotransmission in the substantia nigra measured while participants played a computer game. A subset of these associations were termed the 'transcriptional program associated with neurotransmission' (TPAWN) and were reproduced in analyses from a second LBP cohort.

Single nucleus RNA-sequencing dataset from 371 subjects used in Stage 1 of differential expression analysis to identify genes associated with neuroticism in neocortical cell types. Pseudobulk matrices were generated by aggregating UMI counts for each gene across cells in each cell type, filtered for subjects with at least 10 cells and genes expressed in at least 10% of subjects. Blood transcriptome modules M5, M8, M1, M10, M13, M16, M17, and M21 were identified and characterized for their association with AD/MCI status, cognition, and neuroimaging phenotypes.

Peripheral blood transcriptome data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) was used alongside MCSA data to identify genes associated with AD or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) diagnosis, cognitive, and harmonized neuroimaging measures in two cohorts, followed by meta-analysis. Gene co-expression modules were identified using WGCNA in ADNI and assessed for association between module eigengenes and AD/MCI measures.

Seven bulk brain RNAseq cohorts were used to confirm the preservation of coexpression modules across blood and brain tissues. These cohorts enabled validation that blood-derived gene co-expression modules identified in MCSA and ADNI were preserved in brain networks, establishing M1, M5, and M8 as modules preserved in brain network modules.

Mass spectrometry data from excised protein bands analyzed for 3-nitrotyrosine-containing proteins. The study identified nitrated protein bands at 300, 60, 18, and 15 kDa molecular weights. The 18 kDa band was identified as peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase A. Mass spectrometry assessment criteria included: (a) molecular weight consistency with electrophoretic mobility, (b) ion score relative to other proteins in the band, and (c) known presence in adult brain tissue. Comparative ion and emPAI scores were used to assign proteins with confidence scoring.

The htext-formatted hsa00001 KEGG database was downloaded on October 4th, 2021, via the KEGG web server and parsed into structured data tables in python. Gene symbols provided by KEGG were mapped to Ensembl identifiers with a mapping file generated using the HUGO web server on June 10th, 2020. dataset_context_from_paper: Whole genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on extracted genomic DNA using a high-throughput sequencing platform following standard library preparation protocols. dataset_context_from_paper: Multi-cohort study of 2684 cognitively unimpaired participants (median age 69.6 years, 63% female) followed for a median of 5.4 years (maximum 13.5 years). Analyses included 227 participants from the Biomarkers-for-Older-Controls-at-Risk-for-Dementia (BIOCARD) cohort. Participants were categorized into 3 diagnostic categories: cognitively normal individuals who remained cognitively normal (n=187), individuals who progressed from normal cognition to Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) or dementia during follow-up (n=13), and individuals with MCI/dementia at baseline (n=27). Participants were scanned on a 3T MRI (Philips) in a longitudinal study design. On average, participants had 2 scans (range = 1-4) collected over 3.1 years of follow-up. CMRO2 was estimated from the arterio-venous difference in oxygen content, using a non-invasive MRI technique. The study reports CMRO2 changes from a total of 526 measurements, the largest CMRO2 dataset to date. Linear mixed effect models were used to examine longitudinal changes in CMRO2 over time, as well as the effect of impairment (MCI/dementia) on CMRO2.

The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset was used as one of the cohorts in this study. Radiomic features were extracted from segmented tibialis anterior muscle (TM) of participants using PyRadiomics library, extracting 93 radiomic features spanning first-order intensity statistics, shape descriptors, and texture metrics. Feature selection and model training were performed independently within the ADNI cohort using cross-validation, stability selection, and L1 penalization to minimize overfitting and data leakage. Subgroup analyses were performed stratifying by baseline age, sex, race, BMI, APOE ε4 carrier status, and baseline MMSE score.

The Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study served as the second cohort in this analysis. Radiomic features were extracted from segmented tibialis anterior muscle using identical preprocessing parameters as the ADNI cohort. Feature selection and model training were performed independently within ARIC using cross-validation, stability selection, and penalization. Subgroup analyses stratified participants by baseline age, sex, race, BMI, APOE ε4 carrier status, baseline MMSE score, and baseline SPPB (Short Physical Performance Battery) score.

The dataset includes structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) data and resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data with cortical thickness, brain structural network features, and functional brain network characteristics. data_repository: Banner Sun Health Research Institute, Sun City, Arizona
dataset_context_from_paper: Tissues from autopsied donors were provided by Banner Sun Health Research Institute (SHRI), Sun City, Arizona. Paraffin-embedded tissue sections (6µm) from three male and three female samples each of control (ND), Parkinson's Disease (PD), Alzheimer's Disease (AD), and Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB) disease-matched mid-temporal gyrus (MTG), duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and sigmoid colon samples were obtained. Donor ages ranged between 62 and 95 years of age, Braak stages I-VI, and PMI from 2.07-4.12 hours. Human tissue use was approved by the University of North Dakota (UND) IBC2304-0009 Institutional Biosafety Committee (IBC).

PHF-1 immunohistochemistry (1:500) was performed on tissue sections with antigen retrieval using 80% formic acid for 20 minutes. Immunoreactivity for each antibody was quantified by three blinded examiners, who assigned a score of 0 for no staining, 1 for sparse staining, 2 for moderate staining, and 3 for frequent staining. The three blinded scores were averaged from 3 sections for each intestinal region in each group. Stained tissue slides were scanned with a Nanozoomer 2.0HT slide scanner and viewed using Hamamatsu NDP.view2 software to score antibody staining.

ADNI data are disseminated by the Laboratory for Neuro Imaging at the University of Southern California. This study uses glucose binding potentials and brain parcel volumes from ADNI to uncover novel aspects of MBI (Mild Behavioral Impairment). The research examines neurometabolic and morphological correlates by analyzing FDG BP ND values and Schaefer parcel volumes in cognitively normal (CN) cohort, investigating links between neurometabolism and brain structure associated with MBI.

40 ALS and 32 non-disease age-matched control plasma samples were procured from Northeast ALS Consortium (NEALS) biorepository. Plasma biomarkers including neurofilament light chain (NfL), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), phosphorylated Tau (pTau181) and total Tau were measured using Quanterix digital immunoassays. Plasma NfL and GFAP levels were significantly elevated in ALS samples compared to non-disease controls, with NfL elevated ~7x relative to GFAP ~1.8x in cases versus controls. GFAP:NfL ratio showed lower values significantly associated with disease samples (mean=3.4) versus controls (mean=9.7).

Participants were included from the EMIF‐AD PreclinAD cohort, a longitudinal study in cognitively healthy older monozygotic twins. The study included 124 subjects (age 68.3±6.4, female 54%) with baseline amyloid assessments and follow‐up imaging at mean 4.4±0.5 years. Dynamic [18F]Flutemetamol PET scans were used to visually assess amyloid status and quantify global and regional binding potential (BP_ND) at baseline and follow‐up. Standard resting state functional MRI pre‐processing was performed with fMRIprep, and individual connectivity matrices were generated as pairwise timeseries correlation between 100 regions in the Schaeffer atlas.

Individual connectivity matrices were generated as the pairwise timeseries correlation between 100 regions in the Schaeffer atlas, and binarized using a proportional threshold of 0.25. Regional degree, the number of connections of each region, was taken as a continuous measure of functional 'hubness'. Degree was computed within the 100 individual regions, and averaged within 7 resting state networks.

dataset_identifier: Nine well-established longitudinal cohorts of aging
dataset_context_from_paper: Diffusion MRI data from nine well-established longitudinal cohorts of aging were free-water (FW)-corrected and harmonized. This dataset included 4,702 participants (age=73.06 ± 9.75) with 9,671 imaging sessions over time. FW and FW-corrected fractional anisotropy (FA FWcorr) were used to assess differences in white matter microstructure by sex, race, and APOE-ε4 carrier status. Sex differences in FA FWcorr in association and projection tracts, racial differences in FA FWcorr in projection tracts, and APOE-ε4 differences in FW limbic and occipital transcallosal tracts were most pronounced.

dataset_identifier: Vanderbilt Memory and Alzheimer's Center Dataset
dataset_context_from_paper: Plasma proteomic data from study participants quantified via two distinct methods (mass spectrometry and Olink). Data is sensitive in nature and requires qualified researchers trained in human subject confidentiality protocols. All plasma proteomic measures were standardized using Z score normalization before analysis. MS quantification required 26 batches with proteins log2-transformed and batch effect correction applied using ComBat with covariates including age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, Framingham Stroke Risk Profile Score, APOE-ε4 carrier status, and cognitive status. Olink Explore 3072 platform data reported as Normalized Protein eXpression (NPX) values on log2 scale, run across 4 plates in single batch.

We included participants with a FTLD‐related syndrome from the ALLFTD study. We included 1411 participants, totalling 2063 visits. The patient's age at the initial visit was 64.7±9.4 years and 44.0% were females. Females were 69.2% of the informants, and the relationship was 79.1% spouse or partner, 10.6% children, 4.1% were siblings and 6.2% other. We included participants with a CDR PLUS NACC‐FTLD higher than 0, information on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores, and the Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire (NPI‐Q).

The data that support the findings of this study are available in AD Knowledge Portal – backend at https://doi.org/10.7303/syn23627957. PPMI data, downloaded on 05 October 2021, was used to identify a NBS subnetwork showing functional connectivity differences between PDVH (Parkinson's Disease with Visual Hallucinations) and PDNOVH (Parkinson's Disease without Visual Hallucinations) groups. The authors assessed whether this PPMI-derived NBS subnetwork replicated in an independent dataset (ICICLE-PD). Method 1 analysis revealed a significant difference in masked FC within the PPMI-defined NBS network between PDVH and PDNOVH groups (β = −0.11, P < 0.05), with FC significantly reduced in the PDVH group.

ICICLE-PD data are available by contacting the study lead at Newcastle. This independent dataset with N = 104 participants was used for replication analysis of the PPMI NBS subnetwork. Covariates included age, sex, UPDRS-III, MoCA scores, LEDD and education. Two replication approaches were used: (i) calculating total FC within the NBS network for each individual and applying linear models to test group differences, and (ii) using NBS toolbox to directly compare PDVH and PDNOVH group differences. A post hoc NBS analysis in a smaller matched subset (Sample 2) revealed significant reduction in connectivity within the PPMI NBS subnetwork in PDVH compared to PDNOVH.

Mutation non-carriers had higher education and higher baseline MMSE (Mini-Mental State Examination) performance compared to mutation carriers, and mutation carriers had a higher number of visits compared to non-carriers.

dataset_context_from_paper: A total of 578 plasma samples from 110 participants were analyzed using Biognosys' P2 workflow. Mass spectrometry-based proteomics provided valuable insights into protein- and peptide-level changes associated with cognitive decline, illuminating biological pathways involved in the transition from healthy aging to mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Key pathways identified include lipid metabolism, extracellular matrix remodeling, axonogenesis, and synaptic activity.

Subjects were categorized into two groups based on NIA-Reagan Criteria: control (age 50 years and older, with no or age-associated neuropathological abnormalities; Tau-related Braak tangle Stages 0–III) and AD (Braak tangle stage of IV–VI). A considerable number of subjects were also diagnosed with a history of hypertension (HTN) according to medical records. Data were collected between 1989 and 2015. Clinical and pathological reports including patient history, diagnosis, and de-identified personal information were available for retrospective analysis.

We examined the associations between regional Aβ and tau burden measured by positron emission tomography (PET) in 192 participants without dementia (14 with mild cognitive impairment [MCI]) in the BIOCARD cohort, of whom 52 (27%) were Aβ positive. Amyloid status was assessed using standardized uptake value ratios (SUVR) obtained from the medial orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), lateral OFC, precuneus, posterior cingulate, anterior cingulate, parietal, temporal, and superior frontal regions using 11C‐PIB PET. Tau burden was quantified using 18F‐MK6240 PET across 29 brain regions, assigned to each of the Braak stages. Associations were examined with stepwise and hierarchical regressions, covarying for age, sex, education, and ApoE4 status.

The amyloid finding replicated independently in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset (Centiloid β = −8.6, p = 0.01). This dataset was used to validate the primary finding that antiseizure medication users showed lower amyloid levels compared to non-users.

In 52,537 participants in the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) study, we compared cerebrospinal-fluid biomarkers, amyloid and tau positron emission tomography (PET) between ASM users and non-users using inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting with gradient-boosted propensity scores. ASM users showed directionally lower amyloid across multiple brain regions, amplifying markedly in APOE ε4 carriers (Centiloid β = −25.7, p = 0.007). All three temporal tau-PET composites were significantly lower in users (META-temporal β = −0.05, p = 0.01).

Data used in the preparation of this article were obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. The ADNI was launched in 2003 as a public-private partnership, led by Principal Investigator Michael W. Weiner, MD. The primary goal of ADNI has been to test whether serial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), other biological markers, and clinical and neuropsychological assessment can be combined to measure the progression of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and early Alzheimer's disease (AD). In this study, covariates x_i included demographic variables, Alzheimer's disease (AD) status, gene expressions and structural magnetic resonance image (sMRI), while response variables y_i included points along the outline of the hippocampus. The study analyzed these multimodal data using encoder architecture with shape and size models, incorporating age, sex, AD status, and APOE-ε4 dosage as predictors.

Population-based, racially-diverse cohort in medically underserved communities used for clinical validation of the Pitt-p-tau217 assay. Cohort of older adults >65 years attending a memory clinic used for clinical validation of the Pitt-p-tau217 assay. This was the fourth independent real-world cohort (n=503 total) used to evaluate assay performance and clinical utility in real-world populations.

Whole genome sequencing data from 101 unrelated symptomatic participants with ADAD mutations and 5,050 asymptomatic unrelated control participants without ADAD mutations of non-Hispanic European ancestry. Genome-wide association study assessed the effect of common genetic variants (minor allele frequency <0.005) on AD risk using a logistic regression model.

Cohort included 101 unrelated symptomatic participants with ADAD mutations. Age at onset analysis performed using linear regression model, and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis conducted. Segregation analyses were conducted within families.

The Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) study is an ongoing population-based prospective cohort study that began in 1994 and aims to identify risk and preventive factors for dementia. ACT randomly selects and enrolls Kaiser Permanente Washington (KPWA) health plan members age ≥ 65 years. During the one year-period spanning December 2022 through December 2023, 320 new participants were enrolled with a racial and ethnic distribution of 25% Asian, 12% Black, 16% Hispanic, 2% Pacific Islander or Native American and 49% White. The study examines how newly enrolled cohort members compare to the KPWA population with respect to age, sex, area deprivation index (ADI) and health status. A core aim is to expand enrollment to 600 new members from historically minoritized groups by April 2026, such that these groups represent > 20% of the active sample (n = 3,000).

The ARTFL LEFFTDS Longitudinal Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration (ALLFTD) Research Study enrolled participants from 28 sites across the United States and Canada (study enrollment 2015 to present). The present study included 234 carriers of mutations in the C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT genes from this cohort. ALLFTD data have been harmonized through the FTD Prevention Initiative (FPI). Participants had brain imaging acquisitions and clinical/genetic data available. The study used these data to develop and validate Bayesian linear mixed-effects (BLME) cluster volume as a marker for predicting disease onset in frontotemporal lobar degeneration.

The Genetic Frontotemporal Dementia Initiative (GENFI; data freeze = 7) enrolled participants from 25 sites across Canada and Europe and spanned 2 study phases: GENFI 1 (2012–2015) and GENFI 2 (2015–2023). Participants were included from both study phases. The present study included 234 carriers of mutations in the C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT genes from this cohort. GENFI data have been harmonized through the FTD Prevention Initiative (FPI). Data included brain imaging acquisitions and clinical/genetic information used to develop predictive models for disease onset.

Research studies at the UCSF Memory and Aging Center (MAC) contributed participants to the present study. Participants were enrolled in longitudinal studies of FTLD who had similar brain imaging acquisitions and clinical/genetic data available as in the ALLFTD and GENFI studies. The study included 234 carriers of mutations in the C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT genes, with MAC data harmonized through the FTD Prevention Initiative (FPI).

DIAN EXR is a web-based registry with global outreach to ADAD families and investigators designed to identify families with ADAD and to determine the causative mutations through a genetic discovery program. As part of the Bio-Hermes study, sponsored by the Global Alzheimer's Platform Foundation, Cognivue Clarity was administered to 964 individuals who also had amyloid PET, plasma amyloid and tau measures, ApoE genotyping, MMSE, Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ), and Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Task (RAVLT). Cognivue Clarity performance was compared between (1) clinically-defined, (2) biomarker-defined, and (3) clinicopathological-defined groups. The sample had a mean age of 72.0 ± 6.7y, 15.5 ± 2.7y education, 55.9% females and 23.0% individuals from underrepresented groups. Clinical groups included 42.8% Healthy, 31.6% MCI, and 25.5% Probable AD. Amyloid PET was positive in 62.7%. Three subtests [Shape Discrimination (p=.002), Visual Salience (p=.005), Adaptive Motor Control (p=.004)] and their mean (p<.001) differentiated True Controls from Preclinical AD with an area under the curve of 0.634 (95%CI:0.570-0.698, p<.001) and were moderately correlated with Amyloid PET Centiloid (r=-.308) and pTau217 (r=-.315).

Large-sample, multicenter, long-term follow-up longitudinal cohort study (such as LEADS) needed with strict stratification of patients by clinical phenotype, to systematically track the dynamic trajectory of multimodal imaging changes from the preclinical stage to the dementia stage of the disease, and clarify the temporal relationship between imaging abnormalities, pathological progression, and cognitive decline in sporadic early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD).

This study used de-identified retrospective imaging data from ADNI in accordance with applicable data-use agreements. Amyloid PET acquisition protocols were harmonized across tracers using Centiloid framework standards and reference datasets from the GAAIN Centiloid Project for STN-PET reconstruction. For the GAAIN Centiloid Project reference data, PiB scans followed the standard 50–70 min post-injection acquisition window defined by the Centiloid Level 1–2 reference datasets. GAAIN FBP, FBB, and FMM datasets were processed using tracer-specific acquisition windows aligned to the Centiloid framework, with 50–60 min for FBP, and 90–110 min for FBB and FMM.

This study used de-identified retrospective imaging data from GE HealthCare datasets in accordance with applicable data-use agreements. GE HealthCare FMM used a 30 minute acquisition ~ 90 min after injection with static images generated from motion-corrected dynamic frames.

We used data from the Critical Path for Alzheimer's Disease (CPAD). This dataset comprises thousands of participants with AD or MCI from the placebo arms of numerous RCTs aimed at AD treatment. The names of the administered drugs or trials have not been disclosed. Most participants were diagnosed with AD at baseline, while a small proportion had MCI. We also retrieved baseline data on the use of symptomatic anti-dementia drugs prior to the beginning of trials, including donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine, and memantine. The diagnostic criteria for AD or MCI are uncertain and may vary across studies, and many of the enrolled participants were clinically diagnosed with AD as defined by the NINCDS-ADRDA criteria.

In future studies, replicating the current results could be beneficial using datasets from the placebo arms of RCTs for various anti-amyloid drugs similar to those of the CPAD, such as the YODA Project, which includes the placebo arms from two RCTs of bapineuzumab, one of the anti-amyloid drugs for AD.

The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; U19 AG024904) is a longitudinal multi-site observational study funded by the NIA in 2004. The major goals were to: (1) develop optimum methods for obtaining, processing, and distributing images and biomarkers in conjunction with clinical and cognitive data across multiple sites; (2) validate imaging and biomarker data; and (3) provide rapid public access to all data and samples. ADNI protocols include collection of biological fluids (CSF; blood) for DNA analysis and assays of AD biomarkers. Magnetic resonance imaging and amyloid PET scans were processed through uniform pipelines. Amyloid PET data from different radiotracers were converted to the Centiloid scale to harmonize tracer and data processing. CSF biomarker analytes were processed identically by the ADNI Biomarker Core at the University of Pennsylvania.

The Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network (DIAN) was initially funded by the NIA in 2008 and adopted protocols developed by ADNI. DIAN established an integrated database to facilitate analyses within, between, and among various data domains and to disseminate data to qualified investigators while maintaining confidentiality, including mutation status. DIAN collected biological fluids (CSF; blood) for DNA analysis and assays of AD biomarkers following ADNI protocols. Magnetic resonance imaging and amyloid PET scans were reprocessed by the DIAN Imaging Core at Washington University to guarantee uniform pipelines and ensure equivalency with ADNI cohorts. Pristine CSF aliquots from DIAN participants were processed identically for biomarker analytes. The longitudinal DIAN and ADNI databases were compared to examine whether autosomal dominant AD (ADAD) and late-onset AD (LOAD) share the same pathobiological construct.

The NULISAseq CNS disease panel was applied to 264 plasma samples from two independent cohorts (Human Connectome and MYHAT-NI), encompassing cross-sectional and longitudinal specimens. Wilcoxon rank sum tests and Spearman rank-based correlations were used to determine the significance of the association between NULISAseq measurements and neuroimaging-based assessment of AD pathologies.

The NULISAseq CNS disease panel was applied to 264 plasma samples from two independent cohorts (Human Connectome and MYHAT-NI), encompassing cross-sectional and longitudinal specimens. Wilcoxon rank sum tests and Spearman rank-based correlations were used to determine the significance of the association between NULISAseq measurements and neuroimaging-based assessment of AD pathologies. Classical AD biomarkers (p-tau181, p-tau217, p-tau231, GFAP, NEFL, and amyloid beta peptides Aβ40 and Aβ42), along with cytokines IL6 and TNF, were also measured using alternative immunoassays (Simoa and Quest) in a subset of samples for cross-platform validation.

Primary genetic association tests were performed using PEACOK (version 1.0.7). PEACOK 1.0.7 is available on Zenodo and GitHub. This software tool was used for conducting genetic association analyses in the study.

Variant- and gene-level summary statistics are available in the supplemental tables and on Zenodo. These statistics represent the primary results of the genetic association analyses performed in the study.

We accessed the joint-genotyping v4 release in April 2024.

A custom-built Amazon Web Services cloud compute platform running Illumina DRAGEN Bio-IT Platform Germline Pipeline v3.7.8 was used to align the reads to the GRCh38 genome reference and to call small variants. Sample-level filters were applied to derive a subset of UKB suitable for analysis.

For AoU, we included variants that met the following variant-level QC metrics: GQ ≥ 20, DP ≥ 10, AB ≥ 0.2 for heterozygotes, ExcessHet <54.69 and QUAL ≥60 for single nucleotide variants and QUAL ≥69 for indels. We restricted to variants in positions overlapping CCDS transcripts. We have received an exception to the Data and Statistics Dissemination Policy from the All of Us Resource Access Board to demonstrate the results of our collapsing analysis using All of Us short-read WGS data.

Consensus co-expression module definitions from the Accelerating Medicines Partnership-Alzheimer's disease (AMP-AD) Consortium. These modules were used to conduct gene and gene set enrichment analyses for GWAS signals and to identify driver genes associated with Alzheimer's disease pathology.

ADAMS was the first population-based study of dementia in the United States to incorporate comprehensive in-home neuropsychiatric, cognitive, and clinical evaluations by trained examiners. A multistage probability sample of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), a large, nationally representative longitudinal survey of older adults in the United States. The baseline ADAMS evaluation was a multi-hour, in-home assessment conducted from 2001 to 2008. Of 1,770 individuals who participated in the first wave of ADAMS, 624 received an in-study diagnosis of dementia (defined as a score of 0.5 or higher on the Clinical Dementia Rating Scale [CDR]) and were included in the analysis. Participants underwent physical, neuropsychological, and neurological examination. Informants provided information about medical and family history, cognitive and functional changes, medication use, and behavioral and psychiatric symptoms. Vision was measured by self-report and using a near card. Dementia was ascertained through cognitive testing with expert consensus, and neuropsychiatric symptoms were screened using the Neuropsychiatric Inventory.

ADNI data are contributed by the NIA-funded ADRCs (Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers) across multiple institutions. ADNI data are disseminated by the Laboratory for Neuro Imaging at the University of Southern California. Code used for data analysis was deposited in Zenodo. The analysis included evaluation of sarkosyl-insoluble fractions from 54 FTLD-TDP cases grouped by rs3173615 genotype, high-throughput tandem mass tag–based multiplex proteomics and mass spectrometry with off-line fractionation to quantify approximately 8500 proteins, Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway analysis on the insoluble TMEM106B interactome, and statistical analyses examining relationships between TMEM106B core deposition, pTDP-43 burden, and tSTMN2 transcript abundance.

Using IgG as a negative control to exclude proteins that bind nonspecifically, we identified 1309 proteins that specifically interact with TMEM106B in the sarkosyl-insoluble fraction (adjusted P < 0.05). Data file S2 contains the complete list of TMEM106B interacting proteins identified through mass spectrometry analysis of sarkosyl-insoluble fractions from FTLD-TDP cases.

On recruitment to DIAN, DNA samples were collected, which were genotyped using a TaqMan assay for DIAN participants (Applied Biosystems [Waltham, MA, USA]). Out of these proteins, 61 were associated with ADAD pathogenic mutation status independent of symptomatology, whereas 15 were associated with clinical symptoms within mutation carriers. The analysis examined differences across affected ADAD genes including PSEN1, PSEN2, and APP carriers.

The AMYPAD PNHS represents the largest European longitudinal dataset phenotyping individuals at risk of AD-related progression. The dataset integrates prospective and historical data from 32 European sites across 10 countries, comprising 10 Parent Cohorts including EPAD LCS, EMIF-AD (60++ and 90+), ALFA+, FACEHBI, FPACK, UCL-2010-412, Microbiota, DELCODE, and the AMYPAD Diagnostic and Patient Management Study. The initial dataset includes 3366 participants (55% females, 67±8 years), with 2629 having at least one follow-up visit (2.6±1.9 years). The dataset incorporates brain imaging, clinical, cognitive, and fluid biomarker data. Of those, 1618 underwent baseline amyloid PET, 888 with follow-up. Distribution of participants based on amyloid PET status at baseline yielded 60% negative (<12CL), 24% grey-zone (12-50CL), and 16% positive (>50CL) cases. Access to the data is available through the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative.

PhysioNet challenge 2012 data used for evaluating time series imputation models. CPAD dataset consists of 36 sub-tables including clinical events, lab results, imaging results, and other data domains collected over up to four years. Contains 11,369 patients. Authors focused on the lab result table with 37 most frequent features selected: Albumin, ALP, ALT, AST, Bilirubin, BUN, Cholesterol, Creatinine, DiasABP, FiO2, GCS, Glucose, HCO3, HCT, HR, K, Lactate, Mg, MAP, Na, NI-DiasABP, NIMAP, NISysABP, PaCO2, PaO2, pH, Platelets, RespRate, SaO2, SysABP, Temp, TroponinI, TroponinT, Urine, WBC. dataset_identifier: University of Wisconsin—Madison Alzheimer's Disease Research Center PET imaging data
dataset_context_from_paper: PET imaging data from the University of Wisconsin—Madison Alzheimer's Disease Research Center can be requested using an online application process. Participants from a large longitudinal cohort receiving [11C]PiB scans underwent a terminal [18F]NAV4694 amyloid PET assessment. The dataset includes longitudinal amyloid PET imaging measurements across multiple timepoints with transition from [11C]PiB to [18F]NAV4694 radiotracers. dataset_identifier: National Institutes of Aging - Stool Microbiome Study
dataset_context_from_paper: Stool samples were collected by participants during regular study visits. After shotgun metagenomic sequencing, microbial taxonomy (species) and microbial functional potential (pathways) were annotated using the bioBakery3 workflow. The Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA) neuroimaging cohort has provided key evidence suggesting that individuals who later or subsequently develop cognitive impairment (MCI, dementia, or impaired not MCI/dementia) exhibit distinct neuroimaging patterns preceding clinical diagnosis. Early brain atrophy patterns, reduced white matter (WM) integrity and higher amyloid burden are associated with cognitive decline. DTI data was quantified using parameters: number of gradients = 32; max b-value = 700 s/mm2; TR/TE = 7450/75 ms; flip angle = 90°; image matrix = 320 × 320 × 70; voxel size = 0.81 × 0.81 × 2.2 mm. An automated pipeline, PreQual, was utilized to extract ROI-based characteristics of DTI scalar values, including FA, MD, RD, and AD within WM regions. The study examined DTI metrics across commissural, association, and projection pathways. A total of 154 LME models were used to assess 103 unique ROIs as outcomes. Participants were categorized as cognitively normal (CN), subsequently impaired (SI), or with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). The study examined cross-sectional baseline group differences and longitudinal effects with potential moderating effects of sex and baseline plasma amyloid status on MRI-based metrics.

The cohort included 509 cognitively normal (CN) BLSA participants aged 50+ who had longitudinal cognitive assessments, including adjudication for cognitive status, and 3T MRI scans. Of the 509 CN, 80 individuals developed subjective impairment (SI) during follow-up (median time to SI: 4.6 years). MRI-based metrics included DTI parameters (FA, MD, RD and AD) for white matter integrity, cortical thickness, regional volumes, and machine learning-derived atrophy scores. A total of 154 MRI-based biomarker ROIs were examined. Linear mixed-effects models examined associations between cognitive status and longitudinal MRI biomarkers, adjusting for baseline age, sex, education years, APOE e4 status, and race. Longitudinal analyses revealed significantly faster declines in DTI white matter tract measures and cortical thickness in SI compared to CN individuals, with sex-specific patterns in trajectories associated with cognitive status.

Mount Sinai Brain Bank (MSBB) RNA-seq dataset containing 1,282 samples from multiple brain regions covering 316 unique individuals. Data uniformly processed through the AMP-AD RNA-Seq Harmonization Study with conditional quantile normalized (CQN) expression values. Filtered to include 304 frontal cortex samples functionally connected to the DLPFC for generalization analysis. 15 out of 47 cytokines (31.9%) were associated with Braak or CDR in this dataset.

AMP-AD RNA-Seq Harmonization Study used to uniformly process both Mayo Clinic and Mount Sinai Brain Bank datasets, producing conditional quantile normalized (CQN) expression values for subsequent analysis.

The BRCA dataset was obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) through the Broad GDAC Firehose. For the classification task, clinically relevant PAM50 subtype labels were used, which divide samples into five molecular subtypes: Normal-like, Basal-like, HER2-enriched, Luminal A, and Luminal B. Only samples with complete multi-omics coverage across mRNA, DNA methylation, and miRNA expression were retained for analysis. This dataset is frequently used in breast cancer subtype prediction and multi-view learning research due to its well-annotated structure and biological diversity. The authors evaluated similarity metrics (Cosine Similarity, RBF, and hybrid constructions) for GCN-based multi-omics integration, finding that Cosine Similarity consistently outperformed other metrics on this dataset, achieving superior classification accuracy, F1-score, and AUC.

The ROSMAP dataset was used alongside the BRCA dataset to evaluate the performance of different similarity metrics in GCN-based multi-omics integration frameworks. Cosine Similarity achieved superior classification accuracy, F1-score, and AUC on the ROSMAP dataset while displaying the lowest performance variance across multiple random splits.

Data from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging are available on request by proposal submission through the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging website. All requests are reviewed by the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging Data Sharing Proposal Review Committee. The study data were used for longitudinal aging research and proteomics analysis.

The Scaffold file is available in the MASSive Proteomics repository. Trypsinized samples were analyzed by liquid chromatography mass spectrometry using a Thermo Scientific Exploris 480 Orbitrap mass spectrometer. Tandem mass spectra were analyzed and validated using Scaffold (version 5.3.0) to provide weighted spectral counts for statistical analysis.

The Scaffold file is available in ProteomeExchange. Tandem mass spectra were analyzed using X! Tandem Alanine and searched against the National Center for Biotechnology Information human refseq database with peptide false discovery rate = 0.0% and protein false discovery rate = 0.3%.

ARIC proteomic data are available through the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) Biologic Specimen and Data Repository Information Coordinating Center. Participant-level demographic, clinical, and proteomic data measured by SomaScan were used to relate levels of GDF15 to the full proteome across biofluids. Spearman correlation analyses were implemented with absolute value rho = 0.35 for plasma. Of 180 experimentally determined rhGDF15-enriched pathways, 120 were able to be reproduced using ARIC plasma proteomic data. At least three proteins in a pathway had to have been measured by both mass spectrometry and SomaScan to be considered reproducible.

Structural MRI data from 813 participants (mean ± SD age = 70.67 ± 6.07 years, 52% females) from the DELCODE cohort. Participants were cognitively unimpaired (CU; n = 285) or patients with subjective cognitive decline (SCD; n = 342), mild cognitive impairment (MCI; n = 118), or dementia of the Alzheimer's type (n = 68). The Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) algorithm was applied to this structural MRI data to uncover atrophy subtypes. Atrophy subtypes were compared in baseline demographics, fluid AD biomarkers, and domain-specific cognitive performance. PACC-5 trajectories over up to 240 weeks were examined.

SuStaIn modelling was repeated in participants from the Swedish BioFINDER-2 study for replication and generalizability testing. In BioFINDER-2, analogous atrophy subtypes and cognitive correlates were identified. Group- and subject-level model generalizability were excellent, indicating reliable performance in novel data.

snRNA-seq FASTQ files for the GTEx samples available from dbGaP with the accession phs003749.v1.p1. These single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from GTEx were used as part of the study's analysis of allele-specific expression.

Parkinson's disease cohort raw data available in the ASAP Collaborative Research Network (CRN) Cloud in the 'ASAP Parkinson Cell Atlas in 5D (PD5D)' dataset. The Parkinson's data includes single-nucleus RNA sequencing data used for ASE analysis.

Parkinson's data available in the ASAP CRN Cloud with hybrid selection targeting 101 SNP/gene pairs identified as eQTLs in PD GWAS loci. Sequence data generated for 91 individuals in the PD dataset with hybrid selection applied to target relevant regions of genes.

R package scAlleleExpression (v1) built for downstream analysis of allele-specific expression. Java application for processing long-read data that takes in a BAM file annotated with cell barcodes, UMIs, and genes of origin, as well as a phased VCF. The tool generates gene-level expression information and ASE information at both SNP and gene levels.

NACC developed and maintains a large database of standardized clinical and neuropathological research data collected from each ADRC. A minimum dataset of 67 variables was collected from the ADRCs since 1984. A much richer longitudinal uniform dataset (UDS, comprising 725 variables) has been collected since 2005. In 2025, the centers implemented a new version, UDS version 4, which includes over 1500 variables and is aligned with the latest scientific advances in the field and our evolving understanding of best clinical practice.

data_repository: National Centralized Repository for Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias (NCRAD)
dataset_context_from_paper: NIA created the NCRAD in 1990 as the national repository of ADRC participant DNA and cell lines. NIA has substantially expanded NCRAD by increasing the number and types of samples it collects and distributes, as well as adding a biomarker assay laboratory that centralizes and standardizes biomarker assays and enables cross-laboratory comparability studies.

data_repository: National Institute on Aging Genetics of Alzheimer's Disease Data Storage Site (NIAGADS)
dataset_context_from_paper: The NIAGADS was established in 2012 to ensure that qualified researchers could access the genotypic data generated as part of the NIA's Alzheimer's Disease Genetics Portfolio, including ADRC participants. NIAGADS is hosted at the University of Pennsylvania and works collaboratively with researchers around the world to facilitate access and share genomic and associated omics data related to AD/ADRD as well as healthy aging.

The genetic and genomic data are shared through the Alzheimer's Disease Genetics Consortium (ADGC) and the National Institute on Aging Genetics of Alzheimer's Disease Data Storage (NIAGADS). ADRCs collect genetic data, such as APOE genotype and genome-wide association studies from research participants.

Datasets used for training BrainAgeNeXt. Most datasets used are publicly available. The private datasets are available upon reasonable request and require appropriate ethical approval or data use agreements. The training set was used to train the network for 200 epochs using the L2 loss function, with a batch size set to 4, on one NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPU for approximately 6 days.

The internal validation set consisted of 5% of the training set, randomly sampled but balanced to ensure representation across each 5-year interval throughout the lifespan. The internal validation dataset was used exclusively for model evaluation and was not included in the training process. The best model was saved based on the lowest average of the internal and external validation losses.

The external validation dataset included MRI scans from an unseen site during training (n = 498), covering an age range of 6–84 years. The external validation dataset was used exclusively for model evaluation and was not included in the training process. The best model was saved based on the lowest average of the internal and external validation losses, ensuring robust performance across diverse datasets.
The testing set consists of MRI scans (n = 1,523) acquired at 10 sites unseen during training. Testing datasets were used for final model evaluation.

Anonymised study data for the primary analyses presented in this report are available on request from any qualified investigator for purposes of replicating the results. The BioFINDER study was supported by the Swedish Research Council (2016-00906), the Knut and Alice Wallenberg foundation (2017-0383), and other Swedish funding bodies. The study includes data on Alzheimer's disease, preclinical AD, prodromal AD, and AD dementia patients with measurements including Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE), Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) status, and [18F]RO948 SUVR imaging values in temporal meta-ROI.

O.H. contributed to 'acquisition of patient data from the Swedish BioFINDER study' and the study involved participants with MMSE scores, ADAS immediate recall, ADAS delayed recall, ADAS naming, TMT-A, animal fluency, and AQT cognitive assessments. The dataset included demographic, clinical, CSF, and imaging variables with missing data imputed using fully conditional specification single-imputation method. Imaging markers included cortical thickness measurements and [18F]flortaucipir PET imaging.

Supplementary results tables (tables 8, 9, and 10) containing separate diagnostic group analyses for prodromal AD and AD dementia, as well as nonparametric regression model results and MRI scanner type covariate analyses. These tables provide detailed statistical results for cognitive assessments (MMSE, ADAS memory and language tests, TMT, AQT, animal fluency) correlated with imaging markers (cortical thickness, [18F]flortaucipir PET).

Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using the R package irGSEA (V1.1.3), which uses four distinct methods (AUCell, Ucell, ssgsea, and singscore) to calculate gene set scores. This approach allowed identification of gene sets that exhibited significant enrichment across multiple gene set enrichment analysis methods.

The robust rank aggregation algorithm from the RobustRankAggreg package (V1.2.1) was used to integrate the results of the differential analysis, allowing identification of gene sets that exhibited significant enrichment across multiple gene set enrichment analysis methods.

Differential expression analysis was conducted using the R package Libra (V1.0.0) with a pseudo-bulk strategy for enhanced statistical power. Cell types with > 50 cells in each group were retained for analysis. Raw counts were aggregated across individual samples within each cluster to generate pseudo-bulk profiles, enabling application of robust bulk RNA-seq framework with edgeR.

snRNA-seq data processing, clustering, and cell type annotation were performed using SCANPY (V1.10.4) through a four-step quality control (QC) pipeline. The pipeline implemented stringent cell-level filtering criteria including unique molecular identifier counts (1500–110,000), gene counts (1100–12,500 genes), and mitochondrial gene percentage (< 2%).
Potential doublets were identified and removed using Scrublet (v.0.2.3) with default parameters during the quality control pipeline for snRNA-seq data processing.

The BLSA is an invaluable resource for the study of human aging with uniquely rich measures taken longitudinally on a continuous replenishment cohort since 1958. The study leadership has initiated efforts into making the BLSA data more FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable), growing a BLSA data ecosystem that enables scalable sharing, and leveraging and developing platforms for accessing the ecosystem. Current platform functions empower researchers to find and access BLSA data, metadata, protocols, code and supporting materials to make new discoveries.

Authentic 3D T1 brain structural data from the ADNI database was utilized to investigate the impact of LDL-C levels on the entorhinal-hippocampal complex in individuals with prodromal AD (MCI) and CN subjects. Following data quality assessment, FreeSurfer (version 7.1) toolkit was employed to execute the recon-all pipeline analysis for quantifying the volume of hippocampal subregions.

Genetic data for hippocampal volumes were derived from a large-scale population-based GWAS conducted in 2021, utilizing the UK Biobank dataset. This data was used to validate the causal impact of LDL-C levels on the volumes of the left and right hippocampus using the MR method.

Summary-level genetic data for AD with cases totaling 71,880 and controls 383,378 were obtained from the GWAS study conducted by Jansen et al. This dataset was used as outcome data in the Mendelian randomization analysis.

GWAS summary data for disease phenotypes from the FinnGen R9 database were incorporated as exposure factors, specifically selecting those with a sample size exceeding 2000. Six categories of phenotypes were systematically excluded including medication-related phenotypes, reimbursement codes, AD/dementia-related phenotypes, non-disease-related measurements, repetitive phenotypes, and death-related outcomes.

Non-normalized gene expression data from 41 datasets (8 blood datasets and 33 brain datasets from 20 independent brain studies covering six brain regions) with at least 8,000 protein-coding genes each. These datasets were identified through electronic literature search of PubMed and querying of GEO, ArrayExpress, and Synapse platforms using keywords 'Alzheimer's disease', 'gene expression', 'transcriptom*', 'RNA sequencing', 'microarray', 'blood' and 'brain'. A total of 3,101 common protein-coding genes present in all 41 datasets were retained for WGCNA analysis to identify gene-modules and investigate preservation of gene-module partitions across studies.

Gene markers of eight major brain cell-types (endothelial cells, pericytes, oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells, microglia, astrocytes, excitatory neurons, and inhibitory neurons) downloaded from PsychENCODE and used as reference gene-sets for cell-type enrichment analysis in AD brain. Median effect sizes from meta-analysis were computed for genes present in at least three of six brain regions.

Mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository. Samples from the discovery cohort were analyzed using FASP, HPLC separation, and DIA analysis with an Astral platform mass spectrometer. Protein quantification was performed using LFQ and analyzed with Perseus. LFQ values were log2 transformed, and a two-sided Student's t test was used to evaluate statistical changes in relative protein abundance between groups with a significance threshold of p < 0.05. Protein groups were retained for statistical analysis only if quantified in at least 70% of samples in one or more study groups.

An independent, previously published proteomic dataset obtained from the AD Workbench—a publicly available resource from the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative (ADDI)—comprising patient samples collected at the Alzheimer Center Amsterdam (ACA). Selected features from the discovery and validation cohorts were applied to this independent dataset for patient classification using four machine learning algorithms.
All data supporting the findings of this study are available upon request from the corresponding author. The data are not publicly available due to privacy or ethical restrictions.

Whole genome sequencing (WGS) data from the International LBD Genomics Consortium. Raw sequence data in FASTQ format were processed following the Centers for Common Disease Genomics (CCDG) pipeline standard. Genomes were aligned to the GRCh38DH reference genome using the Broad Institute's functional equivalence standardized pipeline incorporating GATK Best Practices. A subset of WGS was analyzed using Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) to visualize portions of the HHV-6 genome present in the WGS, with comparisons made to HHV-6A reference genome NC_001664.4 and HHV-6B reference genome NC_000898.1.

A file including the complete PathSeq results generated during this study is available for download at https://data.ninds.nih.gov/. PathSeq analysis was applied to detect pathogenic sequences within the whole genome sequencing data.

66 regional (Desikan-Killiany atlas) tau-PET standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) values were extracted from participants in the Swedish BioFINDER-2 study: 429 cognitively normal (CN), 91 subjective cognitive decline (SCD), 168 mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 182 AD. Values were adjusted for mean choroid plexus signal and converted to tau-positive probabilities using two-component Gaussian mixture models.

Regional MAPT and APOE were extracted from Allen Brain Atlas, and Aβ from Aβ-PET. The study used regional biological information to parameterize the SIR model to influence tau synthesis, clearance, spreading, or misfolding.

Aβ from Aβ-PET was extracted and used to parameterize regional biological information in the computational model. Allowing regional Aβ to moderate tau spread improved performance compared to baseline model among Aβ+ individuals.

dataset_identifier: PPMI Cohort - Project 196 Targeted Proteomics: Olink Explore 384 Cardiometabolic panel
dataset_context_from_paper: Data, methods, and manuals regarding PEA proteome analysis from the PPMI Cohort are available online from the PPMI database. The PPMI Cohort included 33 HC and 33 patients with PD with longitudinal DDC measurements of up to 8 years (2 follow-up measurements per patient: median follow-up time [IQR] = 4 [4, 4] years). EDTA plasma samples analyzed in April 2021. For subsets of samples (n = 250; analyzed in April 2021), CSF DDC PEA measurements were available. DDC is part of the cardiometabolic panel which simultaneously measures 369 proteins. Mean intra- and inter-assay CV% were 3.8% and 5.6% in the PPMI Cohort, respectively.

For subsets of samples from the bPRIDE Cohort (n = 75; analyzed in December 2017 and August 2018), CSF DDC PEA measurements were available. IMAGEN DNAm analyses involved regressing out technical confounders (recruitment sites and waves) before conducting WGCNA, hierarchical clustering, and pattern similarity analyses. All DNAm analyses in IMAGEN were adjusted for sex, recruitment site, cell-type composition (first two PCs), the first four DNAm PCs (capturing major technical and biological variance), the first four genotype PCs (population stratification), and wave. T1-weighted MRI images were processed with FreeSurfer (version 6.0). Functional enrichment analyses were performed using missMethyl R package for GO and KEGG enrichment for each DNAm cluster.

For PPMI, analyses controlled for age, sex, race, education, recruitment site, cell types, and the first four DNAm PCs in analyses of depressive symptoms. Functional enrichment analyses were performed with the R package missMethyl (version 1.34.0) for GO and KEGG enrichment.

The ADNI data is available from the website and was used in conjunction with IMAGEN and PPMI datasets for analyses involving DNA methylation patterns, clustering analyses using WGCNA, and functional enrichment analyses.

Multicenter study comprising multiple cohorts with tau PET, MRI, amyloid PET, and prospective longitudinal MMSE scores across the full AD clinical spectrum. The study included cognitively unimpaired (CU), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer disease (AD) participants. Data were analyzed centrally at Lund University using a uniform pipeline, with cohort effects adjusted for in statistical models. MMSE served as the outcome measure as it was the only cognitive test available across all cohorts.

Religious Orders Study (ROS) - Data collection was supported through funding by NIA grant P30AG10161 (ROS). Additional phenotypic data can be requested at www.radc.rush.edu. The ROS cohort was used in meta-analysis of neuropathology traits including pTau pathology (n=1266), neuritic plaques (n=1266), pTDP pathology (n=1176), and α-synuclein pathology (n=1225) in association with genetic variants.

Used in meta-analysis with n=1266 for pTau pathology and neuritic plaques.
Memory and Aging Project (MAP) - Data collection supported by NIA grant R01AG17917 (MAP). Part of the ROSMAP consortium used in neuropathology trait analysis.

Meta-analysis performed on harmonized neuropathology traits across Leuven Brain Collection, ADSP, ADGC and ROSMAP cohorts.

Meta-analysis performed on harmonized neuropathology traits across multiple cohorts.

Alzheimer's Disease Genetics Consortium (ADGC) - Used in meta-analysis of neuropathology traits with sample sizes: pTau pathology (n=2191), neuritic plaques (n=2195), pTDP pathology (n=797), and α-synuclein pathology (n=2185). Meta-analysis performed on harmonized neuropathology traits across Leuven Brain Collection, ADSP, ADGC and ROSMAP cohorts.

dataset_identifier: AD Knowledge Portal - Bulk RNA sequencing data
dataset_context_from_paper: Bulk RNA sequencing data is available via the AD Knowledge Portal (https://adknowledgeportal.synapse.org). The AD Knowledge Portal is a platform for accessing data, analyses, and tools generated by the Accelerating Medicines Partnership (AMP-AD) Target Discovery Program and other National Institute on Aging (NIA)-supported programs to enable open-science practices and accelerate translational learning. RNAseq metadata, test table DEG output, and GSEA results for 5xFAD/CLU-h2kb-Ki vs 5xFAD mice. DEGs between cell groups were identified using FindMarkers function in Seurat using the Wilcoxon Rank Sum test with multiple comparisons adjusted (FDR) p-value cutoff of 0.05.

The remaining dataset has 52,078 cells (17,479 iMGs, 33,837 iNs, and 762 iAs) with an average number of mapped genes detected per cell of 1,924 for iMGs, 2,309 for iNs, and 2,684 for iAs, and average total unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) per cell of 3,644 iMGs, 4,199 iNs, and 5,477 iAs. After filtering, normalized and scaled data were clustered using the 3000 most highly variable features. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) was run on the first 20 principal components.

dataset_context_from_paper: Mass spectrometry proteomics data from brain and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples analyzed by LC-MS using nano-flow HPLC (Dionex 3000 system) interfaced with Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid mass spectrometer. Data was recorded in data-dependent mode and processed using Proteome Discoverer 2.2 software. Protein identification performed using Mascot v.2.6.1. Dataset includes peptide sequences and protein accessions for neuroligin proteins (Nlgn1, Nlgn1-2, Nlgn1-3, Nlgn2) identified from brain sample and CSF sample through SDS-PAGE gel analysis and mass spectrometry.

Roughly a million LC-MS/MS files available across Metabolights repository. The Dorrestein lab developed MASST (mass spectrometry search tool) to query MS/MS spectra across entire public metabolomics repositories including Metabolights. ReDU platform standardizes vocabularies for metadata of data deposited in the public domain to facilitate interpretation of spectral matching results.

Roughly a million LC-MS/MS files available across National Metabolomics Data Repository (NMDR)/Metabolomics Workbench. MASST tool queries MS/MS spectra across this repository along with Metabolights and GNPS/MassIVE to enable reverse metabolomics for discovering species distributions, health phenotype associations, and organ/biofluid distributions.

Roughly a million LC-MS/MS files available across GNPS/MassIVE repository. The Dorrestein lab uses MASST to query MS/MS spectra across public metabolomics repositories including GNPS/MassIVE to facilitate reverse metabolomics applications for discovering molecular distributions and health phenotype associations.

Domain-specific MASST platform with approximately 3,600 curated files. FoodMASST was created with specialized controlled vocabularies to facilitate discoveries in food metabolomics. These domain-specific MASSTs rely on community efforts to curate metadata and link them to LC-MS/MS raw data files, generating detailed reports about whether detected molecules originate from food sources.

This analysis made use of CNV-Finder (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.14182563). Pretrained Long Short-term Memory models in CNV-Finder were applied, which were trained separately for deletions and duplications, using features based on B Allele Frequency, Log R Ratio, and dosage statistics. Deletions were identified using a Log R Ratio of < −0.2, duplications with a Log R Ratio of > 0.2, and insertions with a B Allele Frequency of 0.15–0.35 or 0.65–0.85. The final output of CNV-Finder includes app-compatible files for visualization using an interactive web application.

An overview of the analysis and any additional scripts can be found in the GP2 public domain on GitHub (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17478293). The analysis included a computational workflow developed to identify and prioritize pathogenic missense variants and indels, optimized using a subset of probands (n=13) with five pathogenic missense variants previously identified through wet-lab screening conducted by the South African PD research group.

In 2022, the Accelerated Medicines Partnership for Alzheimer's Disease (AMP-AD) consortium published a deep multilayer analysis of over 1000 post mortem human brain samples from individuals diagnosed with AD, asymptomatic AD (AsymAD), and control subjects. Through integrating genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic approaches, this study identified novel protein network modules strongly correlating with AD pathology and cognition. Among these, Module 42 (M42) – the 'matrisome' – showed the strongest correlation with pathology. M42 protein abundance, but not RNA levels, was found to be highly elevated in post mortem brain samples from AsymAD and AD cases and strongly influenced by the APOE genotype.

The authors used ADNI data as one of multiple cohorts for brain network harmonization, conditioning reconstruction and network measure prediction on site encodings to address scanner and acquisition protocol differences across sites.

BLSA data were used as one of the cohorts in this study for brain network harmonization analysis. The dataset was included in the multi-site, multi-scanner analysis where site encodings were standardized across different imaging locations and scanner manufacturers.

The HABS-HD cohort is the largest dataset collected at a single-site, scanner manufacturer and acquisition protocols that the authors considered in this study. During inference, the model conditioned each sample's reconstruction and network measure prediction on the HABS-HD site encoding, which was used as the common reference site for harmonization across all connectomes.

NACC data were included in the multi-cohort analysis for brain network harmonization. The cohort provided site labels that were followed in the study's site definition and separation by cohort. Data were conditioned on site encodings to standardize network measures across different imaging protocols.

OASIS4 data were used as one of the cohorts in the multi-site brain network harmonization study. The dataset was included in the analysis where different site encodings representing distinct combinations of imaging location, scanner manufacturer, scanner model, and diffusion acquisition parameters were standardized.

ROS/MAP/MARS cohort data were included in the brain network harmonization analysis. The cohort provided site labels that were followed in the study's site definition. Data were separated by cohort and conditioned on site encodings to address differences in scanner manufacturers and diffusion acquisition protocols.

WRAP data were used as one of the cohorts in the multi-site brain network harmonization study. The dataset was included in the analysis where site encodings representing different imaging locations, scanner manufacturers, and acquisition protocols were standardized across the study population.

dataset_identifier: Accelerating Medicines Partnership for AD data portal
dataset_context_from_paper: As a molecular signature of AD pathology, we used brain region-specific differential gene expression data comparing AD patients to cognitively healthy controls, obtained from the Accelerating Medicines Partnership for AD data portal. This dataset was used to establish the genome-wide AD gene expression signature that was computationally matched to drug-induced transcriptional responses to identify candidate compounds for therapeutic repurposing.

We also utilized the Library of Integrated Network-Based Cellular Signatures (LINCS; https://lincsproject.org/) consortium's L1000 platform as a high-throughput gene expression profiling tool, which quantified mRNA levels of 978 landmark genes to capture transcriptional changes in cells in response to diverse perturbing agents. Compounds that produced inverse expression patterns, upregulating genes downregulated in AD and downregulating genes upregulated in AD, were prioritized as candidates for therapeutic repurposing by matching the genome-wide AD gene expression signature to drug-induced transcriptional responses.

The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), under the Accelerating Medicines Partnership - Alzheimer's Disease (AMP-AD), provides multi-modal datasets, including multivariate longitudinal neuropsychological tests and multi-omics data (metabolomics and lipidomics). The authors leverage these multi-modal data resources to develop a modeling framework for assessing dementia risk from the mild cognitive impairment (MCI) stage. The analysis integrates four distinct omics data modalities from ADNI: p180, bile acids, and lipidomics on two distinct platforms. Preprocessing involved excluding features with complete missingness, performing logarithmic transformations, scaling for normality, and excluding features deviating more than five standard deviations from the mean. MOFA analysis identified five key factors accounting for 95% of the variance.

The present analysis used data from two cohorts that have a similar women-to-men ratio, age ranges, the era of data collection, and follow-up periods, but different characteristics in race, education level, and body size and composition. In the longitudinal association between the rate of change in muscle mass and BMD, while the correlation coefficients were higher in the NILS-LSA study than those of the BLSA study, we found similar trends in terms of bone sites and sex differences, indicating that the results from one cohort study were replicated in the other cohort with different race. The availability of longitudinal data allowed the evaluation of change over time in both muscle mass and BMD.

Individuals from BioFINDER-1 (N=752) with CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay results were included. T1-weighted MRIs were processed with voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and region of interest (ROI) analyses. The association between alpha-synuclein pathology and CH4/4p volume was replicated in BioFINDER-1. Analyses were corrected for age, sex, intracranial volume, CSF Aβ42/40, phospho-tau181 and cognitive status.

Individuals from BioFINDER-2 (N=1388) with CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay results were included. VBM analyses in the whole cohort revealed a specific association between alpha-synuclein pathology and the cholinergic CH4/4p nuclei. ROI-based analyses revealed that alpha-synuclein pathology was associated with smaller CH4/4p volumes and smaller CH1/2/3 volumes in BioFINDER-2. In CU individuals, alpha-synuclein pathology was associated with smaller CH4/4p volumes and entorhinal cortex thickness.

Individuals from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; N=823) with CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay results were included. T1-weighted MRIs were processed with voxel-based morphometry and ROI analyses. The association between alpha-synuclein pathology and CH4/4p volume was replicated in ADNI. In CI individuals, CH4/4p volumes partially mediated the association of alpha-synuclein pathology with executive functioning. Executive functioning was assessed with the harmonized composite executive function score (ADNI).

A healthy community sample of cognitively unimpaired adults free from major CNS disease from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging was examined. The primary findings included n = 486 participants (age = 65.5 ± 16.2 years; 54% female; mean follow-up time = 4.3 ± 1.7 years). Among 421 participants with ≥2 fMRI visits (age = 71.7 ± 11.4 years; 55% female; follow-up time = 3.9 ± 1.6 years), longitudinal changes in connectivity were assessed. Plasma biomarkers of AD pathology (Aβ 42/40, phosphorylated tau [pTau-181]), astrogliosis (GFAP), and neuronal injury (NfL) were measured using Quanterix SIMOA assays. Intranetwork connectivity was derived from 3T resting-state fMRI from 7 functional networks using a predefined cortical parcellation mask. Cognitive performance was assessed concurrently with fMRI scans.

Variants annotated using ANNOVAR for population-level frequency (gnomAD), in silico function (VEP), and conservation (CADD score).

Patient cohorts were stratified into AD and cognitively normal control groups. Pathway Commons database was leveraged to generate domain-specific knowledge graphs. In the Pathway Commons network, each edge is annotated with PubMed IDs of references supporting its existence. Of the 19,087 nodes in the Pathway Commons knowledge graph, there was evidence for brain expression for 13,317 (69.77%). The network was used as the base for constructing biodomain-specific graphs and identifying key driver nodes through weighted knowledge-driven association (wKDA) analysis.

HPA tissue microarray data was used to annotate nodes in the knowledge graph for evidence of expression in the brain. This was one of three sources used to establish brain expression evidence for nodes in the Pathway Commons network.

Meta-analysis of AMP-AD datasets was performed to identify evidence of differential expression in AD brains. This was used as one of three approaches to annotate nodes for evidence of brain expression in the knowledge graph construction.

SEA-AD dataset was used to provide evidence of expression in brain cell types. This was one of three data sources used to annotate nodes in the Pathway Commons knowledge graph for brain expression evidence.

Gene ontology (GO) terms were categorized into biodomains based on the GO ID of enriched terms from gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using the AD Target Risk Score as a ranking statistic. The resulting biodomain categorization (syn25428992) was used to seed the generation of biodomain-specific network graphs.

Data used in the preparation of this article were obtained from the Global Parkinson's Genetics Program (GP2). Specifically, we used Tier 2 data from GP2 release 10. The study included individuals with clinically diagnosed movement disorders and neurologically unaffected controls from the MD-GAP study and collaborating brain banks within GP2. MD-GAP integrates clinical, pathological, and genetic data from autopsy-confirmed cases with neurodegenerative diseases, focusing on movement disorders. Demographic data, main clinical diagnosis, primary pathology and co-pathology were provided by brain banks. Clinical diagnoses included PD, PDD, DLB, PSP, Corticobasal syndrome (CBS), MSA, and Controls. Brains were donated between 1985 and 2024. All cases were genotyped using the Illumina Neurobooster array (NBA) and/or underwent genome sequencing in GP2.

Pathological staging and co-pathology data is in Release 11. The dataset includes pathological diagnoses such as Lewy body disease (LBD), PSP, MSA, CBD, and Other, along with Braak NFT staging information used for association analyses with genetic variants.

United States Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol (HCAP, n=3,267) used to develop and test metric measurement invariance of the Latent Dementia Index (LDI). The dataset includes cognitive and functional data from 13 cognitive and 10 functional items used to construct the LDI for cross-national comparison of dementia risk factors.

MexCog study (n=2,042) from Mexico used alongside HCAP to test metric measurement invariance of the LDI across United States and Mexico populations. The same 13 cognitive and 10 functional items from the MexCog battery were used to measure the LDI. Additionally, a Mexican clinical validation sample (51 cognitively normal, 49 MCI, and 50 dementia patients) received the MexCog battery to evaluate LDI validity, with LDI factor scores significantly predicting MCI (β=-2.62, p<0.001) and dementia (β=-5.93, p<0.001) versus cognitively normal status.

Cross-sectional, population-based study data from 5 population-based catchment areas participating in the 10/66 study: Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Peru, and Puerto Rico. Data were collected at 2 time points: 2003 to 2006 and 2016 to 2020. Of 23,709 eligible individuals identified, 17,817 were assessed. The analytic sample included 16,950 participants (wave 1: n = 10,374; wave 3: n = 6,576; mean age 76.0 years; 63.7% women). Participants were community-dwelling adults aged 65 years or older, identified through exhaustive door-to-door enumeration. Pooled crude dementia prevalence increased from 10.6% (2003-2006) to 16.9% (2016-2020). Data were analyzed between March 2025 and May 2026.

The study data are not publicly available for download, but might be retrieved from the principal investigator professor Oskar Hansson. The dataset includes cognitive test results (ADAS naming, Animal Fluency, TMT A, TMT B, SDMT) from multiple cohorts (A-E) with varying pathology status. Cohort A represents the entire population, Cohort B shows no progress in Clinical Dementia Rating over 2 years, Cohort C has no preclinical AD (normal CSF Aβ42/40 and P-tau), Cohort D has no vascular pathology, and Cohort E has no measurable pathology. Cutoffs were created from 500 bootstrap samples and compared across cohorts.

CSF Aβ42, Aβ40, and P-tau were analyzed using Elecsys immunoassays on all participants. CSF NfL was analyzed with ELISAs (NF-light® ELISA kit; UmanDiagnostics AB, Umeå, Sweden). The procedure and analysis of CSF followed the Alzheimer's Association Flow chart for CSF biomarkers. Data are presented as mean (SD) across different cohorts stratified by pathology status.

BioFIND (Fox Investigation for New Discovery of Biomarkers in Parkinson's Disease) is an observational clinical study designed to discover and verify biomarkers of Parkinson's disease (PD). The study was carried out at eight academic sites in the United States. Recruitment began in 2012 and closed in March 2015. BioFIND collected clinical data and biospecimens, including blood and cerebrospinal fluid, in 118 well-defined, moderately advanced people with PD and 88 control volunteers. Enrolled PD subjects met the United Kingdom PD Society Brain Bank (UKPDBB) clinical diagnostic criteria, modified to require all three classic motor signs of parkinsonism (i.e., bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor), by history or examination, instead of just two signs. Clinical and biomarker data from the BioFIND study were accessed through the Laboratory of Neuro Imaging (LONI) Image & Data Archive database (ida.loni.usc.edu).

Seven epigenetic aging measures were derived from peripheral blood DNA methylation data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort. Linear mixed-effects models were applied to examine associations between epigenetic aging measures and global cognition, including baseline-plus-change-from-baseline models and within-person versus between-person decomposition models. Higher epigenetic aging was consistently associated with lower overall MoCA scores, with associations concentrated in the between-person component rather than within-person changes.
