A single wild-type reference cell line, KOLF2.1J, established by the iPSC Neurodegenerative Disease Initiative (iNDI) to standardise iPSC lines used across the neurodegenerative disease community. The authors generated a 'trio' of lines (parental, mutated, revertant) for C9orf72 repeat expansion mutations, with revertant lines in which mutations are corrected back to the non-disease allele, creating crucial controls for attributing phenotypes to disease mutations.

Custom reference sequence was constructed based on the Ensembl C9orf72 reference (ENSG00000147894), incorporating the two regions flanking the hexanucleotide repeat. Reads were aligned to this custom reference using minimap2 with the 'map-ont' preset for detecting hexanucleotide repeat motifs and determining repeat length in C9orf72-associated ALS/FTD samples.

Paired 7T and 3T T1-weighted images were acquired from 178 participants (134 clinically unimpaired, 48 impaired) from the Swedish BioFINDER-2 study. To synthesize 7T-resolution images from 3T images, we trained two models: a specialized U-Net, and a U-Net mixed with a generative adversarial network (U-Net-GAN) on 80% of the data. We evaluated model performance on the remaining 20%. For n = 11 participants, amygdalae were automatically segmented with FastSurfer on 3T and synthetic-7T images, and compared to a manually segmented ground truth. To assess downstream performance, FastSurfer was run on n = 3,168 triplets of matched 3T and AI-generated synthetic-7T images, and a multi-class random forest model classifying clinical diagnosis was trained on both datasets.

These values appeared higher than the literature norm, where the PSNR was 22.9–23.2, and the SSIM was 0.78 in T1w to T2w, and 23.9–24.2 and 0.79, respectively, in T2w to T1w synthesis.

The other dataset comprised brain MRIs from 318 participants (aged 60–70 years, 125 women) in the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). Experiments using the PPMI dataset yielded equivalent results, but they provided an opportunity to further evaluate the potential of the models in handling pathological images based on a highly regarded dataset. Our findings with PPMI were also similar to the literature (PSNR = 19–30; SSIM = 0.65–0.91).

The study conducted a metabolome-wide genetic association study (MWAS) to detect metabolic features in urine excretion associated with CRC genetic variants. Urine contains metabolic breakdown products from a wide range of foods, drinks, drugs, environmental contaminants, endogenous waste metabolites, and bacterial byproducts. High-resolution 1H NMR urine spectra were analyzed for associations with CRC SNPs, identifying 70 annotated urinary metabolites. Key findings included associations between rs10411210 and urinary sucrose excretion (P = 1.23 × 10−7) and inverse associations of rs78368589 (SLC6A18) with tyrosine and leucine.

Mean [18F]AV1451 uptake was extracted from ADNI [18F]AV1451 scans. A separate sample of 90 individuals from ADNI was used to test associations with cognition. Linear models compared [18F]AV1451 signal across all 40 ROIs to tests of global cognition and episodic memory, adjusting for age, sex, and education.

The dataset was divided into training set (70%) and test set (30%) using the 'caret' package in R. Samples were classified into 'hypoxia-low' (182 samples) and 'hypoxia-high' (128 samples) groups using unsupervised clustering based on hypoxia hallmark genes. ROC analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic value of critical genes identified through machine learning.

MRI acquisition followed the standardized PPMI structural T1-weighted protocol implemented across participating sites, as defined by the PPMI Imaging Core. All clinical assessments and T1-weighted MRI acquisitions were concurrent, ensuring that the patients were drug-naive at the time of evaluation. The dataset was used to investigate neuroanatomical patterns associated with impulse control disorder (ICD) and apathy in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients using explainable artificial intelligence techniques applied to deep learning models for structural brain image analysis.

dataset_context_from_paper: Structural MRI, resting-state fMRI, tau-PET, and amyloid-β (Aβ)-PET data from 733 participants aged 50+ from the BioFINDER-2 study were used: 402 cognitively unimpaired (CU, CSF Aβ+=89), 157 with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 174 with AD dementia, with 523 follow-up tau-PET scans (323 CU, 109 MCI, 91 AD); individuals with MCI or AD dementia were all CSF Aβ+. fMRI data were pre-processed, and surface parcellated in subject-space. Template FC (CU Aβ- group-average) and each participant's individual FC were used to build an individualised 'hybrid' FC; template and subject-specific regional FC profiles were integrated by statistically estimating the contribution of each in explaining the participant's tau-PET. FC-based results were compared against using canonical PET patterns estimated from the distribution of regional PET values across the cohort.

Participants included 9008 males and females aged 17–74 y (median age: 42 y) whose data was included in a cross-sectional analysis. C-reactive protein (CRP) and fibrinogen were used as blood biomarkers of inflammation. Linear regressions showed inverse associations between total daily intake and both CRP (β: −0.00702; P < 0.001) and fibrinogen (β: −0.00221; P = 0.038).

The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset was used as the primary dataset for this study. MRI-free SUVRs were compared to MRI-based SUVRs across the entire ADNI dataset and when restricted to the ADNI cognitively unimpaired (CU) sample. SUVR templates were generated using ADNI [18F]FTP data in four diagnostic groups. The multi-template approach was evaluated within ADNI, with R2 and ICCs comparing MRI-free approaches to MRI-based SUVRs computed across all tau-specific ROIs examined. The templates were created using ADNI data, which may explain higher R2 and ICC values between MRI-free and MRI-based SUVRs in ADNI compared to the independent A4 cohort.

An independent cognitively unimpaired (CU) cohort from the A4 study was used to validate the MRI-free processing pipeline. In the independent A4 dataset of CU individuals, intraclass correlations (ICCs) ranged from 0.69–0.93, indicating moderate to excellent correspondence between MRI-free and MRI-based SUVRs. The A4 CU dataset was examined to assess pipeline differences for early detection, with the CU group additionally divided into A- and A+ subgroups. Higher R2 and ICC values were observed between MRI-free and MRI-based SUVRs in ADNI compared to A4.

16S rRNA sequencing data obtained from stool samples of 1,065 participants in the Rotterdam cohort. Used to characterize metabolic properties of host-microbiome co-metabolism by creating personalized microbiome-WBMs. After filtering on species-level, taxonomic diversity was reduced from 359 taxa to 151 taxa with an average read count per sample of 49.5% (SD = 9.7%). Microbiome reads were mapped onto AGORA2 resource using the MARS pipeline.

Strain-resolved metabolic reconstruction resource containing 7,302 high-quality refined genome-scale metabolic reconstructions of microbial strains known to inhabit the human gut. Microbiome data was mapped against AGORA2 using the MARS pipeline. Strain reconstructions were combined into pan-species reconstructions that include the union of all unique reactions, metabolites, and genes of the set of strains within a given species.

dataset_identifier: UCSF Alzheimer Disease Research Center Study

HEAD is a multicentric study comprising nine performance sites with 679 participants enrolled over 26 months, exceeding proposed enrollment by 9.5%. Recruitment targeted 620 individuals between 18-28 or 50-90 years, classified as Young/CU/MCI/Dementia. The study involves clinical assessment utilizing the NACC Uniform Data Set, blood collection for banking of plasma/serum/buffy coat/whole blood, and MRI acquisition based on ADNI4. All participants undergo amyloid-PET and head-to-head tau-PET with multiple tracers (MK-6240, Flortaucipir, PI-2620, RO948). N = 551 (81%) of enrolled participants have completed initial timepoint with 1,489 total acquired head-to-head tau-PET scans (mean acquisition window=34.9 days). Longitudinal data collection initiated in N = 95 participants with 18-month follow-up. Clinical characteristics include group distribution, APOEε4 carriership, plasma biomarker distribution (Aβ42/40 ratio/NfL/GFAP/PTau217), consensus visual rating of amyloid-PET, and Braak stage classification.
Clinical assessment in HEAD study utilized the NACC Uniform Data Set for standardized data collection across all nine performance sites.
MRI acquisition in HEAD study was based on ADNI4 protocol. PET data is reconstructed and processed uniformly similarly to ADNI4.

Blood collection for banking of plasma/serum/buffy coat/whole blood samples from all 679 HEAD study participants. n=761 amyloid-positive (A+) participants from the Swedish BioFINDER-2 study who had undergone (longitudinal) tau PET and cognitive testing, of whom n=253 were cognitively unimpaired (CU A+) and n=508 were cognitively impaired (CI A+). Investigators participate in beta testing for data exploration and designing cohorts and experiments that link specimen and biomarker data.

This study used machine learning to analyze health data from the UK Biobank, focusing on people with Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia.

83 patients with DLB and 86 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were included. Cortical measures were compared between DLB and controls using vertex-based general linear modeling and region-based analysis, correcting for scan site, age & sex.

Mouse mass spectrometry proteomics data deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository. Raw mass spectrometric files were searched against the mouse proteome using MaxQuant (2.1.4.0) with label-free quantification. A peaksPTM search was performed using variable modifications including hydroxylation, oxidation, phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and other post-translational modifications. The final protein list combined peaksDB and peaksPTM searches. Label-free quantification was achieved using PEAKS Studio Quantification with mass error tolerance of 10 ppm and retention time shift tolerance of 2.0 min. Normalization was performed using total ion chromatograms (TICs) and log transformation. The identified proteins, peptides, and protein peptides list are provided as Supplementary Files 2-7. CS56 immunoprecipitation was performed on light microsomal fractions, identifying all four CSPG core proteins of the lectican family (Vcan, brevican, aggrecan, and neurocan).

Human mass spectrometry proteomics data deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository. Raw mass spectrometric files were searched against the human proteome (Uniprot, downloaded on September 29th 2022) including contaminants by MaxQuant (2.1.4.0). Label-free quantification with default settings was used with Trypsin/P digestion protease allowing up to two missed cleavages. Carbamidomethyl (cysteine) was included as fixed modification and oxidation (methionine) and protein N-terminal acetylation were set as variable modifications. FDR of protein and peptide identifications were filtered at 0.01. iBAQ (Intensity Based Absolute Quantification) and match between runs options were enabled. Further downstream analysis was performed with iBAQ values using Perseus v2.0.7.0. CS56 immunoprecipitation confirmed the presence of Vcan, brevican, and neurocan in postmortem human amygdala samples.

The HENA data set consists of two parts–a graph, describing biological interactions between genes, proteins, single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), gene probes, and a set of node attributes providing additional information about the genes. Gene interactions include protein-protein interactions, co-expression, and epistasis. The data record combines preprocessed GWAS data set related to Alzheimer's disease, a data set of genes showing positive selection, and a data set of gene expression in brain regions. Each node represents a gene, protein, SNP or probe uniquely identified by its Ensembl gene name, characterized by a vector of 237 attributes including ENSG ID, gene name, biotype, SNP ID, GWAS p-value, positive selection p-value and expression in 231 brain regions.
Epistasis, co-expression and aggregated gene expression data sets were computed by SIB and Quretec using original data sets from ADNI, TGEN, HBTRC, MEM and ABA data sources.
PPI from IntAct data source were preprocessed and added to the collection. Protein-protein interaction data from IntAct were integrated into the heterogeneous network.

Node attributes originate from GWAS, positive selection and gene expression in brain regions from ABA. Aggregated gene expression in six whole-brain microarray datasets was used to characterize nodes with expression values in 231 brain regions.

dataset_context_from_paper: MTD is a web-based, multi-device (smartphone, tablet, and computers) digital platform used for remote self-administration of cognitive assessments. The MTD cognitive screening battery includes the Stricker Learning Span (SLS) and Symbols (SYM) subtests, typically completed in 15–20 minutes. The SLS is a computer adaptive word list memory test and the SYM test measures processing speed and working memory. The MTD screening battery composite score (MTD Comp) shows robust associations with the Mayo Preclinical Alzheimer's disease Cognitive Composite (Mayo-PACC) and multiple neuroimaging biomarkers including amyloid PET, tau PET, hippocampal volume, and white matter hyperintensity volume. MTD sessions completed between 5/25/21 and 6/15/25 were included in analyses. Inclusion criteria required a complete baseline MTD session with MTD Comp not missing and at least one complete and consecutive follow-up session, a valid session as previously defined, and absence of dementia at baseline.

The OASIS-3 dataset is publicly available through the data access form. The OASIS-4 dataset is publicly available through the data access form. The Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-4) dataset is a clinically representative cohort with neuroimaging and longitudinal clinical data. The HYDRA algorithm was applied to this dataset to identify neuroanatomical subtypes using volumetric data from patients, seeking to reveal distinct neuroanatomical subtypes and their distinct clinical and cognitive longitudinal trajectories.

Fox Insight Date Exploration Network dataset containing de-identified survey responses from the Fox Insight platform, an ongoing digital observational study gathering anonymized survey data on health, lifestyle, and past exposures from people with and without self-reported Parkinson's Disease (PD). The study captures verbatim patient experiences of motor and non-motor symptoms including tremor, gait changes, fine motor issues, and pain, with variation by age and biological sex.

Raw and processed data have been deposited at the NIH Neuroscience Multi-omic Archive (NeMO). The deposition includes both open-access and controlled-access components. Open-access components consist of: Single-cell-level count data on gene expression ('DGE' (gene-by-cell) matrices of UMI counts in h5 format), Metacells by cell type for snRNA-seq village experiments ('DGE' (gene-by-cell) matrices of UMI counts in h5 format), CAG-repeat length measurements from individual cells (in tab-delimited text format), Assignments of cells to individual donors and cell types (in tab-delimited text format), Donor meta-data (age, sex, Vonsattel grade, in tab-delimited text format). Data that are potentially individually identifying (such as sequencing reads that contain allelic information) are in the controlled-access components.

Genes with an adjusted P-value of ≤ 0.05 in either sIl10R vs. control or sIl4R vs. control comparisons were included in the Pearson correlation analysis.

dataset_context_from_paper: Nuclear DNA samples were obtained from a cross-sectional cohort (N = 296) of individuals aged 65-85 from the National Centralized Repository for Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias (NCRAD). Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) was performed on the 5' UTR of COX7A1. Sanger sequencing was performed on a subset of samples to confirm variant length. Fragment analysis was performed on all samples and analyzed in GeneMapper to categorize the number of UTR repeats on each chromosome.

dataset_context_from_paper: Cognitive (MoCA z-score) and demographic (sex, age, education, and APOE status) data were obtained from corresponding participants from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC). The dependent variable was the Montreal Cognitive Assessment z-score (MoCA z-score) and independent variables were APOE status (APOE e4 carrier vs non-carrier) and dichotomized COX7A1 UTR hexanucleotide repeat number (high repeat number and low repeat number).

dataset_context_from_paper: Proteomics dataset from the BioFINDER 1 cohort used for validation of differential expression analysis. Measurements included 2,943 proteins for CSF samples and 92 proteins for plasma samples using the Olink platform. Differential expression analysis was performed on protein levels comparing all LBD, de novo LBD, and atypical parkinsonism to controls. ROC curve analyses with 5,000 bootstrapped samples were conducted to examine the ability of proteins to discriminate between different groups.

BioFINDER cohort study. Authors tested the relationship between biomarkers in the BioFINDER cohort and found that CSF Aβ38 was significantly correlated with Aβ42 (r = 0.44, p < 0.0001) and with P-tau (r = 0.37, p < 0.0001). Analysis included diagnostic groups: AD, MCI, and SCD. Anonymized data from BioFINDER study available by request from qualified academic investigators subject to GDPR and ethical review board approval.

Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort used for independent validation of biomarker relationships. Authors found CSF Aβ38 was significantly correlated with Aβ42 (r = 0.54, p < 0.0001) and with P-tau (r = 0.53, p < 0.0001). Association between CSF Aβ38 and CSF Aβ42 was highest in SCD (r = 0.70) and AD (r = 0.66) compared to MCI (r = 0.47).

Data used in the preparation of this article were obtained from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database. The study performed region-of-interest (ROI) analysis targeting bilateral substantia nigra (SN) and globus pallidus (GP) according to the Automated Anatomical Labeling Atlas 3 (AAL3), extracting ALFF (amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation) and GM (gray matter) volume for statistics. The analysis included exclusion criteria based on technical quality control (head motion > 2 SD) and statistical outlier removal. The validation framework used a demographically matched subset (n = 29 per group) comparing healthy controls (NC), female Parkinson's disease (FPD), and male Parkinson's disease (MPD) groups.

The LID GWAS summary statistics are publicly available on GWAS catalog. The GWAS was conducted across multiple cohorts including the Parkinson's Disease Biomarkers Program (PDBP), Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) and Harvard Biomarker Study (HBS) cohorts.

Genes involved in the dopaminergic transmission pathway were obtained from Explore the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB, version 2023.1), a collection of annotated gene sets for use with Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) software. The pathway included genes: CDK5, FLOT1, PARK7, CHRNB2, ADORA2A, CRH, CRHBP, DRD1, DRD2, DRD3, DRD4, DRD5, TOR1A, RASD2, PNKD, GDNF, ARRB2, PRKN, PTGS2, RAB3B, PINK1, SLC6A2, SLC6A3, SLC6A4, SNCA, TH, CNTNAP4. This was used to construct a pathway polygenic risk score using the PRSet feature of PRSice2.

Collaboration with the EPND-biomarker consortium to analyze over 150 human CSF samples from AD and control patients. Measured levels of Aβ1-40, Aβ1-42, pTau181, and total tau, and conducted proteomic profiling using the O-link and SomaScan platforms. AD patients were stratified into Aβ+Tau+ and Aβ+Tau- groups to identify biomarkers associated with Aβ and/or tau aggregation. Approximately 10% of measured CSF proteins (~250 proteins) showed significant differences (p < 0.05) between AD and control samples. CSF samples with elevated tau levels exhibited altered levels of proteins involved in the complement cascade, cytokine-cytokine receptor interactions, cell adhesion, and vesicular transport.

Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative 2/3 (ADNI2/ADNI3). ADNI3 is a continuation of the ADNI2 study conducted from 2016 to 2022. Image preprocessing for ADNI2 MPRAGE images was not necessary for ADNI3 MPRAGE images, as internal corrections were applied. While some subjects from ADNI2 are included in ADNI3, they were not included in the evaluation dataset to avoid data leakage.

The dataset includes monocyte SASP (senescence-associated secretory phenotype) protein measurements with peptides mapped to human and bovine proteomes, with non-human peptides removed for analysis.

Cross-validation analysis using plasma proteomic data from BLSA performed using the newer generation of the SomaScan panel. BLSA cohort data were used to train linear models that significantly predicted several clinical traits in InCHIANTI. Full proteomic replicate data, quantification, and statistics are available in Table S1. The study identified 220 monocyte SASP candidates detected in both BLSA and InCHIANTI cohorts.

InCHIANTI is a population-based study of older individuals living in the Chianti geographic area of Italy, assessed using the 1.3k SomaScan assay, an earlier version of the assay containing a subset of the total protein measurements in BLSA. Cross-validation analysis identified 220 monocyte SASP candidates detected in both cohorts. Linear models trained on BLSA cohort significantly predicted several clinical traits in InCHIANTI.

Researchers tested for differential item functioning (DIF) using structural equation modeling (SEM) to develop a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) model, finding that a harmonized measure of the CSID has fixed factor loadings between countries but different item thresholds.

Using data from the Mexican Cognitive Aging Study (MexCOG) (n = 1,259) in Mexico. The study examined informant reports of cognitive functioning of the Community Screening Instrument for Dementia (CSID). Results suggest that informants in Mexico are systematically underreporting symptoms of cognitive decline compared to the United States when controlling for directly assessed cognitive functioning.

Resting-state fMRI data were preprocessed using the toolkit of RESTplus version 1.28 on MATLAB 2022b platform. The dataset includes resting-state fMRI scans from three groups: cognitively unimpaired (CU), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients. Analysis focused on altered fronto-temporal functional connectivity patterns among these groups, with nodes in frontal lobe (Superior Frontal Gyrus, Middle Frontal Gyrus, Inferior Frontal Gyrus, Orbital Gyrus, Precentral Gyrus, Paracentral Lobule) and temporal lobe (Superior Temporal Gyrus, Middle Temporal Gyrus, Inferior Temporal Gyrus, Fusiform Gyrus, Parahippocampal Gyrus, posterior Superior Temporal Sulcus).

Connected speech samples obtained from picture description tasks were analyzed for both acoustic features (such as speech rate and silence duration) and linguistic features (such as semantic content). The dataset includes speech recordings from cognitively normal aging, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients used to detect subtle language changes and predict progression to AD. Measures of semantic processing and verbal fluency tasks were used for early identification of AD risk.

dataset_context_from_paper: Publicly available gene expression datasets were searched in NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) (accessed on 3 February 2023). Datasets included human schizophrenia versus control studies of postmortem brain samples from Brodmann area 10, Brodmann area 22/STG, cerebellum, parietal cortex or cingulate cortex with a minimum of seven samples of individuals with schizophrenia and available preprocessed gene expression data. Meta-analysis integrated gene expression across datasets, calculating effect size (Hedges' g) as the standardized difference between disease vs. control samples using random effects model.

Publicly available gene expression datasets from the CommonMind Consortium (CMC) were included in the meta-analysis. CMC data were generated with funding from Takeda Pharmaceuticals Company Limited. Datasets met inclusion criteria for human schizophrenia versus control studies of postmortem brain samples with preprocessed gene expression data available.

This work uses data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), including patients with PD, patients with prodromal PD, and healthy controls. Collected data include demographics (age, sex, and ethnicity), clinical data on Parkinson's disease symptoms and severity (motor assessments, non-motor symptoms, freezing of gait, and falls), and data on prodromal Parkinson's disease symptoms (REM sleep behavioral disorder [RBD], constipation, depression, and hyposmia). If there were multiple assessments for the same variable, the earliest was used for analyses. Data used in the preparation of this article was obtained on 25 July 2025 from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database.

PET imaging dataset from patients scanned with 18F-NAV4694 and 18F-Florbetapir tracers. Images were acquired 50 minutes post-injection (200MBq ± 10% for NAV; 370MBq ± 10% for FBP) with 20-minute static scan for each tracer. Acquisition was performed on Philips Gemini (NAV: 103; FBP: 61) and Allegro (NAV: 47; FBP: 4) scanners at Austin Health, and Siemens Biograph mCT (FBP: 85) at the Brain Research Institute in Melbourne. Images were reconstructed using RAMLA for Philips scanners and OSEM for Siemens. Dataset was used to evaluate inter-tracer consistency when using composite reference region for FBP analysis.

All data generated or analyzed during this study are included in this published article and its supplementary information files. Transcriptome analyses were based on 12,272 protein-coding genes expressed in ≥50% of biological replicates with one or more counts per million (CPM). Principal component analyses (PCA) were calculated using 500 most variable genes. Differential gene expression was performed using DESeq2 with FDR ≤ 0.05 threshold. Genes passing FDR threshold were analyzed by EnrichR and ToppGene.

Media from iMGL cultures were analyzed by OLINK Explore 3072 platform, a high-throughput, multiplex protein immunoassay-based proximity extension assay including a protein library of 2944 protein assays. Technical QC was passed for 2902 of the 2944 assays. Proteins with detectability in all mutant samples, all WT samples, or in all samples were included (n = 1490). The cohort included 509 cognitively normal (CN) BLSA participants aged 50+ who had longitudinal cognitive assessments, including adjudication for cognitive status, and 3T MRI scans. Of the 509 CN, 80 individuals developed subjective impairment (SI) during follow-up (median time to SI: 4.6 years). MRI-based metrics included DTI parameters (FA, MD, RD and AD) for white matter integrity, cortical thickness, regional volumes, and machine learning-derived atrophy scores. A total of 154 MRI-based biomarker ROIs were examined. Linear mixed-effects models examined associations between cognitive status and longitudinal MRI biomarkers, adjusting for baseline age, sex, education years, APOE e4 status, and race. The study investigated MRI-based macro- and micro-structural predictors that distinguish SI from cognitively normal older adults, revealing significantly faster declines in DTI white matter tract measures and cortical thickness in SI compared to CN individuals.

The BioFINDER-2 study enrols participants in five subcohorts. The recruitment process of this cohort was designed to have 50% APOE ε4 carriers.

The UCSF NDBB provides autopsy services to all patients and research participants at the Edward and Pearl Fein Memory and Aging Center. Research participants enter through many programs, including the Alzheimer's Disease Research Center (ADRC), that span healthy aging cohorts and participants with FTD or atypical AD syndromes. We searched the UCSF NDBB to identify all cases from 2005 to 2022 that had TDP-43 inclusions. A random sample of 25 patients per clinical research network were selected at periodic intervals and adjudicated as in traditional clinical trial for validation purposes. As of October 2023, the TOPMed panel includes approximately 180,000 participants, with 29% of African, 19% of Latino/Admixed American ancestry, 8% of Asian ancestry, and 40% of European ancestry.

Each item is measured on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree), and subscale scores are standardized. The GPACS-D results were calculated by averaging individual physician results per the validated scoring algorithm. The cross-site results were calculated by taking an equally weighted average across the seven sites. Results are presented in Table 1 showing baseline attitude towards care was the highest of the three subscales, confidence in clinical abilities received the lowest scores, and engagement scores were modestly higher.

An AD test-retest cohort (N = 10x2) was used to assess within-subject repeatability of Centiloid (CL) calculation using five different target/reference region combinations. Test-retest analysis yielded absolute biases < 5CL for all region combinations except when using Cerebellar Gray as reference region. Within-subject coefficients of variation ranged between [2, 5.9]% and 95% repeatability coefficients from [5.9, 18.8]CL.

An amnestic MCI cohort (N = 80) was used to assess reproducibility in terms of absolute agreement in continuous CL values, and reliability for dichotomizing scans into amyloid positive or negative using thresholds of 11, 25 and 37 CL. Moderate-to-strong correlations between pairs of CL values were observed with R² in [0.87, 0.99] range, and agreement in +/- status between CL sets ranged from 89-99% (kappa: 0.63-1.0).

Commercial regulatory-approved software was applied to 18F-flutemetamol scans to assess the effect of target/reference regions' combinations on repeatability, reproducibility, and reliability of the Centiloid metric. Five different target/reference region combinations were tested: two custom-made tracer-specific target regions combined with either whole-cerebellum or pons; and three combinations of GAAIN cortex with either GAAIN whole-cerebellum, GAAIN-pons or GAAIN-Cerebellar Gray.

R squared values for PPARG and PRKAG2 were extracted for each participant to represent the strength of image-transcriptome co-localization. Generalized additive models (GAMs) were used to evaluate the co-expression trajectory of PPARG and PRKAG2 across study visits with an accelerated longitudinal design.

Brain transcriptome data was obtained from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA), which is currently considered the most comprehensive transcriptional brain map available. AHBA was developed using six adult human donor brains to provide expression data from tens of thousands of genes measured from thousands of brain regions. The Multimodal Environment for Neuroimaging and Genomic Analysis toolbox v3.1 was used to correlate gray matter volume with patterns of AHBA expression from the PPARG and PRKAG2 genes. Principal Components Analysis was performed on a region-by-gene expression matrix to identify components explaining at least 95% variance across the AHBA donors. Representative probes were selected in a data-driven manner considering between-donor homogeneity and the distributions of probe data.

The PPMI model training/testing cohort consisted of 1260 participants, of which 76% had manifest PD with a mean disease duration of 1.2 (±1.6) years. Overall, 68.7% of the overall PPMI cohort (and 88.0% with PD of those with manifest PD) had positive CSF a-syn SAA status results. Variables from the full multivariable model included age- and sex-specific University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT) percentile values, sex, self-reported presence of constipation problems, LRRK2 genetic status and pathogenic variant, and GBA status. Internal performance of the model on PPMI data to predict CSF a-syn SAA status had an AUROC of 0.920, and sensitivity/specificity of 0.881/0.845.

Models were externally validated in a cohort of participants from the Systemic Synuclein Sampling Study (S4) that had also measured CSF a-syn status using SAA. The external S4 cohort included 71 participants (70.4% with manifest PD for a mean 5.1 (±4.8) years). When the model was applied to the external S4 cohort, it performed well, achieving an AUROC of 0.976, and sensitivity/specificity of 0.958/0.870.

Data products were organized with systematic naming conventions using patient GUID, sample vial ID, and assay type abbreviation. Example: raw transcriptomics FASTQ file CASE-NEUAA599TMX-5310-T_P10_1.fastq.gz. Answer ALS is a multicentre cohort study used for model building and internal-external cross-validation to assess generalisability of weight loss prediction models across clinical cohorts.

Data for model building and internal–external cross‐validation were obtained from the Oxford Motor Neuron Disease (MND) Centre referral‐based clinical database (Health and Social Care Northern Ireland Research Ethics Committee B Reference number 15/NI/0096), collected 2003–2019 and downloaded 7th July 2023. The Oxford MND Centre referral-based clinical database was used for model building and internal-external cross-validation to understand generalisability of models built across clinical cohorts.

Multi-center cohort used as the primary training dataset for developing biomarker cut-offs and diagnostic models. The complete bPRIDE dataset was used to establish model coefficients and derive cut-offs at Youden index for amyloid beta, phosphorylated tau, neurofilament light chain, and glial fibrillary acidic protein biomarkers. Cut-offs derived from bPRIDE were subsequently applied to independent validation cohorts (UNIPG, ALFA+, and BIODEGMAR) using both standard model training and fixed cut-off validation methods.

First independent validation cohort used for external cross-validation. Both validation methods were applied to UNIPG: Method 1 involved validating model coefficients trained on bPRIDE data, and Method 2 used fixed biomarker cut-offs derived from bPRIDE. Demographic characteristics and study-specific AUC values for disease group prediction are provided in supporting information tables.

Second independent validation cohort used for external cross-validation with validation Method 2 (fixed cut-off method). Biomarker cut-offs derived from bPRIDE were applied to create binary biomarkers (low/high) within ALFA+ cohort before calculating AUC values. Performance of analyzed markers in this cohort has been previously published.

Third independent validation cohort used for external cross-validation with validation Method 2 (fixed cut-off method). Biomarker distributions were tested and compared across cohorts. Performance of analyzed markers in this cohort has been previously published.

Samples were split across multiple lanes when being run on the Illumina HiSeq; once the data were received, the samples were concatenated to have a single file for paired-end analysis.

Nanostring Mouse AD Panel genes were ranked based on regression coefficients calculated for each factor, and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) was performed on this ranked dataset. The use of GSEA ensured that pathway effects were assessed relative to the genes on the panel, as the panel was enriched for AD-relevant genes.

X2K is a web-based bioinformatics algorithm that uses the hypergeometric P-value from the ChIP-seq experiments (ChEA) database to find the top transcriptional factors. Using the ChEA database, the X2K bioinformatics tool identified transcriptional factors that influence common DEGs expression of obesity, T2D, and AD. The top 20 TF candidates were chosen using transcription factor enrichment analysis (TFEA) based on the hypergeometric P-value.

Using the drug signature database (DSigDB), therapeutic targets were identified based on DEGs generally shared among obesity, T2D, and AD. Drug signature database is a global database that helps identify targeted communications. It is a unique gene set and valuable resource for analyzing new genes and connecting therapeutic compounds to their target genes. There are now 22,527 gene sets, 17,389 different compounds, and 19,531 genes in DSigDB. Drug signature database gene sets ultimately meld with GSEA software, allowing transcriptional activation to be linked to drugs for pharmacologic applications and research purposes.

The FunRich interactive bioinformatics tool was used against the human genomic and proteomic data sets, which was merged with the FunRich background, to identify the potential biological signaling pathways associated with commonly shared DEGs.

Proteomic data from quantitative proteomics study using tandem mass tags (TMTs) analyzing peptides from day 30 motor neurons from wild-type and p97 R155H mutant cell lines (KOLF2.1 or 392.1). Samples were labeled with TMTs and analyzed by liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry (LC/MS-MS). More than 200 proteins were significantly altered (Log 2 fold change mutant: wild type > 0.7) between mutants and wild-type in both cell lines. Higher plasma biomarker stages were associated with more abnormal imaging and clinical AD features, consistent with the expected disease progression.

Lipid dysregulations, particularly in phosphatidylcholines, lysophosphatidylcholines, triglycerides, and sphingomyelins, were observed across all groups.

PandaOmics offers a comprehensive data processing pipeline that facilitates the identification of potential therapeutic targets and biomarkers by leveraging dynamic omics data, including gene expression, proteomics, and methylation data. The platform conducts a systematic search for relevant datasets and assembles a comprehensive data inventory specifically tailored to the disease, condition, or compound of interest. The list of databases used by PandaOmics is provided as Supplementary Table 1. The omics-based models leverage various data types, including gene expression, methylation, proteomics, and genetic information extracted from the meta-analysis.

In total, there are 23 disease-specific models employed in the ranking process, broadly categorized as omics-based and text-based approaches. The omics-based models leverage various data types, including gene expression, methylation, proteomics, and genetic information. These models are further enhanced by incorporating biological graphs derived from signaling pathway and protein–protein interaction (PPI) network databases and knowledge graphs generated through the analysis of scientific publications. The text-based models depend on extracted relations from publications, clinical trials, and grant applications while considering source credibility and trends. Supplementary Table 2 provides the list of PandaOmics disease-specific target ID models available through the user interface of the platform.

CSF proteomics data were downloaded from the ADNI database. CSF proteomic profiling was conducted using the SOMAscan 7K platform, measuring the abundance of approximately 7000 proteins from 728 participants. Out of the 7008 aptamers obtained from 728 participants, aptamers within the lower quantile (Q1) with the lowest standard deviations were excluded to filter out non-variable proteins, leaving a total of 5256 aptamers, which were used to construct network-based co-abundance network modules using weighted gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA). Normalization and quality control procedures were performed to address plate effects and technical variability. The raw data were divided into two matrices: one containing experimental samples and another for non-sample controls. SomaLogic performed initial data normalization using hybridization controls for intra-plate adjustments and median signals to correct for inter-plate variability, with an external reference used for further normalization to account for biological variation.

The study investigated cerebello-basal ganglia and cerebello-cortical connectivity using ROI-to-ROI and seed-to-voxel pipelines. Effects of age, disease duration, cognitive status, motor symptom severity, and dopaminergic medication were assessed. Analysis revealed cerebellar lobule VI and vermis VI showed robust positive connectivity with the pallidum, and disease duration showed region-specific effects on connectivity patterns across cognitively normal PD and PD with cognitive dysfunction.

Transcriptomics raw data from MSBB study. RNA-seq libraries were prepared using TruSeq RNA Sample Preparation Kit v2 (Illumina). rRNAs were depleted using Ribo-Zero rRNA Removal Kit. Single-end non-standard reads of 101 bp were generated by Illumina HiSeq 2500. Only data from the parahippocampal gyrus (PHG, BA36) were selected for this study. RNA-seq data from sporadic AD and control cases were processed and analyzed. Raw read counts for transcripts/genes were generated using STAR, and normalized gene expression levels were computed in FPKM format.

Transcriptomics raw data from ROSMAP study. RNA-seq datasets from the cohort were processed and aligned using in-house RNA-seq pipeline. Reference genome GRCh38 and GENCODE 33 annotation were used. All read sequences were aligned to the human reference genome using STAR (v.2.7.1a). Raw read counts for transcripts/genes were generated using STAR, and normalized gene expression levels were computed in FPKM format. RNA-seq data from sporadic AD and control cases from ROSMAP cohort were processed and analyzed under the same analytical pipeline.

Personalized genome assembly for the KOLF2.1J iPSC line. The authors generated a complete diploid assembly with accompanying genomic, epigenetic, and transcriptomic data. Lambert et al. conducted a large-scale GWAS meta-analysis to elucidate AD genetic architecture. Integrating data from 17 case-control cohorts and four population-based studies encompassing 54,162 total individuals (17,008 AD cases, 37,154 controls), the study identified 11 novel susceptibility loci for AD risk, such as SLC24A4, FERMT2, and INPP5D. Additionally, they confirmed previous GWAS-identified genes, including apolipoprotein E (APOE), BIN1, CLU, CR1, and MS4A6A.

BioFINDER cohort used for analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) proteins including Aβ42, t-tau, and p-tau181 in cognitively unimpaired (CU), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) dementia subjects. Mixed effects models of CDR-SB or MMSE were constructed for CU and MCI subjects in strata of A± and T±. Analysis included covariates of age, sex, APOE ε4 genotype, and CSF protein of interest. Due to insufficient N, A−T+ subjects and AD dementia subjects were not modeled.

Metabolomics data used in preparation of this article were generated by the Alzheimer's Disease Metabolomics Consortium (ADMC). The NIA supported the Alzheimer's Disease Metabolomics Consortium which is a part of NIA's national initiatives AMP-AD and M2OVE-AD. The study analyzed 991 frequent metabolites (missingness ≤30%) after quality control steps. Metabolites were measured using NIST Standard Reference Material (SRM) 1950 sample with coefficient of variance (CV) filtering (CV >30% excluded). Data underwent log2 transformation and K-nearest neighbor (KNN) based imputation for missing values. Genome-wide association study (GWAS) was performed for all 991 metabolites to identify genetic associations (P <5×10−8). Percentage explained variance (EV) of metabolites by genetic features was calculated using gradient boosted decision trees (GBDT).

Fecal samples were collected from the RS-III cohort with detailed collection and sequencing procedures described previously. This sequence data was subjected to a new 16S rRNA profiling pipeline. Raw reads were demultiplexed, primers and barcodes trimmed using tagcleaner v0.16. Filtered reads were processed through DADA2 package version 1.18.0 for quality filtering, denoising, clustering and merging. Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) were assigned taxonomy from SILVA version 138.1 rRNA database using RDP naïve Bayesian classifier.

Dosage information was extracted from genotype imputed data for prioritized SNPs in RS participants. Genome-wide association study (GWAS) was performed using HASE software. In summary statistics, variants were retained with imputation quality R2 >0.3 and minor allele frequency (MAF) >0.05. SNP clumping was performed using PLINK 1.9 with p-value threshold of 5.0×10−8 and linkage disequilibrium (LD) threshold (r2) of 0.2 in 500KB region. A total of 415 independent SNPs reached significance threshold (P <5.0×10−8) for 991 metabolites.

Summary statistics for Alzheimer's disease datasets are available at the EBI GWAS Catalog under the study index GCST90027158. This dataset was used in a comprehensive multi-omics analysis investigating potential causal pathways linking DNA methylation, gene expression, and protein abundance to AD risk. The study integrated evidence from three molecular layers in blood (protein, expression, methylation) to prioritize causal candidate genes, with genes categorized into Tier 1 (significant associations across all three omics layers) and Tier 2 (significant protein-level associations plus associations at either methylation or expression level).

The validation datasets are available at the FinnGen database, which requires an application for access. FinnGen was used as an independent population-based cohort for replication of findings. Several associations, including those for SERPINF2 (cg00443543 and cg18278729), DAPK2 (cg26167930), and TMEM106B (cg23422036), were successfully replicated using FinnGen summary statistics.

The ten BSMN data repositories are accessible in the NIMH Data Archive (NDA). The datasets include whole genome sequencing (WGS), whole exome sequencing (WES), RNA-seq, linked read, single cell WGS-seq, and SLAV-seq of bulk tissue or fractionated samples. Two neurotypical, thoroughly sequenced subjects that can be used as references are present in collections 2458 and 2698. Metadata tables connect subject Globally Unique Identifiers (GUIDs) with relevant de-identified donor, tissue sample, sequencing assay information, and S3 links to sequence data (FASTQs), alignment files (BAM/CRAM), index files (BAI/CRAI/TBI), alignment summary text files, and variant calls (VCFs).

NDA Study 967 contains all data of the BSMN and will be particularly useful to researchers interested in the BSMN data. This cross-collection subset of data was established using the NDA's Study feature.

NDA Study 814 contains data that was uniformly processed using an identical alignment pipeline across the entire consortium. This workflow starts with separating fastq files by flow cell lane, with individual lanes aligned to GRCh37d5 with bwa v3.7.16a, followed by sorting by read group, merging by sambamba v0.6.7, marking PCR duplicates with PICARD v2.12.1, and performing indel realignment and base quality recalibration following GATK best practices (v3.7).

Computational tools have been developed for processing BSMN data. A list of these tools and their repositories is available on the Synapse site at https://bsmn.synapse.org/Explore/Tools and is included in Table 7.

Cohort dataset used for imputing genes from the SST-PRS. Authors conducted over-representation analysis (ORA) on genes from the SST-PRS imputed in the IRL-GRey cohort, examining enriched pathways with adjusted p-values to assess pathway significance and gene counts per pathway.

The VIVA-MIND trial study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03919162) on April 18, 2019. In phase 2A, 180 participants will be randomized using a 1:1 allocation to active treatment or placebo. Following phase 2A, an interim futility analysis will be undertaken with a Stage Gate decision for whether to continue to phase 2B. In phase 2B, there will be enrollment of 234 additional participants, using the same inclusion criteria as phase 2A, to a total sample size of 414. These newly-enrolled phase 2B participants will be randomized 1:1 to active treatment or placebo. The recruitment and enrollment of participants is occurring through sites of the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study network, with 22 clinical sites in phase 2A and a planned 55 clinical sites in phase 2B.

The study included 1195 participants from the BioFINDER‐2 (BF2) cohort. BF2 was split into 80% train and 20% test sets. The three variable blocks (clinical, plasma and MRI) were used as features (together and separately) to predict two tau‐PET characteristics: 1) tau load in the temporal cortex 2) hemispheric asymmetry of temporal tau load in tau positive participants. External validation was performed in the BF2 test set. The best performing model was a combination of plasma and MRI variables in a CatBoost regressor, which achieved SUVR mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.155 and R‐squared = 0.700 on unseen data.

Analysis of lumbar spinal cord and cortex of 12-month-old (GR)400 and (PR)400 mice revealed a striking increase in ECM terms specifically in the spinal cord. The pQTL summary statistics from the deCODE study are available at https://www.decode.com/summarydata/. Plasma protein concentrations in the deCODE study were measured using the SomaScan v4 aptamer-based proteomic platform. Standard SomaLogic normalization procedures were applied, including hybridization normalization, median signal normalization across samples, and calibration across assay plates.

The dorsal prefrontal cortex pQTL summary statistics (syn64600176) are available at https://www.synapse.org/. The brain pQTL data were derived from post-mortem samples. Proteins measured in post-mortem tissues may be affected by processes such as protein degradation, enzymatic autolysis, and microbial activity that occur during the post-mortem interval.

The pQTL summary statistics from the Fenland study (syn51761394) are available at https://www.synapse.org/. Plasma protein concentrations in the Fenland study were measured using the SomaScan v4 aptamer-based proteomic platform with standard SomaLogic normalization procedures applied.

The pQTL summary statistics from the UKB-PPP (syn51364934) are available at https://www.synapse.org/. In the UKB-PPP dataset, proteomic measurements were generated using the Olink proximity extension assay platform. Raw counts were converted to normalized protein expression values using Olink's MyData Cloud software with built-in internal controls used to monitor assay performance.

To characterize tissue expression patterns of proteins with and without colocalized pQTL signals, we analyzed gene expression data from the GTEx project (version 8), which includes RNA-sequencing data across 54 non-diseased human tissues. We applied an established approach to normalize gene expression levels across samples and tissues.

The ROSMAP dataset was obtained from AMP-AD Knowledge Portal for the classification of Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients versus normal control (NC). The dataset includes mRNA expression data, DNA methylation data, and miRNA expression data. Authors selected the top 50 features with highest importance scores across these three omics types for enrichment analysis, which corresponded to 2861 genes after annotation and mapping.

PAM50 breast cancer subtypes were obtained through the TCGAbiolinks R package v2.12.6.

Omics data of LUAD (lung adenocarcinoma) was obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA) through Broad GDAC Firehose. The dataset is used for lung adenocarcinoma pathological stage classification with Stage I, Stage II, and Stage III/IV.

METABRIC is an independent breast cancer cohort from the Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium, used for external validation of models trained on BRCA, with the same PAM50 subtype classification task using mRNA and DNA methylation data.

PEARL was first evaluated on synthetic data generated by InterSIM, a method for generating synthetic multi-omics datasets that simulate real biological data. Three types of omics data were considered: methylation, gene expression, and protein data, with various cluster mean shifts and noise levels across sample sizes of 300, 500, and 800, resulting in a total of nine synthetic datasets.

The source data and code of the computational framework PEARL is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zqq121017/PEARL. The archival version of the code is preserved on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19875866 (zqq121017 2026).

Postprocessed protein expression data from the AD Knowledge portal (Synapse ID: syn25006864). Proteins with missing values in more than 70% of samples were discarded. Z-score normalization followed by quantile normalization was performed to visualize the proteome data.

Gene expression profiles from ROSMAP cohort samples were analyzed to identify cluster-specific differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in AD. The workflow identified 312 DEGs in subgroup 1 and 1,038 DEGs in subgroup 2, with 524 DEGs identified when merging all samples of the ROSMAP cohort. ROS/MAP RNA-seq samples were used to evaluate distribution of single sample enrichment scores of layer makers across subgroups.

Spatial transcriptomics samples of DLPFC from normal participants available from a published study (sample ID 151673, Maynard et al.). Z-score normalized expressions of top 50 genes of each subgroup and gene set enrichment analysis were performed using this spatial transcriptomics data. Layer markers from Maynard et al. were used for pairwise comparison of log2 fold changes between clusters.

Parallel runs of the miR-QTL analysis were performed using reads mapped to miRBase database Release 22.1. Annotations specific to miRBase tended to be lowly expressed in brain samples. The authors chose to use the MirGeneDB set for subsequent colocalization and integration analyses since including poor quality annotations would reduce the power and interpretability of these analyses; however, all data are made available as a resource for future studies.

Parallel runs of the miR-QTL analysis were performed using reads mapped to the curated MirGeneDB database version 2.1. MirGeneDB contains less than 30% of the annotations in miRBase due to its more stringent inclusion criteria. After filtering both annotation sets using a minimum abundance threshold, there was a much larger overlap in the tested miRNAs, with 75% of miRNAs tested in both runs. The authors chose to use the MirGeneDB set for the subsequent colocalization and integration analyses since including poor quality annotations would reduce the power and interpretability of these analyses.

960 individuals were selected from the Swedish BioFINDER-2 study with at least two tau-PET scans (follow-ups were at 1 year (N = 66), 2 years (N = 924), 4 years (N = 335); 6 years (N = 60)). Two intersecting data subsets were selected: 773 individuals having at least two amyloid-PET scans for estimating amyloid duration, and 434 CSF-amyloid-positive individuals for comparison with timelines across the whole population. Regional tau-PET SUVR abnormality was computed in five established data-driven regions using mixture modelling. A novel explicit-duration version of the temporal event-based model (T-EBM) was used to determine the order and timeline of global amyloid-PET and regional tau-PET abnormality.

The study included 838 amyloid-β-positive participants from the BioFINDER-2 cohort who had undergone tau-PET ([18F]RO948). Participants were classified on clinical staging (cognitively normal to dementia) and biological staging (early to advanced). The cohort was used to compare individuals with congruent biological and clinical stage ('Reference' group) to those with more advanced clinical impairment than biological stage ('Clinical > Biological') and those with opposite pattern ('Biological > Clinical') on demographics, neurodegeneration measures (cortical thickness, TDP-43 MRI signature, NfL), alpha-synuclein CSF status, GFAP, white matter lesions, infarcts and microbleeds. Results showed 37.7% in Reference group, 51.3% in Clinical > Biological group, and 11.0% in Biological > Clinical group.

The screening interview included the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) in the version developed for field surveys. The screening interview also included a selection of additional questions recommended by the MRC Alzheimer's Disease Workshop as described previously. Coverage of language skills was extended by adding two objects to be named to the original MMSE objects. Praxis was extended by adding writing to dictation (a name and address) to the MMSE item writing a sentence. The coverage of memory was extended with three additional items: (a) asking subjects to recall the four objects they had named earlier in the session; (b) asking subjects to recall the name and address they had written earlier in the session; (c) a set of five questions assessing semantic memory or general knowledge. At screen, subjects were assigned an organicity score using the organic symptoms component of the AGECAT computerised algorithm. MRC CFAS investigators undertook the fieldwork and oversaw the scientific integrity of the study.

dataset_context_from_paper: Raw small RNA count matrices for combined imported and harmonized across two batches of sequencing. Small RNA libraries were prepared from total RNA using QIAseq miRNA UDI Library Kit, with adapters ligated to 3' and 5' ends of mature miRNAs, followed by reverse transcription with UMI-containing primers. Libraries were sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq platform using paired-end 150 bp reads. Lowly expressed RNAs were excluded based on counts per million (CPM) reads (at least 1 CPM across minimum 20% of samples). Data cleaning and normalization performed using edgeR and limma packages. Differential expression analysis performed between age groups (Young <40 years, Middle 40-69 years, Old ≥70 years) accounting for confounding covariates including RIN, age, sex, and library preparation using limma-voom with empirical Bayes moderation and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR adjustment (threshold 0.05).

The 10/66 cohort is an open-access database containing longitudinal data from multiple assessment waves including baseline, follow-up, and 3rd wave/refreshment cohort. Data includes household assessments, participant interviews covering age, socioeconomic status, health, disability (WHODAS-II), quality of life (DEMQOL), cognitive functioning (CSI'D', 10-word list-learning test), mental health (GMS), clinical examinations including neurological assessment (NEUROEX) and physical assessment, biological assessments (haematological tests, biochemical tests, ApoE genotyping, metabolic syndrome markers, age-related decline biomarkers), and informant interviews with caregiver questionnaires and behavioral/psychological symptom assessments (NPI). Study of 263 participants from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (mean age 72.7 ± 10.1 years, 53.6% women). Outcomes included measures of cardiorespiratory fitness (maximal oxygen consumption [VO2peak]) and energetic efficiency (energetic cost of walking and resting metabolic rate [RMR]). Cross-sectional associations examined between sleep metrics and CRF, walking energetics, and RMR, with exploration of moderation by age, sex, and race.

321 individuals with AD, DLB, PD, and controls from 6 centers of the EPND study. Controls were defined as normal cognition and normal Aβ42/40, whereas AD as abnormal Aβ42/40 without meeting clinical criteria of DLB or PD. Linear regression models adjusted for age and sex were used. Associations were post-hoc compared between individuals with low (≤23), intermediate (24-27), and high (≥28) MMSE scores.

RNAseq data from post mortem brain donors used to identify distinct RNA expression profiles associated with dimensional Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) clinical domain scores in Alzheimer's disease. Differential gene expression analyses were performed in the aINS and dACG brain regions across five clinical domains using ImpulseDE2. Pathway enrichment analysis was conducted using Metascape with multiple databases including Gene Ontology, KEGG, Reactome, and Wikipathway. The study combined natural language processing of electronic health records with RNA sequencing to identify molecular mechanisms associated with neuropsychiatric symptoms in AD.

Analysis code for RNAseq data processing and differential expression analyses is available at the Klengel Lab GitHub page. The code implements RDoC-based NLP algorithms to obtain quantitative measures of clinical domain scores from medical records, as well as the computational pipeline for identifying RNA expression profiles associated with clinical phenotypes.

PET imaging study using [18F]RO948 performed on a digital scanner (Discovery MI; GE Healthcare) 70 to 90 minutes following injection in a large number of patients recruited into BioFINDER-2. Standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) images were created using the inferior cerebellar cortex as the reference region. The DAC-SP Early Detection program was initiated in 2021 in seven healthcare systems across six countries. DCA results across the seven sites are presented in Table 1. The program implemented digital cognitive assessments in primary care and other non-specialty settings. Approximately 60% of the patients in the DAC-SP Early Detection program tested abnormal or borderline for cognitive issues. Patients were eligible for a DCA if they were over 60 years of age, able to hear and see well enough to complete the assessments, and had no prior diagnosis of dementia. An AD test-retest cohort (N = 10x2) was used to assess within-subject repeatability of Centiloid (CL) quantification across seven pipelines. Test-retest analysis revealed absolute biases <5 CL, within-subject coefficients of variation 2.6-4.4% and 95% repeatability coefficients 8.1-16.1 CL.

An amnestic MCI cohort (N = 80) was used to assess reproducibility in terms of absolute agreement in continuous CL values. Agreement in +/- status between software was 92-99% (kappa 0.84-0.97) in this dataset. Strong group-level associations in continuous CL estimates were observed across pairs of software (R2 ≥0.93).

Cases from the BioFINDER-1 cohort enriched for amyloid loads around published positivity thresholds (0-50CL) (N = 110) were used to assess reliability for dichotomizing amyloid scans into positive and negative at three thresholds of 11, 25 and 37 CL. Inter-software reliability in dichotomization was >92% for scans across a wide range of CL values, but the percentage was lower for scans with amyloid loads closer to the range of typical positivity thresholds.

The bulk RNA-seq dataset was obtained from the AMP-AD (Accelerating Medicines Partnership-Alzheimer's Disease) project, with the necessary permissions obtained to download the raw counts table for both AD and control samples. Each cohort provided RNA expression data for a total of 60,675 genes. Data quality filtering removed genes with less than 1 RPM (reads per million) counts in at least 50% of samples per tissue, resulting in 389 overlapping genes from protein-coding genes and lipid droplet related genes. Analysis compared expression levels between Braak stage 0-2 (control samples) and Braak stage 5-6 (AD samples) using Limma package with TMM normalization and Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. Differentially expressed genes were identified with adjusted p-value < 0.05 and absolute log2 fold change > 0.25 across five cohorts and multiple brain regions including parahippocampal gyrus, superior temporal gyrus, and temporal cortex.

A set of 16,465 protein-coding genes detected in the human brain was obtained from the human protein atlas, which was used to compile a list of 389 overlapping genes when intersected with 558 lipid droplet related genes under 6 GO terms.

RNA-Seq data from the PPMI database was accessed in PD patients and healthy controls. The authors analyzed 45 pre-defined non-motor traits previously identified. WGCNA was used to find modules of co-expressed genes with those non-motor traits with very strong filtering to determine the quality of data-derived. Co-expression networks were constructed, followed by the identification of modules of interest, such as those showing statistical significance and associated correlation with NMS traits. Gene significance and module membership were calculated to identify hub genes.

Missense mutation data in PFBC-associated genes (SLC20A2, PDGFRB, PDGFB, MYORG, XPR1, JAM2, CMPK2, and NAA60) were collated from the PFBC Variant Database and supplemented with literature searches. Annotation encompassed minor allele frequency, PolyPhen2 pathogenicity, ClinVar classification, transcriptome expression, amino acid changes, protein structure prediction, solvent accessibility, functional sites, and post-translational modifications. PFBC mutations exhibited an increase in missense mutations causing mutual conversions between nonpolar and polar amino acids, and in helical protein structures.

Gene expression datasets related to PD and melanoma were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. Differential expression analysis was performed using R, followed by enrichment analysis to identify key pathways. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were constructed for shared DEGs. Hub genes were identified using Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression. Correlation analyses were performed for programmed cell death (PCD) and immune cell infiltration using single sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) and CIBERSORT.

Data (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.10962119, release 7) used in the preparation of this article were obtained from the Global Parkinson's Genetics Program (GP2). Samples from GP2 release 6 with imputation calls from the TOPMed server were stored in PLINK2 format (pgen, psam, and pvar files) for each ancestry available. Data was extracted for SNPs within the chromosome base pair ranges for each gene locus and extracted into PLINK2 .raw files. Samples were matched on their GP2SampleID and matched per SNP on the matching chromosome, base position, reference allele, and alternate allele.

Samples from GP2 release 6 with imputation calls from the TOPMed server (Das et al., 2016) hosted on Biowulf were stored in PLINK2 format (pgen, psam, and pvar files) for each ancestry available. Data was extracted for SNPs within the chromosome base pair ranges for each gene locus. Cluster Buster genotypes were compared to imputed genotypes with concordance rates calculated on a per SNP level. For SNPs to be considered 'high-performing', concordance rates between predicted genotypes and imputed genotypes needed to be 90% or higher.

Samples from GP2 release 6 were sequenced and called with DeepVariant-GLnexus (Hampton Leonard et al., 2024). These samples with whole genome sequence genotype calls hosted on Terra were stored in PLINK2 format (pgen, psam, and pvar files) for each ancestry available. Data was extracted for SNPs within the chromosome, base pair ranges for each gene locus and extracted into PLINK2 .raw files. Predicted genotypes were compared to WGS genotypes with concordance rates calculated on a per SNP level.

Each sample processed by GP2 was genotyped by the Illumina NeuroBooster Array SNP genotyping platform (Sara Bandres-Ciga, 2023). Primary sample identifiers, SNP genotypes, and metrics are collected and stored in parquet files. To minimize bias and ensure the representation of rare variants, 44 samples were randomly selected per the eleven available ancestries (Afro-Caribbean, African, Ashkenazi, Admixed American, Complex Admixture History, Central Asian, East Asian, European, Finish, Middle East, South Asian). SNPs were selected to include those within APOE, GBA, LRRK2, and SNCA, for a total of 1,064 SNPs across 484 individuals directly genotyped on the NeuroBooster array.

MedDiet plasma metabolomic dataset with 466 samples that passed quality control. Key findings: 4 metabolites (TrpBetaine, CE(17:1), PCaaC40:5, PCaeC42:3) mediated association between diet and frailty index. Metabolomic signatures explained 28-38% of dietary pattern variance.

Fruit and vegetable intake metabolomic study with 43 metabolites retrieved through targeted metabolomics (mainly lipid species) and 22 metabolites from untargeted metabolomics. Analysis identified metabolites that changed significantly between frail and fit populations. Hippuric acid emerged as key mediating metabolite between fruit-vegetable intake and frailty status, with low plasma hippuric acid associated with frailty and decline in fruit-vegetable intake.

SNAC-K data are sensitive; thus, they cannot be shared publicly but raw and analyzed deidentified data can be requested by qualified researchers. The request will be reviewed to ensure confidentiality obligations and intellectual property. A datasharing agreement must be signed before data release. The study harmonized chronic conditions using ICD and ATC codes, as well as study visit data. LASSO models were developed in SNAC-K cohort to identify biomarkers associated with the rate of disease accumulation. BLSA data are available to qualified researchers through submission of proposals. The baseline characteristics of the BLSA study sample are reported in Supplementary Table 7. Due to limited biomarker availability in the BLSA, it was not feasible to replicate the full LASSO models developed in SNAC-K cohort. Instead, the results of the LASSO analysis were validated by assessing the predictive accuracy of the LASSO-derived model in this independent cohort using MSE as the accuracy metric. The chronic conditions available in BLSA were harmonized using ICD and ATC codes, as well as study visit data to align with those in the SNAC-K dataset.

Neurobanco is part of the Antioquia Neuroscience Group (GNA) and is located at the University Research Headquarters (SIU) of the University of Antioquia (Medellín—Colombia). It was established in 1995, is focused on the study of neurodegenerative diseases, and has the largest repository of brains from a family group with AD (more than 140 brains from those affected with the E280A mutation in PSEN1). DIAN‐LatAm is part of the global DIAN observational study and is aimed at establishing a Latin American multicenter registry of DIAD families by collecting comprehensive clinical, psychometric, neuroimaging, and biomarker data. The DIAN‐LatAm network aims to create a cohort‐ready population to implement the DIAN‐Trail Unit (DIAN‐TU) platform in the region. The DIAN‐TU platform was launched in 2012 to implement therapeutic trials for DIAD individuals and help in the identification of disease‐modifying agents that can also be translated to sporadic AD. To date, the DIAN‐LatAm centers include those in Puerto Rico, Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, and Argentina.

The National Dementia Biobank (BND) in Mexico has focused on research on biomarkers and non‐invasive methods for the early diagnosis of AD. The BND highlighted collaboration with several entities, such as the Latin American and Caribbean Brain Bank Network, the Brain Bank of the Dominican Republic, the Brain Bank of Peru, DIAN, and several academic institutions.

DNA Bank Neurogenetics, founded in 2020, became the first DNA biobank of the public healthcare system in Peru. It supports various collaborative research projects, such as the Latin American Research Consortium on the Genetics of Parkinson's Disease (LARGE PD) and the Peruvian Alzheimer's Disease Initiative (PeADI).

HEK293 cells (CRL-1573, ATCC) were transfected with GFP-fusion constructs of canonical PLCG2 and D65-PLCG2. After 24 h, media was replaced with HBSS with or without 20uM A23187 calcium ionophore (Sigma) for five minutes to assess Ca+2 response and cellular localization of the PLCG2 isoforms.

Working with human brain cDNA, researchers identified several PLCG2 isoforms that began with the LNC. PCRs were performed on cDNA samples corresponding to 30 ng of RNA with primers spanning exons 1-33 of PLCG2 to detect novel PLCG2 splice variants. Multiple isoforms were identified including canonical PLCG2, D65-PLCG2, and variants with different LNC exon combinations and intron retention patterns.

Clustering of the integrated dataset was performed using a shared nearest neighbor approach and clusters were visualized using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). Clusters were manually assigned cell type identities based on differential expression of established cell type marker genes.

For neuronal subtypes, the broad neuron classification categories identified in the Allen Brain Atlas Transcriptome Explorer of the 'Human-M1-10x' dataset (e.g., PVALB+ inhibitory neurons = InN.PVALB) were used when appropriate to assign cell type identities to clusters.

PD status and symptom prevalence in the 23andMe database is based on self-report. 23andMe PD self-report measures have shown excellent correlation with clinical evaluations. From examining the number of participants with PD that viewed their 23andMe genetic health risk reports, 46% were aware of their LRRK2 p.G2019S and GBA1 p.N409S carrier status, and 32% were aware of their APOE E4 carrier status.

Brain tissue RNA-seq data from the MSBB (Mount Sinai Brain Bank) cohort used to characterize transcriptomic features including lncRNA expression, eRNA expression, alternative polyadenylation (APA) events, and A-to-I RNA editing across six brain regions. The MSBB cohort used ribosomal RNA (rRNA) depletion library preparation method, allowing capture of a broader range of RNA molecules including nonpolyadenylated transcripts such as eRNAs. Expression levels, PDUI values, and editing levels were analyzed and deposited in the ADatlas portal. The dataset includes thousands of significant differential events for ncRNAs and PTM events between AD traits across brain regions.

Brain tissue RNA-seq data from the Mayo cohort used alongside MSBB data to characterize transcriptomic features including lncRNA expression, eRNA expression, alternative polyadenylation (APA) events, and A-to-I RNA editing across brain regions. The Mayo cohort used polyA selection library preparation method, which enriches for polyadenylated transcripts. Fewer eRNAs were identified in Mayo samples compared to MSBB samples due to the differing RNA-seq library preparation techniques. Data was deposited in the ADatlas portal allowing users to browse, search, query, and download ncRNAs and PTMs across six brain regions.

The PPMI dataset is a comprehensive, open-access study aimed at identifying biomarkers of PD progression. Patients included recently diagnosed, unmedicated PD patients. The dataset covers demographics, medical and PD history, motor and non-motor assessments (such as MDS-UPDRS, Hoehn & Yahr staging, cognitive and mood evaluations), medication use, and additional features like sleep and olfactory tests. It also includes imaging (123I-Ioflupane SPECT, MRI) and biospecimen data (CSF, blood, urine) gathered at baseline and regular follow-up visits over several years. Data were collected every 3 months for the first 2 years and then subsequently every 6 months. Images were captured on a clinical SPECT/CT scanner 3-4 h after 123I-Ioflupane injections at doses between 111 and 185 MBq, at both baseline and after 1 year. The authors used this dataset to develop prediction models for Parkinson's disease progression, merging it with a real-world dataset for analysis.

The data that support the findings of this study are available on request from the corresponding author. The data are not publicly available due to privacy or ethical restrictions. A real-world dataset was merged with the PPMI dataset for this study. Clinical subtypes from this dataset were included in the analysis alongside PPMI data. All participants in this dataset were N+ (striatal neurodegeneration positive based on 123I-ioflupane SPECT imaging).

SNP rs595765 is not present in 1000 Genomes, but examination of other top SNPs reveals three distinct LD blocks in this region used for validation of genetic variants in AD and stroke GWAS analysis. The dataset served as a reference for allele frequency comparison and variant presence validation.

Agora calculates a target AD risk score that ranges from 0–5 and is based on various multi-omic results, including GWAS studies, QTL studies, phenotypic evidence from human and/or animal models, transcriptomic data from RNA-seq profiling, and proteomic data from label-free quantitation (LFQ) and Tandem Mass Tagging (TMT) shot-gun profiling methods. This integrated resource was used to assess multi-omic evidence for Alzheimer's disease.

The integrated Seurat object included 101,292 cells (55,716 for AD, and 45,576 for Control) with 30,412 features. Data were processed using Seurat package version 5.0.2, filtered for cells with less than 200 expressed genes and genes expressed in less than 3 cells. Following normalization, 2,000 top variable features were identified, integration was performed, doublets were removed, and 36 clusters were identified with resolution 1.

Zebrafish dataset was processed using the same methods and parameters as the human transcriptome for creating a Seurat object. Main cell types were identified using marker genes including s100b and gfap for astroglia, sv2a, nrgna, grin1a, grin1b for neurons, pdgfrb and kcne4 for pericytes, cd74a and apoc1 for microglia, mbpa and mpz for OD, aplnra for OPC, myh11a and tagln2 for vascular SMC, lyve1b for lymph endothelial cells, and kdrl for vascular cells.
