MRI scans from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-4) project were used to apply two distinct clustering approaches, HYDRA and CHIMERA, to delineate the spatial pattern of brain atrophy attributable to Alzheimer's Disease. Both methods identified two disease subtypes with marked atrophy within medial temporal areas, notably the hippocampus, and variations in superior frontal, middle temporal, parietal cortex, and precuneus regions. The findings demonstrate data-driven approaches to derive clinically meaningful patterns of neurodegeneration in heterogeneous AD presentations.

This analysis used data openly available from PPMI; data used in the preparation of this manuscript were obtained on July 3, 2023 from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database. PPMI is a longitudinal, observational, multi-center natural history study of PD. PPMI Online refers to a large cohort of individuals recruited online, from which subgroups are further selected based on qualifying criteria to participate in various investigations of the progression of clinical features, imaging outcomes, or biologic and genetic markers possibly related to PD. In the study reported here, only data from participants in PPMI Online aged 60 years or older who did not have a PD diagnosis were included. Participants completed online questionnaires to collect demographics and vital statistics, and medical and family history. An UPSIT (revised version) was provided in person or mailed to eligible participants to complete. This analysis was conducted by the PPMI Statistics Core and used actual dates of activity for participants, a restricted data element not available to public users of PPMI data.

The Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA) is an open observational cohort study of community-dwelling volunteers that are followed every 1–4 years depending on their age. The sample considered in the study consists of 1769 participants (5090 follow-ups) with completed data for physical examination, health history assessment, and donated a blood sample. The study examined the longitudinal association of neutrophil, lymphocyte absolute count, and their ratio with longitudinal risk for multimorbidity and mortality. The NL ratio increased with age and was associated with a higher risk of mortality, while a lower NL ratio was inversely correlated with multimorbidity. Neutrophils increased with aging and an increase in their absolute number predicted mortality risk.

Data used in the preparation of this article were from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database. Participants included were from the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging (MCSA) and had plasma markers measured by mass spectrometry (IP‐MS; C2N), had an amyloid‐PET scan, and had a tau‐PET negative scan (SUVR<1.29, temporal meta‐ROI) at the baseline, along with one or more follow‐up tau‐PET scans. 255 MCSA participants (122 female [47.8%]) were included with a median age of 71.9 (IQR: 65.8, 78.8) years old, of which 37 progressed to tau‐PET positivity. At baseline, 238 (93.7%) were cognitively unimpaired. Cox proportional hazard models were used to evaluate the relationship between C2N plasma %P‐Tau217 and APS2 and incident tau‐PET positivity.

The analyses were repeated in the BioFINDER‐2 cohort for validation. Among 605 participants who were tau negative at index date in BioFINDER‐2 (316 (52.2%) cognitively unimpaired), with a median age of 70.2 (IQR: 60.5‐76.4), 33 progressed to tau positivity with higher %p‐tau217 (HR: 1.8 [95% CI: 1.5, 2.17]), amyloid‐PET centiloid (HR: 2.3 [95% CI: 1.77, 2.97]), and lower Aβ 42/40 (HR: 0.42 [95% CI: 0.21, 0.85]) at index date all associated with an increased risk of progressing to tau‐PET positive.

The Global Parkinson's Genetics Program (GP2) is a major endeavor aiming to discover novel insights into the genetic drivers of PD and to make this knowledge globally available and actionable. This ambitious program aims to perform genotyping and/or sequencing in ∼200,000 individuals with PD and prioritizes the inclusion of populations worldwide that historically have been underrepresented in genetic studies. The bulk of collected samples were initially planned to undergo genotyping using a high throughput and cost-effective custom-designed content platform (i.e., the NeuroBooster array), and it is now anticipated that many samples will be sequenced, thus increasing the power to detect nearly all forms of genomic variation in an unbiased manner.

The procedure for the gait analysis performed in the BLSA gait laboratory has been described previously. Usual-paced gait speed was assessed by asking participants to walk at their normal, comfortable pace over a 10-meter gait laboratory walkway. Fast-paced gait speed was assessed by asking participants to walk as fast as possible without running. A Vicon 3D motion capture system with 10 digital cameras (Vicon 612 system, Oxford Metrics Ltd., Oxford, U.K.) measured the 3D locations of markers positioned on the skin and non-reflective, form-fitting spandex pants to assess landmarks of lower extremity segments (60 Hz sampling frequency). Gait parameters included gait speed, stride length, and stride width. The Generalized Gait Stability Score (GGSS) was computed to evaluate the integrated essential spatiotemporal gait parameters for both usual and fast-paced walking. During the repeated chair stand test participants start in a seated position, keep their arms folded across their chest, come to a full standing position then sit down in the chair again. The sample includes both male and female participants.

The AIBL study is a consortium between Austin Health, CSIRO, Edith Cowan University, the Florey Institute (The University of Melbourne), and the National Ageing Research Institute. Analysis of biomarker, MRI, and cognitive data from cognitively unimpaired (CU) adults enrolled in the AIBL study identified a sample of older individuals (n = 65) whose Alzheimer's disease was emerging. The emergent AD group was aged approximately 72 years old at baseline and provided relevant data over an average 8-year follow-up period. Participants were classified as CU with Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) global score of 0, had Aβ levels below 15 CL at baseline, and attended at least one subsequent visit for Aβ-PET, MRI, and cognitive assessment. Longitudinal data were collected up to the most recent time point at which all three assessments were completed within a 12-month window.

The SomaScan assay detects approximately 7,000 proteins using aptamer-based technology called slow off-rate modified aptamers (SOMAmers). The ADNI dataset was used as the training set for developing a scorecard with a point-based scoring system and risk-probability mapping for predicting cognitive progression. The scorecard's point-based scoring system and its associated risk-probability mapping were derived solely from the ADNI training set with no retraining, parameter optimization, or scorecard threshold adjustments performed for external validation. Predictive features included LDEL, LOGIMEM, FAQ, TRAILB, ANIMALS alongside demographic covariates (Age, Sex, Education, Race).

The NACC dataset served as a strictly independent external validation cohort for the scorecard developed from ADNI. The pattern of missingness in the NACC dataset was evaluated using standardized mean differences and found to not be missing completely at random. Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) was employed to address systematic missingness, generating m = 5 imputed datasets using Bayesian posterior sampling. The model's calibration was assessed on five imputed NACC datasets, with mean and standard deviation reported for AUC, Accuracy, and Brier scores across these evaluations. The same predictive features (LDEL, LOGIMEM, FAQ, TRAILB, ANIMALS) and demographic covariates were used.

The English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) was characterized as a novel longitudinal CHIP cohort through genetic analysis of 13270 longitudinal peripheral blood samples from participants aged over 50. Using logistic and robust regression analysis, the study showed that statin therapy is associated with reduced TET2 CHIP clonal expansion in a gene specific manner. The dataset was used to analyze the effect of statin therapy on clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) and its association with myocardial infarction and stroke incidence in individuals with CHIP.

Regions of interest (ROIs) were defined using the human Brainnetome atlas (BNA) which consists of 210 cortical and 36 subcortical regions bilaterally. Compared to traditional anatomical parcellations (e.g., Desikan atlas), the BNA provides a more neurobiologically informed framework by capturing the fine-grained organization of the brain's network architecture. It has been widely used in neuroimaging research for ROI-based analysis, connectomics, and network-level comparisons in both healthy and clinical populations.

Structural T1-weighted magnetic resonance images were acquired on a 1.5 Tesla, 3 Tesla, or 4 Tesla system. MR images were bias-corrected, segmented into gray matter (GM), white matter (WM) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and normalized to Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) using an optimized geodesic shooting procedure in CAT12 toolbox via Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM). Gray matter images were modulated with voxel values multiplied by Jacobian determinants resulting from the spatial normalization to preserve relative GM volumes from the original images. Gray matter volumes were extracted from the participants' segmented and modulated structural images.

Classification performance metrics include accuracy, recall, and specificity.

Single cell and single nucleus RNA sequencing datasets from 110 GB (glioblastoma) patients. Used to assess senescent cells using three established gene lists, performed differential gene expression and conducted gene set enrichment analysis. Senescence scores were compared across different cell types and patients. Microglia were specifically enriched for senescence gene sets among glial cells, with a proinflammatory GB microglia subtype identified through data harmonization showing high similarity with AD microglia and highest senescence scores.

Single cell and single nucleus RNA sequencing datasets from 89 individuals with varying stages of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). Following data integration with GB datasets, senescent cells were assessed using three established gene lists, differential gene expression performed, and gene set enrichment analysis conducted. Senescence scores were compared across different cell types and patients. Quantitative analysis of immunohistochemistry measurements in the AD dataset confirmed that samples with high senescence score showed significantly higher density of tau pathology and altered microglia morphology.

The dataset was used for benchmarking methods and applying transfer learning to adapt pretrained models to smaller, clinical datasets.

The dataset contains microstate analysis data with parameters including duration (mean duration of a specific microstate that remains stable), coverage (the percentage of time spent when a given microstate is dominant), and occurrence (the number of times the microstate appears per second) organized per age group and per frequency band. The NACC centralized data repository contains a large relational database of standardized clinical and neuropathological research data that includes comprehensive clinical, sociodemographic, neuropsychological, and biomarker data. For this study, sociodemographic, clinical (neurological signs/symptoms, cerebrovascular risk factors), and neuropsychological data were used from the baseline visit. Neurological signs and symptoms were assessed through neurological examination. CVRFs included hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterol, BMI ≥ 30, years of smoking, history of stroke, history of TIA, and Hachinski Ischemic Score. After excluding amyloid negative participants, differences were found in DSF, DSB, Animal Fluency, Vegetable Fluency, BNT, TMT-A, TMT-B, and Digit Symbol tests.

Data from the Anti-Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (A4) Study are available to qualified investigators through the A4 Study data sharing platform. The study includes baseline demographic, clinical, and biomarker characteristics from a cohort followed over 240 weeks. Enrichment subgroups were analyzed based on plasma pTau217 levels and digital memory assessment (DMA) performance. The dataset was used to empirically derive pass/fail rates for alternative enrichment funnel scenarios and to evaluate PACC (Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite) decline trajectories across different enrichment strategies. Resource demands analysis showed the full cohort required approximately 38,000 clinical visits and 25,000 amyloid PET scans, while enriched designs substantially reduced these requirements.

SHARE cohort data used for analysis of COVID-19 hospitalization and mortality outcomes. The dataset provided mortality data for COVID-19-related deaths, though the number of COVID-19-related deaths was relatively small and results were sensitive to imputations for missing covariates. SHARE had the largest sample size for hospitalization analysis among the three cohorts studied.

Health and Retirement Study (HRS) cohort used for COVID-19 analysis. The study notes that lack of end-of-life data from HRS prevented the analysis of COVID-19 mortality in this cohort. Cognitive assessment data (word recall) was collected across the cohort, though age-stratified analyses were not conducted due to limited sample sizes in each age group.

English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) cohort used for COVID-19 hospitalization analysis. The study notes that ELSA included only 39 hospitalized individuals, limiting the statistical power for this cohort. Like HRS, lack of end-of-life data from ELSA prevented analysis of COVID-19 mortality. Cognitive data (word recall) was collected across the cohort.

The Whitehall II data-base includes extensive socio-economic data, which will allow testing of relevant hypotheses that cross over to risk factors employed in medical epidemiology, and cover the entire adult life course from early adulthood (age 35) to old age. The study follows the Medical Research Council (MRC) Policy on data sharing, i.e. images and other data will be available for analysis by other groups after completion of the study. The Whitehall MRI substudy will have the availability of a fine-grained chronological clinical and life-style record with very detailed cognitive assessment and comprehensive MRI data covering structural and functional brain connectivity.

RNA-seq data have been uploaded to the FAIR Data Sharing Portal within the Alzheimer's Disease Workbench, which is supported by the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative. Gene and TE abundance were estimated from BAM files using TEcount with GENCODE release 34 annotation and a prebuilt TE annotation index. Reads were aligned to the GRCh38 build of the human reference genome using STAR version 2.7.3a. Gene lists were generated from DESeq2 analyses and ranked by log2 fold-change for Gene Set Enrichment Analysis using GSEAPreranked tool with Hallmark Molecular Signatures Database supplemented with gene sets representing senescence-associated secretory and type I interferon response pathways.

Datasets used in this study are openly available at https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds004504 (accessed on 20 June 2023). For analysis, a 5 min segment of data was selected for each participant, as the shortest recording duration was 5.1 min. Data curation was performed to ensure accuracy and relevance of the datasets used.

The data utilized in this study were sourced from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) database, specifically drawing from the NACC Uniform Data Set (UDS) and MRI Data Set. Participants aged above 55 and under 95 with no diagnoses of neurological disorders at baseline were included if they had longitudinal cognitive assessments as well as baseline demographics information and subjective cognitive decline (SCD) assessments. PET or CSF based measures of amyloid positivity provided by the NACC were used to determine amyloid classifications (A+, Amyloid Positive; A− Amyloid Negative).

The data utilized in this study were sourced from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) database, specifically drawing from the NACC Uniform Data Set (UDS) and MRI Data Set. Measurements were obtained from the NACC database. PET and CSF based binary indicators of elevated amyloid and tau were obtained from the NACC database, provided by the NACC ADRCs.

The authors focus on encoding-aware preprocessing for longitudinal cohort data like ELSA because categorical variables need to be encoded before correlation analysis, since correlation measures might not be directly comparable across categorical and continuous data types. The study uses ELSA data to develop machine learning models (XGBoost and Random Forest) for predicting depression, analyzing features such as negative social interactions (NSoc), future outlook (FuEn), motivation for social and cultural activities (MoActVar), overall sleep quality (heslpf), self-reported general health (Hehelf), and frequency of internet use (scint) as predictors of depressive symptoms measured by CES-D items.

The EEG data used in this study are openly available through the OpenNeuro repository. Specifically, the dataset from Miltiadous et al. (2023) [ds004504] was used. The dataset was used as the primary dataset for analyzing EEG-based metrics to differentiate between FTD and AD in comparison to age-matched controls, employing complexity-based techniques including DFA and HFD analysis on global brain activity as well as rostral and caudal sensor data.

To validate the results from the Miltiadous et al. (2023) dataset we utilized a second open-source dataset from Vicchietti et al. (2023). This dataset consisted of 19-channel recordings under the 10–20 electrode placement system. Participants include 12 healthy elderly controls with their eyes closed, 12 controls with their eyes open, 80 probable AD patients with their eyes closed, and 80 probable AD patients with their eyes open, wherein 8 s of data was provided for each. The data was sampled at 128 Hz. The replication of key findings, specifically the increase in theta power and the reduction in alpha power and signal complexity in AD, suggests that the observed EEG alterations are not specific to a single dataset or acquisition protocol.

The research data were made available through ELSA, and as such, our study data cannot be made available for access. ELSA is described as one of the significant cohort and routine clinical practice databases characterized by very large and heterogenous set of variables collected across long periods of time, changes in data collection policies, and updates to the data schema. The study used ELSA data for observational retrospective clinical studies exploring complexities of multiple long-term conditions (MLTCs) and dataset harmonisation and curation tasks involving tens of thousands of variables.

Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) is identified as one of the significant catalysts for observational retrospective clinical studies, providing access to vast amounts of data known as big data in the field of data science. CPRD is characterized as a routine clinical practice database with very large and heterogenous set of variables collected across long periods of time, used for leveraging healthcare big data to discover insights into diverse clinical questions.

Secure Anonymized Information Linkage (SAIL) is noted as one of the available cohort and routine clinical practice databases that has been a significant catalyst for observational retrospective clinical studies. SAIL provides access to vast amounts of healthcare big data characterized by very large and heterogenous set of variables collected across long periods of time, enabling research into multiple long-term conditions (MLTCs).

Study participants and data from the EPINEF cohort study were used in this research examining the relationship between polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) exposure and cognitive outcomes including amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD). The dataset includes measurements of PAH metabolites (1-hydroxypyrene, 1-hydroxyphenanthrene, 2-hydroxyfluorene, 2-naphthol) and cognitive status classifications.

This study included 17,170 GNPC participants with SomaLogic 7K plasma proteomics, comprising controls and patients with AD, PD, FTD, ALS, or Stroke. The study develops AI models on data from the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium (GNPC) to predict major forms of dementia, accounting for multiple underlying pathologies. ProtAIDe achieved simultaneous balanced classification accuracy (BCA) >0.7 and AUC >0.8 across all six targets with ∼200 proteins. Despite being trained only on baseline data, ProtAIDe's baseline embeddings predicted longitudinal CDR progression with an AUC of 0.76±0.09 (N = 2052). The study demonstrates that ∼200 key proteins in blood can differentiate major forms of dementia at the patient-level.

803 non-demented participants from the European Prevention of Alzheimer's Dementia (EPAD) cohort (age 64.7±7.3 years, 57.0% females, 34.2% APOE4 carriers) who underwent genome sequencing, CSF Aβ1-42 and p-Tau181 measurements, and structural and diffusion MRI. Participants were analyzed to assess the effect of pathway-specific polygenic risk scores, Aβ1-42 and p-Tau181, and their interactions on white matter integrity at the bundle and fixel levels using linear models corrected for age, sex, total intracranial volume, and APOE-ε4 carriership.

Bellenguez polygenic risk scores constructed using 85 genetic variants associated with Alzheimer's disease. After excluding those mapping to APOE loci, genetic variants were grouped based on biological function into 6 pathway-specific PRSs (amyloid, clearance, immune activation, inflammation, migration and signal transduction pathways) to assess their effect on white matter fiber density and fiber cross-section.

Between 2006 and 2010, the UK Biobank study recruited more than 0.5 million participants, aged 40-70, from the general population at 22 assessment centres across England, Scotland, and Wales. Data collection involved questionnaires, interviews, regular assessment centre visits, and health record linkages, covering diverse psychosocial, sociodemographic, physical, and genetic variables. The study was used to analyze the relationship between sugar rationing and cardiovascular disease (CVD), including outcomes such as atrial fibrillation (AF) and heart failure (HF).

Analysis code and data are available in a public, open access repository at https://github.com/yangleipzig/sugar-rationing-CVD-analysis-code. This repository contains the computational resources and processed data used for the sugar rationing and CVD analysis study.

The original contributions presented in the study are publicly available at the OpenNeuro Dataset. Preprocessed datasets from OpenNeuro were used for analysis. The dataset includes 23 patients with FTD (Frontotemporal Dementia) and 29 healthy controls (CTLs) from the Second Department of Neurology, AHEPA General Hospital, Thessaloniki, Greece. Spectral power ratios were calculated from EEG data to determine the occurrence of FTD, with analysis of four consistently significant spectral power ratios (F-theta/T-alpha, F-alpha/T-theta, F-theta/F-alpha, and T-beta/T-gamma) showing AUC values over 0.7 for diagnostic discrimination.

SomaScan proteomic data is publicly accessible through the GNPC and Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative (ADDI) data-sharing platform. The study represents the largest single site CSF proteogenomic exploration to date using an aptamer-based proteomic platform evaluating a fixed number of analytes. The dataset includes CSF proteogenomic data with comprehensive quality control and reproducibility scoring. Several SomaScan proteins and genetic markers were evaluated for replication in an independent cohort (WashU dataset).

Independent cohort used for replication of SomaScan proteins and genetic markers. Several SomaScan proteins and genetic markers could not be evaluated for replication in this independent cohort due to QC failures.

Fully independent cohort (n=8,475 non-overlapping control samples) used for AD MR analysis to mitigate sample overlap issues with Bellenguez et al. AD meta-GWAS. LD estimation was conducted using PLINK2 on non-overlapping control samples from the GR@ACE cohort.

Genomic regions were downloaded from the TableBrowser tool to export data from the University of California Santa Cruz (UCSC) Genome Browser annotation track database. Human genome filtered in GRCh38/hg38 (Dec. 2013) assembly with Genes and Gene prediction group selected. The knownGene table from GENCODE V46 track was used to download complete genome region including hg38.knownGene and hg38.kgXref variables.

Protein information downloaded from TableBrowser by selecting the SwissProt Aln. (unipAliSwissprot) table from the UniProt track. Chromosomal coordinates for these proteins were included in the GRCh38/hg38 (Dec. 2013) assembly.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarker measurements from 3,004 subjects assayed on the Roche Elecsys platform to measure levels of amyloid-beta peptide 1–42 (Abeta42), total tau protein (tTau) and phosphorylated tau protein (pTau). The dataset includes demographic variables and biomarker measurements subject to detection limits: 10/3,004 observations of Abeta42 are left censored and 349/3,004 observations are right censored; 31/3,004 observations of tTau are left censored and 4 are right censored; and 110/3,004 observations of pTau are left-censored and 5 are right censored. Authors applied Gaussian mixture models to identify disease subtypes and account for censoring, demographic effects, and unknown disease status in African American individuals who are underrepresented in AD biomarker studies.

The public clinical EEG dataset used in this study is available at the OpenNeuro repository (dataset ds004504). The dataset contains EEG recordings from patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and healthy controls (HC). Authors selected 10-second snapshots from the EEG recordings for analysis and validated consistency between selected snapshots and whole-recording spectral distribution for representative subjects (sub-027, sub-030, sub-049, and sub-083). The dataset is completely anonymized and publicly available.

All data used for this work are publicly available upon signing data sharing agreement on https://cam-can.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/dataset/. Structural MRI data were acquired using a 3 T Siemens TIM Trio scanner with T1-weighted MPRAGE sequences. The study tested whether cognition mediates the association between gray matter volume (GMV) and depressive symptoms and whether this mediation pathway is moderated by age. Cam-CAN research was supported by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BB/H008217/1).

Data from the GNPC include proteomic samples from clinically healthy individuals, and those diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), mild cognitive impairment–subjective cognitive impairment (MCI-SCI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). All cohorts and data were anonymized with letter codes by GNPC prior to analysis. All samples underwent standardized preparation and processing protocols and were stored at −80°C until proteomic profiling was performed.

dataset_context_from_paper: The data that support the finding is available from GATEWAY TO GLOBAL AGING DATA. This study utilized three large, nationally representative datasets with a relatively long follow-up period (mean: 9.01 years). The study employed a longitudinal measure of cancer incidence and conducted stratified analyses based on the presence or absence of cardiometabolic disease (CMD). Multiple sensitivity analyses were conducted to demonstrate the robustness and stability of the observed associations.

The harmonized GNPC data used to generate these findings were provided to consortium members in June 2024 and will be made available for public request by the AD Data Initiative by 15 July 2025. Members of the global research community will be able to access the metadata and place a data use request via the AD Discovery Portal. Access is contingent upon adherence to the GNPC Data Use Agreement and the Publication Policies. The study leverages large-scale cross-sectional plasma proteomic datasets across neurodegenerative diseases (AD, FTD, PD) using the SomaScan platform, providing broad proteome coverage.

Independent proteomic dataset from the UK Biobank (Olink platform) was used to assess consistency of protein associations across different cohorts. For AD, 63.3% of the selected proteins showed consistent directional effects when compared with GNPC findings. The work by Yi-Han et al. was conducted on the Olink platform, demonstrating concordance rates of 55% in Discovery (UK Biobank).

Independent proteomic dataset from the Knight ADRC using the Alamar platform was used for orthogonal validation. Memory-clinic ACE CSF cohort (N=1,372) with deeply characterized cerebrospinal fluid samples. Data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), a population representative survey used to examine the association between hair cortisol and resilience to chronic pain. Hair cortisol samples were collected from participants and analyzed alongside mental health measurements (CESD-8) and chronic pain assessments. The analytical sample included 4,539 observations with participants aged 50-99 years. Hair cortisol measurements ranged from 0.03 to 658.80 picograms per milliliter. The study notes that hair cortisol could not be collected in 20-25% of the eligible sample, with older men and women more likely to be missing hair samples. Inverse probability weighting (IPW) was used as the preferred missing data compensation method.

Data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study Innovation Panel (UKHLS-IP), a population representative survey with similar patterns of association with hair cortisol measurements conducted from the same laboratory as ELSA. The analytical sample included 473 observations with participants aged 50-93 years. Hair cortisol measurements ranged from 0.85 to 6871.50 picograms per milliliter. Mental health was measured using GHQ-12 caseness scores. The study used differing measures of mental health across surveys (GHQ-12 for UKHLS-IP versus CESD-8 for ELSA) but found consistency in patterns observed across both studies.

Single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from 1,378,211 nuclei across 84 donors in the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas (SEA-AD) Middle Temporal Gyrus dataset used to profile SLC13A5 and seven citrate metabolism genes across a continuous AD pseudoprogression score. SLC13A5 expression was restricted to astrocytes (∼20% prevalence) and concentrated in the Astro 2 supertype (24.0%), a homeostatic subtype. Analysis revealed SLC13A3 and ACO1 showed progressive donor-level declines correlating with Braak stage and Thal phase. APOE4 carriers exhibited lower SLC13A5 prevalence specifically within Astro 2 nuclei (median 17.6% vs. 25.9%). No difference in Astro 2 SLC13A5 expression was detected between cognitively resilient and expected-AD donors with equivalent high Braak burden.

Results confirm framework generalizes effectively to independent datasets with differing acquisition protocols.

Data from the placebo arm of EXPEDITION3 AD clinical trial. Participants were patients with mild dementia and biomarker evidence of amyloid burden. Participants were identified as those who demonstrated clinically meaningful cognitive decline (CMCD) or cognitively stable (CS) at final visit of the trial (week 80). Eight hundred ninety-four of the 1,072 participants in the placebo arm had necessary follow-up data, aged on average 72.7 (±7.7) years and 59% female. 55.8% of those participants showed CMCD at the final visit. Machine learning-based classifiers were trained using 70% of the EXPEDITION3 placebo sample with 5-fold cross-validation using demographics, APOE genotype, neuropsychological tests, and biomarkers (volumetric MRI). Trained models were validated in an internal validation sample within EXPEDITION3 data, showing high sensitivity and modest specificity.

A subpopulation from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) was used as an external validation sample. A subset of matched ADNI participants (ADNI AD, N = 105) were aged 74.5 (±6.4) years and 46% female. Models that were validated in ADNI AD showed high sensitivity, modest specificity, and positive predictive values of at least 15% higher than the base prevalence in ADNI AD. This served as an independent external validation dataset for machine learning models trained on EXPEDITION3 data.

Amyloid-PET scans obtained with two radiotracers [18F]Flutemetamol (n = 772) and [18F]Florbetaben (n = 568) from the AMYPAD Prognostic & Natural History Study, a pan-European multi-site study of non-demented older individuals (CDR < 1, age ≥ 50). MNI152-registered SUVR images were processed using FSL MELODIC with n-dimensional spatial group-level independent component analysis (gICA) independently for each radiotracer. The analysis identified nine-dimensional gICA robustly identifying five cortical components (frontal, parietal, occipital, unilateral left and right temporal cortices) and four non-cortical components (projection fibers, commissural fibers, lateral ventricular borders, and meninges). Components were analyzed for relationships to each other, global Aβ burden measure with Centiloid, and regional gray matter volumes independently of age, sex and estimated intracranial volume.

China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) data used for sample selection and analysis. To generate domain-specific knowledge graphs we leveraged the Pathway Commons database. In total this resource captures 1.2 million interactions among over 19 thousand proteins. Of the 19,087 nodes in the Pathway Commons knowledge graph, there was evidence for brain expression for 13,317 (69.77%).

Multi-centre amyloid PET imaging dataset created through collaboration across six centres (University of Geneva, BioFINDER, AMPLE, AMYPAD PNHS, MCSA, GEHC). The dataset includes amyloid PET scans acquired using [11C]PiB, [18F]Flutemetamol or [18F]Florbetapir, and MRI scans from approximately 130 DLB patients, along with approximately 150 AD patients and approximately 150 controls. Additionally, 99 patients positive for the CSF α-Synuclein Seeding Amplification Assay were included. Patient data were anonymized, and a harmonised database was created including demographic characteristics, clinical history, and results from neuropsychological assessments. The processing workflow includes rigorous quality control, formatting, normalisation to MNI space, harmonisation with differential smoothing, and MRI-based segmentation. The dataset enables study of amyloid PET patterns at global, regional and voxel level for investigating neuropathological underpinnings of DLB, improving diagnostic accuracy, and guiding patient stratification in anti-amyloid trials.

The application generates prediction intervals (PIs) for each outcome within the frequentist NMA to account for heterogeneity in intervention estimates.

dataset_context_from_paper: The ADNI dataset was used to train and test CNN classifiers to discriminate between progressive mild cognitive impairment (pMCI) and stable mild cognitive impairment (sMCI). The authors trained classifiers on original MRI scans, diced scans, and generated images from GAN-VAN and GAN-NOV models. The classifiers were trained for 60 epochs with stochastic gradient descent optimizer, validated and tested 5 times with different random seeds. Classification performance was assessed on ADNI test partitions. The study notes that others have achieved varying accuracy between 0.5–0.8 when predicting MCI progression to Alzheimer's disease using ADNI, with one study achieving 81% accuracy when classifying between pMCI and sMCI on ADNI.

The study achieved 64% classification accuracy with generated images from GAN-NOV when tested on the NACC dataset, demonstrating the framework's ability to generalize to unseen, heterogeneous datasets. The authors note that while the generator obtained reasonable predictions on the NACC dataset, its broader applicability needs further verification on other datasets.

The 'Happy' item showed a loading of 0.380 in CHARLS compared to 0.707 in ELSA and 0.783 in HRS, indicating substantial variation in this positively keyed item across cohorts.

HRS data from the University of Michigan Health and Retirement Study available under their conditions of use. ELSA data from the UK Data Service. The study used ELSA as one of three cohorts for cross-cohort MGCFA on six common CES-D items measuring depression. ELSA showed a 'Happy' item loading of 0.707, intermediate between CHARLS (0.380) and HRS (0.783). Cross-cohort analysis supported configural invariance (CFI = 0.981, RMSEA = 0.052, SRMR = 0.046) and partial metric invariance.

The NACC database comprises the Uniform Data Set (UDS) and Neuropathology (NP) Data Set together with additional modules and biomarker and imaging data. Subsets of UDS participants have voluntarily shared magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and calculated brain volumes, β-amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) scans, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarker data, and additional modules on participants with frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) and Lewy body disease (LBD). The database allows researchers to investigate pathology across a wide spectrum of disease and comorbidities. NACC data are freely available to researchers, and approximately 650 peer reviewed publications have used data from the NACC database. The NP Data Set was used to define PART (Braak NFT stage and absence of CERAD plaques) and LATE, with TDP-43 data collected optionally until 2014, after which it became standard.

UDS data can be linked to genetic data housed at the Alzheimer's Disease Genetic Consortium (ADGC). NACC data together with genetic data from the ADGC have played major parts in past efforts of studying the genetics of neuropathology. These genomic data are publicly available by qualified access and are a valuable resource for the dementia research community.

Phase Ib/IIa, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, MAD, parallel-group trial of Trontinemab (RO7126209, RG6102, brain shuttle gantenerumab), a bispecific mAb designed to cross the BBB more efficiently. More than 200 participants with prodromal or mild-to-moderate AD (MMSE score ranging from 18–28 and amyloid PET positive) have been enrolled and given multiple-ascending intravenous doses with doses ranging from level 1 to level 4. The primary outcome is the percentage of participants with adverse events.

DIAN-TU trial: 5-year Phase II/III study testing a combination of solanezumab and gantenerumab. The study began as a two-year Phase II biomarker study and was later expanded into a Phase III registration trial with cognitive endpoints measured after at least 4 years of treatment. The 210 participants were asymptomatic and mildly symptomatic carriers of autosomal dominant mutations in AD genes (AΒPP, PSEN-1, and PSEN-2). Administration commenced with a dosage of 400 mg solanezumab every four weeks, subsequently escalating to 1,600 mg during the midway point of the trial. In 2020, study investigators announced the trial had failed to meet its primary endpoint, showing no statistically significant treatment-related change on the DIAN Multivariate Cognitive Endpoint (DIAN-MCE).

UK Biobank is referenced as a major dataset resource. The COINSTAC platform (Collaborative Informatics and Neuroimaging Suite Toolkit for Anonymous Computation) is described as enabling 'federated analyses' combined with 'data harmonisation, and using representational biostatistical models' to identify 'impactful environmental signatures that can be evaluated for their replicability and generalisability across study designs, cultural settings, and molecular levels.'

Using FDG-PET data from the ADNI, Blazhenets et al. showed that FDG-PET in combination with amyloid PET and non-imaging variables may improve the prediction of conversion from MCI to AD and support the stratification of patients according to their conversion risks. Levin et al. used FDG-PET in the ADNI dataset to subtype AD in 'typical', 'limbic-predominant' and 'cortical-predominant' types that correlate with the brain atrophy subtypes and the different clinical trajectories.

These scans are from the Neuroimaging of Inflammation in Memory and Other disorders (NIMROD) study cohort. It highlights the characteristic patterns of atrophy with relative preservation of the hippocampus in DLB, severe hippocampal atrophy in AD and temporal pole atrophy in FTLD.

Machine learning analysis of the UK Biobank (n = 123,459) identified metabolic biomarkers associated with depression. The study analyzed 249 metabolic markers in 7,945 depressed patients using non-negative matrix factorization and machine learning to reveal three depression subtypes: Subtype 1 (fatty acid dysregulation), Subtype 3 (hyperlipidemia), and Subtype 2 (intermediate phenotype). Diagnostic models incorporating these metabolites along with traditional risk factors achieved AUCs of 0.658 and 0.716 for lifetime and current depression, respectively. The UK Biobank is described as 'the largest metabolomics database at present.'

The Whitehall II cohort was used as an independent validation cohort for depression subtypes identified in the UK Biobank. The study developed 24 subtype-specific diagnostic models and validated them in this independent cohort. Diagnostic models incorporating metabolic markers outperformed binary classification in the Whitehall II cohort, with AUC improvements of 12.8-39.6%.

We used the Alzheimer's Disease Genetics Consortium (ADGC) multi‐ancestry TOPMED‐imputed dataset to generate ancestry‐specific heritability estimates for AA ( N = 6,343), AsA ( N = 3,197), NHW ( N = 32,913) and HL ( N = 1,944) participants and to quantify shared AD genetic architecture. Cross‐ancestry analyses examined high‐quality common variants (minor allele frequency [MAF]>0.05) using a method accounting for ancestry‐specific genetic architecture. Authors created genetic relationship matrices (GRMs) standardized to ancestry‐specific allele frequencies and conducted bivariate genomic‐relatedness‐based restricted maximum‐likelihood (GREML) analyses, adjusting for sex, age and principal components to assess genetic heterogeneity in Alzheimer's Disease across ancestry pairs.

Raw data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) were analyzed using Repeated Measures Latent Class Analysis (RMLCA) to examine distinct classes of respondents with similar patterns of SNAP behaviours over time. The analysis included n = 4759 participants and employed MPlus v8.5 software and R version v4.0.3 for conducting the RMLCA. The study examined disease proportions across identified clusters using pairwise Wald tests with Bonferroni correction.

dataset_context_from_paper: Data collection for the Head Impact and Trauma Surveillance Study is funded by the following grants: NINDS/NIA: R01NS119651, NINDS/NIA: R01NS132290. The study included 2072 participants (127 PRO, 680 COL, 1174 HS, and 91 YTH) who completed assessment tasks including the GDS-15 screening tool.

The GDS-15 is a self-report screening tool used to identify symptoms of depression in older adults. This measure consists of 15 yes-or-no questions evaluating the emotional and cognitive aspects of depression. The number of 'yes' responses are summed, with total scores ranging from 0 to 15. Normal scores range from 0 to 4 while scores ranging from 5 to 8 suggest mild depression, 9 to 11 indicates moderate depression, and 12 to 15 suggests severe depression. 2072 participants (127 PRO, 680 COL, 1174 HS, and 91 YTH) completed this task.

Summary statistics from European ancestry (EA), African American, and East Asian cohorts from the Alzheimer's Disease Genetics Consortium were integrated using a PRS-CS weighted summation approach to develop an APOE-independent multi-ancestry polygenic risk score (PRS) for AD.

Stratified analyses showed associations between PRS and AD risk, cognitive performance (memory, executive function, language), and AD-related brain MRI measures.

The dataset analyzed during the current study is available in the OpenNeuro repository. The dataset was used to train and evaluate machine learning classifiers for distinguishing between Alzheimer's disease (AD), Frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and healthy controls (HC) using functional connectivity metrics derived from EEG data. Multiple classification approaches were tested including logistic regression, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbours, Gaussian naïve Bayes, convolutional neural networks, and bidirectional long short-term memory networks. Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSOCV) was employed to assess classification performance across different frequency bands and functional connectivity metrics (including amplitude envelope correlation, coherence, correlation, covariance, cross-spectral density, entropy correlation coefficient, mutual information, phase locking value, and weighted phase locking value).

Original data for A4 and LEARN are stored publicly on synapse.org. The A4/LEARN cohort is a large multi-site study employing FBP PET imaging. The large sample size of A4/LEARN compensated for the reduced gray-to-white matter contrast and signal dynamic range differences between FBP and PiB by allowing for robust derivation of ROI thresholds using GMM. Authors used this dataset to evaluate the EXT approach for Aβ staging and to analyze the relationship between pTau217 concentration and Aβ PET SUVR measurements.

Original data for A4 and LEARN are stored publicly on synapse.org. The A4/LEARN cohort is a large multi-site study employing FBP PET imaging. The large sample size of A4/LEARN compensated for the reduced gray-to-white matter contrast and signal dynamic range differences between FBP and PiB by allowing for robust derivation of ROI thresholds using GMM. Authors used this dataset to replicate findings in an independent cohort and to evaluate EXT-based Aβ staging.

The EXT approach was previously developed in the HABS sample using PiB. Authors sought to evaluate whether this approach would be robust when applied to the A4/LEARN multi-site study employing FBP, a historically more accessible 18F-labeled radiotracer prone to higher non-specific binding in white matter.

SHARE data were included in a random-effects meta-analysis examining the association between life satisfaction and dementia risk. The study included newly analysed European samples from SHARE along with five other studies, totaling seven samples (N = 74,392) across 15 countries. Life satisfaction was measured at baseline in dementia-free participants who were prospectively followed to identify incident dementia. The meta-analysis found that greater life satisfaction was associated with a lower risk of developing dementia (HR = 0.76, 95% CI = 0.67–0.84).

ELSA data were included in a random-effects meta-analysis examining the association between life satisfaction and dementia risk. The study included newly analysed European samples from ELSA along with five other studies, totaling seven samples (N = 74,392) across 15 countries. Life satisfaction was measured at baseline in dementia-free participants who were prospectively followed to identify incident dementia. The meta-analysis found that greater life satisfaction was associated with a lower risk of developing dementia (HR = 0.76, 95% CI = 0.67–0.84). Pooled data from 16 countries derived from three harmonized cohort studies: the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). These surveys were developed using a shared methodological framework originally modeled on the US HRS. Harmonization across the studies occurs both ex ante (through coordinated study design) and ex post (through the standardized public-use datasets). This process ensures consistency in variable construction, covering socioeconomic characteristics, physical and mental health indicators, retirement status, healthcare utilization and biomarkers, thereby enabling robust cross-regional analyses.

A total of 15 genome-wide significant loci were identified, with 7 already reported to be associated with LOAD and 8 novel loci.

The PsychAD project generated a population-level single-nucleus RNA-seq dataset comprising over 6 million nuclei from the prefrontal cortex of 1,494 individual brains, covering a variety of AD-related phenotypes that capture cognitive impairment, severity of pathological lesions, and the presence of NPSs. Using emerging deep learning approaches, the authors analyzed the PsychAD data to score single-cell phenotype associations and identified phenotype associate cells (PACs). The dataset was used to analyze personalized single-cell functional genomics involving cell type interactions and gene regulatory networks, learn latent representations of individual functional genomics (embeddings), and associate genetic variants with changes of cell type-gene regulatory networks across individuals.

SDMap collects drug perturbation-related genes from the CMap LINCS L1000 (level 5) dataset. The Level 5 dataset contains corrected z-score vectors, which are generated through a procedure that calculates differential expression values for genes by comparing each gene's expression in the corresponding sample with respect to the entire plate population. For each drug-related instance in the LINCS L1000 dataset, genes with a corrected z-score of ≥2 (or ≤−2) are identified as upregulated (or downregulated) differentially expressed genes in a specific signature. The compound information within the LINCS L1000 dataset, including details such as cmap name, target, and moa, was also obtained from the database.

SDMap acquires spatial transcriptomic sequencing datasets from GEO. For each spatial transcriptomic dataset, detailed information such as patient ID, sample ID, tissue type, primary/metastatic lesion, and sequencing technology is integrated into SDMap. For the count expression matrices in these datasets, the SCTransform function from the R package Seurat is used to normalize the expression data. SDMap has collected a total of 989 spatial transcriptomic slices across 35 tissue types, including 969 slices of spot-resolution spatial transcriptomic data and 20 slices of single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomic data, involving 5,490,079 spatial locations and cells.

SDMap acquires spatial transcriptomic sequencing datasets from 10x Genomics. For each spatial transcriptomic dataset, detailed information such as patient ID, sample ID, tissue type, primary/metastatic lesion, and sequencing technology is integrated into SDMap. SDMap has collected a total of 989 spatial transcriptomic slices across 35 tissue types, including 969 slices of spot-resolution spatial transcriptomic data and 20 slices of single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomic data.

Publicly available EEG dataset used to perform two classification tasks: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) vs. Healthy Controls (HC) and Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD) vs. HC. The authors applied their proposed framework using seven different segment lengths with both 10-fold cross validation and leave-one-out-validation techniques. The dataset was segmented using 30 second segments with 15 second overlap, consistent with prior studies. The proposed framework outperformed two previous studies that had used this same dataset for the same classification tasks. Each participant freely consented to data publication, and the data contains no identifying information.

Bulk RNA sequencing data from 3 brain regions: the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), and the head of the caudate nucleus (CN) are available on the AMP-AD Knowledge Portal (syn23650893). These data were used to analyze cell-type-specific gene expression profiles linked to AD endophenotypes.

Single-nucleus RNA sequencing data derived from 424 post-QC ROSMAP participants from DLPFC brain specimens. Eight major cell types were included in the analyses: cux2+/cux2-excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), and endothelial cells. Exclusion criteria applied to genes with expression in fewer than 10% of all cells and cells that had over 20,000 or fewer than 200 total RNA unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), or if more than 5% of their reads mapped to mitochondria.

The Human Protein Atlas (HPA) provides bulk RNAseq data collected across 253 different tissues and spanning 19,023 genes. Authors accessed the data release that includes only information from HPA study participants instead of the consensus data to avoid sample overlap with GTEx. For each gene, expression was measured across all 253 tissues from the HPA and tissues were scored on a sliding scale from 0 (lowest measured gene expression) to 1 (highest) to validate tissue contexts in which AD-GReX associations were identified.

NeuroimaGene, an atlas of associations of GReX with NIDPs, was leveraged to characterize genes previously identified in AD TWAS through their associations with AD-associated NIDPs. This atlas was used to identify instances where transcriptomic profiles of AD-associated genes demonstrated statistically significant associations with AD-associated neuroimaging-derived phenotypes in the UKB.

The global neurodegenerative proteomics consortium (GNPC) is a multi-cohort initiative to gather CSF and plasma proteomic data for more than 40,000 samples from 23 different sites across the globe. GNPC data contains both cross-sectional and longitudinal samples including over 300 million proteomic measurements profiled using SomaScan 7K and 5K platforms. The GNPC aims to uncover disease biomarkers by merging and enhancing proteomic data collected from thousands of patient samples across global dementia cohorts. GNPC covers a wide range of cardiovascular diseases and cognitively healthy individuals, and includes data related to different neurodegenerative disorders, e.g. AD, PD, FTD, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

PPMI is a comprehensive study designed to identify biomarkers for PD. Launched in 2010 with support from the Michael J. Fox Foundation, the study seeks to recruit around 4,000 participants from more than 33 centers for detailed clinical and imaging assessments, as well as an additional 50,000 individuals for genotyping and other PD-related evaluations. Participants undergo various procedures, including CSF collection, MRI scans, motor function tests. This cohort utilized an earlier version of the SomaScan platform (5k), which measured 4,785 unique aptamers corresponding to 4,131 unique protein targets. A total of 1,075 participants were included in the present study, including 575 PD, 168 CO (52 were A − T − ), and 332 prodromal individuals.
The code used for analyzing the proteomic data is available on Zenodo.

Raw MS data and pre- and post-processed protein expression data and case traits related to this manuscript are available at this location. The results published here are in whole or in part based on data obtained from the AMP-AD Knowledge Portal. The AMP-AD Knowledge Portal is a platform for accessing data, analyses, and tools generated by the AMP-AD Target Discovery Program and other programs supported by the National Institute on Aging to enable open-science practices and accelerate translational learning. Data are available for general research use according to requirements for data access and data attribution.

The Swiss samples were projected onto a UMAP space generated from Emory samples using overlapping proteins (n = 167) as features, with 115 out of 120 cases mapping to one of the predefined Emory subtypes.

All data are openly published as microdata at https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/ with no direct contact with all the participants. The dataset includes clinical and biochemical measurements including BMI, CRP, FBG, Ghb, HDL, LDL, TCHO, TG, TyG, and WC.

The Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium (GNPC) created one of the largest proteomic datasets in the world with approximately 300 million unique protein measures from 23 partners and nearly 40,000 biosample analyses. The first version of the Harmonized Dataset (HDS) includes approximately 40,000 unique proteomic analyses on the SomaScan 5k and/or 7k proteomics array platform, in addition to a smaller subset studied with Olink and mass spectrometry methods. All samples are accompanied by 50 phenotypic indicators including demographic, cognitive data, clinical scores, and disease-specific genotype. The complete harmonized dataset was securely provided to consortium members via the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative's online platform, the AD Workbench for data refinement and analysis. After one year of embargoed intra-consortium analysis, the HDS will be made accessible by the broader research community as a shared, global resource (July 2025).

The Accelerating Medicine Partnership AD (AMP‐AD) consortium is taking an agnostic approach to look at the AD brain proteome in up to 2000 individuals using both a high‐throughput label‐free and isobaric tandem mass tag mass spectrometry (MS)–based approaches across the disease continuum. Tissues are being obtained from several large brain banks and longitudinal cohort studies including the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA), Adult Changes of Thought (ACT), Mount Sinai Brain Bank (MSBB), Banner Sun Health Research Institute (Banner), Emory Brain Bank (Emory), University of Pennsylvania (UPenn) and Mayo Brain Bank (Mayo), and the Rush University ROS/MAP cohort. Using systems biology approaches and predictive modeling, clusters of inter‐related proteins were found to be associated with key clinical and pathological phenotypes.

As new genes are identified, new models will be engineered to strategically express combinations of gene variants associated with AD, including those identified in humans as polygenic risk factors.

The original survey datasets from CHARLS, HRS and ELSA are all free of charge and available from the Global Ageing Data Portal. The study examined the association between frailty and depression across culturally diverse cohorts, using CHARLS as one of the primary data sources for this cross-national comparison.

The original survey datasets from CHARLS, HRS and ELSA are all free of charge and available from the Global Ageing Data Portal. ELSA was used as part of the multi-country analysis to examine the consistency of the frailty-depression relationship across culturally diverse populations.

Proteomics data from colon tissue collected using CODEX. Used for clinical outcome prediction task evaluating HEIST model performance on tissue-level classification, measured by AUC-ROC. Part of evaluation on datasets including proteomics data Charville (Colon), UPMC (Neck), and DFCI (Neck) collected using CODEX.

Proteomics data from neck tissue collected using CODEX. Used for clinical outcome prediction and tissue-level classification. HEIST surpasses foundation models scGPT-spatial and CellPLM by 25.4% and 30% respectively on UPMC tasks by constructing co-expression networks directly from observed proteins and incorporating all available markers.
Proteomics data from neck tissue collected using CODEX. Used for clinical outcome prediction task evaluating HEIST model performance on tissue-level classification, measured by AUC-ROC.
Skin cancer data collected using MIBI (Multiplexed Ion Beam Imaging). Used for clinical outcome prediction task evaluating HEIST model performance on tissue-level classification, measured by AUC-ROC.

Spatial transcriptomics data of placenta collected using Xenium. Used for clinical outcome prediction task evaluating HEIST model performance on tissue-level classification. Predictions made using frozen cell embeddings and an MLP classifier, reporting AUC-ROC.

Large-scale spatial transcriptomics pretraining dataset comprising 13.3M cells from 10x Genomics. Part of HEIST pretraining dataset of 22.3M cells from 124 tissue slices across 15 organs. The large scale and diversity of the dataset improve the reliability and robustness of learned representations, enabling better transferability to downstream tasks.

Large-scale spatial transcriptomics pretraining dataset comprising 8.7M cells from Vizgen. Part of HEIST pretraining dataset of 22.3M cells from 124 tissue slices across 15 organs. Contributes to diverse collection of high-resolution spatial transcriptomics datasets generated using single-cell technologies such as MERFISH and Xenium.

Spatial transcriptomics pretraining dataset comprising 360K cells from the Seattle Alzheimer's Brain Atlas. Part of HEIST pretraining dataset of 22.3M cells from 124 tissue slices across 15 organs. Contributes to large and diverse collection of high-resolution spatial transcriptomics datasets for pretraining.

The proposed model was evaluated on an openly available dataset with 36 AD (Alzheimer's disease), 23 FTD (Frontotemporal dementia), and 29 HC (healthy controls) age-matched subjects. Leave-one-subject-out cross validation yielded classification performances for 3 binary classification problems: AD/FTD: 74%, AD/HC: 85%, FTD/HC: 74%. The dataset consists of resting-state EEG data used to train Riemannian geometry classifiers on functional connectivity features across different frequency bands (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma) to differentiate between AD, FTD, and HC.

Anonymized patient data from the study is not publicly archived due to IRB restrictions on sensitive patient data. Data are available upon request by submitting a UCSF MAC Resource Request form. Analysis codes, scripts, and digital study materials are available on the publicly accessible digital repository 'Open Science Framework' (OSF). These materials support the study's analysis of node-to-network functional connectivity scores and gray matter volume harmonized across two MRI scanners using ComBat.

Raw scRNA-seq data (FASTQ files) generated from CD45+ cells isolated from autopsy samples and reported by Tuddenham et al., 2024. This dataset was used as part of the study examining associations of scHPF factors with AD-related traits and was replicated in downstream analyses.

Raw scRNA-seq data (FASTQ files) generated from CD45+ cells isolated from autopsy samples, newly generated scRNA-seq data from CD45+ cells, ScHPF factor scores for projected datasets, and raw and processed MERFISH data made available on Synapse.

New sample set of ROS-MAP participants with snRNA-seq data produced at Columbia University (n=212). Used to replicate significant associations of scHPF factors with AD-related traits. The GPNMB High factor (scHPF_26) was replicated as significantly associated with pathological AD and amyloid levels.

Repurposed dataset of ROS-MAP participants with snRNA-seq data produced at MIT (n=130 independent samples after removing overlapping samples). Used for replication of factor associations with AD-related traits and assembled with CUIMC1 and CUIMC2 datasets in meta-analysis (n=766 unique participants total).

ROS-MAP participants with snRNA-seq data assembled with CUIMC2 and MIT datasets in meta-analysis (n=766 unique participants total) to summarize all available data and prioritize factors significantly associated with AD-related traits.

PRS for AD susceptibility and for CSF-Aβ42 and ptau181 were computed for 867 non-demented AMYPAD participants. Linear regression models tested associations with amyloid burden (Centiloid) adjusting for age, sex, and education. Participants were predominantly cognitively unimpaired (CDR=0, 85.1%), with low amyloid burden (CL<10, 60%), and 42.4% carried at least one APOE-ε4 allele. This study investigates the association between polygenic risk scores (PRS) and amyloid burden in a preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD) cohort.

PRS for AD susceptibility (Kunkle et al., 2019) were computed for 867 non-demented AMYPAD participants. PRS Kunkle had 50 of 99 SNPs mapped to genes, enriched for negative-regulation-of-amyloid-beta-formation (p = 1.9x10⁻⁶) and amyloid-precursor-protein-catabolic-process (p = 2.8x10⁻⁶). PRS amyloid and PRS Kunkle at pT=5x10⁻⁸ and 1x10⁻⁵ performed comparably across brain regions (R² >0.14).

PRS for CSF-Aβ42 and ptau181 (Jansen et al., 2022) were computed for 867 non-demented AMYPAD participants. PRS were calculated with and without the APOE region under three p-value inclusion thresholds. Model performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation.

Data from the 2004 and 2018 survey waves of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) were used in this study. These years were chosen for being the earliest and most recent (non-COVID) harmonized waves with all relevant factors available for both datasets. The study analyzes nationally representative cross-sections of the older adult population (aged 65+) at each time point. Between 2004 and 2018, five refresher cohorts were added to the existing pool of ELSA participants (22% of respondents in the English analytic sample participated in both study waves).

Data from the 2004 and 2018 survey waves of the U.S.-based Health and Retirement Study (HRS) were used in this study. These years were chosen for being the earliest and most recent (non-COVID) harmonized waves with all relevant factors available for both datasets. The study analyzes nationally representative cross-sections of the older adult population (aged 65+) at each time point. Between 2004 and 2018, two refresher cohorts were added to the HRS (33% of respondents in the U.S. analytic sample participated in both study waves).

Code and guidance to harmonize and compare the ELSA and HRS datasets is available through the Gateway to Global Aging data resource. This resource provides harmonized data and methodology for comparing the two longitudinal studies across countries.

The datasets presented in this study can be found in online repositories. The names of the repository/repositories and accession number(s) can be found at: doi: 10.7303/syn52229757. The three validation samples were used to evaluate evidence for the reliability and validity of the MTB Sequences measure. Internal consistency reliability was indexed using split-half reliability (corrected with the Spearman-Brown formula) in Studies 1 and 2, with 1,000 random permutations for splitting the data. The dataset supports the Mobile Toolbox (MTB) cognitive assessment library, which enables remote data collection on smartphones for monitoring cognitive functioning over time and identifying pathological cognitive decline.

The Cam-CAN dataset, which includes both imaging and behavioral data, can be accessed at camcan-archive.mrccbu.cam.ac.uk/dataaccess/. This study utilized data from the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) cohort. For the Cam-CAN cohort, a GE-EPI sequence was used with the following parameters: 64 slices with 2.3 mm thickness; TR = 1400 ms; TE = 39.4 ms; flip angle = 69°; FOV = 202 × 202 mm²; and voxel-size = 2.3 mm isotropic.

The LEMON (Leipzig Mind-Brain-Body) cohort from the Max Planck Institute was used as replication cohort. The LEMON dataset is available for public download via an Amazon Web Services S3 bucket at: fcp-indi/data/Projects/INDI/MPI-LEMON. For the LEMON cohort, DWI data were acquired using a multi-band accelerated sequence combined with in-plane GRAPPA (acceleration factor = 2). The acquisition protocol included 88 axial slices with an isotropic voxel size of 1.7 mm isotropic, 60 diffusion gradient directions at a b-value of 1000 s/mm² and 7 additional images with a b-value of 0 s/mm². For the resting state functional MRI, participants closed their eyes and sat for 15.5 min.

Mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics study using postmortem human brain tissue samples (synaptosomes) analyzed by label-free quantitation (LFQ). The MS data were processed to arrive at 2260 total quantified proteins. Only proteins with fewer than 50% missing global pooled peptide reference standard sample measurements were included in analyses. The dataset comprises 66 total injections making up RAW LC-MS/MS LFQ files. Coefficients of variation were assessed for 2623 proteins having at least four of eight nonmissing values, with 50% of proteins having CV <20.9%, mean CV of 25.1%, and 76.4% of well-measured proteins below 30% CV threshold. The study examined disease-associated changes in protein expression related to Alzheimer's disease (AD) and cognitively normal aging using correlation network approaches (WGCNA) to cluster the proteome into biologically relevant modules.

The original data for this study are available on their official websites: the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. This analysis uses data or information from the Harmonized ELSA dataset and Codebook, Version G.3 as of June 2023 developed by the Gateway to Global Aging Data. Population-based Cam-CAN (The Cambridge Center for Aging and Neuroscience) cohort with deeply phenotyped data on approximately 700 adults, aged 18 to 88 years. This dataset was used to study the relationship between pulse pressure and cognitive impairment via white matter disruption, with measurements including heart rate variability, peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD), and cognitive outcomes.

A subset of data generated for this study are available at https://github.com/DebsKing/Pulse_pressure_impairs_cognition_via_white_matter_disruption.git. All summary measures and R code for regression models and structural equation models (SEMs) are publicly available at this repository. Statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.0.2) and RStudio.

PSMD (peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity) was calculated using the release 1.8.2 available at https://github.com/miac-research/psmd/releases. This tool was used to process white matter imaging data from the Cam-CAN cohort.

BEYONDD was intentionally designed to address the translational gap in neurodegenerative biomarker research through community-based ascertainment, decentralized multimodal phenotyping, and participant-centered engagement strategies capable of identifying neurodegenerative vulnerability earlier and within heterogeneous populations in community-based settings. The study focused on midlife adults with subjective cognitive concerns (sCBC) and was approved by Institutional Review Boards of participating institutions. All participants provided electronic informed consent prior to participation, with additional consent obtained for in-home biospecimen collection and optional in-clinic evaluations. The present report focused primarily on feasibility- and implementation-related outcomes, with downstream biomarker analyses and clinic-based validation outcomes to be reported separately.

The NACC database is funded by NIA/NIH Grant U24 AG072122. NACC data are contributed by the NIA-funded ADRCs across multiple centers. The study used data from the Uniform Data Set version 3 (UDSv3) which captures clinical information including arthritis status (clinician-flagged as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid, or other inflammatory subtypes) and other health conditions. The database does not include polysomnography (PSG) or actigraphy data for obstructive sleep apnea assessment, nor imaging or serological confirmation for arthritis diagnosis, relying instead on clinician-suspected diagnoses.

ELSA data are available from the UK Data Service 10.5255/UKDA-SN-5050-35. The dataset was used for cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses examining biological age and physiological systems. Authors conducted analyses using PCA-derived biological age measures across diverse physiological systems, with both cross-sectional and longitudinal study designs to assess effects and potential survivor bias.

Code is available from 10.5281/zenodo.17986826. The code was used to implement analyses for deriving biological age using PCA methods on physiological data and conducting cross-sectional and longitudinal statistical analyses.

Data, analysis code, and research materials from three studies validating the MTB Arranging Pictures test for assessing episodic memory via smartphone. Studies 1 and 2 were approved by Northwestern University IRB (STU00207455), study 3 by UCSF IRB (20–30058). Participants completed MTB assessments at baseline and at approximately two-week follow-up on iOS devices. The dataset includes performance data from participants aged 18-59+ years on the Arranging Pictures task, which involves remembering and arranging sequences of pictures in original order. Convergent validity was assessed using NIHTB V3 PSM. Analyses were conducted in R with publicly available code included.

The dataset used in this study is publicly available through the ELSA project. The authors employed multiple imputations with chained equations, generating 25 imputed datasets to minimize bias and preserve statistical power. The dataset contained missing data that was handled through imputation procedures. The robustness of primary findings was affirmed by sensitivity analyses.

Data came from the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN; Shafto et al., 2014) dataset. The rs-fMRI sequence was performed using a Gradient-Echo Echo-Planar Imaging (EPI) sequence with a TR of 1970 ms, TE of 30 ms, flip angle of 78°, FOV of 192 × 192 mm, and 3 × 3 × 4.44 mm voxel size. This sequence acquired a total of 261 volumes over 8 min and 40 s, with each volume containing 32 axial slices. The dMRI imaging was performed using a twice-refocused sequence with a TR of 9100 ms, TE of 104 ms, FOV of 192 × 192 mm, and voxel size of 2 × 2 × 2 mm, with 30 directions of 66 axial slices having a b-value of 1000, 30 directions of 66 axial slices having a b-value of 2000, and 3 images of 66 axial slices having a b-value of 0. Parcellation-based blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) time-series data were used for the dynamic functional connectivity analyses and were bandpass filtered to include frequencies between 0.1 and 0.01 Hz. Structural connectivity (SC) measures of streamline probability and distance were calculated from the dMRI data.

Researchers interested in accessing the data used in this study can apply for access to the ELSA by visiting their website. It is free to access. The ELSA dataset was used in this study for machine learning model development to predict stroke risk based on obesity indices and multimodal health data.

NACC was established in 1999 by the NIA (U01 AG016976) to harmonize and centralize data collected by ADRCs. Its Uniform Data Set (UDS), collected longitudinally during standardized annual evaluations at ADRCs, includes data on over 50,000 individuals and post mortem data for more than 8000 Clinical Core participants. NACC hosts one of the world's largest, oldest, and most comprehensive datasets on AD/ADRD. GAAIN has partnered with NACC to make ADRC data more easily searchable and accessible through GAAIN's open-access infrastructure, allowing investigators to identify relevant datasets, build cohorts, and establish new research collaborations.

NACC hosts data from other NIA-funded studies such as CLARiTI and SCAN. These datasets are part of the harmonized data infrastructure that provides access to high-quality clinical, biomarker, and neuropathologic data.

Retrospective cohort study applying the eligibility criteria of the CLARITY-AD trial to participants with early AD from the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging (MCSA). The most common reasons for exclusion were chronic diseases and neuroimaging findings, using T2* GRE sequences on 3 T scanners for quantifying cerebral microbleeds (CMBs).

A similar retrospective study on a European cohort applying AAT trial eligibility criteria found that the proportion of patients eligible for anti-amyloid therapy varied from 8% (6.2–9.9) for lecanemab to 15% (12.4–17.5) for donanemab. The proportion of patients not eligible based solely on neuroradiological criteria was about 1/3, mainly conditioned by the presence of small vessel disease (SVD), using T2*-GRE sequence on 1.5-T MRI scanners.

To predict ancestry of these samples, we merged the data with 1000 Genomes Phase 3 (1000G) reference samples. The A4 Study is a secondary prevention trial in preclinical Alzheimer's disease, aiming to slow cognitive decline associated with brain amyloid accumulation in clinically normal older individuals. Participants provided permission to share their de-identified data to advance treatment for Alzheimer's disease. Specific acquisition parameters by site can be found at ida.loni.usc.edu ('A4 Study Materials'). All structural and functional images were preprocessed using T1 MPRAGE anatomical scans, skull-stripped through optiBET and registered to an MNI template. High-resolution segmentation of the amygdala and hippocampus was performed using Freesurfer 7.2. The data are made available through the Laboratory for Neuro Imaging at the University of Southern California.
