This strategy maximised the information available while maintaining a consistent feature space across datasets.

The study population included patients from two independent data sources: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative database (ADNI), which includes rich data on AD progression. Before defining the study cohort, the authors ensured that ADNI and NACC had similar data collection processes and a large overlap in variables useful for the study. A unified set of variables was constructed based on the union of variables available in NACC and ADNI. Variables present in only one cohort were retained, and missing values in the other cohort were imputed during preprocessing.

Physiological aging index was derived and tested using the ELSA study population. The index combines blood-based biomarkers (fibrinogen, C-reactive protein, glycated hemoglobin) with physiological function tests (grip strength, respiratory function, pulse pressure, blood pressure). Analyses of this index show its association with incident functional and mobility limitations, memory impairment, and diverse chronic conditions in the ELSA study population, indicating its relevance to aging processes.

MRI data from N = 1208 older adults were available at baseline. MRI data from 1112 participants were available longitudinally (number of sessions = 5945). Data collected over 4.5 years from the Anti-Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's study (A4). White matter hyperintensity (WMH) was extracted using HyperMapper. Microhemorrhages (mH) were identified by experienced radiologists at Mayo Clinic. Linear regression compared WMH at baseline with respect to mH presence and level. Longitudinal WMH accumulation was obtained from a linear mixed effect model and assessed against last visit mH. Logistic regression assessed relationship between baseline WMH and emergence of mH during follow up. All models corrected for age, sex, grey matter volume, composite cortical amyloid PET, and APOE e4 status.

Pre-existing, anonymized, publicly available EEG dataset used for neurodegenerative disease detection. Authors used this dataset with deep learning models for enhanced disease detection, noting that the standardized pre-processing routine enhances comparability and reliability across studies.

Alzheimer's Disease Genetics Consortium (ADGC; N=27,383; 60.6% female; mean age=75 [SD=12]; 37.8% cases; 80% European ancestry). English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) database containing waves 0-11 spanning 1998-2024. Authors used this dataset to investigate the temporal associations between cognitive function (CF), positive affect (PA), and depressive symptoms in an aging population. The study employed multiple imputation to handle missing data across five complete datasets and conducted sensitivity analyses comparing complete-case data with imputed data. Results showed CF significantly predicted depressive symptoms at T2 (β = −0.052, SE = 0.008, P < 0.001) and T2-CF negatively predicted T3-Depression (β = −0.054, SE = 0.009, P < 0.001), with PA mediating the bidirectional association between CF and depressive symptoms.

Data was used from the Cognitive Function and Ageing Study (CFAS), focusing on adults aged 65 years and over. Data from CFAS I and CFAS II was used to understand the relationship between education (a marker of socio-economic status) and polypharmacy. Individuals were categorised on the number of years in full time education, and baseline cohorts (wave 1) from each study were compared, to identify the longitudinal effect. Logistic regression was used to assess the association between polypharmacy and education. Results showed that increased number of years of full-time education was associated with a decreased likelihood in polypharmacy, with those having <10 years of full-time education showing higher odds of polypharmacy compared to individuals with 10-11 years of full-time education (OR 1.61, 95% CI 1.44-1.80) in CFAS II.

Cross-sectional UK Biobank (n = 44,952) used to train chronological age and mortality models on organ-specific proteomics. Organ-specific proteins were defined based on GTEx data where expression in one organ was at least fourfold higher than in all others. Models were developed predicting chronological age and mortality, retaining only proteins with consistent correlation (r > 0.30) with chronological age and mortality. Brain-, artery-, and kidney-specific models predicted chronological age slightly better than previous models.

GTEx data used to define organ-specific proteins. Proteins were classified as organ-specific if their expression in one organ, based on GTEx data, was at least fourfold higher than in all other organs. This organ-specific protein definition was then used to build models for predicting chronological age and mortality.

The dataset was used to analyze associations between presence and intensity of previous and current non-chronic low back pain (LBP) with physical activity outcomes including log of total daily activity counts (LTAC), time spent in light/moderate/vigorous daily physical activity, and compliance with PA guidelines. Participants were classified into categories: No LBP (no episodes in previous year), Previous LBP (experienced LBP in past year but not at time of interview), and Current LBP (experiencing LBP at moment of study interview). Analyses were performed using generalized linear models and logistic models adjusted by age, sex, race, obesity, number of painful body sites, smoking history, and self-reported depression.

A physiological age acceleration measure was derived using clinical indicators from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA). Data were collected at wave 2 in nurse visits (blood-based biomarkers and physiological testing) or at the main ELSA interview (cognitive testing). The physiological age index was created using cardiovascular system measures (pulse pressure, systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, mean arterial pressure), respiratory system measures (forced vital capacity, forced expiratory volume in one second), haematologic system measures (haemoglobin concentration, fibrinogen, C-reactive protein, ferritin), metabolic system measures (fasting glucose, glycated haemoglobin, total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglyceride), muscle and fat measures (grip strength, waist circumference), and cognitive system measures (memory tests of immediate and delayed recall). The physiological age acceleration/deceleration measure was created by subtracting chronological age from physiological age, with analyses showing association with incident functional and mobility limitations, memory impairment, and diverse chronic conditions.

An exploratory factor analysis investigated the underlying structure of available data within ELSA on individuals' physical activity and everyday mobility. The aim was to understand whether the measures included in ELSA can be understood to map onto a single underlying construct or whether there appear to be two, or more, underlying dimensions. Factor analysis was used as a data-reduction technique to explore the underlying dimensions of the data by ascertaining the minimum number of hypothetical constructs that can account for the observed variation between a set of measured variables. Factor scores were derived using SPSS v 28, with the syntax included in supplementary material. The relationships between the factors identified and other covariates in the dataset were tested to determine whether there is evidence for two separate measures of everyday mobility and physical activity that independently are associated with other variables of interest such as quality of life.

121 cognitively unimpaired participants, aged 22–94 years, from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging and the Genetic and Epigenetic Signatures of Translational Aging Laboratory Testing (a mean follow-up duration of 4.3 ± 6.3 years). The HCAP data facilitate classifying individuals as having dementia, MCI, or normal functioning. These classifications are generally not formal medical diagnoses, but the classification variable has sufficient validity and reliability for research purposes. The classification allows researchers to study the prevalence of dementia and MCI, their determinants (including modifiable risk factors), their consequences, and their cost to individuals, households, and society. For HCAP participants, the classification variable from the HCAP can be merged into the core data set. The paper focuses on missing data treatment in HCAP studies, including item nonresponse, missing subinterviews, and imputation of dementia classification in parent studies. Interviewer observations were embedded in survey instruments including task-specific observations and observations applicable to certain types of tasks such as vision impairment or language barriers.

The larger sample size of the parent data set allows for subgroup analyses that are not possible using only the HCAP sample, for example, estimating dementia prevalence for each state or similar administrative/geographic subunit. The classification variable from HCAP is missing for individuals who did not participate in the HCAP, creating a standard missing data problem that the authors address through imputation approaches.

Shotgun metagenomic data are available from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under accession number PRJNA1271016. Reads were mapped to taxa and genetic pathways using MetaPhlAn4 and humann3 databases. De novo metagenome assembly was used to identify metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) of microbial taxa using SPAdes, Bowtie2, and MetaBAT2, resulting in 1464 high-quality MAGs. Gene annotation with hidden Markov models using MUSCLE and HMMER was applied to identify putative genes encoding the production of butyrate and propionate. MAGs were annotated as butyrate-producing genomes if they contained all four genes encoding for enzymes involved in the acetyl-CoA pathway (thl, bhbd, cro, but) or as propionate-producing genomes if they contained all three genes in the succinate pathway (mut, epi, mmd) or both genes in the propanediol pathway (PduCDE, PduP). Associations between microbial genes and biomarker status were tested, and MAG levels were validated against SCFA levels in samples.

The Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium conducted a large-scale proteomic analysis of approximately 35,000 biofluid samples from 23 cohorts. This study revealed that the ratio of cerebrospinal fluid to plasma proteins changes with age in healthy controls, with an increase in 848 proteins associated with coagulation, chemokines, and neurodegeneration. The increase in peripherally derived proteins also suggests age-associated blood-brain barrier disruption. Furthermore, the consortium identified common alterations in inflammatory responses, glycolysis, and extracellular matrix pathways across diverse neurodegenerative diseases, including AD, PD, and frontotemporal dementia.

The GNPC has brought together over 40,000 samples from over 20 different international cohorts to create a fully anonymized Harmonized Dataset (HDS). The first version includes over 40,000 unique samples on the SomaScan 5k and/or 7k proteomics array platform. All samples are accompanied by >40 phenotypic indicators including demographic, cognitive data, clinical scores, and disease-specific genotype. The HDS spans multiple neurodegenerative disorders including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). With over 300,000,000 unique protein measures, the GNPC represents the largest protein biomarker discovery effort for neurodegenerative diseases to date. Secure access to GNPC data is facilitated through the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative's online platform, the AD Workbench. De-identified datasets submitted by each participating cohort were harmonized and further anonymized by professional data vendors. After one year of intra-consortium analysis, the HDS will be accessible by the broader research community as a shared, global resource.

Emory and Banner cohort RAW data files were analyzed separately using MaxQuant v1.6.0.1 and 1.5.3.30. RAW files were searched against a concatenated target-decoy Uniprot human reference database (downloaded 4/15/2015) containing 90,411 FASTA sequence entries. In total, 53,499 peptides mapping to 4,774 protein groups were identified among Emory case samples. After filtering for proteins quantified in >50% of samples with <50% missing values across LC-MS/MS runs, 4,382 unique proteins were identified and robustly quantified in the Emory cohort.

Banner cohort RAW data files were analyzed using MaxQuant with Thermo Foundation 2.0 for RAW file reading. The Andromeda search engine was used to search against the Uniprot human reference database. In total, 99,130 peptides mapping to 5,711 protein groups were identified in the Banner cohort. After filtering for proteins quantified in >50% of samples, 3,710 unique proteins were identified and quantified in the Banner cohort.

The Uniprot database (downloaded 4/15/2015) included all Swissprot-curated (canonical) plus Trembl (unreviewed) sequences, totaling 90,411 FASTA sequence entries. Additional entries for unique peptides from ApoE E2 and E4 allelic gene products were included in the database.

439 participants from the AMYPAD consortium with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) available. Structural and functional connectomes comprising 100 nodes from the Schaefer atlas were built using QSIprep v0.19.0 and fMRIPrep v23.0.1. Global cortical amyloid burden was assessed using the Centiloid scale. Linear models were used to investigate the effects of age, sex, and baseline amyloid burden on global, network-level, and regional SDI, correcting for APOE ε4 carriership and global Clinical Dementia Rating score.

Structural-Decoupling Index (SDI) was computed using a graph signal processing framework, which projects functional data onto the structural connectome, filtering it into coupled and decoupled components. The ratio of these components yields regional SDI values, reflecting the degree of decoupling between brain structure and function, with lower SDI indicating higher coupling and vice versa.

Participants completed the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) consisting of 14 items (seven anxiety and seven depression symptoms). The authors examined symptom severity across age groups using pairwise comparisons with false discovery rate correction, and computed symptom networks for younger and older adults using mutual information to capture dependencies between items. Community detection analysis using the Louvain algorithm identified distinct clusters of depression- and anxiety-related symptoms. The authors note that 'the Cam-CAN cohort was originally designed to study cognitive ageing, which limits the depth of available affective symptom data' and that 'the study's reliance on voluntary participation introduces potential selection bias.'

To correct for selection bias, we analyzed the prevalence of RBD in PD patients from the DeNoPa cohort. PD patients with RBD were compared with PD without RBD. The study included 504 PD patients who had video-polysomnography (vPSG), with 37 excluded due to missing REM or artifacts during REM, resulting in 467 patients analyzed. RBD was present in 406/467 (86.9%) PD patients. PD + RBD patients were older than PDnonRBD (69 ± 7.7 vs. 64 ± 9.2 years, P < 0.01), were more likely to have postural instability [234 (59.1%) vs. 19 (33.9%), P < 0.01], and were treated more often with antidepressants (other than SSRIs) [141 (34.7%) vs. 7 (13%), P < 0.01].

Demographic data were obtained from the LRRK2 Cohort Consortium Database. All new data obtained from this study have been deposited in the LRRK2 Cohort Consortium Database and are located in the LCC Box folder. The dataset was used to analyze associations between cytokine concentrations and Parkinson's disease, including those carrying mutations of LRRK2.

All other resources and codes used, including information about all the publications related to Figure S2, in this study can be found at 10.5281/zenodo.17102285. This includes code and resources for the GPT-assisted literature review and analysis of cytokine associations with Parkinson's disease.

The most relevant papers were retrieved from the PubMed Central (PMC) database through an application programming interface (API) using keywords: (cytokine name) AND (LRRK2 AND Parkinson) OR (LRRK2) OR (Parkinson). The search was limited to a maximum of 50 papers per cytokine. Full texts, excluding references, were processed by the GPT model to extract cytokine-related information and associations with Parkinson's disease.

English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. 7th Release. NatCen Social Research, University College London, Institute for Fiscal Studies. (2023). The dataset was used in research examining relationships between diet and health outcomes in aging populations, with analysis of depression scales (CES-D) and Mediterranean Diet Index (rMED) measures.

Cohort of cognitively and physically healthy older adults from the UK (n = 79) used to examine brain topology profiles underlying high dual-functional stability (DFS). Neuroimaging data and cognitive and physical task performance were analyzed using graph theory analyses of diffusion tensor imaging connectomes to assess brain network segregation and integration through clustering coefficients and shortest path lengths. Support vector machine and regression models differentiated high DFS subgroup from low and mix DFS subgroups with 65.82% accuracy.

Cohort of cognitively and physically healthy older adults from the US (n = 48) used to examine brain topology profiles underlying high dual-functional stability (DFS). Neuroimaging data and cognitive and physical task performance were analyzed using graph theory analyses of diffusion tensor imaging connectomes. Support vector machine and regression models differentiated high DFS subgroup from low and mix DFS subgroups with 84.78% accuracy and predicted cross-task DFS score at 58.06% and 70.53% for cognitive and physical stability, respectively.

The Perturb-seq dataset is available through the Broad single cell portal as txt files. The study applies causarray to a Perturb-seq study investigating autism spectrum disorder/neurodevelopmental delay (ASD/ND) genes in developing mouse brains, performing single-cell-level perturbation analysis with significant gene detection and functional enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes under perturbation conditions.

The gene expression count matrices of ROSMAP-AD datasets can be obtained from supplementary website, which have been deidentified to protect confidentiality—the mapping to ROSMAP IDs and complete metadata can be found on Synapse as Seurat objects (rds files). The study applies causarray to a case-control study of Alzheimer's disease (AD) using human brain transcriptomic datasets, validating findings across three independent datasets for identifying causally affected genes and uncovering biologically meaningful pathways.

The SEA-AD datasets of nuclei-by-gene matrices with counts and normalized expression values from the snRNA-seq assay are available through the Open Data Registry in an AWS bucket (sea-ad-single-cell-profiling) as AnnData objects (h5ad files). The study validates causarray findings across three independent AD datasets, including SEA-AD, showcasing robustness and reproducibility in identifying causally affected genes.

DPP/DPPOS has provided the protocols and lifestyle and medication intervention manuals to the public through its public website. The DPPOS abides by the NIDDK data sharing policy and implementation guidance as required by the NIH/NIDDK. Following clinical examination, video recordings were uploaded to a HIPAA compliant Box repository. The completion of each exam was documented on the Visit Inventory Form with the video embedded within the form which triggers an automated evaluation workflow managed by the Multimodal Integrated Data Acquisition System (MIDAS). MIDAS synchronized the video files with corresponding NB8 clinical forms and managed physician assignments.

The mouse Smart-seq single-cell transcriptomic dataset is available at the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession id GSE115746. This dataset was used with MMIDAS to uncover 92 distinct transcriptomic categories, with two VAEs achieving 94% consensus score on categorical assignments. Mutual information analysis shows strong alignment between MMIDAS-inferred categories and reference cell types.

The raw and processed mouse 10x isocortex dataset is deposited in the NeMO Archive for the BRAIN Initiative Cell Census Network. This dataset was analyzed using MMIDAS to identify transcriptomic categories and establish reproducible discrete representation of cellular diversity through cross-validation and Silhouette score analysis.

The inhibitory Patch-seq transcriptomic dataset is available at https://dandiarchive.org/dandiset/000020/. This dataset was used in the MMIDAS analysis to identify discrete and continuous factors of cellular variability and characterize inhibitory neuron transcriptomic diversity.

This dataset was analyzed using MMIDAS to dissect discrete and continuous factors of variability for identification of key genes associated with disease progression in Alzheimer's disease.

These data were used to identify APOE4-specific mechanisms through machine learning-based proteome profiling across plasma, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and brains of APOE4 carriers and non-carriers with no-impairment, AD, FTD, and PD diagnoses.

The bioinformatic pipelines have during the recent years been transitioned from the previously reported MIP pipeline to the current nextflow-based pipeline, which we have made publicly available on the nf-core pipeline repository. The pipeline includes calling of single nucleotide variants (SNVs), insertions and deletions (INDELs), short tandem repeats (STRs), uniparental disomies and structural variants (SVs) including deletions, duplications, inversions as well as insertions of mobile elements (MEI), variants in the mitochondrial genome, and SMN1 and SMN2 copy number estimation.

We studied 705 adults in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging with data for diet, fecal microbiome (shotgun metagenomic sequencing), and key covariates. The analytic sample comprised participants with mean age 71.0 years (SD = 12.8 years), 55.6% female and 67.5% non-Hispanic White participants. Diet data were derived from food frequency questionnaires used to calculate healthful plant-based diet index (hPDI) and unhealthful plant-based diet index (uPDI). Fecal microbiome data were generated using shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Plasma TMAO measurements were also collected. Regression models examined associations between plant-based diet indices and microbiome α-diversity (richness and evenness measures), β-diversity (Bray–Curtis and UniFrac measures), species-level composition, and plasma TMAO, adjusted for age, sex, education, physical activity, smoking status, body mass index, and total energy intake.

Raw diffusion-weighted MRI data in BIDS format from a cohort of subjects covering the adult lifespan (18-94 years old). The dataset was used to compare multiple diffusion MRI (dMRI) techniques and metrics including DKI, NODDI, FA, NDI, ODI, Fiso, MSD, and MSK across different white matter tracts. Authors analyzed age-related changes in these metrics and performed principal component analysis to assess whether various metrics provide complementary information across different white matter tracts with varying degrees of crossing fibres and free-water contamination.

Code repository containing all diffusion-weighted data pre-processing steps and analysis scripts used for processing and analyzing the Cam-CAN dMRI dataset. Includes methodology for dMRI metric extraction and statistical analysis of age effects on white matter microstructure.

The EEG data used in this study are derived from public domain resources. The dataset is available at https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds004504/versions/1.0.8, accessed on 11 September 2024. The study applied a machine learning framework with an alignment module, generation module, and fusion module (total 0.79 M learnable parameters) to analyze EEG data. The research involved five-fold cross-validation with strict hyperparameter tuning procedures to prevent overfitting in small-sample medical dataset scenarios.

Data was obtained from the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936. Significant PGSs were constructed in LBC1936 to validate findings from ELSA. PGSs in LBC1936 were derived using the same method and software as ELSA — PRSice-2. The study used this cohort to test polygenic scores as predictors of frailty index in a multivariate framework.

The English Study of Ageing data was used as the primary dataset. 26 PGSs were identified that either corresponded to traits commonly included in frailty indices or were phenotypically associated with frailty. The aim was to capture broad coverage across frailty-relevant domains (physical health, cognition, psychosocial factors). PGSs in ELSA were derived using PRSice-2 software. Significant PGSs from ELSA were then constructed in LBC1936 to validate findings.

A GWAS of the Frailty Index in the UK Biobank tested various PGSs as predictors of FI in univariate linear regression models and found that PGSs for BMI, Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), Waist Hip Ratio (WHR), menarche, grip strength, age at first sexual intercourse, parents' survival and educational attainment were associated with the FI. The present study improves on this PGS approach by extending it to a multivariate framework using the most recent GWAS.

The research examined marginal mean scores of intrinsic capacity for the 1940 and 1950 birth cohorts with 95% confidence intervals.

The datasets used in this study are publicly available through the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) database. Data can be accessed through the NACC Data Request process. Key features include: NACCAGE (age at visit), REMDATES (remembering dates/appointments), BILLS (managing bills/checks), DECIN_1.0 (reported memory decline), TAXES (managing tax records), HRATE (resting heart rate), BPDIAS (diastolic blood pressure), TRAVEL (traveling out of neighborhood), SMOKYRS (total years smoked cigarettes), EDUC (years of education), NACCMMSE (total MMSE score), MMSEORDA (orientation subscale score – Time), MEMUNITS (total number of story units recalled), TRAILA and TRAILB (trail making test A and B – total number of seconds to complete), VEG (total number of vegetables named in 60 s), and ANIMALS (total number of animals named in 60 s). The data were used to train and validate machine learning models (Gradient Boosting Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and others) for cognitive status classification across three resource levels, achieving AUC scores ranging from 91.53% to 93.98% for distinguishing between cognitively intact, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia classifications.

The GTEx brain RNA-seq data were obtained from the database of Genotypes and Phenotypes (dbGaP) under the accession number phs000424.v8. These data were used for eQTL mapping analysis of lncRNAs, circRNAs, and protein-coding genes across brain tissues.

RNA-seq data from neuronal and non-neuronal cell types from the SuperAgerEpiMap project, available at https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn25672226. These omics datasets were incorporated into the study for comprehensive eQTL analysis.

Gene loops identified by proximity ligation-assisted ChIP-seq (PLAC-seq) in neurons from the repository available at https://github.com/nottalexi/brain-cell-type-peak-files were used to support eQTL analysis.
Single-nucleus ATAC-sequencing (snATAC-seq) data for various neuronal cell types from http://catlas.org/catlas_hub/ were used as part of the omics datasets for this study.

Full lncRNA- and circRNA-eQTL summary statistics, GTFs, and genomic sequences of lncRNAs are available at https://yanglab.westlake.edu.cn/ncrna_eqtl.html. This represents the primary dataset generated by the authors containing eQTL results for non-coding RNAs identified through meta-analysis of seven cohorts.

The Cam-CAN Stage 2 and Stage 3 study collected comprehensive cognitive, neural, and physiological data from participants. Data collection included: physiological measures (weight, height, blood pressure), behavioral assessments (visual short-term memory, emotion expression recognition, face recognition, fluid intelligence, sentence comprehension, emotional reactivity and regulation, motor learning), MRI imaging (T1-weighted structural images, T2-weighted structural images, diffusion-weighted images, magnetisation transfer ratio images, resting state and task-based fMRI), and MEG data (resting state and sensorimotor task). Saliva samples were collected for future genotyping analyses to understand genetic influences on cognition and ageing. Background demographic information was obtained from regional Public Health Observatory data to link participants to general population data.

Data used in this work were from the Lifespan Brain Chart Consortium (LBCC), which includes multiple publicly available MRI datasets. The Alzheimer's Disease Repository Without Borders (ARWiBo) was one of three datasets included in the study. The work included experiments varying in their reference and test datasets, with ARWiBo used as either reference or test dataset across different experiments to validate the ReForm method for calibrating reference intervals to new samples.

Data used in this work were from the Lifespan Brain Chart Consortium (LBCC), which includes multiple publicly available MRI datasets. The work included experiments varying in their reference and test datasets, with NACC used as either reference or test dataset across different experiments to validate the ReForm method for calibrating reference intervals to new samples.

Data came from the nationally representative English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) waves 6 (2012–2013) to 9 (2018–2019). Sample comprised ELSA core members with valid blood samples in waves 6 and 9 (n = 1,162). Group-based trajectory modelling was used to determine trajectories of informal caregiving hours from waves 6 to 9. Logistic regression models investigated associations between informal caregiving trajectories and inflammatory biomarkers (C-reactive protein [CRP], fibrinogen, and white blood cell count [WBC]) in wave 9, adjusting for sociodemographics, wave-6 inflammation, and wave-9 non-inflammatory biomarkers.

Post hoc data from MEG analysis of the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) dataset. The data represents results from Hidden Markov Model (HMM) inference conducted on MEG recordings, with model selection based on minimizing free energy and identifying eight states that resolved rich and specific spatio-spectral features across states. The analysis involved 5 inferences for K = 8 states, examining networks and frequency content in resting-state MEG data.

MEG data from this cohort was processed using Hidden Markov Model inference to identify brain states and their spatio-spectral features.

Methylation probe data from a prospective study identifying cg06581459 (located between CD70 and DENND1C) as the most significant methylation probe (p adj = 4.45×10⁻⁷). Study included 26 probes with genome-wide significance. Replication in cross-sectional study (current vs AZA-naive) was successful for 8 out of 26 probes (enrichment p = 2.61×10⁻⁵), including cg06581459, cg08018827/cg08018828 (PLK2, GAPT), cg11201447 (PVT1), and cg06138367 (DENND2D, CHI3L2, CEPT1).

Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of colonic epithelium from children with diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) integrated with comprehensive bioinformatics approaches to investigate alterations in protein expression.

Shotgun metagenomic microbiota sequences from fecal samples of 20 newly diagnosed, untreated children with ulcerative colitis (UC) and 20 controls. Significantly enriched bacterial species and bacteriophages identified by Boruta algorithm were selected and annotated to biologic functions in MetaCyc and Gene Ontology (GO) databases related to UC pathogenesis. Spearman correlations performed between selected species and biologic functions.

Data are openly available to researchers via the UK Data Service. The study involved statistical analyses conducted using Stata version 17.0, with statistical significance defined as a two-tailed P-value < 0.05. The research appears to involve family member data, as indicated by the abbreviation 'OIFM other immediate family members' in the supplementary materials.

ARIC Cohort (n = 5778) used for validation of dementia and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) prediction risk scores. The cohort was stratified into groups: No MCI and No dementia (3329, 57.7%), Dementia & MCI (482, 8.3%), Dementia without MCI (409, 7.1%), and MCI without dementia (1558, 26.9%). Multiple predictive tools were applied including CogDrisk, ANU-ADRI, CAIDE, and LIBRA scores. CAIDE risk score produced the highest odds ratios for predicting MCI in both complete case and imputed analyses.

PATH Cohort (n = 1545) used for validation of dementia and MCI prediction models. Cohort composition: No MCI and No dementia (1353, 87.6%), Dementia & MCI (11, 0.7%), Dementia without MCI (34, 2.2%), and MCI without dementia (147, 9.5%). CAIDE score yielded the highest odds ratios for predicting MCI, while ANU-ADRI score produced the highest AUC followed by CogDrisk and CAIDE.

Whitehall II cohort (n = 6387) used for validation of dementia and MCI prediction risk scores. Cohort stratification: No MCI and No dementia (6192, 97.0%), Dementia & MCI (22, 0.3%), Dementia without MCI (39, 0.6%), and MCI without dementia (134, 2.1%). Complete case analysis produced slightly lower AUCs compared to multiple imputed analysis across all risk scores. In the imputed dataset, AUCs were generally similar for CogDrisk, ANU-ADRI, CAIDE, and LIBRA.

The harmonized GNPC data used for validation analyses are available through the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative/AD Discovery Portal. This cohort constitutes the largest dataset of SOMAscan proteomic profiles from individuals with neurodegenerative diseases (AD, FTD, Parkinson's disease dementia, Parkinson's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) and cognitively unimpaired controls, collected across study sites in the USA, UK, and Europe. CSF and/or plasma samples were obtained from each participant at a single time point, along with demographic and limited clinical information.

Gene clusters containing 237 brain-expressed genes and 154 bone marrow–expressed genes were retrieved from the Human Protein Atlas database. Fisher's exact test was used to assess enrichment by comparing the identified genes from the proteomic data with gene sets from the Human Protein Atlas database.

Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database containing whole-blood expression datasets used for validation experiments. The study divided PPMI into two cases: PPMI-A with 1745 patients, 4674 genes, 4 labels, and 24 MB sample size; and PPMI-B with 4332 patients, 4674 genes, 7 labels, and 59.6 MB sample size. Raw gene expression data were normalized using the normalize_per_cell function, after which the top 1600 highly variable genes were selected. These blood transcriptomic datasets were employed as benchmarks for constructing classification models for disease states and detecting PD-PACE subtypes. The data are accessible through the AMP-PD platform but subject to specific access restrictions and require permission from the Accelerating Medicine Partnership Parkinson's Disease Knowledge Platform.

Parkinson's Disease Biomarkers Program (PDBP) database containing whole-blood expression datasets used for validation experiments. The PDBP dataset includes 1025 patients, 7000 genes, 4 labels, and 34.3 MB sample size. These blood transcriptomic datasets were employed as benchmarks for constructing classification models for disease states and detecting PD-PACE subtypes. Raw gene expression data were normalized and filtered to identify genes with significant expression variability associated with disease-specific information. The data are accessible through the AMP-PD platform but subject to specific access restrictions and require permission from the Accelerating Medicine Partnership Parkinson's Disease Knowledge Platform.

Accelerating Medicine Partnership Parkinson's Disease Knowledge Platform (AMP-PD) serves as the central access point for both PPMI and PDBP datasets. The data supporting the findings of this study are available through the AMP-PD platform, though their accessibility is subject to specific restrictions. The data were used under license for the current research and are not publicly available. Data may be obtained from the corresponding author upon reasonable request and with the permission of the Accelerating Medicine Partnership Parkinson's Disease Knowledge Platform.

All source data and quantifications related to this article are available at Mendeley. The dataset includes genome-wide bioinformatics analysis results identifying genes with PRE (Pumilio Response Elements) in their 3′ UTR, with 4,279 unique putative mRNAs identified and 2,187 candidate targets conserved between humans and mice. Also includes Ingenuity Pathway Analysis results, PUM1 coding variants extracted from exomes and genomes of patients with Parkinson's disease (n = 3,484; 739 from Columbia and 2,745 from AMP-PD), and variant filtering results against control databases.

Single-cell RNA sequencing data from human dopaminergic neurons were acquired from Kamath et al. (GEO accession no. GSE178265) and analyzed using the Seurat package (version 5.0.1) in R (version 4.3.1). Data normalization was performed using the Normalize Data Seurat function with default parameters on the RNA assay. Variable features were identified using FindVariableFeatures, and data scaling was conducted with ScaleData. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using RunPCA with 20 principal components to reduce dimensionality. Metacells were constructed using the hdWGCNA package for weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), selecting genes expressed in at least 5% of cells.

Data from wave 1 to wave 9 (2002–2018) of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing were used. Global cognition, assessed by orientation, memory, and executive function, was measured in each wave. Incident COPD and asthma was ascertained using self-reported physician diagnosis and further verified by the records of corresponding medication use and spirometry measurement. During a median 12.5-year follow-up, 389 incident COPD and 329 incident asthma cases were recorded among 7,948 individuals (mean age 63.0 years, 56.2% women). The study explored temporal patterns of cognitive change before and after incident COPD and asthma onset, measuring annual rates of change in global cognition, orientation, memory, and executive function.

Positive psychological wellbeing was assessed using Office for National Statistics (ONS) wellbeing measures across three domains: affective wellbeing, eudemonic wellbeing, and evaluative wellbeing, each measured on a 0-10 scale. Depressive symptoms were measured using the 8-item Centre for Epidemiological Studies Depression (CESD-8) scale with a cutoff of 4 or more symptoms to denote probable clinical depression.

Dataset from the UK Data Service analysed to assess positive psychological wellbeing and depressive symptoms. Data came from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) which included both in-person, internet and telephone interviews. Analyses were weighted to account for non-response and to match the sample to the English population. The study examined trajectories of wellbeing changes in older men and women living in the community during and after the pandemic.

The study included 2484–2491 participants who were retiring and completed at least one dietary assessment before and at least one assessment after retirement. Participants provided data on dietary measures at 3.7 (SD 0.6) times of the possible four study waves during a 32-year follow-up, with a maximum of −16 to +16 years from retirement.

The PsychAD dataset provides high-resolution cellular taxonomy, identifying 8 major cell classes and 67 subtypes from single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and genotype data from dorsolateral prefrontal cortex samples of 1,494 human donors. This dataset spans over 6.3 million nuclei from donors with diverse diagnoses, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder, alongside neurotypical controls. The dataset offers insights into transcriptional and genetic alterations associated with neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders and highlights shared molecular pathways. Donor metadata, such as neuropsychiatric symptom profiles and neuropathological assessments, enrich the dataset's value for targeted disease investigations. Open-access tools enable users to explore cell-type-specific gene expression, identify phenotype-associated cells, and map new datasets to the PsychAD reference framework. Publicly accessible through the AD Knowledge Portal, it supports collaboration and re-use, providing a foundation for novel integrative analyses, tool development, and discovery of therapeutic targets.

dataset_context_from_paper: The NACC Neuropathology data set represents one of the largest multi-center databases of carefully curated neuropathologic information that is freely available to researchers worldwide. The database contains neuropathologic evaluations for aging-related neurodegenerative diseases including cerebrovascular disease (arteriolosclerosis, microbleeds, microinfarcts), hippocampal sclerosis, TDP-43, and FTLD. A 2014 update to the NACC Neuropathology Form expanded diagnoses of Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia.

ELSA cohort data was analyzed to examine the association between elevated incident cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM) and cumulative HbA1c/HDL-C ratio. The study found that elevated incident CMM is significantly linearly associated with higher cumulative HbA1c/HDL-C ratio and its value at visit 1 in ELSA. The cumulative HbA1c/HDL-C ratio was identified as an optimal predictor that significantly improves the AUC, NRI, and IDI in ELSA. Baseline characteristics and missing data comparisons are presented in supplementary tables.

HRS cohort data was analyzed to examine the association between elevated incident cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM) and cumulative HbA1c/HDL-C ratio. The study reveals consistent findings indicating that elevated incident CMM is significantly linearly associated with higher cumulative HbA1c/HDL-C ratio and its value at visit 1 in HRS and pooled analysis. The cumulative HbA1c/HDL-C ratio significantly improves the AUC, NRI, and IDI in HRS. Subjects with CMM occurrence prior to or during the 10-year baseline surveys were excluded.

This dataset was used in validation analysis where PLS1 and PLS2 regression models were applied to analyze morphometric similarity and its correlation with fluid intelligence. The validation analysis showed that PLS1 and PLS2 accounted for 33.88% and 27.39% of the variance in fluid intelligence respectively, with significant positive correlations (r=0.59 and r=0.45, p<0.001).

The codes for PLS regression analysis are openly available at this GitHub repository. These codes were used for analyzing morphometric similarity data and performing PLS1 and PLS2 regression analyses to examine correlations with fluid intelligence.

The sarcopenia database was split into two tables: training (2995 samples) and validation (1999 samples), with 40% of samples reserved for validation. The database was imported from an Excel 2022-formatted file. The dataset contained skewed/unbalanced data with many more observations of one class. Machine learning models including RUSboost and feature selection using MRMR algorithm were applied to predict sarcopenia. The authors demonstrated that training a model with only selected features did not lose accuracy compared to using all features in the database. The resulting model provided robust prediction in terms of true and false positives as shown in ROC curve analysis, useful for automatic initial screening of potential patients.

This adjustment was necessary because initial embeddings generated without this covariate exhibited sex-specific clustering within shared cell types, indicating that sexual dimorphism was a dominant driver of transcriptional variance that masked disease-relevant signals.

The ALTRA cohort comprised 89 donors and 2,029,864 cells collected across two study sites, including ACPA-negative healthy controls, ACPA-positive at-risk individuals who either remained non-progressors (NONC) or subsequently progressed to clinical RA (CONV), and ACPA-positive early RA individuals (ERA). Applied to peripheral blood mononuclear cells for evaluating scVIP framework on autoimmune disease transcriptional signals.

The SoundLife cohort contributed 96 healthy control donors totaling 4,634,837 cells after stratification to improve data balance across cohorts. Because all NONC, CONV, and ERA individuals in this cohort were ACPA-positive, scVIP was trained jointly on two RA-related classification tasks: distinguishing ACPA-negative healthy controls from ACPA-positive individuals, and distinguishing NONC from ERA disease states.

Extensive battery includes cognitive assessments, amyloid (NAV4694) and tau (MK6240) PET imaging, MRI, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), plasma, and DNA. Gene-based test of association for MTUS2 gene were conducted using EPACTS software with sex, age, education, and principal components adjusted analyses using the sequence kernel association test SKAT and incorporating the efficient Mixed‐Model Association eXpedited (EMMAX) algorithm. The association of MTUS2 with LOAD observed in LLFS was validated using six different independent cohorts.
Alzheimer's Biomarkers Consortium‐Down Syndrome (ABC‐DS) was one of six independent cohorts used to validate the association of MTUS2 with late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) observed in LLFS.
The Religious Orders Study/Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP) was one of six independent cohorts used to validate the association of MTUS2 with late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) observed in LLFS.
The Washington Heights/Inwood Columbia Aging Project (WHICAP) was one of six independent cohorts used to validate the association of MTUS2 with late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) observed in LLFS.

The National Institute on Aging Alzheimer's Disease Family Based Study (NIA‐FBS) was one of six independent cohorts used to validate the association of MTUS2 with late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) observed in LLFS.

Data from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging may be requested through the study website: blsa.nih.gov. Computed tomography (CT) scans including images of the abdomen (L4-L5) and thigh (mid-femur) are acquired by the Radiology Department of MedStar Harbor Hospital (Baltimore, MD) using a Somatom Sensation 10 CT scanner. Tissue types and regions are segmented and quantified using customized machine learning algorithms specific to each body region with manual review and correction as appropriate. Variables of interest include areas of abdominal subcutaneous and visceral fat, thigh subcutaneous and inter-muscular fat areas, as well as thigh muscle area (mm²), and thigh muscle intensity, Hounsfield unit (HU), an indicator of lipid content.

Data were used from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), an ongoing longitudinal cohort study of 12,099 people aged 50+ who had previously participated in the Health Surveys for England (HSE) in 1998, 1999, and 2001. In ELSA, data has been collected every two years since the baseline assessment in 2002, over the course of 16 years. The sample of participants was limited to those who: i. Participated in Wave 1; ii. Were core cohort members (partners were excluded); and iii. Did not self-report dementia at baseline. All participants provided informed consent prior to data collection, and ethical approval for Wave 1 was provided by the Multicentre Research and Ethics Committee. The majority of data are free to access via the UK Data Service.

The SEA-AD MTG dataset analyzed in this study is publicly available via the Allen Brain Cell Atlas. The dataset contains single-nucleus RNA-seq data from human middle temporal gyrus (MTG) with donor-level metadata including Braak stage (I–VI), CERAD score (1–4), Thal phase (0–5), APOE genotype, cognitive status (No dementia/Dementia/Reference), age at death, and post-mortem interval (PMI). The study provides cell-type-resolved, single-nucleus characterization of SLC13A5 expression and seven additional citrate metabolism genes (SLC13A3, SLC25A1, ACLY, ACO1, ACO2, IDH1, IDH2) across 24 cell subclasses and six astrocyte supertypes. The full dataset matrix contains 1.37M × 36,601 dimensions with CP10K-normalized, log1p-transformed expression values.

EEG recordings from patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), Frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and cognitively normal controls (CN). The dataset was used to develop and validate classification models for distinguishing AD/CN, FTD/CN, and AD+FTD/CN using accuracy (ACC) metrics across five batches. The EEG signals were acquired following a standardized protocol with full documentation of demographic characteristics, experimental setup, participants, and signal acquisition process. The dataset is BIDS-compliant and publicly available on OpenNeuro with accompanying data descriptor paper providing complete metadata.

In an analysis of UK Biobank data, the association for the inflammation-anxiety relationship was weaker compared to that between inflammation and depression, and it was entirely attenuated following adjustment for depression. The UK Biobank dataset was used to examine the relationship between inflammation markers (CRP) and mental health outcomes (anxiety and depression), with findings showing disorder specificity in the inflammation-depression association.

data_repository: Laboratory for Neuro Imaging at the University of Southern California
dataset_context_from_paper: The A4 Study is a secondary prevention trial in preclinical Alzheimer's disease, aiming to slow cognitive decline associated with brain amyloid accumulation in clinically normal older individuals. Participants provided permission to share their de-identified data. The study includes neuroimaging data (amygdala connectivity maps, amyloid PET imaging to classify amyloid-positive and amyloid-negative groups) and clinical measures of depression and anxiety. Data are made available through the Laboratory for Neuro Imaging at the University of Southern California. Authors conducted seed-based functional connectivity analyses examining amygdala-to-ROI connectivity and identified clusters showing differences between amyloid groups, with medial amygdalar to RSC connectivity correlating inversely with anxiety scores.

Data collection began in July 2023 and will continue through March 2026. Participants are emailed baseline questionnaires with embedded hyperlinks to the Mayo Clinic SRC Qualtrics platform. Survey data includes baseline, 6-month and 12-month assessments from caregivers of people living with late-stage Alzheimer's disease. Monthly surveys collect data on lucid episode frequency and attributes (prevalence, content, antecedents, consequences, duration). All survey data will be imported from Qualtrics into SPSS for analysis. Longitudinal analysis will examine incidence of lucid episodes, characteristics of PLWD and caregivers that predict episodes, and associations between lucid episodes and caregiver outcomes including burden, distress, and grief.

Secondary analysis conducted in the English Longitudinal Study of Aging (ELSA; analytic N = 14,992), a large representative panel study of adults 50 years and older in the United States, Europe, and Israel. Within this sample, discontinuous growth curve modeling was used to estimate loneliness trajectories across adulthood and the impact of stroke on loneliness trajectories. In ELSA, loneliness levels were higher after stroke onset relative to before stroke onset.

dataset_context_from_paper: Secondary analysis conducted in the Survey of Health, Aging, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE; analytic N = 103,782), a large representative panel study of adults 50 years and older. Within this sample, discontinuous growth curve modeling was used to estimate loneliness trajectories across adulthood and the impact of stroke on loneliness trajectories. Across the sample, participants who experienced stroke reported higher levels of loneliness relative to participants who did not experience stroke.

Secondary analysis conducted in the Health and Retirement Study (HRS; analytic N = 22,179), a large representative panel study of adults 50 years and older in the United States, Europe, and Israel. Within this sample, discontinuous growth curve modeling was used to estimate loneliness trajectories across adulthood and the impact of stroke on loneliness trajectories. In HRS, loneliness levels were higher after stroke onset relative to before stroke onset, and participants who experienced stroke reported higher levels of loneliness.

dataset_context_from_paper: The Whitehall II Study provided participant data for depression assessment. The Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) was used to assess depressive symptoms in Whitehall participants at phase 7 (2002/2004), phase 9 (2007/2009), phase 11 (2012/2013) and phase 12 (2015/2016). The self-report scale is composed of 20 items covering symptoms of depression, with participants rating frequency using a four-point scale. Participants with a CES-D score ≥ 16 or treated by anti-depressants between 2002/2004 and 2015/2016 were defined as depressive symptom cases. Current medications use was self-reported and coded using the British National Formulary to determine anti-depressant use.

The BLSA dataset includes participants with a wide range of non-debilitating medical conditions used to develop neural network models for predicting gait speed trajectories as a marker of healthy aging. The dataset incorporates relevant predictor and outcome variables for model development. Authors used this longitudinal cohort to identify healthy versus accelerated aging trajectories and their biomarkers. The dataset represents a largely normative aging population with measurements restricted by IRB to permissioned access only due to ethical considerations for informed consent to share human data.

The PD-HI (Parkinson's Disease Health Index) is a disease-specific patient-reported outcome (PRO) measure designed from the ground up using a large-scale patient-centered approach involving participants in variable stages of their disease. It was developed to adhere to FDA guidance regarding the development and validation of PROs for use in drug labeling claims and was designed specifically to detect small but clinically important changes in patient health in response to therapeutic intervention. The PD-HI comprehensively assesses disease burden in many important symptomatic domains in PD and emphasizes non-motor symptoms such as fatigue and sleep impairment. The research provides initial evidence of the content validity, construct validity, test-retest reliability, and usability of the PD-HI as a disease-specific PRO for PD clinical trials and clinical care. Requests for access, licensing, or further information can be directed to HealthIndexes@chet.rochester.edu.

Summary statistics from the Oslo cohort are made available at www.github.com/pihlstrom. The Oslo cohort is incorporated in the largest and most recent PD GWAS meta-analysis and was used to generate polygenic risk scores (PRS) using independent weights from summary statistics of the Chang et al. meta-analysis.

Raw methylation data will be made publicly available through the Gene Expression Omnibus repository upon publication of the article. Methylation profile scores (MPS) were generated using summary statistics from Vallerga et al. as weights, following an identical processing pipeline for the Oslo data.

The PPMI data are available through an application process. For the PPMI cohort, whole blood DNA methylation data from two different projects are available as Tier 1 data in the PPMI online portal. The Illumina MethylationEPIC data from 'MJFF project 120' was analyzed, which included the largest number of PD and control samples from PPMI baseline visits. The final PPMI data set included 779,321 CpGs in 269 PD patients and 109 controls.

Meta-analysis summary statistics from the Vallerga et al. EWAS are publicly available. Methylation profile scores (MPS) were generated with the '--score' command in OSCA, using summary statistics from Vallerga et al. as weights.

Meta-analysis summary statistics from Chang et al.'s GWAS, including data from 23andMe Inc., are made available through 23andMe to qualified researchers under an agreement with 23andMe that protects the privacy of the 23andMe participants. Independent weights from summary statistics of the Chang et al. meta-analysis were used to generate polygenic risk scores (PRS), including only SNPs associated with PD at a genome wide significance threshold (P < 5 × 10−08).

A multidisciplinary team assigned a diagnosis to each participant using established PPA diagnostic criteria. For this cross-sectional study, information only from the first visit was included. The data support findings in a cohort of patients with PPA variants.

Raw proteomic data deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository. The proteomic dataset supports conclusions about proteins significantly correlated with age in human hippocampus, analyzed through linear regression models adjusted for PMI and sex, with gene set enrichment analysis performed on 2091 linear models assessing association between age and protein levels.
Lipidomic data deposited to Synapse with Project SynID: syn52087674 (10.7303/syn52087674). The lipidomic dataset supports the conclusions of the article regarding lipid profiles in relation to age.

Processed tandem mass tag labelling proteomic data from the Emory Alzheimer's Disease Research Center (ADRC) cohort accessed through the PRIDE repository for both protein and peptide group data. This dataset was used for comparison with proteins correlated with age in the hippocampus study.

Molecular Signatures Database (v7.5.1 MsigDB, released January 2022) providing gene sets used for gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA). Protein sets were obtained from gene sets in MsigDB, with gene sets containing less than 15 or more than 200 genes excluded from analyses.

Shotgun metagenomic data available from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under accession number PRJNA1271016. Data were analyzed using de novo metagenome assembly with SPAdes, Bowtie2, and MetaBAT2 to identify 1464 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Gene annotation with hidden Markov models using MUSCLE and HMMER was applied to identify genes encoding production of butyrate and propionate. Reads were mapped to taxa and genetic pathways using MetaPhlAn4 and humann3 databases. MAGs were annotated as butyrate-producing or propionate-producing genomes based on presence of specific enzymatic pathway genes. Analysis tested associations between microbial genes for SCFA production and biomarker status (A+ or T+), with propionate production pathway showing association with lower risk of amyloid positivity (OR [95% CI] = 0.52 [0.32, 0.85], p = 0.01).

The largest collection of incident PD proteomic datasets to date with exceedingly long-term follow-up and rigorous case ascertainment. The study analyzed proteomic profiles using SomaScan 7K assay across multiple follow-up intervals to identify protein biomarkers associated with Parkinson's disease. Of 291 unique proteins previously linked to PD, 191 proteins were assessable in the EPIC4PD data. The dataset includes 38 proteins recently reported as putative predictive PD biomarkers, with 11 showing at least nominally significant associations in one or more follow-up intervals including HPGDS, CD209, TPPP3, EPS8L2, FCRL1, BAG3, TNXB, IL13RA1, NEFL, PPY, and RET. Data can be accessed by external researchers after approval by the EPIC4ND working group and the EPIC steering committee.

Three GNPC case-control datasets comprising 2,592 participants (335 prevalent PD cases and 2,257 controls) with proteomic profiles analyzed using similar methodology as the discovery phase analyses. Used for replication and validation of protein biomarkers identified in the EPIC4PD dataset.

UK Biobank proteomic dataset using Olink platform containing 38 proteins previously reported as putative predictive PD biomarkers. Re-analyzed proteomic data from UKB was used for comparison and validation against EPIC4PD SomaScan-based findings. Discrepancies between this study and UKB likely reflect methodological differences between proteomic platforms used (Olink versus SomaScan).

Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network database (v12.0, accessed May 6th, 2025) used to build networks based on all FDR-significant EPIC4PD biomarkers. Interactions with a minimum interaction score of 0.4 were included based on sources: 'textmining', 'experiments', 'databases', 'co-expression', 'neighborhood', 'gene fusion', and 'co-occurrence'.

The Whitehall II data are available through UK Data Service and requests to the study team. Researchers wishing to access the data can apply for access through the UCL website. The dataset includes longitudinal follow-up data with six distinct missing data patterns categorized into complete data (71%, n = 4954), partial data (21%, n = 1474), and no follow-up (8%, n = 251). Missing baseline covariates were imputed via multiple imputation with chained equation (MICE) with random forest algorithm, assuming data were missing at random (MAR). Ten imputed datasets were generated based on lower than 10% total missingness in baseline covariates.

Of the 363 CI participants with a consensus classification fitting one of the specific disease types, the breakdown was as follows: 88 AD; 107 PPA (31 logopenic variant PPA, 33 semantic variant PPA, 17 non-fluent variant PPA, nine unspecified PPA, three semantic bvFTD, 11 AD language variant, and 11 MCI predominantly language); 84 bvFTD (80 bvFTD only and four bvFTD + ALS); 60 CBS/PSP (25 CBS and 35 PSP); and 24 PD/DLB (21 PD and 3 DLB). For concurrent validity with TabCAT Match total correct, authors assessed UDS-3 measures of memory (Story Recall, Figure Recall), language (naming, semantic fluency), and visuospatial ability (figure copy). Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores were used to classify participants from clinically normal (CDR 0) through dementia (CDR 2).

TabCAT Match total correct, TMT-A total time, TMT-B total time, Digit Span total, and lexical fluency were used as predictors for classifying Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) stages. Standardized and weighted receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves adjusted for all demographic variables were used to depict the area under the curve (AUC) for classifying CDR 0 clinically normal versus CDR ≥ 0.5 mild cognitive impairment or dementia, and various other CDR stage comparisons.

Multi-shell connectome diffusion MRI data from 80 participants (55 CU (32 F, mean age 66.7 +/- 6.6; 25 CI (8 F, mean age 73.6 +/- 7.3)) in the ADCP were pre-processed using DESIGNER processing guidelines. The study tested associations between disruptions to white matter along the AD clinical continuum (cognitive unimpaired (CU): cognitive impaired (CI) – Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) and AD) and cognition using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and multi-tissue neurite and orientation dispersion and density imaging (mtNODDI) models. Analysis revealed significant interaction between clinical status and cognitive test outcomes on the mtODI metric, with CI individuals showing higher mtODI levels in cerebellar and brainstem regions and lower cognitive performance compared to CU individuals.

China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study data were analyzed to examine associations between frailty, depressive symptoms, and cardio-oncology comorbidity. The study included analysis of baseline frailty associated with cancer risk and the protective effects of healthy lifestyle on cancer risk outcomes.

English Longitudinal Study of Ageing data were analyzed during the current study as part of a multi-cohort analysis examining healthcare outcomes, population structure, and baseline risk factor distributions across different healthcare systems and socioeconomic contexts.

Health and Retirement Study data revealed that baseline frailty was associated with higher cancer risk (HR = 1.61, 95% CI: 1.27, 2.02), with further elevation upon frailty progression. Healthy lifestyle significantly attenuated the adverse effect of frailty on cancer risk, with protective effects observed for lung, colorectal, and liver cancers (pooled HR = 0.74, 95% CI: 0.71, 0.78).

UK Biobank data from 352,277 participants were analyzed to identify inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, neutrophil count) and brain structural changes (reduced hippocampal volume) that mediate the association between frailty and depressive symptoms. The study also showed that individuals with depressive symptoms alone had significantly higher risk of incident cardiovascular disease.

Participants from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS, N = 5,658, mean age = 73.23, standard deviation [SD] = 6.22) completed measures of gait speed, semi-tandem balance, and cognitive status at baseline. Cognitive status was assessed over up to 15 years. Baseline slower gait speed (HR HRS = 1.52, 95% CI = 1.32–1.75, p < .001) and balance impairment (HR HRS = 1.58, 95% CI = 1.26–1.96, p < .001) were related to a higher risk of incident dementia, adjusting for demographic factors.

Participants from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA, N = 3,667, mean age = 69.90, SD = 7.02) completed measures of gait speed, semi-tandem balance, chair stand, and cognitive status at baseline. Cognitive status was assessed over up to 15 years. Baseline slower gait speed (HR ELSA = 1.73, 95% CI = 1.37–2.18, p < .001), balance impairment (HR ELSA = 1.97, 95% CI = 1.24–3.14, p < .01), and worse performance on the chair stand (HR = 1.56, 95% CI = 1.23–1.99, p < .001) were associated with a higher risk of incident dementia.

We used data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing to investigate associations between child abuse and dementia (N:5,448). Indirect pathways through four mediator categories (education, health behaviours, mental health and cardiovascular health) were examined. We used regression modelling to estimate associations between child abuse, mediators and dementia, and causal mediation analysis using the g-formula to estimate the joint indirect effect through the mediators. Individuals who experienced child abuse had, on average, an 80% higher hazard of dementia, compared to those who did not (RTE HR:1.80, 95% CI:1.21-2.39).

dataset_context_from_paper: Cognitively unimpaired (CU) older adults cohort (n=1,643) with mean age 71.49±4.72 years, ~60% female, mean education 16.63±2.74 years. Study outcomes included Preclinical Alzheimer's Cognitive Composite (PACC), Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study (ADCS) Activities of Daily Living Prevention Instrument (ADL-PI), Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), plasma phosphorylated-tau at threonine 217 (p-tau217), Aβ-PET ([18F]-florbetapir), tau-PET ([18F]-flortaucipir), and gray matter volume (GMv) via structural magnetic resonance imaging. Data from the ELSA Study accessed through the UK Data Service for researchers meeting criteria for accessing confidential data. The dataset was used to develop and validate machine learning models for predicting healthy ageing. The original dataset was divided into a training dataset (70% of the sample) and a test dataset (30% of the sample), balanced within each category of the outcome variable. Variables excluded from analysis included ethnicity (near-zero variance) and haemoglobin, C-reactive protein, HDL, and triglyceride levels (approximately 30% missing data). The training dataset underwent preprocessing using missForest imputation method with RF algorithm, achieving a PFC of 0.082473 (8% misclassification rate). Models were tested using 10-fold cross-validation with performance metrics including sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, PPV, NPV, ROC, ROCAUC, and PRAUC.

The mouse PMC MERFISH dataset contains spatial transcriptomics data used to identify cell-cell interactions (CCI) between neurons. GITIII identified interactions between L4/5 IT and L2/3 IT neurons that upregulate Rorb expression in L2/3 IT neurons. The dataset contains 254 genes measured across multiple cells and was used for benchmarking CCI inference methods at the cell-type level.

The SEA-AD MERFISH dataset is a human brain spatial transcriptomics dataset from the middle temporal gyrus. GITIII identified interactions between L4 IT and L2/3 IT neurons associated with RORB upregulation in L2/3 IT neurons. The dataset contains 140 genes and was used to demonstrate cross-species generalizability of the GITIII method.

The NSCLC (non-small cell lung cancer) CosMx spatial transcriptomics dataset was used to benchmark cell-cell interaction inference methods. GITIII achieved the most negative Spearman correlation coefficient among all compared methods. The dataset was used to identify interactions between tumor cells and macrophages, as well as between tumor cells and endothelial cells, demonstrating cross-dataset generalizability.

The human breast cancer spatial transcriptomics dataset generated by Xenium contains 313 genes measured across three slides with two replicates of 5 μm sections from sample 1, including 274,492 cells from 19 annotated cell types. Among the 313 genes, 33 were identified as ligand genes. GITIII achieved the most negative Spearman correlation coefficient in this dataset and identified interactions between tumor cells and macrophages and endothelial cells.

English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), a cohort study following individuals two–yearly from 2002. Data were collected by a mix of face-to–face interview and nurse assessments. Data collected for core ELSA members across nine waves from 2002–2019 were used, including individuals who joined via refreshment sampling in waves 3, 4, 6, 7 and 9. Each wave of data collection took place across two years. The authors used anonymised publicly available data under the conditions of ELSA ethics approval. The authors did not have access to data that could identify participants at any stage.

Study participants and their families participated in the UCSF Memory and Aging Center and other research programs from which data were sourced for this project. A subset of 81 participants underwent longitudinal brain magnetic resonance imaging using a Siemens Prisma 3T scanner at the UCSF Neuroscience Imaging Center. Whole-brain T1-weighted images were acquired with specific parameters (TR = 2300 ms, TI = 900 ms, TE = 2.98 ms, flip angle = 9°, FOV = 240×256 mm). Regional brain volumes of interest including bilateral hippocampi were quantified. T2-weighted FLAIR images were also acquired. The study examined within-person associations between change in daily step count and depressive symptoms (GDS scores), as well as associations with white matter hyperintensity volume and hippocampal volume.

The Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study (DPPOS) is a longitudinal cohort study that has accumulated data over 25 years with a focus on diabetes prevention. The study successfully implemented UDSv3 forms with full fidelity to harmonize data with the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) and preserve longitudinal data. DPPOS includes cognitive assessments, medical history, medication data, and lifestyle and medication intervention information from persons with type 2 diabetes and pre-diabetes. The dataset includes cognitive adjudication performed by a centralized team, UDSv3 form data for diagnosis of cognitive syndromes, and research brain imaging biomarkers including MRI and amyloid PET in approximately one-third of the cohort. Plasma biomarkers of amyloid burden are available in 82% of participants.

The National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) Uniform Data Set (UDS) version 3 forms were implemented in DPPOS to harmonize data with NACC and enable integration with datasets from all Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers (ADRCs) in the United States. The UDSv3 data from DPPOS includes cognitive syndrome diagnosis forms (form NR1) and complementary questionnaires integrated with existing DPPOS electronic data capture forms, legacy cognitive tests, and medical history and medication data.

The study contributed to pooled analyses examining longitudinal associations of psychological distress with cognition and dementia.

In ELSA, persistent distress (β=−0.008 [−0.016; −0.002]), but not intermittent distress was associated with cognitive decline. Psychological distress and global cognition were standardised to facilitate cross-study comparisons.

NICOLA is a longitudinal cohort study resource containing multi-omic data including genetic-epigenetic-transcriptomic data linked to biochemical biomarkers and extensive phenotype information. The bioresource has identified multiple biological markers associated with more than 30 different phenotypes and has contributed to identifying novel biomarkers for cardiovascular, eye, and kidney-related outcomes. The dataset includes anonymised data from study participants and biological samples (biological, clinical, and multi-omic). Researchers can apply for access by submitting a Research Proposal to the NICOLA Data Access Committee. All data is collected, stored and disseminated in accordance with UK GDPR, Data Protection Act (2018), Human Tissue Authority Codes of Practice, and the NICOLA Data and Sample Access Policy.

Amyloid-PET scans obtained with two radiotracers [18F]Flutemetamol (n = 772) and [18F]Florbetaben (n = 568) from the AMYPAD Prognostic & Natural History Study, a pan-European multi-site study of non-demented older individuals (CDR < 1, age ≥ 50). MNI152-registered SUVR images were generated using the whole cerebellum as reference. Spatial group-level independent component analysis (gICA) was performed independently for each radiotracer with dimensionality ranging from n=1-15. A 9-dimensional gICA robustly identified five cortical components (frontal, parietal, occipital, unilateral left and right temporal cortices) and four non-cortical components (projection fibers, commissural fibers, lateral ventricular borders, and meninges). Component loading was estimated via spatial regression of the resulting components on individual amyloid-PET scans.

Circulating proteomic profiles were measured using the SomaScan aptamer-based platform version 4.1 (SomaLogic) for the high-throughput quantification of approximately 7000 proteins. Targeted proteomics were performed on CSF and plasma samples from 354 participants of the Brain Stress Hypertension and Aging Program (BSHARP) to analyze 276 proteins. Three 92-Olink panels were used measuring markers of neuronal injury, cardiometabolic and inflammation. The proximity extension assay (PEA) technology was used to quantify proteins in 9 plates of plasma samples and 6 plates of CSF samples. Protein data is presented as Normalized Protein Expression (NPX), an arbitrary unit on the Log2 scale. A bioinformatic pipeline generated data-driven protein modules clustering the 276 proteins into 5 modules (M1-M5, ranging from 80 to 14 proteins) that varied in their degree of association with age, race, CSF AD biomarkers (Aβ42, Tau, and pTau) and clinical phenotypes such as disease progression, cognitive function, and the Aβ42/Tau Ratio. Crossover dataset with 80 participants scanned within 2 days bridging two different protocols on GE and Siemens scanners. Three Olink Target 96 panels were selected for the proteomics assays (Cardiovascular II, Neurology I, and Neurology Exploratory), covering a total of 276 unique proteins. Enrichment analysis for Gene Ontology Biological Process, Molecular Function, KEGG, Reactome, and WikiPathways were performed on proteins significantly linked to social support.

Among 459 participants (mean age 68 years; 55% women) in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, mitochondrial function was quantified as skeletal muscle oxidative capacity via post-exercise phosphocreatine recovery rate (τ PCr) in the vastus lateralis muscle of the left thigh, using 31P magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Accelerometry was collected using a 7-day, 24-h wrist-worn protocol and summarized into activity amount, intensity, endurance, and accumulation patterning metrics. Linear regression, two-part linear and logistic models, and linear mixed effects models were used to estimate associations between τ PCr and each physical activity metric.

PET-to-histology registered datasets used for analysis. The methodological workflow involved imaging acquisition followed by registration of PET imaging data to histological data. Analyses were conducted using SAS. ALAN exposure cutoffs were calculated at 25th percentile: 2.8 nW/cm²/s; 50th percentile: 11.7 nW/cm²/s; 75th percentile: 23.9 nW/cm²/s. Prevalence ratios and 95% confidence intervals were calculated for each ALAN quartile using individuals in the lowest quartile as the reference group.

Study design accounted for repeated measures and complex survey design including clustering.
