dataset_context_from_paper: The CES-D-8 (Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale - 8) is a brief self-report instrument for assessing symptoms of depression in the general population, administered in all eleven ELSA waves. During the eighth wave, 7223 participants attended the study, during the ninth wave 7289, during the first COVID-19 wave 5825, and during the second COVID-19 wave 5594. The CES-D-8 comprises eight items that measure the occurrence of symptoms of depression in the past week in a dichotomous response format (yes/no) with total scores ranging from 0 (no symptoms) to 8 (all symptoms present). It covers depressive affect (enjoyed life, felt depressed, happy, lonely, and felt sad) and somatic complaints (everything was an effort, restless sleep, and could not get going). Data imputation was conducted to include all cases in all networks, with imputation analysis based on wave 8 data (N = 7223).

Cognitive Function and Ageing Study (CFAS) undertook baseline interviews in populations aged 65+ years in England and Wales (1989-1994). Three areas (CFAS I) were selected for new sampling two decades later (2008-2011) with same geographical boundaries, sampling and approach methods (CFAS II). At 2 years CFAS I interviewed 5,156 (76% response) with 5,288 interviewed in CFAS II (74% response). Data on medication use and dementia status was assessed at each wave. Low dose aspirin (<150 mg) use was associated with a reduction in dementia incidence rate in women from 60.99 (95% CI: 47.6, 78.2) per 1000 person-years to 44.1 (95% CI: 2.0, 45.4) in 1993 and from 44.5 (33.7, 58.7) to 38.6 (27.2, 54.9) in 2013.

Bulk RNA-seq data supporting the findings of this study are available in the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) repository under accession number GSE314708. Total RNA from the cortex (CX) and hippocampus (HP) of 7-month-old wild-type (WT), 5xFAD, and 5xTFEB mice was extracted using TRIzol reagent. RNA-Seq data were processed using ExDEGA software for quality control and primary expression profiling. Differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 with normalization and variance stabilization. A total of 299 genes were upregulated and 334 downregulated in 5xTFEB compared to 5xFAD. Gene Ontology enrichment analysis identified upregulated terms including autophagy, lysosomal organization, endosome-lysosome transport, and ubiquitin-related functions, while downregulated terms included apoptotic process, inflammatory response, cytokine production, and immune receptor activity.

WM tract integrity of 19 WM regions pertaining to seven WM tract pathways was assessed using DTI scans processed and segmented using a state-of-the-art pipeline.

Authors quantified histopathological characteristics including neuron density, glial cell density, α-synuclein burden, and tau burden in substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and reticular nucleus (RN), and correlated these with in vivo MRI metrics including R2* (apparent transverse relaxation rate) and QSM (quantitative susceptibility mapping).

Population-based sample used to compare non-imaging indicators (VRFs, gait, behavioral, and plasma markers) of vascular cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID) based on their association with small vessel disease (SVD)-related white matter damage across different age strata. The study focused on two VCID markers: white matter hyperintensity (WMH), a well-established SVD biomarker, and fractional anisotropy of genu of corpus callosum (Genu-FA), a regional diffusion MRI marker that captures early systemic vascular injury. Secondary goal was to identify a comprehensive set of non-imaging indicators of VCID that could aid in risk stratification and screening participants for clinical trials.

Study participants and data from the Mayo Alzheimer's Disease Research Center contributed to this research examining non-imaging indicators of VCID and their association with SVD-related white matter damage.

The study used the resources of the REP medical records-linkage system, which is supported by the National Institute on Aging (NIA; AG 058738), by the Mayo Clinic Research Committee, and by fees paid annually by REP users. This system was utilized for screening and identifying participants at higher risk of VCID using available non-imaging measures from electronic health records.

ROSMAP dataset containing 152,459 microglia nuclei from six regions of brain tissue of 138 early AD, 79 late AD and 226 control subjects. Used for identifying homeostatic, inflammatory, phagocytic, lipid processing and neuronal surveillance microglia states associated with AD-associated senescence via integrative analysis. Additionally, ROSMAP snRNA-seq data from 982,384 nuclei from postmortem prefrontal cortex of 239 AD and 188 non-AD subjects was used to identify microglia as central components to AD associated senescence phenotypes among non-neuron cell types.

Sea-AD dataset containing 82,486 microglia nuclei from 42 dementia, 42 no dementia and 5 reference subjects. Used in integrative analysis with ROSMAP to identify microglia states associated with AD-associated senescence, preserving meaningful biological information of microglia cell states across datasets.

snRNA-seq data from induced microglia (iMGs) derived from iPSCs exposed to myelin, Abeta, and synaptosomes, containing 56,454 microglia across two replicates of untreated and four treated groups. Used to validate findings on cholesterol associated senescence transcriptomic signatures, demonstrating that in vivo cholesterol associated senescence transcriptomic signatures were preserved and altered after treatment with AD pathological substrates.

The study analyzed temporal parameters of microstates (duration, occurrence, coverage, relative duration, and relative occurrence) and their association with MMSE scores. GFP peaks and grand mean templates were applied for backfitting to compute temporal parameters using both four-class and seven-class clustering methods.

1000 Genomes Unrelated European High Coverage dataset serving as an LD reference panel for the OTTERS workflow. Used to visualize colocalizing AD GWAS and eQTL signals and to support transcriptome-wide association study analyses for Alzheimer's disease.

GTEx (v8) data accessed from dbGaP accession number phs000424.v7.p2 on 04/03/2018. The Genotype-Tissue Expression Project data was used as part of the analyses, though specifically excluded from the eQTLplot visualization which used eQTLGen and MetaBrain summary statistics instead.

MetaBrain summary statistics used as input for eQTLplot visualization alongside clinically-adjudicated AD GWAS summary statistics. eQTL p-value thresholds were determined by extracting the p-value most closely corresponding with an FDR of 0.05 for each gene based on the original MetaBrain summary statistics.

Cell line data (HG002, HG0073 and HG02723) openly available through the Terra workspace. These datasets were used for long-read sequencing analysis and de novo diploid assembly construction to characterize structural variation and genomic regions previously inaccessible with short-read methods.

Human brain sequencing datasets under controlled access requiring dbGap application (phs001300.v4). Data available through restricted Terra workspace after approval. These datasets are part of the Center of Alzheimer and Related Dementias (CARD) at the U.S. National Institutes of Health initiative applying long-read sequencing methodologies across thousands of human brain samples with plans to make data openly available for research within the AnVIL cloud platform.

Restricted Terra workspace containing long-read whole genome sequencing data from human brain samples. Part of the CARD initiative applying scalable long-read sequencing and informatics for comprehensive characterization of genomic regions harboring medically relevant mutations.

As part of the published Cochrane review, the following is made available for download for users of the Cochrane Library: full search strategies for each database; full citations of each unique report for all studies (included, ongoing or awaiting classification, or excluded with reasons at the full text screen) in the final review; study data, including study information, study arms, and study results or test data; consensus risk of bias assessments; and analysis data, including overall estimates and settings, subgroup estimates, and individual data rows.

dataset_context_from_paper: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, two other databases and two trials registers from 2014 to 5 March 2024. We performed a forward citation search for papers citing the previous update. We did not apply any restrictions on date of publication, publication status or language. We worked with an information specialist to undertake a comprehensive search strategy across multiple databases, including three trials registers, aligned with Cochrane guidance. The most recent search was conducted in March 2024.

Anonymized NICOLA dataset used to analyze frailty prevalence in Northern Ireland. Approved researchers can access the dataset by completing an application. Data are accessed via a 'safe setting' located within the Centre for Public Health at Queen's University Belfast, with remote access facilitated via secure server. NICOLA data can also be accessed via the UK Longitudinal Linkage Collaboration and the UK Data Service websites. The study conducted formal analysis of NICOLA data to examine all-cause 8-year mortality outcomes and frailty prevalence differences between Ireland and Northern Ireland.

TILDA data accessed via the Irish Social Science Data Archive. CAPI interviews were conducted between October 2009 and February 2011. TILDA data are linked to Irish General Register Office (GRO) death records. The study used TILDA data for formal analysis of frailty and all-cause 8-year mortality outcomes, with a mean follow-up time of approximately 6.94 years (SD = 1.28) as of the cut-off date of 17 March 2018. Publicly accessible dataset files are hosted by the Irish Social Science Data Archive based in University College Dublin and the Interuniversity Consortium for Political and Social Research.

WGS data were deposited under ENA accession PRJEB111205. Whole genome sequencing was performed on stored isolates resistant to cefotaxime and/or ciprofloxacin collected from farm visits. Genomic DNA library construction used Nextera XT Library Prep Kit with sequencing on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 using 250 bp paired end protocol. De novo assembly used SPAdes version 3.7 with quality control by QUAST. Fasta files were analysed using ResFinder 4.1, MLST 2.0, and Clarmont phylogrouping. Sequence alignment used Snippy with SNP distances determined using SNP-dists. Core-genome MLST used chewBBACA with E. coli Prodigal training file. Data are divided by farm type (beef, mixed, sheep) and animal type on mixed farms.

Bioinformatics analysis using single-cell (single-nuclei) transcriptomic data from cortical middle temporal gyrus (MTG) samples collected from post-mortem AD donors in the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas (SEA-AD) consortium was performed to explore the relationship between MAPT and HMGA1 genes, and MAPT gene expression changes across AD progression.

The data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), that underlie the results reported in this study, are available from the UK Data Service for researchers who meet the criteria for access to confidential data. The study used ELSA data to analyze baseline characteristics according to diabetes classification and to estimate trajectories of global cognition and specific domains over time using generalized linear mixed models with repeated measures across more than 8 years of follow-up.

The estimated normative models will be available for the public at the PCNPortal. This research utilized normative modeling approaches across multiple datasets to establish population-based reference standards.

This research was conducted using data from UK Biobank, a major biomedical database, under application number 11559. Healthy Brain Network Biobank (HBN) data. The dataset is described in Nature Scientific Data: Alexander, L. et al. An open resource for transdiagnostic research in pediatric mental health and learning disorders. Scientific Data 4, 170181 (2017).

Data used in the preparation of this article were obtained on August 25, 2022, from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database. PPMI – a public-private partnership – is funded by the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research and funding partners.

The datasets analyzed for this study can be found at DOI: 10.18112/openneuro.ds004504.v1.0.8. The dataset includes EEG data with exploratory data analysis showing distribution of different age groups, distribution of different disease groups, and MMSE score distribution among participants. The dataset was used to validate and test classification metrics for multiple neural network architectures (EEGITNet, EEGNetv4, EEGNetv1).

The Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium (GNPC) cross-sectional profiling workstream studied disease specific plasma proteomic profiles across n = 9,963 individuals (AD = 1,936, PD = 2,186, FTD = 65, Controls = 5,776). Protein expression levels for up to 7,288 analytes were measured using the SomaScan platform. Separate linear regression models were employed to evaluate differences in plasma protein levels between each clinically defined neurodegenerative disease (AD, PD, FTD) and the control group, adjusting for covariates such as age, sex, contributor site, and the first two proteomic principal components. The analysis identified significantly altered proteins across different ND, including elevated SPC25 and SMOC1 in AD, increased PCBP3 and SUMF1 in PD, and decreased NPTXR and OMG in FTD.

The datasets used and analysed during the current study are publicly available from the UK Data Service. Access to ELSA data requires registration and approval through the UK Data Service. The study analyzed ELSA data using group-based multi-trajectory modeling (GBMTM) to investigate composite indices such as TyG-WWI and TyG combined with obesity markers like CVAI and BRI for cardiovascular disease risk prediction.

Data on sCJD patients came from chart reviews of the UCSF rapidly progressive dementia database and UCSF MAC general research databases, which include extensive information on persons with probable or definite sCJD who separately consented to the ongoing use of their data from medical records and/or from research records through an IRB-approved UCSF study of rapidly progressive dementias. Sources of diagnostic information for sCJD included brain tissue pathology, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers of neuronal cell injury (i.e., 14-3-3 Western blot, total-tau, and neuron-specific protein levels), CSF RT-QuIC analysis, internal review of brain MRI(s), and prion protein gene (PRNP) analysis.

Data on sCJD patients came from chart reviews of the UCSF rapidly progressive dementia database and UCSF MAC general research databases, which include extensive information on persons with probable or definite sCJD who separately consented to the ongoing use of their data from medical records and/or from research records through an IRB-approved UCSF study of rapidly progressive dementias.
Group-level imaging data derivatives are publicly available in the Open Science Framework repository. Individual participant-level data are not available due to privacy and ethical restrictions.

TMT isobaric labeling mass spectrometry (ROSMAP) data have been deposited in www.synapse.org. Postmortem DLPFC (Brodmann area 9) proteomics data were measured with TMT isobaric labeling mass spectrometry and were available for 400 (70% women) individuals including 168 cognitively normal individuals, 101 MCI, 123 AD, and 8 had other causes of dementia. A total of 12,691 unique proteins were detected; 7,901 were kept after quality control. The protein abundances were log2 transformed and regressed for batch, study, age at death, and postmortem interval, prior to downstream analyses.

Anonymized TMT isobaric labeling mass spectrometry (BLSA) data have been deposited in www.synapse.org. BLSA study (N = 47) measured postmortem DLPFC protein abundance using untargeted proteomics. Expression levels were regressed for batch, library size, percentage of coding bases, percentage of aligned reads, percentage of ribosomal bases, percentage of UTR base, median 5 prime to 3 prime base, median CV coverage, study (ROS or MAP), and postmortem interval (PMI).

The data are available through the synapse.org AMP-AD Knowledge Portal (www.synapse.org; SynapseID: syn3388564). This portal contains the processed proteomics data from ROSMAP and BLSA studies with expression levels regressed for batch, library size, and other technical covariates.

The BLSA data are available upon request. Applications should be made through the website https://www.blsa.nih.gov/. The dataset was used to generate statistical source data presented in Figures 4, 6, and 7 of the publication.

Supplementary data containing LCA-identified subgroups characterized on the basis of neuropsychiatric comorbidity and functional outcomes. Dataset includes participant-reported lifetime diagnoses of psychiatric conditions (major depressive disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, eating disorders, attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder) and cognitive impairment history (mild cognitive impairment, dementia including Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body disease). Study examines hoarding disorder (HD) with focus on cognitive difficulties in attention and memory domains.

The dataset is publicly available on the OpenNeuro website. This dataset was used to train and evaluate machine learning classifiers (GB, SVM, LR, MLP, KNN) for distinguishing between Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and healthy controls (HC). The best-performing Gradient Boosting model achieved an AUC of 0.88 for AD vs HC classification, SVM achieved 0.83 AUC for FTD vs AD, and LR achieved 0.79 AUC for FTD vs HC. Performance metrics including accuracy, recall, specificity, precision, F1-score, balanced accuracy, and Matthews correlation coefficient were computed across multiple classifier comparisons.

Resting-state EEG dataset from Greece, comprising 88 subjects (29 healthy controls, 36 with Alzheimer's disease, 23 with Frontotemporal Dementia). The study was approved by the Scientific and Ethics Committee of AHEPA University Hospital, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki. This dataset was used as one of five datasets for cross-dataset performance evaluation, where any four of datasets 1-5 were used for training with the remaining dataset reserved for testing.

Cuban Human Brain Mapping Project (CHBMP), a publicly available multimodal neuroimaging and cognitive dataset including 156 healthy participants. This dataset was used for cross-dataset performance evaluation of network frameworks, where datasets 1-5 were shuffled for training with datasets 6 and 7 used as validation sets to test model performance.

dataset_context_from_paper: The final sample size included in the CHARLS database analysis was 9790. Individuals afflicted with severe hepatic and renal dysfunction, malignancy and other serious chronic diseases that may interfere with lipid metabolism and inflammatory status were excluded from the study. The study evaluated the predictive efficacy of RCII (residual cholesterol inflammatory index) in predicting the development of diabetes in individuals of middle and older age groups through ROC curves, comparing AUC of RCII with AUC of RC and hsCRP. All subjects were categorized according to gender to investigate whether RCII could serve as a predictive indicator of new-onset diabetes in diverse gender demographics.

Data from the ELSA Study are available from the UK Data Service to researchers who meet the criteria for access to confidential data. The study examined biochemical markers of interest including total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides levels (mg/dL) as continuous variables. Clinical conditions were documented based on self-reported diagnoses of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, cancer, heart disease, lung disease, stroke, osteoporosis, and osteoarthritis. The analysis investigated relationships between abdominal obesity and vitamin D status (deficiency, insufficiency, sufficiency) and their associations with cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes.

dataset_context_from_paper: UK Biobank cohort study used as one of three nationally representative cohorts. Hospital records were used to capture historical depression diagnoses. In UKB, reliance on electronic health records was used for dementia ascertainment, which may have led to missed cases of undiagnosed dementia. Authors restricted UKB depression diagnoses to those recorded within 2 years before baseline for sensitivity analysis.

English Longitudinal Study of Ageing used as one of three nationally representative cohorts. Dementia was defined algorithmically using objective cognitive tests rather than clinical diagnoses. Study provided long-term follow-up data for examining associations between physical frailty, depression and dementia.

Health and Retirement Study used as one of three nationally representative cohorts. Dementia was defined algorithmically using objective cognitive tests rather than clinical diagnoses, potentially misclassifying individuals with severe cognitive impairment who did not meet formal dementia criteria. Provided long-term follow-up data for the study.

The data that support the findings of this study are openly available on request on the ADNI open-source database. The study used ADNI data as part of the discovery cohort for developing and validating a hyperbolic regression model between baseline CSF-Aβ42 and Aβ-PET centiloid data. Participants had available CSF-Aβ42, p-tau, and t-tau measurements.

Data are openly available through the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative website for AMYPAD-PNHS. The validation cohort included lumbar CSF samples collected and analyzed separately in each PNHS PC according to local procedures. All participants had available CSF-Aβ42, p-tau, and t-tau measurements. For EPAD-LCS and ALFA+, samples were quantified using the Roche Cobas Elecsys System at the Clinical Neurochemistry Laboratory at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden. FACEHBI samples were analyzed using the ELISA immunoassay.

An in-house Matlab code to derive Aβ-aggregation and Aβ-severity scores is available on the AMYPAD website. Modelling was performed separately for the discovery and validation cohort, using in-house code written in MATLAB (version R2022a; The Mathworks, Matwick, MA). The code implements a hyperbolic regression model between baseline CSF-Aβ42 and Aβ-PET CL data, by minimizing the sum of the Euclidean distance of the experimental points to the fitted line.

Publicly available dataset analyzed in this study. The dataset contains neuroimaging data from 617 participants with button press events and post-movement beta rebound (PMBR) measurements. Authors selected trials with at least 15 seconds between button presses to allow PMBR to return to baseline. A total of 626 epochs were extracted from preprocessed data, segmented into 18-second duration epochs with 2-second pre-stimulus intervals. The dataset includes both bimodal and unimodal cue types from the Cam-CAN paradigm.

Proteomic data can be accessed via the AD Knowledge Portal. The proteomic data used in this study were accessed from the AD Knowledge Portal under the terms of the data use agreement. These datasets were collected with the informed consent of participants and ethical approval from the original study institutions, including ROSMAP cohort studies. To integrate the proteomics and PPI data, total values were calculated for each gene symbol in the proteomics dataset. Pearson correlation coefficients were derived from the proteomics data, retaining only data with Benjamini-Hochberg (BH)-corrected p-values of <0.05.

Human AD brain snRNA-seq and microglia snRNA-seq datasets are available at the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession number GSE174367. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) datasets used in this study were obtained from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), where all samples were collected following approved institutional protocols, with participants providing informed consent for research and data sharing.

The human neuropathological and RNA sequencing datasets employed for the linear regression analysis can be found at https://www.niagads.org/datasets/ng00059. Neuropathological and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) datasets used in this study were obtained from NIAGADS, where all samples were collected following approved institutional protocols, with participants providing informed consent for research and data sharing.

A Gene Ontology (GO) analysis was used to explore the biological functions of our targeted gene set. The GO biological process (GObp) dataset version 2023.1 was downloaded from the Molecular Signatures Database (MsigDB). For the analysis, the enrichment function in the clusterProfiler package was used, and values of p < 0.05, after BH correction, were considered significant.

For PPI, STRING filtering was used to obtain physical interactions within Homo sapiens with confidence scores exceeding 0.7, and normalization was performed to set the maximum values to 1 and minimum values to 0. Proteomic and PPI data were integrated using a recently reported method, BIONIC, which integrates multiple biological networks while preserving information using graph attention networks.
Whitehall II data, protocols, and other metadata are available to the scientific community through the Whitehall II data sharing policy. Data missing for 215 men and 138 women in the analyzed cohort.

This observational study used data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), which enrolled patients with PD, healthy controls (HCs), and non-PD participants carrying GBA1, LRRK2, and/or SNCA pathogenic variants (genetic prodromals) at international sites. Study participants were chosen from PPMI enrollees based on the availability of aptamer-based CSF proteomic data, quantifying 4,071 proteins, and classified as patients with PD without GBA1, LRRK2, and/or SNCA pathogenic variants (nongenetic PD), HCs, patients with PD carrying the aforementioned pathogenic variants (genetic PD), or genetic prodromals.

Signatures characteristics of nongenetic PD were quantified as a PD proteomic score (PD-ProS), validated internally and then externally using data of 1,556 CSF proteins from the LRRK2 Cohort Consortium (LCC).

ACE is available as a hosted website at https://sea-ad.shinyapps.io/ACEapp/ with source code and associate annotation tables available on GitHub at https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ACE. A snapshot of the ACE project associated with this manuscript release is stored on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14624012 and on GitHub. This represents a specific version of the project for reproducibility and archival purposes.

To link annotations across 11 studies of AD, we integrated data from ten community-based studies of AD focused on DFC with DFC data from SEA-AD. Raw sequencing data was downloaded from the AD Knowledge Portal hosted on Synapse or from the Sequencing Read Archive (SRA) and processed using the same pipeline as was used for SEA-AD snRNA-seq data. Processed data were similarly QCed and then mapped to SEA-AD cell types using a variation of the Deep Generative Mapping model on MapMyCells.

Publicly available dataset analyzed in this study. The experimental protocol and demographic characteristics of the dataset can be found in Section 2.1. All pre- and post-treatment script probes (4 observations in total, 2 pre-treatment and 2 post-treatment) were recorded either via digital camera (if in-person) or via teleconferencing software. Script probes were transcribed by speech-language pathology undergraduate or graduate students who were trained in detailed transcription procedures. Transcripts were coded for analysis in CLAN by a single graduate research assistant (K.B.) to ensure consistency. The same coding markers were added to the transcriptions to allow CLAN to recognize repetitions, revisions, and phonological fragments. Duration information was also added to each transcription file in CLAN to allow for calculation of words per minute.

All raw sequencing data generated in this study is available at the GEO archive under accession # GSE211140. Gene expression and pseudobulk data for all timepoints from both species is directly searchable via a custom web app. The dataset includes multiomics data (RNA and ATAC) from astrocyte differentiation across multiple timepoints in two species, with quality control filtering applied (nCount_ATAC < 120000, nCount_ATAC > 500, nCount_RNA < 50000, nCount_RNA > 500, TSS.enrichment > 1). Data were processed via CellRanger v6.0.1 and analyzed using Scanpy with PCA, Harmony integration, Louvain clustering, and RNA velocity analysis.

Previously published datasets from P3 ACSA-2 purified astrocytes published by Lattke and colleagues were available from the NCBI GEO under accession # GSE152223. Raw .fastq files were downloaded and analyzed via CellRanger v6.0.1. The published raw data was used to produce .loom files via Velocyto splice calling, which was not done in the original analyses. These files were then processed for RNA velocity analysis and combined with later mouse timepoints via the Harmony algorithm.

Mouse developmental datasets published by La Manno and colleagues were available from the Sequence Read Archive under accession # PRJNA637987. Raw .fastq files were downloaded and analyzed via CellRanger v6.0.1. The published raw data was used to produce .loom files via Velocyto splice calling. These files were processed for RNA velocity analysis, filtered for quality control with Muscat, and combined with later mouse timepoints via the Harmony algorithm. .loom files from the Linnarsson lab website (primary mouse brain atlas) were also downloaded and integrated with these datasets.

The datasets analysed in this study are available in the UK Data Service (SN 8688 and 5050) repository. The dataset was used to investigate associations between diabetes, hypertension, depression, and obesity in relation to cardiovascular disease (CVD) incidence and mortality. Authors analyzed the relationship between these conditions and CVD outcomes, examining both incident CVD cases and CVD mortality, with stratified analyses for stroke incidence separately.

dataset_identifier: Biomarkers Consortium Project: Use of Targeted Multiplex Proteomic Strategies to Identify Plasma-Based Biomarkers in Alzheimer's Disease
dataset_context_from_paper: Correlation analysis revealed strong positive correlations between MMP-1, VEGF, VEGF-C, and bFGF with memory and MMSE (all r>0.33, p≤0.05). Multiple linear regression analysis confirmed significant statistical associations of memory with MMP-1 (β=0.95, p=0.040), VEGF-C (β=1.09, p=0.043), and bFGF (β=1.33, p=0.006), and MMSE with MMP-1 (β=1.18, p=0.028). Angiogenesis biomarkers were associated with both MMSE (β=1.53, p=0.045) and memory (β=1.76, p=0.006).

In the CHARLS, although significantly higher baseline FI was not found among AO (β: −0.225, 95% CI: −0.933 to 0.484, p = 0.534), D/AO (β: 5.265, 95% CI: 3.889 to 6.640, p < 0.001) and D (β: 4.043, 95% CI: 2.995 to 5.090, p < 0.001) had a higher baseline FI, compared with ND/NAO. The datasets analyzed during the current study are available at https://charls.pku.edu.cn/ (accessed on 29 October 2022). The authors especially thank the CHARLS and ELSA team for collecting data and providing data access.

In the ELSA, a significantly higher baseline FI was shown among D/AO (β: 14.942, 95% CI: 12.679 to 17.204, p < 0.001), D (β: 11.984, 95% CI: 9.668 to 14.300, p < 0.001), and AO (β: 1.768, 95% CI: 0.786 to 2.749, p < 0.001). The datasets analyzed during the current study are available at https://beta.ukdataservice.ac.uk/ (accessed on 14 September 2023). The authors especially thank the CHARLS and ELSA team for collecting data and providing data access.

The original data presented in the study are openly available in ELSA PROJECT, available at https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/. The dataset was used for conceptualization, methodology, formal analysis, investigation, and data curation by the research team.

Data from two nationally representative large cohorts in the US and the UK are integrated for the first time in this analysis. The study employed long-term dynamic assessments of depressive symptoms using HRS data to assess robustness of findings through sensitivity analyses. The follow-up endpoint for cancer events was extended to the 15th wave to increase the follow-up duration. The study analyzed developmental trajectories of depressive symptoms and their differential impacts on cancer risk, differentiating associations between total depressive symptom trajectory, somatic trajectory, and cognitive affective trajectory with cancer risk.

The NP list compiled in a previous study was utilized to maintain consistency in follow-up analysis on the Grubman dataset. The dataset was used to characterize cell counts for different cell types co-expressing various levels of neuropeptides in Alzheimer's disease and control donor brains.

MIT ROSMAP Single-Nucleus Multiomics Study dataset. This dataset was included in the analysis of AD development and progression (time), as it characterizes changes of neuropathology and cognitive functions during AD pathogenesis. De-identified metadata for individuals and experiments included from the MIT ROSMAP Multiomics dataset was provided in supplementary materials.

Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project's v8 data release included bulk transcriptomic data derived from tissues sampled from donors aged 20 to 79 years, providing a valuable resource for studying gene expression changes during aging. RNA-seq transcript matrices (transcript per million (TPM)) of 11 human brain regions from a cohort of individuals from the general population were obtained from the GTEx portal. All brain regions from the GTEx v8 data were included for this study, subject to exclusion criteria for data quality including RIN > 6 and complete metadata regarding age, sex, and death classification.

dataset_identifier: Siletti et al. single-cell sequencing dataset
dataset_context_from_paper: Single-cell sequencing of microdissected brain regions by Siletti et al. This dataset was used to analyze the distribution of AHNP neurons across micro-dissected brain regions and to study neuropeptide expression across different brain regions.

The data for this study are available upon request from the BLSA website. All requests undergo a review process performed by the BLSA Data Sharing Proposal Review Committee. The study used BLSA data to assess cross-sectional associations of age with sleep parameters using generalized least squares models. Data included sleep parameters as outcomes, with age as the primary predictor modeled as a restricted cubic spline. Covariates controlled for included race, sex, BMI, CES-D (Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale), and disease status including CVD, respiratory disease, diabetes, liver and kidney disease, and cancer. The sample included 106 Black participants, 23 Asian participants, and 8 other nonwhite participants.

This study examines the relationship between magnetic resonance imaging-estimated brain-predicted age difference (brain-predicted age−chronological age), leg strength, and their interaction on mobility decline using Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging data (N = 645, 78.1 ± 7.54 years, 56% women). Partial Spearman correlations evaluated the relationships between leg strength, brain-predicted age difference (BPAD), gait speed, and time to complete 5 repeated chair stands (5CS). Mixed-effects linear regression models examined associations of baseline BPAD, leg strength, and lifestyle factors with mobility change over time (5.74 ± 2.87 years). Logistic regression modeled predictors of success in a narrow course walking task.

China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) - one of five population-based aging cohorts used in longitudinal analysis. Cohort inclusion criteria included availability of baseline and follow-up data from 2010 to 2020 and collection of a blood-based diabetes biomarker at the baseline wave. The cohort was nationally representative of China's middle-aged and older population.

English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) - one of five population-based aging cohorts used in longitudinal analysis from 2010 to 2020. Cohort inclusion criteria included availability of baseline and follow-up data and collection of a blood-based diabetes biomarker at the baseline wave. The cohort was nationally representative of England's middle-aged and older population. Mortality data for ELSA are not publicly available.

Mexican Health and Aging Study (MHAS) - one of five population-based aging cohorts used in longitudinal analysis. Cohort inclusion criteria included availability of baseline and follow-up data from 2010 to 2020 and collection of a blood-based diabetes biomarker at the baseline wave.

Health and Aging in Africa: A Longitudinal Study of an INDEPTH Community in South Africa (HAALSI) - one of five population-based aging cohorts used in longitudinal analysis from rural South Africa. Cohort inclusion criteria included availability of baseline and follow-up data from 2010 to 2020 and collection of a blood-based diabetes biomarker at the baseline wave.

Health and Retirement Study (HRS) - one of five population-based aging cohorts used in longitudinal analysis. Cohort inclusion criteria included availability of baseline and follow-up data from 2010 to 2020 and collection of a blood-based diabetes biomarker at the baseline wave. The cohort was nationally representative of the USA's middle-aged and older population. These cohorts are part of the HRS International Family of Studies, a network of longitudinal aging studies with similar sampling designs, eligibility, and assessment methods.
Statistical code is available at the Harvard Dataverse. This repository contains the analytical code used in the longitudinal analysis of the five population-based aging cohorts.

data_repository: Instituto de Salud Carlos III (ISCIII, Ministry of Health of Spain)
dataset_context_from_paper: The ACE collection cohort encompasses a comprehensive collection of baseline samples gathered on the day of lumbar puncture, including matched CSF, plasma, serum, saliva, and peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) specimens from 1369 patients. All biospecimens were meticulously paired with contemporary records including demographic, cognitive, and neurological information, along with brain MRI data. The window for acquiring samples and associated clinical record was less than three months for all patients. The cohort maintains regular follow-ups acquiring neurological and neuropsychological data on an annual basis. This dataset was used for multiplex proteomics-based SOMAscan screening assay with a selected panel of 63 candidate proteins to investigate connections between selected proteins and Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI).

To investigate the connection between selected proteins and AD, the authors utilized the STRING database which systematically compiles and integrates protein-protein interactions, including both physical interactions and functional associations. The data are sourced from various origins, including automated text mining of scientific literature, computational predictions based on co-expression and conserved genomic context, databases of interaction experiments, and curated pathways/complexes from established sources.

To partially address the limitation of lack of access to other databases that integrate paired CSF-plasma multiomics data, the authors analyzed differences in protein levels between AD cases and controls across multiple biofluids in the NGI database. They observed significant differences in plasma sIL6RA (p = 0.019) and CSF sIL1RAP (p = 0.048), which provided partial support for their findings related to sIL6RA.

Participant data are linked to UK National Health Service (NHS) electronic health records for all but ten participants (99.9%). The NHS provides most of the health care in the UK, including in- and outpatient care, and record linkage is undertaken using a unique NHS identifier held by all UK residents. Data from linked records were updated on an annual basis, until March 31, 2019.

MEG dataset with n = 646 subjects used as source domain for empirical benchmarks evaluating alignment techniques for domain adaptation. Authors evaluated the practical impact of data alignment methods for boosting generalization capacity of regression models across acquisition protocols (resting state vs. audiovisual & motor tasks). Brain age was used as the prediction target label.

EEG dataset with n = 1385 subjects used in empirical benchmarks to evaluate alignment techniques for boosting generalization capacity of regression models. In the cross-dataset benchmark, TUAB served as the source domain with data from LEMON as the target domain. The datasets shared 15 channels in common which were selected to define covariance matrices of the same shape and similar information.

Leipzig Mind-Brain-Body EEG database with n = 213 subjects used in empirical benchmarks evaluating alignment techniques. In the cross-dataset benchmark, LEMON served as the target domain with TUAB as the source domain. The target set was kept fixed and a bootstrap procedure was implemented on source subjects to estimate standard deviations. Authors evaluated alignment methods on both Riemannian regression and Source Power Comodulation (SPoC) models.

The Cam-CAN dataset contained 643 subjects with MEG recordings, of which 22 did not have sMRIs and 9 failed in the sMRI surface extraction. Access to the Cam-CAN dataset can be requested through their official portal. The dataset was used to investigate age effects on resting-state networks, with analysis including time-averaged and transient network calculations.

Python scripts for reproducing the analysis in the current work starting from the public data are available at this repository. The time-averaged and transient networks calculated in the current work are also provided.

data_repository: Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience data repository
dataset_context_from_paper: Data used in this analysis were obtained from the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience (CamCAN) data repository. The initial cohort contains a population-based sample of individuals across the lifespan. The neuroimaging data were collected during a second wave of data collection from a subsample of the first wave cohort, whose ages ranged from 18 to 87 years. The final sample analyzed in the current study included 576 cognitively healthy participants (MMSE score > 24). Participants were included if they had complete data across all demographic variables, self-reported physical activity engagement, and resting-state functional MRI data from wave 2. The study examined functional connectivity of salience network and frontoparietal network in relation to physical activity energy expenditure using ROI-to-ROI analysis with Schaefer atlas with 300 parcellations.

Cross-sectional and longitudinal CSF samples from the multicentered observational cohort study of the DLB Consortium and similar studies within the Parkinson's Disease Biomarker Program, contributed by academic medical centers in the United States, underwent αSyn-SAA testing. CSF samples from 191 participants diagnosed with DLB (mean age 69.9 ± 6.8, 15% female), 50 age-matched and sex-matched clinical control participants, and 49 younger analytical control participants were analyzed. Seventy-two percent (137/191) of participants with DLB had positive αSyn-SAAs vs 4% of the control groups. Associations between core DLB features and olfaction with αSyn-SAA positivity were evaluated using logistic regression.

dataset_context_from_paper: AD mouse (P301S Tau) RNA-seq dataset used for bioinformatic analyses. The dataset was analyzed using SynGo to examine enrichment of genes associated with synapses and Gene Ontology analysis to identify enriched categories of differentially expressed genes.

AD human microarray dataset used for bioinformatic analyses. From this microarray dataset, downregulated differentially expressed genes (Down DEGs) were identified in frontal cortex of AD samples. Using SynGo, these Down DEGs were found to be synaptic enriched, particularly in synaptic organization, postsynaptic and presynaptic signaling. The dataset was also used in a meta-analysis where both GAD1 and GAD2 were found to be significantly reduced in multiple regions of AD humans.

RNAseq dataset from Mayo Clinic used for bioinformatic analyses. Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of this RNAseq database found that common Down DEGs in AD were enriched in trans-synaptic signaling, GABAergic and glutamatergic synaptic transmission and neurotransmitter release. The study identified significantly decreased expression of GABA-related genes in AD humans consistent with this RNAseq study.

RNAseq dataset from Mount Sinai used for bioinformatic analyses. Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of this RNAseq database found that common Down DEGs in AD were enriched in trans-synaptic signaling, GABAergic and glutamatergic synaptic transmission and neurotransmitter release. Results for GABA-related genes are congruent with this RNAseq study.

Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) SEA-AD dataset used to examine the trajectory of GABA-related gene changes in AD. The dataset revealed that expression of many GABA-related genes exhibited profound reduction in a cell type-specific manner during AD pseudo-progression, including GAD1, GAD2, PVALB, SST, and VIP, while GABRG2 was largely unchanged across various cell types.

Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) dataset used for brain aging prediction model development. Authors employed a random sampling approach to partition 80% of the Cam-CAN dataset as the training set (NC-train) and 20% as the validation set (NC-val). The dataset included only healthy individuals, excluding those with neurological disorders (e.g., Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease), psychiatric disorders (e.g., depression), hematologic disorders (e.g., anemia, leukemia), history of traumatic brain injury, migraines, diabetes, or tinnitus. Ethical approval was obtained locally and an anonymized version was made publicly available.

Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset used as independent test sets for model validation. The trained model was applied to two independent test sets from ADNI: MCI-test and AD-test, each comprising 56 individuals diagnosed with MCI and AD, respectively. Losses on three evaluation metrics (MAE, RMSE, MSE) were computed for these test sets. Additionally, ADNI data was used to examine correlation between chosen brain regions and severity of brain aging, with segmentation and analysis of hippocampus and amygdala regions, followed by age prediction and MAE computation.

This study is based on the UK Biobank (UKB, separated into a discovery cohort and an internal prospective validation cohort). We included 45,906 UKB participants for analysis. The UKB discovery cohort participants had a mean age (SD) of 56.4 (8.1) years at recruitment (2009–2010), and 54.9% were female. The UKB validation cohort participants had a mean age (SD) of 56.8 (7.4) years at recruitment (2006–2009), and 50.8% were female. The UKB identified dementia cases from linkage to electronic health records, including primary care, hospital admissions and the death registry, coded with the ICD‐10 and Read coding system from 2006 to 2010 until December 2022. A MIND‐MetS was constructed using elastic net regression to train the weights for all 168 metabolites in the UKB discovery cohort and assessed its association with incident dementia using Cox proportional hazard models.

This study is based on the Whitehall II study (WHII, serving as an external validation cohort). We included 6193 WHII participants for analysis. The WHII participants had a mean age (SD) of 55.8 (6.2) years at baseline (1997–1999), and 29.0% were female. In the WHII, global and domain‐specific cognitive function was measured using a cognitive test battery in 1997−1999, 2002−2004, 2007−2009, and 2012−2013. The association of metabolites with global and domain‐specific cognitive function z‐scores was assessed using linear mixed models.

Data from FHS can be obtained by contacting fhs@bu.edu and conditions for access include the successful completion of all steps outlined at https://www.framinghamheartstudy.org/fhs-for-researchers/ as well as approval from the FHS Research Committee. Data from FHS was used for model testing. Due to the absence of CDR scores in the FHS dataset, a modified definition was used for cognitive status classification.

These datasets were used to obtain genetic, gene expression, miRNA expression profiles, and pathological measurements for Alzheimer's disease patients.

The starBase database can be accessed through https://rnasysu.com/encori/. This database was used for analyzing miRNA and gene interactions.
The circRNA interactions can be obtained from the CircBank database. This database was used to obtain circRNA interaction data for the analysis.

Hi-C data (GSE87112) disclosed interactions between rs56261258 (PVR) and genes such as ENSG00000216588 (IGSF23), ENSG00000159915 (ZNF233), and ENSG00000062370 (ZNF112). This dataset was used to identify three-dimensional chromatin interactions relevant to identified risk SNPs.

The Health and Retirement Study (HRS) is a publicly available, third-party cohort study used in this secondary analysis. HRS data are available to qualified researchers from the Health and Retirement Study website. Access to core and phenotypic data requires user registration. Access to genetic data requires an approved restricted data application, Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval, and a signed Data Use Agreement. The study analyzed baseline characteristics and differences by APOE allele profile using HRS genetic and phenotypic data.

The English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) is a publicly available, third-party cohort study used in this secondary analysis. ELSA data are available through the UK Data Service website with required registration. Core datasets are available under the End User License. Genetic data require a separate application submitted through the ELSA website. The study analyzed baseline characteristics and differences by APOE allele profile using ELSA genetic and phenotypic data alongside HRS data.

Data were drawn from 9 waves of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing 2002/3–2018/9, including 6,918 different-sex couple dyads (6,468 married and 450 cohabiting). Latent growth curve Actor-Partner Interdependence Models were used to estimate the associations of husbands' and wives' education with each other's memory trajectories, with a focus on economic resources and health behaviors as potential mediators.

The datasets used in the current study may be obtained from third parties (UK Biobank https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/). Researchers can apply to use the UK Biobank resource. This work used data of participants in research studies (UK Biobank, Whitehall II) who have consented to collection and use of their data for research.

Researchers can apply to use the Whitehall II study data. This work used data of participants in research studies (UK Biobank, Whitehall II) who have consented to collection and use of their data for research.

The A4 study collected demographic, clinical, genetic, and biomarker variables across up to six screening visits over a maximum of 12 weeks (90 days). Demographic characteristics collected at initial screening included: participant's age at consent, sex, self-reported race, self-reported ethnicity, education (years), study partner type, marital status, and family history of dementia. An initial blood draw was used to perform genotyping for APOE ε4 carrier status (carrier/non-carrier). The study was supported by a public-private-philanthropic partnership including funding from the National Institute of Aging (R01 AG063689, U19AG010483 and U24AG057437), Eli Lilly, the Alzheimer's Association, and other funders. All participants and their study partners provided written informed consent prior to data collection, which included consent for data sharing.

PBMC3k dataset used as a benchmark dataset for cell type annotation. dataset_context_from_paper: PBMC Atlas used as an annotated reference dataset to derive gene signatures in GMT format for the PBMC3k dataset. CIA and AUCell were both provided with the same signature files independently derived from this annotated reference dataset.

Neuro_Training dataset obtained from the Allen Institute motor-cortex dataset used as an annotated reference to train Garnett classifiers and derive curated signatures for neuronal cell type annotation in the Neuro_Test benchmark.

Neuro_Test dataset from human motor and temporal gyrus used as a benchmark test dataset for evaluating cell type annotation methods. Curated signatures from Azimuth were used for this dataset in the CIA benchmark comparison.

Cancer Training dataset used as an annotated reference to derive gene signatures in GMT format for the KUL3 cancer dataset. Model-based tools such as CellTypist and SingleR were retrained on this same annotated reference used to derive CIA and AUCell signatures, ensuring consistency across approaches.

KUL3 dataset used as a benchmark dataset for evaluating cell type annotation performance. This dataset was used to test CIA's ability to accurately identify cell types by comparing expression profiles against pre-computed signatures.
CBMC dataset containing cord blood mononuclear cells with 13 antibody barcodes used as a benchmark dataset for evaluating cell type annotation methods in the CIA study.

Pre-processed datasets and GMT signature files used in the CIA benchmark study. These files contain the normalized gene expression data and gene signatures in GMT format derived from annotated reference datasets for PBMC, neuronal, and cancer cell types.

Transcript expression data were produced by the CommonMind Consortium and were downloaded from https://www.synapse.org, specifically syn29442530, which was accessed on February 4, 2025. These data have been moved to the NIMH Data Archive. The authors first normalize transcript expression counts, transform them to counts per million, set them on a log 2 scale, and remove the effect of technical covariates.

We included 414 CU participants from the ALFA+ cohort [mean age: 61.1(±4.72), women:60.4%, APOE‐ε4 carriers:54.8%, and amyloid‐positive:34.2%]. A subset of participants (n=341) had longitudinal follow‐up [mean follow of 3.28 years (0.50)]. Blood factors [β2‐microglobulin(β2‐M), CCL2, CCL11, CCL19, Haptoglobin, sVCAM1, CSF2 and TIMP2] were measured using ELISA, MSD, or Simoa immunoassays. Cognitive data included the PACC score and domain‐specific composites (attention, episodic memory and executive function). Amyloid positivity was determined by CSF‐Aβ42/40<0.071. Human tissue analysis using COXPRESdb v8, a gene coexpression database based on DNA microarray analysis and over 200,000 RNASeq runs which collates data to present coexpression relationships based on relative expression patterns of genes and networks and protein–protein-interactions. COXPRESdb v8 was employed for non-specific tissue, top 10 co-expressed genes ranked based on z-scores to generate co-expression networks for ITM2B.

Human macrophage tissue was selected for analysis using HumanBase, a resource that includes genome-scale functional maps and tissue-specific networks across 144 human tissues with statistical prioritisation developed using Bayesian framework on more than 14,000 publications. Over 700 fasting plasma samples from the baseline of Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) 2/GO study were analyzed using targeted mass spectrometry method to provide absolute quantifications of over 150 metabolites from oxylipin and endocannabinoids pathway. The study interrogated the role for inflammation/immune dysregulation and the key enzyme soluble epoxide hydrolase in AD, providing insights into the regulation of this pathway in different disease stages, APOE genotypes and between sexes. The investigation included mild cognitive impaired (MCI) patients to identify metabolic signatures that inform about resilience to progression and conversion to AD.

Plasma sample proteomics assessment in the Knight-ADRC cohort where 3,132 participants and 6,907 aptamers passed proteomics QC. 7,584 aptamers were measured using the SOMAscan 7k platform. Plasma proteomics data from all genetic ancestries were QCed with seven steps including limit of detection, outlier detection, call rate filtering, and back transformation. The protPRSs were significantly associated with actual plasma protein levels for 10 out of 13 protPRSs in this cohort.

The protPRSs were significantly associated with actual plasma protein levels for 7 out of 13 protPRSs in the ALFA + cohort. The protPRSs of HP (both scores), KLOTHO, B2M, VCAM1 and TIMP2 consistently predicted their respective protein levels in both the Knight-ADRC cohort and ALFA + cohort.

GTEx v8 eQTL data was used to establish tissue-specific gene expression patterns and their relevance to TIMP2 protein levels measured in the pQTL analysis. By mapping eQTLs from GTEx to genomic locations identified in TIMP2 pQTL analysis, variations affecting TIMP2 plasma protein levels were assessed for influence on significant differential gene expression across 54 tissue types.

For phasing and imputation, TOPMed server with genome build GRCh38 (imputation panel version R2), imputation quality of R2 ≥ 0.3, and Eagle v2.4 phasing was used. In the post-imputation phase, both genotyped and imputed variants were retained based on genotyping missing rate of ≤90% per variant and MAF of ≥0.0005.

Correlations between methylation and expression were found for nine DMRs in FCX including CCDC169-SOHLH2, CAMTA1, DYSF, ICMT, LINC02139, NDUFA10, PDZD4, SPAG7 and WBP2NL.

A clinical model for incident AF was developed using penalised logistic regression with Lasso modelling (80:20 training/testing). Record linkage identified people with AF during follow-up.
External validation of the clinical model for incident AF was performed in UK Biobank. The model achieved AUROC of 75.4% (75.1-75.6%) in external validation data from UK Biobank.

Scores were normalized to scale in the (0,1] range with 1.0 indicating the most favourable druggability score.

Two PPI networks were constructed for two species (Mm and Hs) based on known PPIs verified by experiments from the STRING database. PPIs with experimental evidence were selected with no cut-off. The graph was simplified by averaging the weights of multiple edges between two nodes.

The gnomAD data file was cleaned for duplicates and annotated for ARG classification. Gene constraint analysis was performed using 'loss-of-function observed/expected upper bound fraction' (LOEUF) and probability of being loss-of-function intolerant (pLI) scores. ARG gene set distributions were compared to 1000 random non-ARG gene sets of equal size using Kruskal-Wallis and pairwise Wilcoxon tests.

AD Atlas is a network-based framework for AD which provides access to integrated multi-omic data for AD and is available at https://adatlas.org/. The AD Atlas was built using as input the ARGs list, the ARG-AD-GWAS list and the risk list including APOE, with settings (Type: gene, Cutoff: genome-wide, Expand: no, Dist: 0). The network included co-regulation edges (dark green), co-abundance (dark blue) and co-expression (dark grey) links and was undirected. Centrality analysis and visualization were performed on the resulting network.

The dataset comprises all cell populations with differential gene expression analysis between DS and CON samples by cluster using DESeq2 pseudobulk analysis with Wald test, threshold padj<0.10, |log2FoldChange| > log2(1.2).

Cells with <750 UMI or >10% mitochondrial reads were removed, and transfer anchors were generated for mapping and label transfer with cell cluster, cell type, and area annotations.

All interactions including network TFs or differentially expressed Chr. 21 genes were extracted and filtered for interactions of Chr. 21 genes with network TFs directly or via one common interacting protein.

Brain and Body Donation Program dataset containing neuropathologically characterized postmortem brain tissue samples. All GWAS summary statistics were uniformly processed using the cleansumstats pipeline. For each dataset, the genome build of the original GWAS was inferred and coordinates were lifted over to the GRCh37 version of dbSNP. The pipeline handled reference allele alignment, allele direction flipping, effect size adjustment, and exclusion of multi-allelic variants, strand-ambiguous SNPs, allele mismatches, variants with duplicated positions, indels, and those with missing test statistics.

dataset_identifier: Rahmioglu et al. endometriosis GWAS meta-analysis
dataset_context_from_paper: GWAS data for endometriosis were obtained from a recent large-scale meta-analysis by Rahmioglu et al, which included 60,674 cases and 701,926 controls of European and East Asian ancestry. To minimize population stratification bias, analyses were restricted to the European subset excluding 23andMe (21,779 cases and 449,087 controls). This study identified 42 genome-wide significant loci encompassing 49 independent association signals, with the strongest signals observed in stage III/IV disease, particularly ovarian endometriosis.

The discovery and validation datasets were defined from the EUR cohort: 75% of the EUR samples were randomly assigned as the discovery set and the remaining samples formed the validation set. GAD EWAS was carried out in the discovery set and beta values from the resulting summary statistics were used as weights to compute the MRS for the samples in the validation set. The total EUR cohort was split into discovery (75% samples) and validation cohorts (25% samples). With 75% of the EUR samples, the discovery EWAS found 6 EWS CpG sites for GAD. The MRS performed well at predicting GAD within MVP, showing a linear regression r-square value ranging from 0.018–0.02 with statistical significance for different P-value thresholds.

Similar procedures were used to generate MRS in an independent cohort from Generation Scotland, using weights from the full MVP EWAS. This independent cohort was used to validate the methylation risk score derived from the MVP discovery EWAS.

The research involved metabotyping analysis to characterize gut microbiome function based on metabolite production levels, examining substrate/metabolite relationships in relation to CVD risk. Biospecimens and data are maintained by the National Institute on Aging (NIA) AgingResearchBiobank.

Label-free proteomics experiment data were analyzed using Scaffold (version 5.3.3) with a protein and peptide threshold of 5% false discovery rate (FDR) and a minimum number of 2 peptides per protein required for quantification. The normalized total ion current (TIC) for all detected peptides in all samples was exported as an Excel table and analyzed in R (version 4.2.2). Samples included AD (Alzheimer's disease) and CN (cognitively normal) tissues from human biological materials provided by the Banner Sun Health Research Institute Brain and Body Donation Program, processed in parallel with matched 'no primary' controls.

Ninety-nine cognitively unimpaired individuals from the ALFA+ cohort with valid 18F-RO-948 and 18F-flutemetamol PET, T1-weighted MRI, cognition, CSF, and plasma biomarkers were included. Participants were initially categorized into AT stages using CSF-based pre-established cut-off values. Regional SUVR of 18F-RO-948 PET was calculated in entorhinal (BraakI/II), limbic (BraakIII/IV), and neocortical (BraakV/VI) regions using the inferior cerebellum as reference region. Amyloid PET was quantified using Centiloids. Pearson correlations were calculated between regional 18F-RO-948 SUVRs and AD biomarkers. ROC analyses adjusted for age, sex, and APOE-ε4 performed to evaluate the capacity of biomarkers in predicting BraakI/II Positive.

The UKB is a prospective health study that recruited over 500,000 volunteers aged 40 to 69 years in the United Kingdom from 2007 to 2010. Genome-wide genotyping, available for all UKB participants, underwent standard quality control (QC) and imputation. Linkage with primary care data is available for ∼230,000 UKB participants, containing clinical events (coded by READ v2 or CTV-3) and prescription records (coded by READ v2, READ v3, BNF, or dm+d). SNP-based heritability (h2SNP) was estimated using genomic relatedness–based restricted maximum likelihood (GREML)–based methods, genome-wide complex trait analysis (GCTA) and genome-wide complex trait Bayesian (GCTB).

GSK sponsored summary statistics generated and/or analysed during the current study. Authors conducted candidate variant analysis, power calculations for association studies, polygenic risk score (PRS) analysis, and heritability estimates using GCTA. The study involved genotyping with quality control procedures and mixed model analysis with repeated measures for individual candidate SNP associations with disease progression.

Raw reads were pseudoaligned to the mouse transcriptome (GRCm38) with kallisto. This reference genome was used for mapping RNA-seq data from mPFC tissue samples.

A total of 1,153 individuals from the ALFA cohort, many within the Alzheimer's continuum, with available genotyping, air pollution estimation and magnetic resonance imaging were included (62.6% women, average age 55.6 years). Functional genetic scores, including plasma pQTLs for inflammatory markers (PRS-CCL2, PRS-IL6, PRS-CCL19), CSF pQTLs for AD pathology (PRS-Aβ42, PRS-ptau), genetic predisposition to clinical AD (PRS-AD), and APOE-ε4 carriership, were assessed. General linear models, corrected for age at MRI visit, sex and years of education, were computed to assess the main effects of air pollution on brain volumes.

This research included 331 CU participants with early AD biomarker profiles from the ALFA+ cohort. Study measures involved baseline Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) and plasma biomarkers, as well as three-year longitudinal Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and neuropsychological evaluation. Episodic memory was evaluated with a composite of standardized tests, computing a longitudinal Reliable Change Index (RCI). Self-perceived cognitive decline was measured at follow-up with the SCD-Questionnaire. The relationship of baseline CSF (Aβ42/40, p-tau181, p-tau181/Aβ42, NfL, GFAP) and plasma (p-tau217, NfL, GFAP) biomarkers with meta-memory trajectory was evaluated using linear regression. Grey Matter volume (GMv) changes were evaluated using Longitudinal Voxel Based Morphometry.

Clinical data and images from participants in both active and placebo arms who consented to additional research were anonymized for upload to the Laboratory of NeuroImaging (LONI) server. These data are now available upon request to external researchers to access and use for additional analysis.

Most of the samples from both active and placebo arms were provided to the National Centralized Repository for Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias (NCRAD). These data are now available upon request to external researchers to access and use for additional analysis.

dataset_identifier: Proteomic profiling dataset from 250 large-vessel-occlusion stroke patients

Study prospectively registered in PROSPERO. LocusZoom plots from the IGAP Stage 1 dataset showed that rs2075650 and rs157581 lie within a dense LD block spanning the APOE–TOMM40–APOC1 region, whereas rs157580 exhibits minimal LD with surrounding variants.

TOMM40 biological domain classification was obtained from the AD Knowledge Portal—AGORA. The Biological Domain framework is an AD–specific system developed by the TREAT-AD Center, which assigns genes to 19 AD-related biological domains. The assignment of genes to domains is performed using curated Gene Ontology (GO) term mappings that link TOMM40 to its corresponding AD-related biological pathways.

Regulatory eQTL/sQTL evidence from GTEx were incorporated to provide biological context. eQTL analysis revealed that rs157580 had the broadest transcriptional footprint, showing significant associations with the expression of APOC1P1, APOE, IRF2BP1, DMPK, and APOC1, while rs2075650 and rs157581 were associated with a more restricted set of genes.

To visualize the exact genomic positions of TOMM40 SNPs, the authors used the UCSC Genome Browser. Genomic annotation was performed according to the GRCh38 genome assembly, with the term 'gene body' referring to the complete transcribed region of TOMM40, including all exons, introns, and untranslated regions (5′ and 3′ UTRs), bounded by the transcription start site and transcription termination site.

The dataset contains metabolomic measurements and SNP genotyping data analyzed for associations with Parkinson's disease dementia (PD-D), Parkinson's disease with cognitive impairment (PD-MCI), and Parkinson's disease cognitively normal (PD-CN) subject groups. data_repository: eDRIS (Electronic Data Research and Innovation Service)
dataset_context_from_paper: A suite of software tools for hosting and managing more than 3 petabytes of data from different sources including imaging data and longitudinal electronic health records. The eDRIS service provides end-to-end extraction of researcher-specified cohorts from large data resources. Data extracts can be requested based on DICOM tag data, routinely collected clinical data (prescribing, hospital admissions), researcher's existing cohort, and/or results of natural language processing classification of structured reports. Example cohort extraction: patients age >40 years with any lung cancer diagnosis, further refined to include patients with CT chest images showing lung nodules.

RNA-seq data have been deposited in NCBI BioProject (PRJNA1253883). The dataset was used to analyze gene expression, including plasma Serinc2 mRNA expression in different subgroups of patients with bipolar disorder and healthy controls, stratified by family disease history, drug treatment, episode of test time (depression, mania/mixed, remission), gender, and age.

Lipidomics data have been deposited in MetaboLights (MTBLS12830). The dataset includes LC-MS/MS analysis results for lipid profiling, with assistance from the Facility Center of Metabolomics and Lipidomics at Tsinghua University.

Population-based cohort following 20,000 individuals living in Catalonia. Atherosclerosis risk in communities (ARIC) study proteomic data used to develop the dementia risk prediction score (dSST). The dSST was generated using plasma proteomic data in a cohort who were middle-aged at time of blood draw and followed for 20 years (total n = 11,277), namely ARIC participants at Visit 3 (1993–1995) followed until Visit 5 (2011–2013). The dSST was also tested in an older cohort from a later wave of the study (total n = 4,985), namely ARIC participants at Visit 5 followed until Visit 6 (2016–2017). Proteins were measured with the SomaScan Assay v4.0 (≈5,000 proteins). Proteins that showed the strongest associations with dementia risk in Cox PH models were included in a single Cox LASSO iteration followed by 10-fold cross-validation, and an AFT model was applied to the reduced feature set of 25 proteins to generate continuous relative risk scores.

Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA) data used in the study. Anonymized BLSA data not published within this article may be shared upon request from qualified investigators. Researchers who wish to use BLSA data are encouraged to develop a pre-analysis plan that can be submitted for approval.

National Institute for Longevity Sciences–Longitudinal Study of Aging (NILS-LSA) data are available from the authors upon reasonable request and with permission of NILS-LSA investigators; as the data are under license for the current study, some restrictions to data sharing may apply.

Supplemental information relevant to AD, including expression levels (RNA, protein) in post-mortem brain tissue, was obtained from the AD Knowledge Portal, a platform for accessing data, analyses, and tools generated by the Accelerating Medicines Partnership Program for AD (AMP-AD) and other NIA-supported programs.

Expression levels in neurovasculature cell types were obtained from the Human BBB, a transcriptomic dataset generated using VINE (Vessel Isolation and Nuclei Extraction)-seq. Welch's independent samples t-test was used to determine if cognate genes encoding proteins were differentially expressed in neurovasculature cell types in AD brain tissue.

For comparative gene expression across cell types, consensus transcript expression levels (normalized Transcripts per Million [nTPM]) from the Human Protein Atlas were used. If a central nervous system (CNS) cell (i.e., astrocytes, excitatory/inhibitory neurons, microglia, etc.) was among the top five cell types with the highest expression of a given gene, it was considered highly expressed in a CNS cell.

Analyses were conducted in 328 CU individuals from the ALFA cohort (mean age=60.8, SD=4.74) with available CSF Aβ, p-tau, resting-state fMRI and longitudinal cognitive assessment (average follow-up time=3.35 years, SD=0.53). Resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) was examined amongst 246 brain regions of the Brainnetome atlas using the CONN toolbox, selecting a cluster threshold of p<0.005, and adjusting for the effects of age, sex, and APOE status.

dataset_context_from_paper: Patient DNA raw sequencing datasets from targeted capture sequencing using HemePACT and HemeBrainPACT assays. Libraries were captured by hybridization with baits specific to either HemePACT (576 genes, 2.88Mb) or HemeBrainPACT (716 genes, 3.44 Mb) panels. Capture pools were sequenced on HiSeq 4000 for PE100 reads. Reads were aligned to hg19 genome (UCSC). Patient DNA raw sequencing datasets and additional information required to reanalyze the reported data are available from the lead contact upon request.

Gene signatures of reactive astrocytes were obtained from references 72 and 73. Scoring of gene signatures across clusters was done by applying the sc.tl.score_genes function from scapy on the clusters of interest. The score is the average log-transformed expression of a set of genes subtracted with the average log-transformed expression of a reference set of genes.

The clinical data that support the findings of this study were obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). The neurovascular uncoupling dataset comprised 403 subjects from ADNI phases 2 and 3, who underwent 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET (FDG), T1-weighted, T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, and arterial spin labeling (ASL) MRI within 180 days. MRI sequences were processed using ExploreASL to obtain cerebral blood flow (CBF) maps, which serve as a surrogate readout of cerebral perfusion. FDG serves as a surrogate readout of glycolytic metabolism. ADNI provided disease classification: cognitively normal (CN) = 95, early MCI (EMCI) = 71, MCI = 112, late MCI (LMCI) = 42, and AD = 83. For the metabolic connectomics analysis and region-set enrichment analysis, the database comprises 431 cases with CN = 98, EMCI = 76, MCI = 129, LMCI = 42, and AD = 89.

The proteomics dataset generated and analyzed during the current study has been deposited in the PRIDE repository (ProteomeXchange Consortium) under the accession number PXD080003. Protein extraction was performed on human brain tissue subjected to either the SiMPL-DREx workflow or a standard single-omic whole tissue control. Paired statistical analysis of ~9,000 quantified proteins revealed no proteins with significant (adjusted p-value < 0.05) 2-fold difference between SiMPL-DREx pellet and whole-tissue extracts. SiMPL-DREx pellet and whole-tissue extracts exhibited median %CVs of 17.19% and 20.46%, respectively.

The metabolomic and lipidomic data is available at the NIH Common Fund's National Metabolomics Data Repository (NMDR) website, the Metabolomics Workbench, https://www.metabolomicsworkbench.org prior to submission. Lipids were identified by MS2 fragmentation (mass error of precursor = 5 ppm, mass error of product = 8 ppm). The intensity of each molecular feature in the lipidomic, metabolomic, proteomic, and total RNA-seq datasets from each of the five donors was plotted against the corresponding feature obtained using the respective gold-standard methods, yielding coefficients of determination (R2) greater than 0.96.

Generation Study 1 screening data and anonymised data collected from Generation Study 1. The screening data are not available for public access due to restrictions in the informed consent.
