This study reanalyzes peripheral blood transcriptome data from the Center for Health Discovery and Well Being (CHDWB) study of 189 health adults from Atlanta, GA, USA. Gene expression profiles were generated with Illumina HT-12 V3 bead arrays. The dataset includes the abundance of transcripts measured with 14,343 probes that are consistently detected across multiple datasets of peripheral blood samples, which were obtained from Tempus tubes (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) that preserve whole blood RNA. The raw data is available at GEO as study accession number GSE35846. The study explores nine different normalization strategies to illustrate how the first phase of analysis of gene expression datasets can influence various aspects of statistical and biological inference.

Whole genome genotypes were measured using Illumina OmniQuad arrays. After quality filtering, 34,548 common variants (MAF > 0.05) on Chromosome 6 were retained for the eQTL analyses. The study reports the total number of associations detected between 34,548 Chromosome 6 SNPs and 732 Chromosome 6 Probes, including total (trans and cis) associations at NLP 8 and cis-associations at NLP 5 or NLP 8 (defining cis as eSNPs within 250 kb of the probe).

Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) reference number for the presented RNA sequencing study. Small RNA derived from both hNSC- and iMGL-derived EV sources underwent RNA-seq analysis to generate unique miR library sets. Selection criteria included miRs with gene counts constituting more than 1% of total miR expression or those expressed in both library sets. Functional enrichment pathway analysis of predicted miRNAs from hNSC- and iMGL-derived EVs was performed using Metascape based on their predicted target genes. In addition to individual gene expression analysis, transcriptomic changes in 20 unique gene sets categorized by cellular functionality were quantified using both weighted and non-weighted gene expression levels to generate Pathway Scores and Directed Global Significance Scores, normalized to vehicle-treated AD expression.

Raw data from this study have been deposited at the NIMH Data Archive (NDA) in collection 5862. An interactive data browser for visualization and analysis is available at https://brainome.ucsd.edu/BrainHydroxyDevelopment. The study used RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to assess gene expression, whole genome bisulfite sequencing (BS-seq) to quantify total modified cytosine (total mC = mC + hmC), and oxidative bisulfite sequencing (OxBS-seq) to measure methylcytosine (mC). Hydroxymethylcytosine (hmC) was estimated using the difference (total mC - mC) at each site. Analysis included 295 X-inactivated genes and 51 escape genes with average expression level greater than 4 CPM.

An interactive data browser for visualization and analysis is available at https://brainome.ucsd.edu/BrainHydroxyDevelopment for the raw data from this study. The browser provides access to RNA-seq gene expression data, bisulfite sequencing methylation data, and analysis of X-inactivated and escape genes across brain cell populations including MGE-GABA neurons (parvalbumin and somatostatin expressing) and glutamatergic neurons.

Human dorsolateral PFC microarray dataset comprising 129 AD and 101 control samples analyzed via Phantasus. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified with DESeq2. DEG lists were interrogated for functional enrichment using EnrichR. Phantasus-generated heatmap was used to visualize key genes.

RNAseq data between WT vs. ADNP-deficient mice. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified with DESeq2. DEG lists were interrogated for functional enrichment using EnrichR. A PPI network for top-enriched categories was built in STRING, and hub genes were identified in Cytoscape using CytoHubba.

RNAseq data between WT vs. 5xFAD mice analyzed for differential gene expression. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified with DESeq2 and interrogated for functional enrichment using EnrichR.

Mass spectrometry proteomics data deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository. This dataset contains the whole proteome of AD mouse models. The raw MS data were searched against protein database by the JUMP software (v1.13.4) utilizing both pattern matching and de novo tag scoring. A composite target/decoy database was used to evaluate FDR in peptide identification with protein FDR below 1%. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified among four genotypes (WT, KO, FAD, FAD/KO) using ANOVA analysis with P-value < 0.05 and log2 fold change > 2 SD, resulting in 876 DEPs. These were classified into four whole proteome clusters using weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) followed by pathway enrichment analysis.

Mass spectrometry proteomics data deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository. This dataset contains the aggregated proteome of the mice. The raw MS data were processed using the same methodology as PXD046539, including JUMP software (v1.13.4) for database searching with composite target/decoy database approach and protein FDR below 1%. Data were analyzed for differentially expressed proteins across four genotypes using ANOVA analysis and classified into whole proteome clusters using WGCNA.

Signalment data for each of the 76 canine urothelial carcinomas and the 24 non-neoplastic bladder samples, detailing breed, sex, neutering status, age at the time of sampling, BRAF V595E mutation test results, CNA results, tissue and tumour measurements, and tumour morphology. The BRFSS is collecting population-level data on subjective cognitive decline (SCD) in all U.S. states and territories, and these data are publicly available for analysis and creation of public health data products. States can continue to collect data on SCD in the BRFSS survey, as outlined in CDC's Healthy Brain Initiative State and Local Public Health Partnerships to Address Dementia: The 2018–2023 Road Map. The public health community and policymakers can use these data and products as a planning and programmatic indicator for community-level action. For researchers and providers, these population-level data can help guide and tailor their efforts by describing trends over time, different symptoms associated with SCD including functional limitations and comorbid chronic conditions, and how people in different subgroups (age, socioeconomic status, education level) respond.

Blood samples were collected in EDTA tubes, centrifuged at 2500 g for 10 min at 4 °C, and the plasma was aliquoted and stored at −80 °C. Proteomic assays were conducted on approximately 55,000 plasma samples using dual-barcoded antibody technology on the Olink platform. A total of 2923 types of proteins were retained for current analyses. Cox proportional hazards adjusting for covariates and logistic regression models were used to identify differentially expressed proteins associated with AD risk and FAS.

Data are available from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. The study conducted proteomic and bioinformatic analyses to explore the potential biological mechanisms through which FAS was associated with AD risk, utilizing data from ADNI alongside UK Biobank.

Systematic review registered to PROSPERO examining polygenic risk scores for depression (PRS D) and gene-by-environment (GxE) interactions. The review refined datasets by selecting studies that: i) calculated PRS D based on whole-genome summary statistics of GWAS using definitions from the spectrum of depressive phenotypes like lifetime MDD, depressive symptoms or alternative methods to measure MD, ii) had no overlap between GWAS discovery sample used for PRS D calculation and target samples of the GxE study for the same phenotype, iii) analyzed GxE interactions.

Large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) on depression phenotypes. A 2019 meta-analysis drawing on 807,553 individuals from three largest GWAS of depression identified 102 independent variants associated with depression, of which 87 replicated in an independent sample. A more recent meta-analysis with n > 1 million participants yielded 233 genetic variants associated with depression. These GWAS summary statistics are used as the basis for PRS D calculation.

DIA analysis on timsTOF SCP (three replicates/sample) quantified 7,108 proteins with 546 excluded due to missing values. Eventually, 5,958 proteins were quantified as overlapping among 3 quantification methods. The quantification data was listed in Table S4. For all 5,958 overlapping proteins, protein fold changes (FC) between AD and control groups were calculated and transformed using log2.

Comparative quantification data from three methods (TMT-reporter, TMTc, and diaPASEF) showing 5,958 overlapping proteins quantified across all methods. Probability density distribution curves revealed standard deviation (SD) was similar between diaPASEF and TMTc quantification methods, but larger than TMT-reporter quantification method. Data demonstrates quantification reproducibility and accuracy evaluation across DDA and DIA approaches.

The CSF proteomics data used in the primary analysis of this study were acquired from the ADNI database. CSF samples were uniformly processed and stored at −80°C. The CSF proteomics levels of 7584 analytes were measured at baseline using the SOMAmer‐based capture array method (SomaScan 7K platform). The 7584 analytes were assayed using SomaLogic's SomaScan platform. All data normalization steps were performed by SomaLogic, and protein levels were reported as Relative Fluorescence Units (RFU). Hybridization normalization was performed at the sample level, followed by median normalization to eliminate assay biases. This discovery cohort was used to identify three robust biological subtypes of Alzheimer's disease with distinct disease progression trajectories.

The data used in this study were obtained from the ADNI database and the PPMI database. Access to both datasets is subject to data use agreements and requires registration and approval. PPMI was used as one of three independent replication cohorts with available CSF proteomic data to evaluate the reproducibility of the identified subtypes using random forest classifiers trained in the discovery cohort.

Filtered raw count data were obtained from the Synapse AD Knowledge Portal under Synapse ID: syn8456637. The source data were derived from 632 individuals enrolled in ROSMAP. Gene expression levels were then normalized using the DESeq2 package in R to account for differences in library size and sequencing depth. RNA was isolated from brain tissues and cell samples using the RNeasy Mini Qiacube Kit (Qiagen) with the Qiacube Connect system. These studies received approval from the institutional review board at Rush University Medical Center. All participants provided informed consent, repository consent, and consent under the Anatomical Gift Act.

dataset_context_from_paper: Raw and analyzed datasets from single-cell RNA sequencing study of prefrontal cortex (PFC) cells. Dataset includes 53,000 cells annotated into seven major cell types using established PFC marker genes. Gene counts were obtained by aligning reads to the GRCh38 genome using Cell Ranger software (v.3.0.2). Data includes both COVID+ and control samples that were normalized separately, log1p transformed, batch corrected using ComBat, and filtered to the top 5000 most variable genes. Cells were filtered to remove those with over 20% mitochondrial or 5% ribosomal RNA, and genes expressed in fewer than 3 cells were excluded. Differential expression analysis was performed with enrichment analysis using gprofiler2 package with GO:BP, REAC, WP, KEGG, and CORUM annotation sources (p-value cutoff 0.05). PCA (k=50), Harmony batch integration, and BB-kNN were applied across individuals, with final UMAP embedding and Leiden clustering performed on the dataset.

The proteomics assessment of plasma samples in the Knight-ADRC cohort included 3132 participants and 6907 aptamers that passed proteomics QC. 7584 aptamers were measured using the SomaScan 7k platform. Plasma proteomics data from participants of all genetic ancestries were QCed through a seven-step process including evaluation of limit of detection, detection of outlier expression levels, removal of analytes and samples with call rates below thresholds, back transformation into raw values, and removal of non-Human analytes. The final matrix was used for proteomic polygenic risk score (protPRS) association analysis with cognitive composites PACC and EM.

Shotgun sequencing data were uploaded to and processed by Qiita (Study ID 13662). Human reads were removed using minimap2 2.17, while adapters, quality filtering, and trimming were performed using fastp 20.1. GS:SFHS is a study focused on identifying gene loci associated with important quantitative traits (QTs) through intensive phenotyping of family members at baseline and follow-up through routine data systems. The study links participant-collected data with routine NHS healthcare data using CHI (Community Health Index) numbers as unique identifiers. Data collection is designed to complement UK Biobank and other studies. The study aims to create a nationwide research platform in emerging technologies of health informatics in genetics research, including linkage of study data to 'real-time' routine healthcare data on an individual basis. Tayside region enables linkage from primary to tertiary care, from birth to death, with CHI numbers routinely added to all research datasets for phenotype enrichment.

UK Biobank is referenced as a general population biobank study with which GS:SFHS data will be linked and will complement. Unlike UK Biobank, GS:SFHS does not focus on gene:environment interactions and is not powered for this. GS:SFHS's main focus on identifying gene loci associated with important QTs means it will complement UK Biobank and other studies.

Data from the 2016 Venous Blood Study of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), a nationally representative cohort of U.S. adults aged ≥51 years (N = 3575 with high-quality DNAm). Epigenetic g scores were computed using CpG weights from a BayesR+ model of general cognitive ability developed in Generation Scotland. Cognitive function was measured with a modified version of the Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status (TICS) at each interview wave; 6-year incident dementia was defined using the validated Langa–Weir algorithm. Linear regression estimated associations with cognitive scores; logistic regression estimated 4-year dementia risk.

data_repository: Trusted Research Environment (TRE) - Scotland Health System
dataset_context_from_paper: Scotland has more than five million people within a single health system, using a single central Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS) for radiography data. This enabled the project team to build a research resource exceeding a petabyte of imaging from 2010 onwards. Image metadata, treatment and diagnostic records can be used to define large cohorts of patients then make the data available remotely to researchers in a Trusted Research Environment (TRE). The project launched in April 2022 and since then a variety of research projects have already used this environment and data representing millions of pounds of funding, some using large cohorts with historical data up to 14 years old, re-assessing historical scans with the benefit of subsequent diagnosis to investigate possible early warning signs of conditions including dementia and pre-cancerous lung nodules.

The dataset was used to compare habitual dietary patterns from Food Frequency Questionnaires with potential omics data applications.

Genomic datasets generated from stored biospecimens collected from n=218 participants during the CALERIE-2 randomized controlled trial of long-term caloric restriction in healthy, non-obese humans. This multi-tissue, multi-omic, longitudinal data resource was created to expand understanding of molecular pathways and biological processes underpinning caloric restriction effects in humans. Data from the placebo arm of trial of Solanezumab for mild dementia due to AD (EXPEDITION-3 trial). Participants were 710 individuals with longitudinal MRI and CDR measures (mean age: 72.57[±7.69] years, 60.1% Female). Participants were classified as showing cognitive decline (CD) if there was any increase in Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR, Sum of Boxes) from baseline to 80 weeks of follow-up. The dataset included baseline volumetric MRI measures and longitudinal changes observed after 80 weeks, along with ADAS-cog scores measured at baseline and Week 80.

Long Life Family Study (LLFS), which aimed to investigate the biological basis of familial exceptional longevity. Using 3,059 US participants, the study performed a multi-stage analysis examining whole genome sequencing, transcriptomic, and lipidomic data. The genome search of 18 lipids yielded two loci: 11q12.2 and 20p12.1. Genes on 11q12.2 were associated with five lipids, including classes of triacylglycerol, phosphatidylcholine, and lysophophatidylcholine. Genes on 20p12.1 were associated with the class of ceramide non-hydroxy fatty acid-sphingosine.

The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort, representing the general population, was examined as an independent dataset for confirmation. The 11q12.2 associations observed in LLFS were confirmed in the ADNI dataset.

The Multiomic Studies of Alzheimer's Disease in Adults with Down Syndrome (omicsADDS), representing the high-risk Down Syndrome cohort, was examined as an independent dataset for confirmation. The 11q12.2 associations observed in LLFS were confirmed in the omicsADDS dataset.

Raw RNA-seq .fastq, processed kallisto abundance.tsv, and abundance.h5 files have been deposited in Gene Expression Omnibus (GSE291195). Transcripts were quantified using Kallisto (version 0.44.0) with default options, with the additional 'bootstrapping' command set to 50. The paired-end sequencing reads for each sample were mapped to the human reference transcriptome (GRCh38.p14). The transcript abundances were imported and summarized to gene-level counts using R library 'tximport.' RNA-seq analysis was performed on iMGL cells treated with rTauM, rTauF, and hTau to identify expression changes in Alzheimer's disease-related genes.

The mass spectrometry data have been deposited in ProteomeXchange (PRIDE database). Using mass spectrometry, the proteome and phosphoproteome of iMGL cells treated with rTauM, rTauF, and hTau were analyzed. A total of 8101 proteins were identified in the cell lysates, with differentially expressed proteins found in each treatment condition (17, 12, and 58 DEPs respectively).

COSMIC is a multi-ethnic cohort study investigating cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease (AD) polygenic risk scores (PRS) across diverse populations. The study has begun investigating the utility and performance of AD PRS derived from populations of different ancestry for predicting cognitive decline. Preliminary meta-analyses indicate that higher genetic risk for AD is associated with decline on both the MMSE and memory tests. COSMIC aims to increase the diversity and sample size for genetic studies and has collaboration plans to extend the scope of dementia genetics to include low and middle-income countries (LMICs) from Asia, South America, and Africa.

Two groups were defined based on residual median values, namely the slow- and the fast-cognitive decliners groups. Protein levels in plasma were measured using Proximity Extension Assay (PEA) technology (Olink). Non-parametric univariate analysis of baseline proteomics data identified 74 significantly different proteins between slow- and fast-cognitive decliners, with 29 proteins upregulated in fast decliners and 45 in slow decliners.

Data used in the preparation of this article were obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. Cardiac and inflammatory biomarker data (NT-proBNP, GDF-15, cardiac troponins, and C-reactive protein) are also available.

The full range of phenotypic, clinical, and biochemical data available for GS (and therefore MeGS) participants has been described previously and is searchable via the GS data dictionary. Differential expression analysis was conducted using DESeq2 v1.38.0 and gene set enrichment analysis using fgsea v1.24.0 with 1,000 permutations.

Single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from human periventricular white matter. This dataset was analyzed alongside bulk RNA-seq and DNA methylation data from the same cohort to characterize gene expression patterns and pathway enrichment.

DNA methylation profiling data from the same cohort as the bulk and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing datasets. This dataset was analyzed in conjunction with transcriptomic data to provide comprehensive molecular characterization.

Researchers wishing to access the DNAm resource and wider Generation Scotland study data can do so by submitting an access application form to access@generationscotland.org (contact person Dr D. McCartney). Access applications are subject to review through GS access processes, which ensure that all research using the resource aims to benefit the health and wellbeing of patients and the public. Approved projects are subject to a Data & Materials Transfer Agreement (DMTA) or commercial contract. Data dictionaries describing the full GS resource are available online.

Instructions for accessing Lothian Birth Cohort data, alongside a Data Request Form template, Data Summary Tables and Data Dictionaries is available from the Lothian Birth Cohort website. Completed Data Request Form applications are subject to review and a Data and/or Material Transfer Agreement.

The ALSPAC study website contains details of all the data that is available through a fully searchable data dictionary and variable search tool. The UK Medical Research Council and the Wellcome Trust provide core support for ALSPAC.

The following summary level data was used in this study: GIANT consortium data files. We queried whether either of these mQTLs have been previously identified to be associated with height or lie within height associated loci.

The following summary level data was used in this study: DNA methylation QTLs. cis-mQTLs were identified for both DNAm loci within a 1 Mb window of the DNAm probe (rs7747636 associated with DNAm levels at cg09612304 and rs57556107 for cg07386640).

The Accessible Resource for Integrated Epigenomics Studies (ARIES) which generated large scale methylation data was funded by the UK Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BB/I025751/1 and BB/I025263/1).

dataset_identifier: MsigDB human Hallmark gene set, v2024.1
dataset_context_from_paper: The fgsea R package was used to perform gene set enrichment analysis against the MsigDB human Hallmark gene set, v2024.1 with 200,000 permutations, using signed adjusted p-values (Log2 FC * −Log10(adj.P.Val)). Significantly enriched gene sets were identified by a Benjamani-Hochberg FDR of ≤ 0.05.
Human reference DNA GM24143 or HG04217 (Coriell Institute) was used as a negative control. Somatic variants were validated by amplicon sequencing.

Reads were mapped to human reference genome build GRCh38 using bwa v0.7.15 and secondary analysis performed under the Churchill framework. Sequence alignments were refined according to community-accepted guidelines for best practices.
The whole-genome sequencing data have been deposited in the NCBI SRA as PRJNA1336751 and are publicly available as of the date of publication.

The sn multiomic, bulk RNA-seq, and bulk methylation data have been deposited at GEO as GSE295840 and are publicly available as of the date of publication. Data were processed using RSEM (v1.3.1) for transcriptome quantification, Bowtie 2 (v2.3.4.3) for alignment, and Picard CollectRnaSeqMetrics for quality control. PLIER analysis was applied to combined z-scored matrices of gene expression and ATAC peaks to identify latent variables associated with known pathways from Reactome and KEGG databases.

Authors propose this as a solution to challenges in validating measures across diverse populations and reducing research participation burden.

dataset_identifier: Not explicitly provided - available from authors on request
dataset_context_from_paper: Metabolomic dataset from LC-HRMS analysis of amino acids and other metabolites. Amino acids were identified by m/z, RT, and tandem mass spectrometry relative to standards (level 1 or 2 identification). Other metabolites were annotated using xMSannotator version 1.3.2 employing mass matching (±5 ppm), coelution analysis (±10 s), and pathway associations. Dataset includes 44 discriminatory metabolites identified by PLS-DA with VIP >2, with amino acid quantification using reference standardization and coanalysis with reference materials (Qstd3 and NIST SRM1950). Samples stratified into three groups: metabolically healthy nonobese (MHN), metabolically healthy obese (MHO), and metabolically unhealthy obese (MUO). Complete list of discriminatory metabolites available in Supplemental Table 2.

Kunkle et al. 2019 summary statistics for the Stage 1 can be obtained from The National Institute on Aging Genetics of Alzheimer's Disease Data Storage Site (NIAGADS)—a NIA/NIH-sanctioned qualified-access data repository, under accession NG00075. Authors used these summary statistics to compute polygenic risk scores (PRS) using multiple methods including PRSice, LDpred-inf, PRS-CS, LDAK and SBayesR.
UK Biobank data used in this study were available under UK Biobank approval (application 15175). The UK Biobank was used as a population cohort for PRS standardisation.

Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) used in this study were available at the database upon registration and compliance with the data usage agreement. ADNI was used as part of a combined case-control cohort. Authors combined and harmonised ADNI with ROSMAP, MSBB and MAYO studies, removing overlapping samples, leaving 271 AD cases and 278 controls with 6,077,045 SNPs for analysis.

1000 Genomes data are publicly available and can be found at http://www.1000genomes.org. The 1000 Genomes Project was used as a population cohort for PRS standardisation. LD was estimated using 1000 Genomes data for PRS-CS method, and the PRS generated were standardised against the 1000 Genomes population data.

All HipSci data were accessed from http://www.hipsci.org (HipSci data access agreement 8759). The HipSci dataset was used as an example of a population cohort for the identification of individuals with high and low AD risk.
TCR raw data are available at the Sequence Read Archive, accession number PRJNA1321765. TCR analysis code is available through GitHub at https://github.com/mvcowley/synucleinopathy-tcrs.

Single-cell sequencing raw data are available at the Gene Expression Omnibus, accession number GSE307000. Code for single-cell sequencing and Nichenet analysis is available through GitHub at https://github.com/Victor-K27/De_Schepper_etal_2025.

Proteomics raw data are available at the Proteomics Identifications Database (PRIDE), accession number PXD069218. Code for proteomic analysis is available through GitHub at https://github.com/UKDRI/Proteomics/blob/main/code%20repositories/UKDRI_DIANN_output_processing.R.
DSP data are available at Dryad (10.5061/dryad.12jm63zb6).

data_repository: National Institute on Aging Genetics of Alzheimer Disease Data Storage Site
dataset_context_from_paper: WGS data for the LASI-DAD are available from the National Institute on Aging Genetics of Alzheimer Disease Data Storage Site, accession number NG00067–ADSP Umbrella. The LASI-DAD dataset serves as an Indian-representative reference panel for linkage disequilibrium (LD) and genotype imputation for the Indian population.

Phenotype data are available at the Gateway to Global Aging website. The LASI-DAD dataset is used to create an Indian-representative reference panel that can serve as a resource for future studies in India as well as methods development, providing robust and representative estimates of genome-wide LD statistics for the Indian population.

The LASI-DAD LD reference panel is available at both GitHub and Zenodo. This reference panel provides LD patterns that match the Indian population and is used for statistical fine-mapping and polygenic risk score (PRS) construction.

The LASI-DAD LD reference panel is available at both GitHub and Zenodo. This reference panel provides LD patterns that match the Indian population and is used for statistical fine-mapping and polygenic risk score (PRS) construction.

The LASI-DAD imputation panel is available on the Michigan Imputation Server. Genotype imputation estimates unobserved genotypes in samples with sparse microarray data and has been widely used in GWASs to boost power, fine-map candidate causal variants, and facilitate meta-analysis across studies.

GIANT consortium data files were used for validation. The improvement in PRS performance when using LASI-DAD as the reference panel was larger for the GIANT data than for the Genes & Health data, as a large proportion of individuals in the GIANT data are of Indian origin.

Genes & Health GWAS summary statistics were used for validation. The Genes & Health data consist of British Pakistani and British Bangladeshi individuals, and showed smaller improvement in PRS performance when using LASI-DAD as the reference panel compared to GIANT data.

1000 Genomes Project is referenced as one of several initiatives that have made extensive efforts to establish reference panels for genetic research. LD blocks were identified from 1000G super-populations by LDetect.

Raw snRNA-seq data, iMG RNA-seq and iMG ATAC-seq data are available in the Gene Expression Omnibus under accession code GSE254205. The snRNA-seq dataset contains 100,317 cells after quality control and batch correction. Data was processed using Scanpy (v.1.9.1) to select the top 2,500 highly variable genes and calculate the top 20 principal components. BBKNN (v.1.5.1) was used for batch correction across samples. Leiden clustering was applied and UMAP embedding was calculated. Cells were annotated into 6 identified cell types including control, AD-APOE3/3, and AD-APOE4/4 subject groups. ATAC-seq experiments were performed in replicate with peaks called using HOMER and IDR used to test reproducibility. Differential enhancer peaks were identified using DESeq2 with FC > 1 and adjusted P < 0.05.

Case-control methylome-wide association studies (MWAS) of antidepressant exposure were performed from blood samples collected between 2006-2011 in Generation Scotland (GS). Whole-blood DNAm levels were assayed by the EPIC/450K Illumina array (N exposed = 661, N unexposed = 9,575). Prospective data from GS was used to test methylation profile score (MPS) association with antidepressant exposure.

Summary statistics were tested for enrichment in an independent MWAS in the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety (NESDA). Whole-blood DNAm was assayed by MBD-Seq in NESDA (N exposed = 398, N unexposed = 414). The self-report MWAS found significant enrichment for the top 1% of CpGs from the NESDA MWAS (OR = 1.39, p < 0.042).

dataset_identifier: FTC, SHIP-Trend, FOR2107, LBC1936, MARS-UniDep, ALSPAC, E-Risk, NTR
dataset_context_from_paper: A methylation profile score (MPS) was derived and tested for its association with antidepressant exposure in eight independent cohorts (FTC, SHIP-Trend, FOR2107, LBC1936, MARS-UniDep, ALSPAC, E-Risk, and NTR) alongside prospective data from GS.

WGBS and population RNAseq data are available in GEO under SRA Bioproject Accession# PRJNA1137953. The dataset was used for gene correlation analysis where 1 kb windows were generated and methylation signal from all CpGs were averaged within each window. Methylation windows were overlapped with hg38 coordinates to retrieve methylation values per promoter. Gene-level methylation values were assessed in relation to donor age, stratified by subset and tissue, with significantly correlated genes filtered for immune-related genes. Differential gene expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 comparing younger donors (<50 years old) and older organ donors (>50 years old) by tissue site. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was conducted on differentially expressed genes between circulating memory (TEM and TEMRA) and TRM (CD69+ CD103+) CD8+ T cells.

Brain 5hmC data have been deposited into the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under the accession number GSE291402. This dataset contains 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) measurements from brain tissue used in the study.
ROSMAP genotype data are available on Synapse under accession code syn11724057. This dataset was used as part of the ROSMAP cohort for genetic analysis.
ROSMAP RNA-seq data are available on Synapse under accession code syn3388564. This dataset contains RNA sequencing data from the ROSMAP cohort used for gene expression analysis.
ROSMAP proteomics data are available on Synapse under accession code syn17015098. This dataset includes protein abundance measurements from the ROSMAP cohort.
ROSMAP histone modification data are available on Synapse under accession code syn4896408. This dataset contains histone modification measurements used in the functional enrichment analysis.

Summary statistics from Bellenguez et al. were accessed through the National Human Genome Research Institute-European Bioinformatics Institute GWAS catalog under accession number GCST90027158. These summary statistics were used in GARFIELD analysis for functional enrichment of regulatory elements.

Reference chromatin map data are available on the Roadmap Epigenomics portal. This dataset includes 1005 annotations such as genetic elements, chromatin states, histone modifications, DNase I hypersensitive sites, and transcription factor binding sites from ENCODE, GENCODE, and the Roadmap Epigenomics Project used in GARFIELD functional enrichment analysis.

Citation networks for papers were generated using searches to the OpenAlex database. The following queries were applied: 'wearable sensors or health monitoring', 'wearable sensors', 'wearable health monitoring', 'wearable health technology', 'wearable sensors and health monitoring', 'wearable medical devices', 'materials for wearable sensors', 'wearable health monitoring technology', 'wearable sensors for healthcare', 'wearable sensors and human health monitoring'. The searches were conducted with a title and abstract filter.

The expression patterns of CAMKK2, transferrin (TF), and transferrin receptor (TFRC) in the adult human hippocampus have been documented using data from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) data from the HPA revealed the presence of CAMKK2, TF, and TFRC in both neuronal and glial populations within postmortem hippocampal tissue.

dataset_identifier: Human Hippocampus Across the Postnatal Lifespan
dataset_context_from_paper: Complementary single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from the UCSC Cell Browser, specifically the Human Hippocampus Across the Postnatal Lifespan dataset, demonstrated overlapping expression of CAMKK2, TF, and TFRC across multiple hippocampal cell subtypes.

Frozen hippocampal tissue samples from CN individuals and patients diagnosed with AD, FTD, and PD were obtained from the NIH NeuroBioBank repositories (Request ID #1883). The cohort included CN individuals (N = 29), EOAD (N = 42), LOAD (N = 31), FTD (N = 7), and PD (N = 9). Classification of AD cases into EOAD and LOAD was provided by the NIH NeuroBioBank and is publicly accessible. Additional hippocampal samples representing various developmental and aging stages - from prenatal to elderly - were generously provided by Dr. Richard Deth through the NIH NeuroBioBank. This developmental cohort included 9 CN individuals spanning a wide age range. All tissue samples were stored at −80 °C until further analysis.

RNASeq data generated by Mayo (Synapse ID: syn5550404) was analyzed. Humanin transcript count matrices were created from bam files by constructing a MDP database in GTF format and implementing the summarizeOverlaps function of the GenomicAlignments package in R. Thereafter, normalized counts were used to conduct linear regression between humanin counts and all nuclear-encoded gene counts. Other covariables included RIN, flow cell, biological sex, and age at death. The coefficient of each gene was used for biological process gene set enrichment analysis via the gseGO function in R, with a FDR of 0.05.

Samples were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 550 platform for 75 single end cycles, quality ensured using FastQC, and mapped to the mouse reference genome (GRCm39) using kallisto. Normalized fold changes were used to estimate differential gene expression for among conditions by using the DESeq2 package in R.

Code for simulations shown in Figs. 1 and 3 and for figure generation is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16794635. This code repository contains computational implementations of the simulation studies and visualization methods presented in the paper.

dataset_identifier: Brain and Body Donation Program at Banner Sun Health Research Institute
dataset_context_from_paper: Antemortem plasma samples (median= 1.4 years prior to death, SD= 1.3) from 253 participants in the Brain and Body Donation Program at Banner Sun Health Research Institute. All participants underwent postmortem neuropathological examination. Samples were collected < 5-years before death. Using the NULISAseq CNS panel, plasma proteins were analyzed to relate to postmortem neuropathology in a cohort with diverse neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's disease, TDP-43 pathology, and Lewy body pathology. Linear Models for Microarray and RNA-Seq Data (LIMMA) were used to identify differentially expressed proteins between pathology-defined groups. Spearman correlations tested exploratory associations with neuropathology scores and ROC curves evaluated plasma biomarker discriminative accuracy.

PBMCs from study participants at the University of California, San Francisco Memory and Aging Center (MAC) were analyzed by scRNA-seq. Raw sequencing reads were aligned to GRCh38-2020-A and feature-barcode matrices were generated using Cell Ranger (v7.1.0) with intronic reads excluded. After QC filtering, clustering of approximately 182,000 PBMCs generated 17 primary clusters consisting of all expected PBMC types. Comparison of relative cluster abundance in EOAD cases versus controls revealed a single cluster (cluster 15) that was robustly expanded in EOAD (P = 0.005; FDR-corrected P = 0.079). Cluster 15 is a subtype of CD4 T-cell expressing uniquely high levels of IFN-signaling genes MX1 and IFI6.

A large, well-characterized multimodal PBMC CITE-seq dataset was used as a reference. The EOAD PBMC dataset was mapped onto this reference dataset to identify proliferating NK cell clusters and validate findings of rare NK cell subpopulation expansion in EOAD cases, specifically in female cases.

The metabolomics database for plasma biospecimens was obtained from the Alzheimer Disease Metabolomics Consortium (ADMC) funded by the National Institute on Aging. The NIH-West Coast Metabolomics Center used an ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography quadruple/time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UHPLC-QTOF MS) instrument to measure the lipid metabolite profile of blood specimens of subjects from ADNI at baseline. Metabolomics lab staff were blinded to diagnostic data. After unblinding and data release, metabolite profiles went through QC checks and data preprocessing including batch-effect adjustment, missing value imputation, and log-transformation. All serum LCFAs data are unitless normalized intensities.

Blood specimens of subjects from ADNI at baseline were used for metabolomics analysis. ADNI data are disseminated by the Laboratory for Neuro Imaging at the University of Southern California. The study is coordinated by the Alzheimer's Therapeutic Research Institute at the University of Southern California.
The two SNPs (rs429358, rs7412) that define the epsilon 2, 3, and 4 alleles were genotyped and the copy numbers of APOE ε4 alleles for each individual were calculated based on genotyping data.

Raw data not included in this article are available on Metabolomics Workbench. Data from human samples and the δ-valerobetaine treatment mouse studies underwent mass spectral feature extraction with peak detection, noise removal, alignment, and median summarization of technical triplicates using adaptive processing for LCMS (apLCMS) v.6.3.3 coupled to quality control processing with xMSanalyzer v.2.0.8. Metabolite annotation was performed with xMSannotator using the Human Metabolome Database as reference.
Homocarnitine chemical information: https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/145650518
Metabolite annotation was performed with xMSannotator using the Human Metabolome Database as reference.

Proteogenomic summary data from the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (UKB-PPP, n = 54,219), which provides detailed mapping of 2923 proteins and their associations with genetic variants within blood plasma. Exposure data for selected DMARD targets were sourced from this large-scale proteogenomic analysis. Lead pQTLs were identified from this dataset to proxy the effects of select DMARD target perturbations, based on independence and strength of association (meeting the genome-wide significance threshold of p < 5 × 10−8). Selection criteria applied included pQTLs within ±1000 kb of the gene region (cis-acting) and a genome-wide significance threshold of p < 5 × 10−8.

Full AD GWAS data can be obtained by requesting access via the National Institute on Aging Genetics of Alzheimer's Disease Data Storage Site (NIAGADS) data repository, ID: NG00075. This dataset was used as outcome data in the Mendelian randomization analysis examining associations between DMARD targets and Alzheimer's disease.

DMARDs and their corresponding encoding gene targets were identified using the DrugBank database. This database was used to identify drug targets for sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab, and tocilizumab, though the table does not encompass all targets of the respective DMARDs, but rather only those with available pQTL data.

Brain Stress Hypertension and Aging program (B-SHARP) dataset containing cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) proteomic data. Raw data including demographics, cognitive categories and raw NPX (Normalized Protein Expression) values are available in Supplementary Data 3. The dataset was used to identify hub proteins and critical proteins associated with age, gender, race, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), Alzheimer's disease progression, and CSF AD biomarkers (Aβ42, Tau, pTau 181). Authors performed pathway enrichment analysis using Enrichr to understand molecular pathways engaged by hub proteins.

Pathway enrichment analysis was performed using Enrichr, a web-based data-analysis tool. Gene Ontology (GO) pathway analysis was performed using Enrichr to understand the molecular pathways that the hub proteins may be engaged in. The top enriched biological and molecular pathways are displayed based on P-value (-log10).

Population-based study of over 500,000 individuals aged 40 to 69, recruited between 2006 and 2010 from 22 centers across the United Kingdom. Samples for genotyping and proteotyping assessments were collected at baseline. Beginning in 2014, a subset of 41,443 UK Biobank participants was selected for a neuroimaging substudy, undergoing research brain MRI at a median of 9.3 years from baseline. From 2020 to 2021, the UKB-PPP (UKB Pharma Proteomics Project) analyzed 54,219 baseline blood samples for proteomic profiling of 2,923 proteins. A subset of 5,443 participants contributed data to both the proteomics and neuroimaging studies. Used in Stage 1 with WMH polygenic risk score and high-throughput plasma proteomics in >50,000 participants, and Stage 4 examining circulating and genetically predicted protein levels in relation to cognitive performance.

Participants were drawn from the NIH NeuroBioBank for the snRNA analyses. Used in Stage 3 to interrogate single-nucleus RNA-seq data from WMH lesions to determine whether candidate proteins are transcriptionally perturbed at the site of injury.

Protein Quantitative Trait Loci (pQTL) derived from the Iceland 36K study were used to derive instruments for exposures and outcomes. Primary set of instruments comprised SNPs in cis association with proteins (+/− 1Mb of the gene-coding region), genome-wide significant (p < 5×10−8) and uncorrelated (r2 < 0.001). Used in Stage 2 for bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses.

From 2020 to 2021, the UKB-PPP analyzed 54,219 baseline blood samples for proteomic profiling of 2,923 unique proteins using Olink proximity extension assays organized into four 384-plex panels corresponding to inflammation, oncology, cardiometabolic, and neurology. Used as alternative source of pQTL instruments when proteins identified in Stage 1 were not measured in the Iceland 36K study.

dataset_identifier: Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center Research Resource Sharing Hub
dataset_context_from_paper: All data included in these analyses are available through the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center Research Resource Sharing Hub. Targeted proteomic analysis was performed with frozen tissue from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex as part of the Accelerating Medicines Partnership–AD Consortium study. A total of 126 genes and a corresponding 226 proteotypic peptides were analyzed. The dataset includes diverse clinical information, lifestyle measures, and 10 ADRD pathologies measured from brain tissue samples. Qualified investigators may create an account and submit requests for deidentified data.

The UKB is a prospective cohort study which has recruited 502,166 participants ages 40 to 69 across the UK. From the full UKB cohort, participants were excluded who had withdrawn consent, were lost to follow-up, were pregnant at baseline, had sex mismatches between genetic and phenotypic data, or had missing information on age or sex, leaving 499,172 eligible participants. Furthermore, we only included patients in the MRI imaging subcohort with structural (T1-weighted) or diffusion MRI data available, resulting in 43,201 participants. Glaucoma diagnosis was determined from three sources: self-report, hospital inpatient records (ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes), and primary care data (Read2 and Read3 codes). Linear regression was carried out to select for MRI measures with a significant association with glaucoma, controlling for age, sex, social deprivation score, polygenic risk score, and glaucoma status. This research has been conducted using the UKB Resource under project number 76765.

Neural differentiation scRNA-seq data have been deposited in ArrayExpress under the accession number E-MTAB-15695. This dataset was generated for this study and contains single-cell RNA sequencing data from neural differentiation experiments used in the CroCoNet analysis.

ATAC-seq data of the cell lines G1c2, G1c3 and C1c3 have been deposited in ArrayExpress under accession number E-MTAB-15654. This dataset was generated for this study and contains chromatin accessibility data used for identifying active transcription start sites and peak-to-gene associations.

Long-read RNA-seq data have been deposited in GEO under the accession number GSE326106. This dataset was generated for this study and used for identifying active transcription start sites in human, gorilla, and cynomolgus iPSCs and NPCs.

Single-cell CRISPRi data, profiling the effects of the POU5F1 perturbation, have been deposited in GEO under the accession number GSE325993. This dataset was generated for this study and used to validate regulatory modules and investigate cis-regulatory effects.

The raw data for the primate brain snRNA-seq dataset are available at the Neuroscience Multi-omic Data Archive (NeMO) under the ID nemo:dat-net1412 and the corresponding processed data can be downloaded from the NeMO Archive repository 'Great Ape MTG Analysis'. This previously published dataset was reused for cross-species comparison in the CroCoNet analysis.

ATAC-seq data of the cell lines H1c2, H2c1, C1c1 and C2c1 are available at ArrayExpress under the accession number E-MTAB-13373. This previously published dataset was reused for identifying active transcription start sites and peak-to-gene associations across species.

POU5F1 ChIP-seq data are available at GEO under the accession number GSE69646. This previously published dataset was reused for scoring binding motifs of central regulators and calculating binding potential across species.

NANOG ChIP-seq data are available at GEO under the accession number GSE99627. This previously published dataset was reused for scoring binding motifs of central regulators and validating regulatory modules.

PAX6 ChIP-seq data are available at the Genome Sequence Archive (GSA) of the China National Center for Bioinformation (CNCB-NGDC) under the accession number CRA002482. This previously published dataset was reused for analyzing transcription factor binding patterns across species.

Raw and processed data are available in GEO (GSE267937). IDAT files were imported into R and processed using an in-house bioinformatics pipeline that utilizes minfi (version 1.48.0), ChAMP (version 2.32.0), posibatch (version 1.0), and ENmix (version 1.38.01), and CETS (version 3.03) packages. After QC, eleven female samples and six male samples were removed due to a high level (> 10%) of failed probes, leaving 57 male (28 PD, 29 control) and 26 female (13 PD, 13 control) samples. The dataset was used to identify differentially methylated cytosines (iDMCs) and analyze epigenetic regulation in Parkinson's disease pathogenesis, examining both 5mC and 5hmC marks.

Area Health Resources Files (AHRF) 2020 to 2021 provided by the Health Resources and Services Administration were used to derive exposure variables. AHRF files contain comprehensive data on health resources and services at the state level in the United States.

Data were derived from the CDC's state-level Chronic Disease Indicators database, which relies on BRFSS surveys conducted in 2019 to 2021. This database was used to derive exposure variables for the study.

KFF (previously called the Kaiser Family Foundation) State Health Facts data from 2019 to 2022 were used. KFF is an independent organization committed to providing non-partisan information that sources its data from multiple federal databases, such as the US Census American Community Survey.

Supplementary File 1 includes proteomics and transcriptomics datasets for AD brain samples and EVs, as well as DAPs and DEGs resulted from the analyses of each dataset, along with normalized counts and their p values. It also includes a cross-comparison of DEGs and DAPs. The identified lists of low and high-abundant proteins from each dataset were separately ranked based on their fold changes. The list of low and high-abundant DAPs and down and upregulated DEGs from each separate dataset were combined into a single file and then subjected to the RRA method. Identified robust DAPs and DEGs with a Bonferroni-corrected p-value less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

Supplementary File 2 includes GO enrichment terms along with statistical significance for DEGs, DAPs, proteins, and transcripts commonly shared by both datasets identified in AD brain samples and EV subpopulations. Gene ontology (GO) functional analyses, including Biological process (BP), Molecular function (MF), and Cellular component of common proteins between AD brain and EV subpopulations, were performed in Enrichr. Biological pathway analysis was then performed in the KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) pathway and Reactome biological pathways database. Enriched terms with an adjusted p-value less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant for low- high abundant DAPs.

Data up to April 2022 from three cohorts within the Tayside Bioresource, University of Dundee was utilised. Genome-wide association analysis identified SNPs associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. Individuals with metformin prescriptions were identified in GP prescription records (UKB data field 42039) based on drug name, Read v2, DMD and BNF codes. Similarly, individuals with injectable vitamin B12 prescriptions were identified. This work was undertaken as part of UK Biobank project application ref 56653 'Pharmacogenomics to improve drug efficacy and safety'.

Data up to April 2022 from three cohorts within the Tayside Bioresource, University of Dundee was utilised for genome-wide association analysis. The analysis identified one non-synonymous SNP in the CUBN gene (rs1801222) that passed genome-wide significance threshold, with 877 additional SNPs reaching suggestive statistical significance.

Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC; BA9) proteomics data and metadata obtained from consensus of 2 cohorts: ROSMAP (Religious Orders Study and Memory and Aging Project) and Banner (Banner Sun Health Research Institute, Arizona). dataset_identifier: Multiple AD sc/snRNA-seq, bulk, and spatial transcriptome datasets
dataset_context_from_paper: AD sc/snRNA-seq, bulk, and spatial transcriptome datasets were all obtained from GEO database. Raw gene expression matrices were downloaded for each dataset. Cells were filtered with nCount_RNA > 500 and percent.mt < 0.7%, with high ribosomal read fraction (>30%) excluded. Data were normalized and scaled using Seurat package with top 3000 highly variable genes identified using vst method. For each cell type, NMF was applied to identify sets of co-varying genes termed 'modules'. Samples with less than 50 cells were removed. Comparative analysis of gene composition across sample-derived modules was performed to define MPs as gene sets exhibiting recurrent co-expression patterns across multiple samples.

Code for cell-type-specific MP identification and spatial transcriptome analyses have been made available on a GitHub repository. The strategy for identifying MPs was designed to first extract co-expressed gene sets from individual samples prior to cross-study integration, minimizing the impact of technical batches by focusing on intrinsic biological patterns within each sample before data aggregation.

Data acquisition protocols, feature definitions, and variable naming conventions have evolved substantially across ADNI phases. For each domain, the corresponding CSV files containing the features were carefully preprocessed and standardized prior to integration. All non-informative variables were removed, including columns unrelated to disease status or progression, such as instrument models, PET field strength, acquisition protocol identifiers, or administrative metadata. All data were stored in tabular format and retrieved as distinct CSV files, each corresponding to a specific domain and ADNI enrollment phase.

Corrected reporter intensities from TMT labelling were normalized using CONSTANd before being log2-transformed for statistical analysis via Linear Models for Microarray Data (limma). Significant changes in total protein and phosphorylation levels were selected using a p value < 0.005.

To compare outputs at the gene level, identifiers were standardised to Ensembl gene IDs. Generation Scotland participants' data used for epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) of metabolic traits. Penalised regression models were trained in Generation Scotland (GS) to generate epigenetic scores (EpiScores) of six metabolic traits using 395,380 CpGs from the 450K methylation array. Each trait was modelled as the response variable with CpG sites as predictors, followed by cross-validation (n folds = 20) with elastic net penalty.

Lothian Birth Cohort 1936 (LBC1936) data (n = 861) used for validation of epigenetic scores (EpiScores) derived from Generation Scotland. CpG sites with non-zero coefficients from penalised regression models were used to derive EpiScores in LBC1936. Missing CpGs were mean imputed in LBC1936.

HELIOS cohort (n = 2,245) used for further testing of epigenetic scores (EpiScores) derived from Generation Scotland and validated in Lothian Birth Cohort 1936. Missing CpGs were mean imputed in HELIOS. Predictors from Bayesian penalised regression models were projected into HELIOS using mean posterior effect sizes as weights for the scores.

EWAS summary statistics from this study will be submitted to the EWAS Catalog upon publication. Previously, 14 of the 37 common CpGs from linear models had been associated with metabolic traits in studies using whole blood samples at P < 3.6 × 10−8 and study N > 1000 reported in the EWAS catalogue.

The dataset contains single-nucleus multi-omic data (paired single-nucleus gene expression and chromatin accessibility) from brain tissue and phNPCs. After pre-processing, filters were applied to retain high quality nuclei based on gene expression count (nCount_RNA >200 and <3 standard deviations from donor mean), ATAC fragment count (nCount_ATAC >100), and percent mitochondrial genes (<5% for tissue or <10% for phNPCs). The dataset includes 3,464 cell type specific differentially expressed genes (DEGs), primarily in excitatory neurons and their progenitors, with 278 detected HSA21 genes. Data was processed using sctransform normalization in Seurat (v4.4.0) and integrated across all donors and timepoints using reciprocal PCA projection with 3000 features.

For the PPMI cohort, the short-read SNCA SV genotypes are available at the LONI IDA. The short-read genotypes were analyzed for structural variants in the SNCA gene.

Analysis pipeline is publicly available at https://github.com/neurogenetics/SNCA_intron4_SV/blob/main/README.md. The pipeline includes basecalling with Guppy/6.1.2, mapping with minimap2/2.24, and manual genotyping visualization.

Clinical trial study (H8A-US-B004) examining amyloid positivity in patients with mild cognitive impairment and mild dementia. The study enrolled patients and assessed cognitive deficits using Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and positron emission tomography (PET) amyloid imaging. Key finding: approximately 52% of patients were amyloid positive, indicating that cognitive deficits in some cases may be attributable to etiologies other than Alzheimer's disease such as vascular dementia or major depressive disorder.

US-based observational study designed as part of the Coverage with Evidence Development by the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services to assess the clinical usefulness of amyloid testing in patients with uncertain cause of cognitive issues. This study captured real-world practice with less intensive clinical and research-oriented assessments, including diverse patient samples, in contrast to clinical trials that use enrichment strategies and central readers to interpret amyloid PET images.

The raw EM micrographs and mitochondrial segmentation labels generated in this study have been deposited in the BioImageArchive under accession number S-BIAD3729. The study performed analyses on end-stage disease tissue using correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM) to examine mitochondrial ultrastructure and pathology in human brain tissue across multiple donors. The dataset includes high-resolution electron microscopy images with corresponding segmentation labels for mitochondrial structures.

All raw (fastq files), batch processing/multiplexing plan (flat file) and processed data (post-QC counts tables and cluster identities) are available on the AD Knowledge Portal. The dataset includes single-nucleus multiome data (snRNA-seq and scATAC-seq) from nuclei pooled from three samples from different donors per library. Raw sequencing data was generated on NovaSeq 6000 with target coverage of approximately 645 million reads per sample for both RNA-seq and ATAC-seq. Processed data includes quality-controlled counts tables and cell cluster identities. Donor demultiplexing was performed using freemuxlet workflow to assign nuclei to original donors based on SNP information.

For the Syndrome analysis, RNA-Seq BAM files were downloaded from GSE33029 and FPKM values were obtained for all 25,227 transcripts reported. After removing 6,862 low expression genes, the remaining 18,365 measures were log2 transformed, median centered, and standardized to z-scores. 83 of the 90 BIT genes present in the profiles were extracted. The first PC for each BIT-defined axis was determined from these transcript abundance measures and plotted across the time course. One sample, GSN818565 (Day 21), was excluded due to very low counts.

CHDWB is reported for the first time in this paper. It is one of 9 studies referred to in the paper showing the location of the population, number of samples, and source of blood RNA. The Atlanta CHDWB dataset was used for Principal Component analysis, with PC1 generated for all genes in each Meta-Module and evaluated for their relationship to the first 5 Principal Components of the full dataset of 14,343 transcripts. Axis 6 was found to be strongly negatively correlated with the 3rd and 4th PC in the Atlanta CHDWB study.

Human brain proteomic data from ROSMAP dataset comprising 376 participants of European ancestry with dlPFC tissue samples. Proteomic sequencing identified cis-regulated proteins associated with genetic variants, yielding 1475 proteins with significant cis-associations. These proteome reference weights were integrated in two-stage PWAS to identify candidate genes associated with postpartum depression (PPD), identifying four candidate genes: MKRN1, CCDC92, CRK, HARS2 at P-FDR < 0.05 threshold.

Genome-wide DNA methylation data of late-onset Alzheimer's disease obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus database. The study analyzed tissue samples from the superior temporal gyrus (STG) region of 34 patients with confirmed late-onset AD and 34 controls without dementia using the Illumina Infinium Human Methylation 450 array platform. After filtering for CpGs at intermediate methylation levels and applying β-value difference thresholds (≥0.2), 2,211 differentially methylated CpGs covering 1,991 genes were identified. These differentially methylated CpGs were used for functional enrichment analysis using Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway analysis, and hierarchical clustering analysis was performed to assess classification performance between AD subjects and controls.

Expression of secretory factors compared between mutation carriers vs isogenic control WT iMGL cultures by paired t-tests with p-value≤0.05 significance threshold.

Generation Scotland is a family-based cohort study that initiated a new wave of recruitment in 2022 using web-based data collection and remote saliva sampling for genotyping. Genotyping of the GS:SFHS samples was carried out by the Genetics Core Laboratory at the Edinburgh Clinical Research Facility, funded by the Medical Research Council UK and the Wellcome Trust. Recruitment for the expansion of the cohort began in May 2022 and continued through December 2023. A person is formally a full member of the GS cohort if they have completed the study consent, baseline survey, and returned their saliva sample for genetic analysis. In total, 840 individuals were excluded for not completing the baseline survey. Data are available on reasonable request through the Generation Scotland website.

Next GS is funded by the Wellcome Trust (216767/Z/19/Z) and represents the new wave of recruitment initiated by Generation Scotland in 2022 using web-based data collection and remote saliva sampling. This expansion cohort was recruited over the first 18 months from May 2022 through December 2023 using multilayered recruitment strategies combining traditional and web-based approaches.

The study was supported by multiple National Institute on Aging grants including components of the Accelerating Medicines Partnership for AD (AMP-AD) Target Discovery and Preclinical Validation Project and the M2OVE-AD Consortium (Molecular Mechanisms of the Vascular Etiology of AD).

Among the nine libraries of human microglia, we selected the PV053 library because it had the best quality. We defined microglia as CD74 high if its CD74 protein abundance was higher than mean + 2 standard deviations of CD74 protein abundance in the library. The differential expression analysis of proteins and RNA was performed using FindMarkers() function of the R package Seurat. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on microglia cells from different brain regions of the same donor using 10x Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3' Reagent Kits v3.1 with Feature Barcode technology for Cell Surface Protein. A total of 10,000–20,000 cells were loaded into one well of the Chip G kit for GEM generation.
The GRCh38 human reference transcriptome was used (also provided by 10x Genomics). Raw sequencing data for each sample were processed using the Cell Ranger software (v.7.2.0) from 10x Genomics.

dataset_context_from_paper: We demonstrated the robustness of the pipeline by capturing data from two different brain banks – the RUSH University AD Center and the New York Brain Bank – and combining results across the two sets of data that provide consistent results regarding the morphology of CD74 high microglia. Tissue sections profiled by immunofluorescence were scanned and analyzed using CellProfiler (version 4.2.5) to identify target cell types. The entire tissue section is scanned, and the component images are segmented to identify the target cell types.

Whole-genome sequencing data for ROSMAP subjects were obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project (ADSP) release 4 (R4), comprising a subset of the NIAGADS NG00067 dataset. All sequencing data in ADSP R4 were centrally processed by the Genome Center for Alzheimer's Disease (GCAD) using the variant calling pipeline and data management tool (VCPA), a standardized pipeline functionally equivalent to the CCDG/TOPMed workflow. VCPA, implemented in Workflow Description Language (WDL) and optimized for the Amazon EC2 cloud environment, accepts sequencing data in FASTQ, BAM, or CRAM formats.

We performed an excess-of-overlap (EOO) enrichment analysis of the haSNPs and mSNPs using a collection of predefined functional annotations from the Baseline-LD v2.2 model among common SNPs (MAF > 0.05) in the 1000 Genomes Project. For each molecular trait (H3K9ac, DNA methylation) and method (fSuSiE, SuSiE-topPC), we defined the 'positive set' for enrichment analysis using variants within 95% credible sets (CSs) that had PIP > 0.5 and complete functional annotations available in Baseline-LD v2.2 common SNPs.
Other data sets used include: GENCODE Ensembl/Havana database, used for genome annotation and gene build information in the analysis pipeline.

DLPFC protein abundance was quantified using selected reaction monitoring (SRM) proteomics. Gray matter tissue from DLPFC was homogenized and proteins were extracted, followed by trypsin digestion. After QC and filtering for proteins quantified in at least 50% of samples, n = 416 subjects with matched genotype and protein abundance data of 7,710 proteins were retained for association analysis and fine-mapping. Peptide relative abundances were (base-2) log-transformed, and centered at the median, then imputation of missing protein levels was performed using grouped empirical Bayes matrix factorization (gEBMF).

The spectra were searched against a human Uniprot database downloaded August 2020. Search parameters included dynamic modifications for methionine, deamidated asparagine and glutamine, phosphorylated serine, threonine, and tyrosine, and static modifications for carbamidomethyl cysteines and N-terminal and Lysine-tagged TMT.

GWAS summary statistics and polygenic risk score weights generated from the current study are deposited on Zenodo. These summary statistics were used to identify genetic variants underlying both bone and brain traits, with SNPs mapped to genes using MAGMA resulting in identification of 58 overlapping genes.

Summary statistics of brain measures for genetic correlation analyses were obtained from the BIG40 dataset. Summary statistics of brain traits and disorders used in genetic correlation and Mendelian Randomization analyses are summarized in Supplementary Data from this resource.

The individual-level data used in the current study, including imaging, genetic and phenotypic data, were obtained from the UKB (application number 71901). This research was conducted using the UKB resource under application 71901. Gene-level association analysis was performed on 19,110 protein-coding genes with a Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold applied across 50 bone measures.
The 1000 Genomes Project phase 3 reference panel was used to calculate LD (linkage disequilibrium) across SNPs and genes in the gene-level association analysis using MAGMA.

To identify genetic variants underlying both bone and brain, we searched the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog (version e110_r2023-07-20) for SNPs that are associated with both bone measures and brain-related traits and disorders. These SNPs were then mapped to genes based on their physical positions using MAGMA.

The Hi-C raw fastq files were deposited at NCBI under accession number of SRP280183. The Hi-C data analyses were performed using public tools including FastQC, HiC-Pro, Juicer tools, and other bioinformatics software for quality assessment, alignment, and interaction analysis of Hi-C datasets.

The raw ATAC-seq data were publicly available in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database with the ID of GSE129041. The ATAC-seq data were used to identify open chromatin regions and integrated with Hi-C data for analysis of contacts of active regions and SNP-promoter interactions.

eQTL data were downloaded from the GTEx database. The GTEx eQTL track was displayed alongside eQTLs from other sources including entorhinal cortex samples of AD cases and matched controls, and prefrontal cortex region of Chinese AD samples for integrative analysis of SNP-promoter interactions.

The genomic locations of AD risk SNPs were mapped to the human genome based on the annotation of dbSNP database. SNPs were filtered for those located in promoter regions (±2000 bp around TSS) and used to identify loops linking SNPs to promoters.

The TSS information was collected from the ENSEMBL database and the promoter regions were defined as from −2000bp to 2000 bp around TSS. Most human genes have multiple promoters, and these promoters were all considered in the analysis.

We included 226 CU postmenopausal parous women and 144 men with children from the ALFA+ cohort. Cognitive change (3-year follow-up) was measured with a PACC-like composite and individual cognitive domains. All CSF biomarkers were measured using the NeuroToolKit and Elecsys® immunoassays (both Roche Diagnostics International Ltd), except GAP-43 (ELISA). Biomarkers analyzed included neuroinflammation (YKL 40, GFAP, and sTREM2), synaptic dysfunction (GAP-43 and Neurogranin), and vascular dysregulation (sICAM1). Independent linear models with t-tau and cognitive change as dependent variables were constructed with age, education, APOE-ε4, reproductive span, and age at first birth as covariates.

dataset_context_from_paper: This PRISMA-DTA-guided evidence synthesis identified 28 eligible studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of AI-based and SAF DR screening pathways. The database and register search pathway identified 5229 records initially (1734 from PubMed, 756 from Embase, 349 from Web of Science, 2232 from Google Scholar, 139 from Scopus, and 19 from Cochrane). After screening and eligibility assessment, 88 reports were successfully assessed for eligibility. The meta-analysis compared pooled diagnostic specificity of SAF screening versus AI-based diagnostic systems for identifying RDR, with specificity estimates expressed as logit-transformed event rates and corresponding 95% confidence intervals.

Single-cell RNA sequencing data is available via European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) accession code PRJEB46758. The dataset contains scRNA-seq data from progenitor cells comparing control (CON) and deletion (DEL) samples (Prog_C1, Prog_C2, Prog_C3, Prog_D1, Prog_D2, Prog_D3). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified between CON and DEL samples, with genes expressed in >5% of cells used for analysis. Genotyping was conducted by Affymetrix for UK Biobank using bespoke Axiom arrays. This research has been conducted using data from the UK Biobank cohort under application reference 17044. Imputed UKBB data were used to calculate polygenic scores (PS) for Alzheimer's disease risk and oestradiol concentration. The imputed data were linkage disequilibrium (LD) pruned with PLINK by retaining the variant with the smallest p-value from each LD block and excluding variants with r2 > 0.1 in a 1000-kb window, using a random sample of 10000 individuals with 'most probable genotypes' computed from imputed allele 'dosages'. SNPs were filtered based on minor allele frequency < 0.01, imputation quality score (INFOscore<0.4) and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium p-value< 10-6.

The PS for AD risk was calculated based on a GWAS of clinically identified AD cases that importantly does not include participants from UK Biobank (Kunkle et al., 2019). PS were calculated using PLINK with four different p-value thresholds (0.5, 0.1, 0.00001 and 5e-7). The PS for AD represents the effect size weighted genome-wide count of common alleles associated with risk for AD at a given p-value threshold carried by an individual.

The PS for oestradiol concentration was based on published summary statistics from a GWAS study on sex hormones (N = 2913) (Ruth et al., 2016). PS were calculated using PLINK with four different p-value thresholds (0.5, 0.1, 0.00001 and 5e-7). No oestradiol specific score was computed for the most stringent p-value threshold since no SNPs were retained. The PS for oestradiol represents the effect size weighted count of alleles associated with higher levels of oestradiol concentration.

Identification was carried out using a project-independent public spectral library with a precursor false discovery rate (FDR) set to 1%. Linear batch-correction was applied using the limma package. Of the 669 identified significant DMPs, nearly 60% are located within CpG islands, about 25% in adjacent CpG 'shore' regions (within 2 kb of islands), and the remainder in CpG 'shelves' (2–4 kb) and 'open sea' regions (> 4kb).

328 CU individuals from the ALFA cohort (mean age=60.8, SD=4.74) with available CSF Aβ, p-tau, resting-state fMRI and longitudinal cognitive assessment (average follow-up time=3.35 years, SD=0.53). CSF Aβ42 and Aβ40 were assessed with the exploratory NeuroToolKit, while p-tau181 was measured with the Elecsys® Phospho-Tau (181P) CSF immunoassay. RSFC was computed amongst 246 brain regions of the Brainnetome atlas using the CONN toolbox. Of the entire sample, 38.4% had positive CSF Aβ42/40 markers. Low CSF Aβ42/40 ratios were associated to a higher RSFC between visual areas and anterior as well as posterior subdivisions of the default-mode network (DMN).

The primary RNA-seq dataset comparing 'Control and CH specimens' is hosted at Harvard Dataverse. Bulk whole-transcriptome RNA sequencing was performed in two independent sequencing sessions interrogating roughly 40,000 annotated genetic loci. First session (N = 4; n = 2 control, n = 2 CH) with roughly 3% genes meeting nominal statistical significance (P < 0.05). Second session (N = 6; n = 3 per group) with approximately 10% genes significant at P < 0.05, and 4% meeting stringent threshold (P < 0.01). Genes involved in xenobiotic metabolism, adipogenesis, and hypoxia pathway signaling ranked top 3 distinguishable sets. Raw reads were trimmed using Trimmomatic version 0.39, aligned to reference human genome GRCh38 using HISAT2 version 2.2.1, and differentially expressed genes identified using DESeq2 version 1.34.0 with false discovery rate threshold of 0.1.

Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was conducted using GSEA software (v4.3.3) with Hallmark gene sets from MSigDB, supplemented by analyses using g:Profiler. Enrichment significance was assessed using permutation-based normalized enrichment scores.

Pathway analysis was performed by processing the full result set from DESeq2 with the Gene Set Enrichment (GSEA) algorithm as implemented by the R/Bioconductor package fgsea version 1.20.0, against the Reactome pathways database.

Mass spectrometry data from cross-linking experiments analyzing alpha-synuclein (aSyn) protein variants. Thermo.raw files were converted to mzXML format and analyzed using xQuest. Post-search manual validation applied xQuest score > 30, mass error between −2.2 and +3.8 ppm, %TIC > 10, minimum peptide length of six amino acids, and at least four assigned fragment ions per cross-link. Five replicate datasets were compared and only cross-links present in all five datasets were used to generate consensus dataset. FDRs estimated using xprophet.

UniProt reference sequence for wild-type alpha-synuclein (aSyn) protein used as search database for xQuest analysis. DMTMM zero-length cross-linking searches were performed against FASTA database containing aSyn (UniProt ID P37840) or with mutant substitutions. WT aSyn sequence served as reference for calculating relative enrichment (RE) scores comparing observed frequency of protein variants to input frequency.

Deep sequencing data from alpha-synuclein variant selection experiments. Paired-end reads were joined using NGmerge with default parameters. A database of expected gene sequences was generated by substituting each codon of WT aSyn with NNS codons. Perfect occurrences of each sequence in sequencing output were counted to determine allele frequencies and calculate relative enrichment scores for protein variants.

Raw and processed data from an epigenome-wide association study (EWAS) using Illumina EPIC array technology. The study involved running 200 arrays to analyze DNA methylation patterns. IDAT files were imported into R and processed using an in-house bioinformatics pipeline utilizing minfi (version 1.48.0) for importing data, quality control, and dye bias correction, ChAMP (version 2.32.0) for singular value decomposition to identify covariates, posibatch (version 1.0) for batch correction, and ENmix (version 1.38.01) for control probe verification. The analysis identified differentially methylated cytosines (iDMCs) across multiple genes including ELANE, GNAS, AGPAT4, WWOX, and SLC15A4, with separate analyses conducted for male and female samples.
Study preregistration and supplementary materials including additional figures, tables of results, and code used for analyses are available through the Open Science Framework.

HG002 Illumina bisulfite sequencing data collected from an AWS open data set generated by ONT. HG002 HiFi data available through the Genome in a Bottle Consortium. Authors assessed variation in the identification of haplotype-specific methylation between R9 and R10 data sets. An extensively validated HG002 WGBS data set generated as part of an epigenomics quality control (EpiQC) study. This dataset was used as a reference for comparison with the ONT bisulfite data set.
